neural networks ultimately perform enormous numbers of operations on scalar values. but manipulating one scalar at a time would be impossible. so we group scalars into vectors and matrices . 0.1.2 vector a vector is an ordered collection of numbers. for example: x= \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 4\\ 7 \end{bmatrix}. this is a 3-dimensional vector: x\in\mathbb r^3. we can also write: x=(2,4,7). the individual values are components: x_1=2,\qquad x_2=4,\qquad x_3=7. why does an llm need vectors? because a token such as: cat cannot directly participate in operations such as: q=xw_q. we first convert the token into numbers. eventually: \text{cat} \rightarrow \text{token id} \rightarrow \text{embedding vector}. for example: \text{cat} \rightarrow [0.21,-0.53,0.72,\ldots]. that vector contains a learned numerical representation of the token. raschka's book follows precisely this progression from token representations into vector operations and later q/k/v projections. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.1.3 matrix a matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers. for example: a= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2&3\\ 4&5&6 \end{bmatrix}. this has: 2\text{ rows} and 3\text{ columns}. therefore: \boxed{a\in\mathbb r^{2\times3}} the notation m\times n means: m=\text{number of rows} n=\text{number of columns}. why do transformers need matrices? because instead of transforming one token vector at a time, we want to transform an entire sequence simultaneously. suppose: n=4 tokens and embedding dimension: d=8. then the input representation is: x\in\mathbb r^{4\times8}. conceptually: x= \begin{bmatrix} ---x_1---\\ ---x_2---\\ ---x_3---\\ ---x_4--- \end{bmatrix}. each row represents one token. so: \boxed{ \text{rows}=\text{tokens} } and: \boxed{ \text{columns}=\text{features} } this shape convention will appear throughout the entire course. 0.1.4 matrix multiplication suppose: a\in\mathbb r^{m\times n} and b\in\mathbb r^{n\times p}. then: ab\in\mathbb r^{m\times p}. the crucial rule is: \boxed{ \text{inner dimensions must match} } because: (m\times n)(n\times p) \rightarrow (m\times p). example let: a= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4 \end{bmatrix} and: b= \begin{bmatrix} 5&6\\ 7&8 \end{bmatrix}. then: ab= \begin{bmatrix} 1(5)+2(7)&1(6)+2(8)\\ 3(5)+4(7)&3(6)+4(8) \end{bmatrix} so: ab= \begin{bmatrix} 19&22\\ 43&50 \end{bmatrix}. notice what happened. for example: (ab)_{11} = 1(5)+2(7). that is a dot product . so matrix multiplication is essentially a huge collection of dot products. 0.1.5 why this becomes q = xw this is our first major connection. suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} and: w_q\in\mathbb r^{d\times d_k}. then: q=xw_q is legal because: (n\times d)(d\times d_k) gives: \boxed{ q\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k}. } this is not arbitrary notation. the matrix multiplication is doing the following to every token simultaneously : x_i \rightarrow x_iw_q. raschka's book explicitly implements these projections using: \texttt{query = x @ w\_query} and shows that changing the number of columns of the weight matrix changes the dimensionality of the resulting query vector. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) this is the first reason i want you to become comfortable with dimensions before we enter attention. 0.1.6 dot product given: x= \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ \vdots\\ x_d \end{bmatrix} and: y= \begin{bmatrix} y_1\\ y_2\\ \vdots\\ y_d \end{bmatrix}, their dot product is: \boxed{ x^\top y = \sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i y_i } for example: x= \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 3\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad y= \begin{bmatrix} 4\\ -1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. then: x^\top y = 2(4)+3(-1)+1(2) =8-3+2 =7. why is dot product so important? because it measures alignment/similarity between two vectors. geometrically: x^\top y = \|x\|\,\|y\|\cos\theta. therefore: same direction \theta=0 so: \cos\theta=1. large positive dot product. orthogonal \theta=90^\circ so: \cos\theta=0. dot product: 0. opposite directions \theta=180^\circ so: \cos\theta=-1. negative dot product. this is exactly why attention uses it later we will calculate: s_{ij}=q_i^\top k_j. meaning: how compatible is query i with key j ? so the attention mechanism starts with something extremely simple: \boxed{ \text{query-key compatibility} = \text{dot product} } the nlp-with-transformers book describes attention scores precisely as dot products between query and key vectors and then builds the attention matrix from those scores. (source: nlp_transformer) 0.1.7 dimensions — the rule you must master suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d}. then: w_q\in\mathbb r^{d\times d_k} gives: q=xw_q with: q\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k}. likewise: k=xw_k gives: k\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k}. now: k^\top\in\mathbb r^{d_k\times n}. therefore: qk^\top has shape: (n\times d_k)(d_k\times n) \boxed{ =n\times n. } that n\times n matrix is the attention-score matrix . this is one of the most important dimensional relationships in the entire course. 0.1.8 why n\times n matters suppose: n=4. then: qk^\top = \begin{bmatrix} s_{11}&s_{12}&s_{13}&s_{14}\\ s_{21}&s_{22}&s_{23}&s_{24}\\ s_{31}&s_{32}&s_{33}&s_{34}\\ s_{41}&s_{42}&s_{43}&s_{44} \end{bmatrix}. interpretation: s_{ij} = \text{how much token }i \text{ relates to token }j. therefore: row 1 = what token 1 is interested in row 2 = what token 2 is interested in etc. this is why attention is fundamentally a token-to-token interaction mechanism . 0.1.9 weight parameters vs attention weights this distinction is extremely important and often causes confusion. weight parameters for example: w_q. these are: \boxed{\text{learned during training}} and remain fixed during a particular inference pass. attention weights for example: a_{ij}. these are: \boxed{\text{computed dynamically for the current input}} and can change for every sequence and position. raschka explicitly warns about this distinction: the w matrices are learned model parameters, whereas attention weights determine how strongly the current context vector depends on different input positions. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.1.10 matrix vs tensor a matrix: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} has two dimensions. a batch of sequences: x\in\mathbb r^{b\times n\times d} has three dimensions. where: b=\text{batch size} n=\text{sequence length} d=\text{embedding/model dimension}. so: \boxed{ \text{tensor shape} = (b,n,d) } is what we will normally use in actual pytorch implementations. the nlp-with-transformers source explicitly discusses batch matrix multiplication for attention, where the batch dimension is handled independently for each sequence. (source: nlp_transformer) 0.1.11 why we care about this for the entire course this seemingly basic material will keep reappearing. transformer q=xw_q lora w'=w+ba quantization w\rightarrow\hat w distillation p_{\text{teacher}} \rightarrow q_{\text{student}} rl \pi_\theta(a|s) grpo r_i(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(o_i|q)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i|q)} everything is ultimately built from transformations of numerical objects. 0.1.12 cheatsheet connection from the master sheet: \boxed{ x:(n,d) } \boxed{ w_q:(d,d_k) } \boxed{ q=xw_q:(n,d_k) } \boxed{ qk^\top:(n,n) } the reason these shapes work is exactly the matrix-multiplication rule we just learned. so when you see the transformer equation later, you should not memorize it . you should be able to reconstruct it. 0.1.13 mini numerical transformer example let's make this concrete. suppose: n=3 and: d=2. let: x= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4\\ 5&6 \end{bmatrix}. suppose: w_q= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}. then: q=xw_q so: q= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4\\ 5&6 \end{bmatrix}. here: d_k=2. therefore: qk^\top will have: 3\times3 entries. for example, if: k=q, then: s_{11} = [1,2] \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = 1^2+2^2 = 5. and: s_{12} = [1,2] \begin{bmatrix} 3\\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = 3+8 = 11. so token 1 has: \boxed{ [5,\;11,\;17] } as its raw similarity scores with the three tokens. this is the first concrete appearance of attention. we have not yet applied: \frac1{\sqrt{d_k}} or: \operatorname{softmax} or: \text{causal masking}. those will be the next concepts. 0.1.14 what we have actually learned we started with: \text{numbers} and reached: \boxed{ \text{token representations} \rightarrow \text{matrix transformations} \rightarrow \text{query/key representations} \rightarrow \text{pairwise token similarities} } the next question is: why should those raw similarities become probabilities? that leads directly to softmax . but before we jump there, we need the probability foundation. master connection our chain so far is: \boxed{ \text{scalar} \rightarrow \text{vector} \rightarrow \text{matrix} \rightarrow \text{matrix multiplication} \rightarrow \text{dot product} \rightarrow \text{similarity} \rightarrow qk^\top } next: \boxed{ qk^\top \rightarrow \text{scaled scores} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{attention probabilities} } later: \boxed{ \text{attention probabilities} \rightarrow av \rightarrow \text{context vector} } and eventually: \boxed{ \text{context} \rightarrow \text{transformer block} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{probability} \rightarrow \text{decoding} } sources used for this step primary mathematical/llm grounding build a large language model (from scratch) — vector/matrix operations, learned weight matrices, q/k/v projections, attention scores. independent depth scoring pending. step 0.2 — probability → log-probability → softmax plan node: i0 · chat order #3 now we move from the linear-algebra primitives we just learned into the probability machinery that turns transformer outputs into meaningful distributions. this step is extremely important because the same mathematical ideas will later reappear in: attention → language-model training → decoding → distillation → kl divergence → rl/ppo/grpo. the master cheatsheet explicitly places these formulas at the mathematical foundation of the transformer and language-model objective. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.1 first: what problem are we trying to solve? suppose the transformer has processed: the cat is and now must predict the next token. the model does not directly output: "sleeping" instead, the final layer produces a vector of arbitrary real numbers called logits : z = \begin{bmatrix} 2.1\\ 0.3\\ 4.2\\ 1.0\\ ... \end{bmatrix} there is one logit for every vocabulary token. for example: token logit the 2.1 dog 0.3 sleeping 4.2 ran 1.0 ... ... but these numbers are not probabilities . they can be: negative positive larger than 1 smaller than 0 so we need a transformation: \boxed{\text{logits} \rightarrow \text{probabilities}} that transformation is softmax . 0.2.2 what is a probability distribution? suppose we have five possible next tokens. a probability distribution could be: p=[0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] a valid discrete probability distribution must satisfy two conditions: p_i\ge 0 and \sum_i p_i=1 so: 0.05+0.10+0.60+0.05+0.20=1 this means: all possible outcomes share 100% of the probability mass. this is exactly the kind of distribution a language model needs when choosing its next token. the supplied minillm material gives a concrete example where the next-token distribution is: [0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] for {the, cat, sat, dog, ran} . (source: minillm-slides) 0.2.3 why does a language model need probabilities? because language generation is inherently uncertain. take: the sky is possible continuations might be: p(\text{blue})=0.60 p(\text{cloudy})=0.15 p(\text{clear})=0.10 p(\text{dark})=0.05 etc. the model is effectively saying: given the context, how likely is each possible next token? mathematically: \boxed{p(x_t\mid x_{<t})} where: x_t = current/next token x_{<t} = all previous tokens this conditional probability is the heart of autoregressive language modeling. the nlp with transformers book describes gpt-style language modeling exactly this way: the model estimates the probability of a token sequence through conditional next-token probabilities. (source: natural language processing with transformers _ building) 0.2.4 autoregressive probability suppose the sentence is: i love cats let the tokens be: x_1=i,\quad x_2=love,\quad x_3=cats we want the probability of the whole sequence : p(i,love,cats) using the chain rule of probability: \boxed{ p(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } so: p(i,love,cats) = p(i)\, p(love\mid i)\, p(cats\mid i,love) this is called autoregressive factorization . it is in your cheatsheet as the language-model objective. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.5 why factorization matters calculating the probability of every possible full sentence directly would be impossible. instead, the model breaks the problem into manageable pieces: \text{whole sequence} becomes \text{next-token prediction at position 1} \text{next-token prediction at position 2} \text{next-token prediction at position 3} etc. so a transformer doesn't need to directly model: p(\text{"the cat sat on the mat"}) as one giant indivisible object. it models: p(\text{the}) then p(\text{cat}\mid\text{the}) then p(\text{sat}\mid\text{the cat}) and so on. this is the foundation of both training and generation . 0.2.6 the problem with multiplying probabilities consider: 0.8\times0.7\times0.9\times0.6\times0.5 =0.1512 now imagine a sequence of 1,000 tokens. you might multiply hundreds or thousands of numbers like: 0.001\times0.02\times0.4\times0.003\times\cdots the result becomes extremely tiny. this creates numerical problems. so we use logarithms . 0.2.7 log-probability take: p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_t p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) apply \log : \log p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \log \left( \prod_t p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) \right) using: \log(ab)=\log a+\log b we obtain: \boxed{ \log p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_t \log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } so multiplication becomes addition. that is enormously more convenient computationally. example suppose: p_1=0.8 p_2=0.7 p_3=0.9 then: p_{\text{sequence}} = 0.8(0.7)(0.9) = 0.504 log form: \log(0.504) which is equivalent to: \log(0.8)+\log(0.7)+\log(0.9) so instead of multiplying many tiny values, we add log-probabilities. 0.2.8 why are log-probabilities negative? because for probabilities: 0<p\le1 and therefore: \log p\le0 for example: \log(1)=0 \log(0.5)\approx-0.693 \log(0.1)\approx-2.303 \log(0.001)\approx-6.908 so: higher probability → log probability closer to 0. lower probability → more negative log probability. this gives us a very useful way to measure how well the model predicted the correct token. 0.2.9 negative log-probability because log probabilities are negative, training usually minimizes: \boxed{ -\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } this is the negative log-likelihood loss for one token . look at what happens: model predicts correct token with probability 0.9 -\log(0.9)\approx0.105 very small loss. model predicts it with probability 0.5 -\log(0.5)\approx0.693 larger loss. model predicts it with probability 0.01 -\log(0.01)\approx4.605 huge loss. therefore: \boxed{\text{better probability for the correct token} \rightarrow \text{smaller loss}} the cheatsheet expresses the per-position loss as: l_t=-\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}) and sequence-average loss as the mean over positions. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.10 now we reach softmax we have logits: z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_v where v is vocabulary size. we need to convert them into: p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_v such that: p_i\ge0 and: \sum_i p_i=1 softmax does exactly this. \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}} {\sum_j e^{z_j}} } this formula appears directly in the mathematical cheatsheet. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.11 understand softmax from the inside out suppose: z=[1,2,3] step 1: exponentiate e^1\approx2.718 e^2\approx7.389 e^3\approx20.086 so: [e^1,e^2,e^3] \approx [2.718,7.389,20.086] step 2: calculate the sum 2.718+7.389+20.086 = 30.193 step 3: divide each by the total p_1=\frac{2.718}{30.193}\approx0.090 p_2=\frac{7.389}{30.193}\approx0.245 p_3=\frac{20.086}{30.193}\approx0.665 therefore: \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}([1,2,3]) \approx [0.090,0.245,0.665] } check: 0.090+0.245+0.665\approx1 0.2.12 why the exponential? this is an important why , not a memorization detail. softmax uses: e^{z_i} for several useful reasons. 1. it guarantees positivity exponentials are always positive: e^z>0 so the resulting probabilities cannot be negative. 2. it preserves ordering if: z_3>z_2 then: e^{z_3}>e^{z_2} so larger logits still produce larger probabilities. 3. it amplifies differences compare: z=[1,2] difference = 1. exponentials: [e^1,e^2]=[2.718,7.389] now the larger value dominates much more strongly. this gives softmax a useful competitive behavior. 4. it normalizes dividing by: \sum_j e^{z_j} forces the results to sum to 1. so softmax is essentially: \boxed{ \text{positive transformation + normalization} } 0.2.13 logits are not probabilities this distinction is essential. suppose: z=[2,1,-1] these are logits. you cannot say: "token 1 has probability 2." that is impossible. after softmax: \operatorname{softmax}(z) produces valid probabilities. so: \boxed{ \text{logit} \neq \text{probability} } pipeline: \boxed{ \text{transformer hidden state} \rightarrow \text{linear projection} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{probabilities} } 0.2.14 a very important transformer connection remember our earlier attention equation: s=qk^t these are also just scores . they are not probabilities. then: a=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}}+m\right) produces attention weights. the attention handbook describes the process as: project → compare → scale → constrain → normalize → aggregate. in particular, row-wise softmax turns the compatibility scores into nonnegative weights that sum to one across allowed keys. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) so softmax appears in two extremely important places: attention \boxed{\text{scores}\rightarrow\text{attention weights}} output layer \boxed{\text{logits}\rightarrow\text{token probabilities}} same mathematical operation. different semantic purpose. numerical correction: softmax([1.2,2.0,0.4,−∞]) ≈ [0.2721184774,0.6056108090,0.1222707136,0]. the third entry is permitted and must not be zero. the inherited displayed result below is retained for traceability. derivation and checked counterpart . correction: correct masked distribution for [1.2,2,.4,-inf] is [.2721184774,.6056108090,.1222707136,0]; the third permitted key does not have zero probability. complete grounded review 0.2.15 attention softmax vs language-model softmax this distinction is worth memorizing. suppose a sequence has n=4 tokens. attention scores for token 3 might be: [1.2,\;2.0,\;0.4,\;-\infty] after causal masking and softmax: [0.31,\;0.69,\;0.00,\;0.00] these tell us how the query distributes its attention over allowable positions. but at the output layer we might have: z=[2.1,0.7,4.3,-1.2,\ldots] softmax turns these into probabilities over the vocabulary . thus: softmax location distribution is over attention positions/tokens being attended to output layer vocabulary tokens this distinction will become very important later when we study decoding . 0.2.16 causal masking + softmax suppose we have: s= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5\\ 3 & 2 & 4\\ 1 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} for a causal language model: token 1 cannot look at future tokens 2 and 3. token 2 cannot look at future token 3. so we use a mask: m= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\infty & -\infty\\ 0 & 0 & -\infty\\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} therefore: s+m = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -\infty & -\infty\\ 3 & 2 & -\infty\\ 1 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} now apply softmax row-by-row. for row 1: \operatorname{softmax}[2,-\infty,-\infty] = [1,0,0] for row 2: \operatorname{softmax}[3,2,-\infty] gives approximately: [0.731,0.269,0] the -\infty effectively produces zero probability. so the causal mask works because: e^{-\infty}\rightarrow0 this is the mathematical mechanism behind preventing future-token information leakage. 0.2.17 softmax has a beautiful property: shift invariance suppose: z=[1,2,3] now add 10 to every number: z'=[11,12,13] softmax gives exactly the same result: \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}(z+c) = \operatorname{softmax}(z) } why? because: \frac{e^{z_i+c}} {\sum_j e^{z_j+c}} can be rewritten as: \frac{e^c e^{z_i}} {e^c\sum_j e^{z_j}} and e^c cancels. this gives us a very useful computational trick. 0.2.18 numerically stable softmax instead of calculating: \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} we usually compute: \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}(z) = \operatorname{softmax}(z-\max(z)) } example: z=[1000,1001,1002] directly computing e^{1000} can overflow numerically. instead subtract 1002: [-2,-1,0] then: \operatorname{softmax}([1000,1001,1002]) = \operatorname{softmax}([-2,-1,0]) same probabilities, much safer numerically. 0.2.19 temperature now introduce another concept that will become central in decoding . temperature modifies softmax: \boxed{ p_i= \frac{e^{z_i/t}} {\sum_j e^{z_j/t}} } where: t>0 case 1: t=1 normal softmax. case 2: t<1 the distribution becomes sharper . example: t=0.5 logits become effectively: [2z_1,2z_2,\ldots] differences get amplified. the highest-probability token tends to dominate. case 3: t>1 the distribution becomes flatter . differences between logits matter less. more probability spreads to lower-ranked alternatives. intuition think of temperature as a control over certainty: \boxed{ t\downarrow \rightarrow \text{sharper} } \boxed{ t\uparrow \rightarrow \text{flatter} } this will later become a major text-decoding mechanism. 0.2.20 one-hot targets now connect probability to training. suppose vocabulary: [\text{the},\text{cat},\text{sat},\text{dog},\text{ran}] the correct next token is: sat represent the target as a one-hot vector: y=[0,0,1,0,0] suppose the model predicts: q=[0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] so: q_{\text{sat}}=0.60 the loss is: \boxed{ l=-\log(0.60) } l\approx0.5108 this exact worked example appears in the supplied minillm material. (source: minillm-slides) notice something interesting: the model predicted probabilities for all five tokens, but for a one-hot target the loss ultimately depends on the probability assigned to the correct token . 0.2.21 why negative log probability is such a good loss suppose the correct answer is sat . prediction a p(\text{sat})=0.9 loss: -\log(0.9)=0.105 prediction b p(\text{sat})=0.5 loss: -\log(0.5)=0.693 prediction c p(\text{sat})=0.01 loss: -\log(0.01)=4.605 this means the loss heavily punishes confidently wrong predictions . that's exactly what we want. a model saying: "i am 99% sure the answer is wrong" should be punished much more strongly than a model saying: "i am only somewhat uncertain." 0.2.22 from one token to the entire sentence for n tokens: l_t=-\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}) average: \boxed{ l = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } this is the standard next-token training objective shown in your cheatsheet. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) therefore the complete training chain is: \boxed{ \text{tokens} \rightarrow \text{transformer} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{probabilities} \rightarrow -\log p(\text{correct token}) \rightarrow \text{loss} } that chain is one of the most important chains in the entire course. 0.2.23 connection to attention now connect today's lesson to yesterday's linear algebra. yesterday: q=xw_q k=xw_k v=xw_v then: s=qk^t today we add: a=\operatorname{softmax}(s/\sqrt{d_k}+m) and: o=av so we have: \boxed{ x \rightarrow q,k,v \rightarrow qk^t \rightarrow \text{scaled scores} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow a \rightarrow av } the attention handbook explicitly emphasizes that the attention weights are intermediate coefficients and that the actual output is av . (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) this is why yesterday's dot product was not the end of the story. 0.2.24 extremely important distinction there are now three different kinds of numbers you must not mix up: 1. learned parameters for example: w_q these are model parameters learned during training. 2. scores / logits examples: qk^t or final vocabulary logits: z these are raw compatibility/evidence scores. 3. normalized weights/probabilities examples: a=\operatorname{softmax}(qk^t) or: p=\operatorname{softmax}(z) these are normalized values. raschka explicitly distinguishes learned weight parameters from dynamic attention weights. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.2.25 the entire mathematical picture so far we can now build the first major chain: token ↓ embedding vector ↓ matrix transformations ↓ q, k, v ↓ dot product ↓ raw attention scores ↓ scale by √d_k ↓ causal mask ↓ softmax ↓ attention weights ↓ weighted sum of v ↓ contextual representation ↓ transformer layers ↓ final hidden state ↓ linear projection ↓ vocabulary logits ↓ softmax ↓ next-token probability distribution ↓ -log(probability of correct token) ↓ training loss once this chain is solid, a huge portion of transformer mathematics becomes much easier. 0.2.26 tensor-shape grounding let's make this precise. suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} then: q=xw_q with: w_q\in\mathbb r^{d\times d_k} so: q\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k} likewise: k\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k} therefore: qk^t has shape: (n\times d_k)(d_k\times n) giving: \boxed{n\times n} then: a\in\mathbb r^{n\times n} and if: v\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_v} then: av = (n\times n)(n\times d_v) giving: \boxed{n\times d_v} these exact shape relationships are summarized in your transformer cheatsheet. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.27 a tiny complete numerical example let's make the entire softmax calculation concrete. suppose the model produces three logits: z=[2,1,0] exponentials: [e^2,e^1,e^0] \approx[7.389,2.718,1] sum: 7.389+2.718+1=11.107 therefore: p_1=\frac{7.389}{11.107}\approx0.665 p_2=\frac{2.718}{11.107}\approx0.245 p_3=\frac{1}{11.107}\approx0.090 so: \boxed{ p\approx[0.665,0.245,0.090] } suppose the correct token is token 2. then: l=-\log(0.245) \boxed{l\approx1.407} so the model receives a substantially larger penalty than it would if the correct token had probability 0.9. 0.2.28 pytorch implementation this is the computation you should be able to recognize immediately in code. import torch import torch.nn.functional as f # raw logits from a model logits = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # convert logits to probabilities probs = f.softmax(logits, dim=-1) print("logits:", logits) print("probabilities:", probs) print("sum:", probs.sum()) # suppose token 2 is the correct answer target = torch.tensor(1) # negative log probability loss = -torch.log(probs[target]) print("probability of correct token:", probs[target]) print("loss:", loss) conceptually: logits ↓ softmax ↓ probabilities ↓ select correct-token probability ↓ -log(...) ↓ loss 0.2.29 a safer practical version in real pytorch training, you usually don't manually do: softmax() -log() for the language-model loss. instead, functions such as cross-entropy loss are designed to operate directly on logits in a numerically stable way. that is one reason the next lesson— entropy, cross-entropy, and kl divergence —is so important. 0.2.30 what you should understand, not memorize at this point you should be able to explain: why probability? because the model needs to represent uncertainty over possible next tokens. why logits? because the neural network naturally produces unconstrained real-valued scores. why softmax? because we need to transform those scores into nonnegative normalized values. why log? because sequence probabilities are products, and logarithms convert products into sums while improving numerical behavior. why negative log probability? because we want high probability on the correct answer to correspond to low loss. why does softmax appear in attention? because raw compatibility scores need to become normalized coefficients before we aggregate value vectors. 0.2.31 one subtle point: attention weights are not automatically "probabilities" in the ordinary semantic sense mathematically, a row of attention weights has the properties: a_i\ge0 and \sum_i a_i=1 so it behaves like a distribution over positions. but we should be careful with interpretation. it does not automatically mean: "the model believes there is a 70% probability that this token is the reason for the prediction." the attention handbook specifically warns against automatically treating attention weights as faithful explanations of model decisions. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) this distinction will matter later when you study transformer interpretability. 0.2.32 master connection you can now see why our first two mathematical lessons were ordered this way. we started: \boxed{\text{vectors}} because embeddings, queries, keys, and values are vectors. then: \boxed{\text{matrices}} because projections and batched transformations are matrix operations. then: \boxed{\text{dot product}} because it creates compatibility scores. now: \boxed{\text{probability}} because scores must often become normalized distributions. then: \boxed{\text{log probability}} because language-model sequence probabilities are products. then: \boxed{\text{softmax}} because it converts raw scores into normalized weights/probabilities. next we need to understand: \boxed{ \text{entropy} \rightarrow \text{cross-entropy} \rightarrow \text{kl divergence} } because those concepts are the mathematical bridge from ordinary language-model training to: knowledge distillation → rlhf → rlvr → ppo → grpo → deepseek-r1. master check — 0.2 try these without looking back. q1 why can't a vector like: [2.3,-1.7,5.2] be directly interpreted as probabilities? independent depth scoring pending. step 0.3 — entropy → cross-entropy → kl divergence plan node: i0 · chat order #4 this is one of the most important mathematical steps in the entire course. you already understand: \text{logits}\rightarrow\text{softmax}\rightarrow\text{probabilities} now we need to answer: how do we measure whether one probability distribution is good, uncertain, or different from another? that gives us: \boxed{\text{entropy}} \boxed{\text{cross-entropy}} \boxed{\text{kl divergence}} and these are not isolated formulas. they form a chain that later becomes: \text{lm training} \rightarrow \text{knowledge distillation} \rightarrow \text{rlhf/rlvr} \rightarrow \text{ppo/grpo} your master cheatsheet explicitly places entropy, cross-entropy, and kl in the probability/information-theory foundation, and later uses kl directly in distillation and rl. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs) 0.3.1 first question: what is entropy trying to measure? suppose a model has two possible outcomes. distribution a p=[1,0] the model is completely certain. distribution b p=[0.5,0.5] the model has no preference. intuitively: \boxed{\text{distribution b is more uncertain than distribution a}} entropy gives us a mathematical way to quantify that uncertainty. 0.3.2 entropy for a discrete distribution: \boxed{ h(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i } where: p = probability distribution p_i = probability of outcome i h(p) = entropy this formula is part of the mathematical foundation in your master cheatsheet. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs) 0.3.3 why the minus sign? we already learned: 0<p_i\le1 therefore: \log p_i\le0 so: p_i\log p_i\le0 without the minus sign, entropy would generally be negative. we want uncertainty to be represented as a nonnegative quantity, so: -\sum p_i\log p_i is used. 0.3.4 perfect certainty take: p=[1,0] then: h(p) = -[1\log1+0\log0] since: \log1=0 the first term is zero. the 0\log0 term is interpreted through its limiting value as zero. therefore: \boxed{h(p)=0} so: a completely certain distribution has zero entropy. 0.3.5 maximum uncertainty for two outcomes now: p=[0.5,0.5] then: h(p) = -[0.5\log0.5+0.5\log0.5] since: \log(0.5)\approx-0.6931 we get: h(p)\approx0.6931 thus: \boxed{ h([0.5,0.5])\approx0.693 } which is larger than zero. therefore: \boxed{ \text{more spread-out distribution} \rightarrow \text{higher entropy} } 0.3.6 three outcomes consider: p=[1/3,1/3,1/3] entropy: h(p) = -3\left(\frac13\log\frac13\right) = -\log(1/3) =\log3 using natural logarithms: \boxed{h(p)\approx1.099} so the maximum entropy increases as more possible outcomes become equally likely. for v equally likely outcomes: \boxed{h_{\max}=\log v} when using natural logarithms. 0.3.7 the intuition behind entropy think of entropy as: how spread out is the probability mass? very concentrated: [0.99,0.01] → low entropy. very spread out: [0.5,0.5] → high entropy. for a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens, a model assigning almost all probability to one token has relatively low entropy, while a model spreading probability broadly across thousands of alternatives has higher entropy. 0.3.8 another interpretation: surprise there is another extremely useful interpretation. the surprise of observing event i is: \boxed{ i(i)=-\log p_i } why? because: highly likely event → small surprise unlikely event → large surprise for example: p=0.9 gives: -\log(0.9)\approx0.105 while: p=0.01 gives: -\log(0.01)\approx4.605 entropy is the expected surprise : \boxed{ h(p)=e_{x\sim p}[-\log p(x)] } expanding the expectation gives: h(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x) so entropy means: if outcomes are actually generated according to p , how much surprise do we expect on average? 0.3.9 now the crucial question: what is cross-entropy? entropy talks about: the distribution itself. cross-entropy asks: what happens when the true distribution is p , but i use another distribution q to assign probabilities? the formula is: \boxed{ h(p,q) = -\sum_i p_i\log q_i } your supplied hands-on machine learning text gives this exact definition and explains that cross-entropy is larger than the entropy of the true distribution when the assumed distribution is imperfect. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron) 0.3.10 why are there two distributions? this is the key conceptual difference. entropy: h(p) = -\sum_i p_i\log p_i uses: p\rightarrow p cross-entropy: h(p,q) = -\sum_i p_i\log q_i uses: p\rightarrow q so: quantity meaning h(p) uncertainty inherent in p h(p,q) how costly it is to encode outcomes from p using q 0.3.11 numerical example let's use: p=[0.7,0.2,0.1] and suppose our model uses: q=[0.6,0.3,0.1] first calculate entropy of p : h(p) = -[0.7\log0.7+0.2\log0.2+0.1\log0.1] numerically: \boxed{h(p)\approx0.802} now cross-entropy: h(p,q) = -[0.7\log0.6+0.2\log0.3+0.1\log0.1] giving: \boxed{h(p,q)\approx0.829} notice: 0.829>0.802 why? because q isn't exactly p . 0.3.12 the beautiful relationship cross-entropy can be decomposed into: \boxed{ h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) } this identity is explicitly used in the supplied minillm material to explain knowledge distillation. (source: minillm-slides) this equation is tremendously important. let's understand it rather than memorize it. 0.3.13 what is kl divergence? kl divergence measures how different q is from p , in an information-theoretic sense: \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i \log \frac{p_i}{q_i} } your supplied active-learning material describes kl divergence as measuring the difference between a true distribution p and an approximating distribution q , and notes that it is zero when the two distributions match. 0.3.14 derive the cross-entropy identity start with kl: d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i \log\frac{p_i}{q_i} use: \log\frac{a}{b} = \log a-\log b therefore: d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i\log p_i - \sum_i p_i\log q_i now recall: h(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i and: h(p,q)=-\sum_i p_i\log q_i so: d_{kl}(p\|q) = -h(p)+h(p,q) rearrange: \boxed{ h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) } there is the identity. 0.3.15 what does this identity actually mean? it says: \boxed{ \text{cross-entropy} = \text{intrinsic uncertainty} + \text{mismatch penalty} } specifically: h(p) is unavoidable uncertainty in the original distribution. and: d_{kl}(p\|q) is the additional cost caused by using the wrong distribution q . this is a fantastic mental model. 0.3.16 what happens when p=q ? suppose: q=p then: d_{kl}(p\|p) = \sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{p_i} = \sum_i p_i\log1 =0 therefore: h(p,p) = h(p) so: \boxed{ \text{perfect match} \rightarrow kl=0 \rightarrow ce=entropy } this exact idea is demonstrated in the supplied minillm slides: when the student exactly matches the teacher, kl is zero but the distillation cross-entropy remains equal to the teacher's entropy. (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.17 let's verify our numerical example we had: h(p)\approx0.8018 and: h(p,q)\approx0.8286 therefore: d_{kl}(p\|q) = h(p,q)-h(p) \approx0.8286-0.8018 \boxed{d_{kl}(p\|q)\approx0.0268} so: 0.8286 = 0.8018+0.0268 exactly. 0.3.18 important property: kl is nonnegative for valid distributions: \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q)\ge0 } and: d_{kl}(p\|q)=0 only when: p=q under the usual conditions. therefore: h(p,q)\ge h(p) this means: using the wrong distribution cannot give you lower cross-entropy than the true distribution's own entropy. 0.3.19 but kl is not a distance this is a common interview/exam trap. people often casually call kl a "distance," but technically it is a divergence , not a metric. why? a metric generally requires symmetry: d(p,q)=d(q,p) but kl generally does not satisfy this. usually: \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q)\neq d_{kl}(q\|p) } this asymmetry becomes extremely important later in knowledge distillation . 0.3.20 forward kl vs reverse kl there are two directions. forward kl \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q) } reverse kl \boxed{ d_{kl}(q\|p) } they are not interchangeable. your minillm materials explicitly distinguish these two and discuss their different behavior. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) 0.3.21 why direction matters consider p as the teacher and q as the student. forward kl: d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_xp(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} the teacher's probabilities p(x) are used as weights. so if the teacher assigns meaningful probability to something and the student gives it almost zero, the student gets heavily penalized. this tends toward covering teacher-supported modes . your supplied minillm material describes forward kl as strongly penalizing missing teacher-supported modes. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) reverse kl: d_{kl}(q\|p) = \sum_xq(x)\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} now the student's distribution determines which regions are emphasized. it strongly penalizes putting probability mass where the teacher says probability is very low. this is associated with mode-seeking behavior in the supplied minillm explanation. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) we will return to this in depth when we reach minillm . 0.3.22 cross-entropy in language-model training now connect today's mathematics directly to transformers. suppose vocabulary: v=\{\text{the, cat, sat, dog, ran}\} correct token: y=\text{sat} one-hot target: p=[0,0,1,0,0] model distribution: q=[0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] cross-entropy: h(p,q) = -\sum_ip_i\log q_i because all p_i are zero except the correct token: = -\log0.60 \boxed{ h(p,q)=0.5108 } this exact example is in the supplied minillm slides. (source: minillm-slides) so ordinary next-token training is just cross-entropy with a one-hot target. 0.3.23 why does one-hot cross-entropy collapse to -\log q_y ? suppose: y=[0,0,1,0] and: q=[0.1,0.2,0.6,0.1] then: -\sum_i y_i\log q_i becomes: - [ 0\log0.1+ 0\log0.2+ 1\log0.6+ 0\log0.1 ] everything disappears except: \boxed{-\log0.6} this is why the ordinary lm loss focuses on the probability assigned to the observed token. 0.3.24 now the big connection: distillation imagine we replace the hard one-hot target: [0,0,1,0,0] with the teacher's output: p_{\text{teacher}} = [0.02,0.05,0.70,0.03,0.20] now the student might predict: q_{\text{student}} = [0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] the loss becomes: \boxed{ h(p_{\text{teacher}},q_{\text{student}}) = -\sum_v p_{\text{teacher}}(v) \log q_{\text{student}}(v) } now every vocabulary item contributes . this is the mathematical reason knowledge distillation carries more information than one-hot supervision. the supplied minillm example explicitly shows that the teacher's entire probability shape—not just the true token—is used. (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.25 why call this "dark knowledge"? suppose the teacher says: p= [0.01,0.02,0.70,0.05,0.22] a one-hot label only says: sat is correct. it loses the teacher's relative judgments among wrong answers. but the teacher distribution tells us: p(\text{sat})=0.70 p(\text{ran})=0.22 p(\text{dog})=0.05 etc. so the student learns: sat is preferred, but ran is also somewhat plausible. that extra structure is what the distillation material refers to as dark knowledge . (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.26 why temperature enters distillation a teacher may produce: [0.999,0.0005,0.0003,\ldots] that distribution is too sharp to reveal much information about secondary choices. temperature modifies logits before softmax: \boxed{ p_i^{(t)} = \frac{e^{z_i/t}} {\sum_j e^{z_j/t}} } with: t>1 the distribution becomes softer. for example: [0.999,0.0005,0.0003] might become something more informative such as: [0.70,0.20,0.10] the exact numbers depend on the logits, but the conceptual point is: \boxed{ t>1 \rightarrow \text{more information in the relative alternatives} } the supplied minillm slides explicitly use temperature to soften teacher outputs and expose relative confidence among alternatives. (source: minillm-slides) this will become a whole topic later. 0.3.27 the same kl appears later in rl this is where today's lesson becomes much more powerful. in reinforcement learning for language models, we often don't want the updated policy to move arbitrarily far from a reference policy. so kl divergence appears as a constraint or penalty. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{reward improvement} - \text{penalty for moving too far} } one common structure is: j(\theta) = e[r] - \beta d_{kl}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) the exact objective varies by method, but the mathematical idea is the same: \boxed{ kl=\text{distribution mismatch} } your master cheatsheet explicitly places kl in both knowledge distillation and rl sections. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) so understanding kl now will make later rl mathematics much easier. 0.3.28 a unifying view we now have: entropy \boxed{ h(p)=e_{x\sim p}[-\log p(x)] } interpretation: how uncertain/spread out is p ? cross-entropy \boxed{ h(p,q)=e_{x\sim p}[-\log q(x)] } interpretation: how much surprise do i incur when data comes from p , but i use q to predict it? kl divergence \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q) = e_{x\sim p} \left[ \log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \right] } interpretation: how much extra information cost/mismatch arises from using q instead of p ? and: \boxed{ h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) } 0.3.29 the complete conceptual graph probability distribution │ ├───────────────┐ ↓ ↓ entropy cross-entropy │ │ │ │ │ ↓ │ kl divergence │ │ └───────┬───────┘ ↓ distribution mismatch │ ┌───────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ knowledge rl distillation ppo / grpo and ordinary language-model training sits underneath: logits ↓ softmax ↓ probability distribution q ↓ cross-entropy with target ↓ loss 0.3.30 one subtle but very important distinction do not confuse these: h(p) with: h(p,q) with: d_{kl}(p\|q) their roles are different. formula what it measures h(p) uncertainty of p itself h(p,q) prediction/encoding cost when true distribution is p , model uses q d_{kl}(p\vert q) mismatch between p and q and: \boxed{ ce = entropy + kl } not: ce=kl however, when optimizing q_\theta with p fixed: h(p) doesn't depend on \theta . therefore: \boxed{ \arg\min_\theta h(p,q_\theta) = \arg\min_\theta d_{kl}(p\|q_\theta) } this is why a distillation cross-entropy objective can be described as equivalent to minimizing forward kl with respect to the student's parameters. the supplied minillm material makes exactly this point. (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.31 why this matters for the entire course you've now built a mathematical bridge: \boxed{ \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{probability distribution} \rightarrow \text{log probability} \rightarrow \text{entropy} \rightarrow \text{cross-entropy} \rightarrow \text{kl} } later: \boxed{ kl \rightarrow \text{distillation} } and: \boxed{ kl \rightarrow \text{rlhf/rlvr} \rightarrow ppo \rightarrow grpo } and later still: \boxed{ grpo \rightarrow deepseekmath \rightarrow deepseek-r1 } so this is not a side chapter of information theory. it is part of the mathematical spine of the whole curriculum. 0.3.32 master numerical example given: p=[0.7,0.2,0.1] q=[0.6,0.3,0.1] we found: \boxed{h(p)\approx0.8018} \boxed{h(p,q)\approx0.8286} \boxed{d_{kl}(p\|q)\approx0.0268} and verify: \boxed{ 0.8286\approx0.8018+0.0268 } this one example contains the entire relationship. 0.3.33 code it import torch p = torch.tensor([0.7, 0.2, 0.1]) q = torch.tensor([0.6, 0.3, 0.1]) # entropy h(p) entropy = -(p * torch.log(p)).sum() # cross-entropy h(p, q) cross_entropy = -(p * torch.log(q)).sum() # kl divergence d_kl(p || q) kl_divergence = (p * torch.log(p / q)).sum() print("entropy:", entropy.item()) print("cross-entropy:", cross_entropy.item()) print("kl divergence:", kl_divergence.item()) print("entropy + kl:", (entropy + kl_divergence).item()) you should observe approximately: entropy: 0.8018 cross-entropy: 0.8286 kl divergence: 0.0268 entropy + kl: 0.8286 0.3.34 one more connection to gradients you already learned in the previous lesson that we minimize negative log probability. cross-entropy gives us the same training objective: l = -\sum_i y_i\log q_i where y is the target distribution. for a one-hot target: l=-\log q_y and with softmax outputs, the gradient with respect to a class logit has the particularly elegant form: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial z_i}=q_i-y_i } this is one of the reasons softmax + cross-entropy is so convenient for training neural networks. the supplied hands-on machine learning text derives the corresponding softmax-regression gradient in terms of predicted probabilities minus target indicators. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron) we will derive this carefully in the calculus/optimization foundation step , rather than skipping the derivation. 0.3.35 your mental model should now be when you see: -\log p think: surprise / penalty for predicting probability p when you see: h(p) think: uncertainty of a distribution when you see: h(p,q) think: how well q predicts outcomes from p when you see: d_{kl}(p\|q) think: how much q differs from p , measured from p 's perspective when you see: h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) think: prediction cost = irreducible uncertainty + mismatch master check — step 0.3 do these before we move forward. q1 which distribution is more uncertain? p_1=[1,0] or: p_2=[0.5,0.5] and why? q2 calculate: h([0.5,0.5]) using natural logarithms. q3 what is the conceptual difference between: h(p) and: h(p,q)? q4 given: p=[0.5,0.5] q=[0.8,0.2] which quantity tells us that q does not perfectly match p ? q5 what happens to: d_{kl}(p\|q) when: p=q? q6 is: d_{kl}(p\|q) = d_{kl}(q\|p) generally true? q7 derive: h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) in two or three mathematical steps. q8 why does ordinary lm cross-entropy with a one-hot target reduce to: -\log q_y? q9 why can we optimize cross-entropy and forward kl interchangeably when the teacher distribution p is fixed? q10 — the big one explain this entire chain in your own words: \boxed{ \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow p \rightarrow \text{cross-entropy} \rightarrow \text{kl} }

(source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.1 the whole idea before the mathematics imagine a single parameter: w and suppose the model's loss is: l(w) you want to make l smaller. so the central question is: if i increase w slightly, does the loss go up or down, and by how much? that is exactly what a derivative tells us. 0.4.2 derivative: the slope for a function: y=f(x) the derivative is: \boxed{ \frac{dy}{dx} } it measures the instantaneous rate at which y changes when x changes. a rough interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{derivative} = \frac{\text{change in output}}{\text{change in input}} } simple example let: f(x)=x^2 then: \frac{df}{dx}=2x at: x=3 we have: \frac{df}{dx}=6 interpretation: around x=3 , increasing x slightly increases f(x) at a rate of about 6 units of output per unit of input. 0.4.3 why slope matters for optimization suppose: l(w)=w^2 then: \frac{dl}{dw}=2w consider: w=5 then: \frac{dl}{dw}=10 the slope is positive. that means: increasing w increases the loss. so to reduce the loss, we should move w in the negative direction. now suppose: w=-5 then: \frac{dl}{dw}=-10 the slope is negative. that means: increasing w decreases the loss. so we should move w in the positive direction. this gives us the fundamental rule: \boxed{ \text{move opposite to the gradient} } 0.4.4 partial derivative a neural network doesn't have just one parameter. suppose: l(w_1,w_2,w_3) now we may ask: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_1} while treating the other parameters as fixed. that is a partial derivative . similarly: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_2} and: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_3} raschka and the supplied hands-on ml material use this idea explicitly: a partial derivative measures how the cost changes with respect to one parameter while considering the others. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron; build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.5 why not just use one derivative? because the model has millions or billions of parameters. suppose: \theta= [w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4] we need: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_1}, \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_2}, \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_3}, \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_4} all at once. we package them into a vector. 0.4.6 gradient the gradient is: \boxed{ \nabla_\theta l = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_1}\\ \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_2}\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_n} \end{bmatrix} } so: \boxed{ \text{gradient}=\text{all partial derivatives collected together} } this is exactly how the supplied sources describe it. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron; build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.7 geometric meaning of the gradient remember the mountain analogy. suppose you are standing somewhere on a mountain. the gradient tells you: \boxed{ \text{the direction of steepest increase} } therefore: -\nabla l points toward the steepest local decrease. this is why optimization uses: \boxed{ \theta_{\text{new}} = \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l } the supplied hands-on ml source gives this exact gradient-descent update. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron) 0.4.8 what is the learning rate? \eta is the learning rate . it determines how large a step we take. so: \theta_{\text{new}} = \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l has two pieces: direction -\nabla_\theta l step size \eta think: gradient tells us where to go. learning rate tells us how far to go. 0.4.9 numerical gradient-descent example take: l(w)=w^2 then: \frac{dl}{dw}=2w start with: w=5 and: \eta=0.1 gradient: \frac{dl}{dw}=10 update: w_{\text{new}} = 5-0.1(10) \boxed{w_{\text{new}}=4} loss changed from: l(5)=25 to: l(4)=16 good—we moved downhill. 0.4.10 another iteration now: w=4 gradient: 8 update: w=4-0.1(8) =3.2 then: l(3.2)=10.24 again smaller. eventually: w\rightarrow0 because: l(w)=w^2 has its minimum at zero. 0.4.11 why this becomes difficult in neural networks in a transformer: l = l(\text{softmax}( \text{transformer}( x,\theta ))) a parameter such as w_q affects: q which affects: qk^t which affects: a which affects: o which affects later layers, which affects: z which affects: p which affects: l so there is a long chain of dependencies. we therefore need the chain rule . 0.4.12 chain rule suppose: y=f(u) and: u=g(x) therefore: y=f(g(x)) the chain rule says: \boxed{ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \frac{du}{dx} } this looks simple, but it is the mathematical engine behind backpropagation. raschka explicitly describes backpropagation as applying the chain rule backward through the computation graph. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.13 tiny numerical example of chain rule let: u=x^2 and: y=3u then: \frac{du}{dx}=2x and: \frac{dy}{du}=3 therefore: \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \frac{du}{dx} = 3(2x) = 6x if: x=2 then: \boxed{ \frac{dy}{dx}=12 } instead of directly differentiating the full expression, we propagated derivatives through intermediate variables. that is exactly what a neural network does. 0.4.14 computational graph let's represent the previous example as a graph: x │ ▼ u = x² │ ▼ y = 3u forward: x\rightarrow u\rightarrow y backward: \frac{\partial y}{\partial y} \rightarrow \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} \rightarrow \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} this is the basic shape of backpropagation. 0.4.15 a neural-network example suppose: z=wx+b then: a=\sigma(z) and loss: l=\ell(a,y) the dependency graph is: x, w, b ↓ z ↓ a ↓ l to find: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} we walk backward. by the chain rule: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial a} \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} } every factor represents one local derivative. 0.4.16 why this is so powerful imagine a model with: 10^9 parameters. we don't want to symbolically re-derive the entire loss function for every parameter from scratch. instead, the computation graph contains local operations. backpropagation reuses intermediate derivatives efficiently. this is why modern deep-learning frameworks rely on automatic differentiation . raschka explains that pytorch tracks operations in a computational graph and can then compute the gradients required for training. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.17 forward pass vs backward pass this distinction is essential. forward pass we compute: x \rightarrow q,k,v \rightarrow attention \rightarrow transformer \rightarrow logits \rightarrow probabilities \rightarrow loss purpose: \boxed{ \text{compute prediction and loss} } backward pass we start with the loss and move backward: l \rightarrow logits \rightarrow transformer \rightarrow attention \rightarrow q,k,v \rightarrow parameters purpose: \boxed{ \text{compute gradients} } 0.4.18 backpropagation so now we can define it properly: \boxed{ \text{backpropagation} = \text{efficient backward application of the chain rule} } it calculates: \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_i} for the model parameters. the supplied raschka source makes exactly this connection and describes reverse-mode automatic differentiation as computing loss gradients by working backward from the output toward the parameters. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.19 why "reverse mode"? suppose we have: \text{many parameters} \rightarrow \text{one loss} a transformer has an enormous number of inputs/parameters, but typically the training objective produces a relatively small number of scalar losses. reverse-mode differentiation is efficient for this structure. conceptually: many parameters ↓ ... ↓ scalar loss then propagate backward: scalar loss ↓ intermediate nodes ↓ many parameters this is the mathematical reason reverse-mode autodiff is so useful for neural-network training. 0.4.20 a complete small example let's create: z=wx with: w=2,\quad x=3 then: z=6 suppose loss is: l=(z-10)^2 therefore: l=(6-10)^2=16 now calculate: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} break the graph: w \rightarrow z \rightarrow l we have: z=wx so: \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}=x=3 and: l=(z-10)^2 so: \frac{\partial l}{\partial z}=2(z-10) at z=6 : \frac{\partial l}{\partial z} = 2(6-10) = -8 chain rule: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial z} \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} =(-8)(3) \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w}=-24 } 0.4.21 what does -24 mean? it means locally: increasing w tends to decrease the loss. so gradient descent does: w_{\text{new}} = w-\eta(-24) if: \eta=0.1 then: w_{\text{new}} = 2+2.4 \boxed{w_{\text{new}}=4.4} the gradient was negative, so subtracting it moves w upward. that is exactly why we always say: \boxed{ \text{gradient points uphill} } and: \boxed{ -\text{gradient points downhill} } 0.4.22 connect this to the transformer now replace our simple w with: w_q a simplified dependency chain is: w_q \rightarrow q \rightarrow qk^t \rightarrow s \rightarrow a \rightarrow o \rightarrow \text{transformer output} \rightarrow z \rightarrow p \rightarrow l therefore we want: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} the chain rule conceptually gives: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial z} \frac{\partial z}{\partial o} \frac{\partial o}{\partial a} \frac{\partial a}{\partial s} \frac{\partial s}{\partial q} \frac{\partial q}{\partial w_q} the actual implementation uses tensor operations and automatic differentiation, but this is the conceptual mathematical structure. 0.4.23 even more concretely we previously had: q=xw_q suppose: l=l(q) then: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} comes from: w_q \rightarrow q \rightarrow l the local derivative of: q=xw_q is essentially governed by x . for the complete matrix calculus, autodiff handles the tensor-shaped derivative bookkeeping for us. this is why learning matrix dimensions earlier was essential. 0.4.24 why gradients can explode or vanish now we encounter another crucial deep-learning issue. suppose chain rule gives: \frac{\partial l}{\partial x} = a_1a_2a_3a_4\cdots a_n if the factors are mostly less than 1: 0.5^{20} becomes extremely small. the gradient can effectively disappear. this produces the: \boxed{\text{vanishing-gradient problem}} if the factors are mostly greater than 1: 2^{20} becomes enormous. that gives: \boxed{\text{exploding gradients}} hands-on ml explicitly discusses these problems as part of deep-network optimization. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron) this will later motivate: initialization normalization residual connections activation choices careful optimization which we will encounter when studying the transformer block. 0.4.25 gradient descent in vector form suppose: \theta= \begin{bmatrix} \theta_1\\ \theta_2\\ \theta_3 \end{bmatrix} and: \nabla_\theta l= \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ -4\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} let: \eta=0.1 then: \theta_{\text{new}} = \theta - 0.1 \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ -4\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} thus: \theta_{\text{new}} = \begin{bmatrix} \theta_1-0.2\\ \theta_2+0.4\\ \theta_3-0.1 \end{bmatrix} each parameter moves independently according to its own derivative. 0.4.26 batch gradient descent the supplied hands-on ml source derives: \nabla_\theta \mathrm{mse} = \frac{2}{m}x^t(x\theta-y) and then: \boxed{ \theta_{\text{next}} = \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta \mathrm{mse} } it describes this as batch gradient descent because the full training set is used at every update. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron) for a modern transformer, we generally use stochastic/minibatch variants rather than computing the gradient over the entire training corpus at every step. the fundamental mathematical update remains the same. 0.4.27 the training loop now we can finally write the conceptual training loop: initialize parameters θ ↓ take a batch of training data ↓ forward pass ↓ compute logits ↓ softmax / loss ↓ compute loss l ↓ backpropagation ↓ compute ∇θl ↓ optimizer update ↓ new parameters θ ↓ repeat mathematically: \boxed{ \theta \rightarrow l(\theta) \rightarrow \nabla_\theta l \rightarrow \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l } this is the fundamental learning loop. 0.4.28 pytorch example let's see automatic differentiation perform the calculation. import torch # parameter w = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=true) # input x = torch.tensor(3.0) # forward pass z = w * x # loss loss = (z - 10) ** 2 print("z =", z.item()) print("loss =", loss.item()) # backward pass loss.backward() print("gradient =", w.grad.item()) # gradient descent update learning_rate = 0.1 with torch.no_grad(): w -= learning_rate * w.grad print("updated w =", w.item()) expected reasoning: w=2 z=6 l=16 \frac{\partial l}{\partial w}=-24 so: w_{\text{new}}=4.4 0.4.29 what requires_grad=true means when we write: w = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=true) we are telling pytorch: track operations involving w so its gradient can be computed. raschka explains that pytorch builds a computational graph by tracking operations on tensors whose gradients are being tracked. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.30 what loss.backward() means this: loss.backward() means conceptually: start at the loss and propagate derivatives backward through the computation graph. so: \boxed{ \texttt{backward()} \approx \text{reverse-mode automatic differentiation} } afterward: w.grad contains: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} 0.4.31 why do we use torch.no_grad() for the update? we do: with torch.no_grad(): w -= learning_rate * w.grad because the parameter update itself should not become another differentiable operation in the training graph. otherwise we would start tracking the optimizer's bookkeeping as part of the computation graph. for now, the important mental model is: forward operations → tracked backward → calculate gradients parameter update → outside the gradient graph 0.4.32 gradient vs parameter never confuse: w with: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} the first is: the parameter itself. the second is: how the loss changes when the parameter changes. example: w=2 but: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w}=-24 these are completely different quantities. 0.4.33 gradient vs learning rate also don't confuse: \nabla_\theta l with: \eta the gradient determines: \boxed{\text{direction and local sensitivity}} the learning rate determines: \boxed{\text{update magnitude}} 0.4.34 why the chain rule becomes the transformer learning mechanism let's now connect everything we've learned. forward: x \rightarrow q,k,v qk^t \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow av \text{transformer blocks} \rightarrow z \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow p p \rightarrow -\log p_{\text{correct}} \rightarrow l backward: l \rightarrow p \rightarrow z \rightarrow \text{transformer} \rightarrow a \rightarrow q,k,v \rightarrow w_q,w_k,w_v and simultaneously toward: embeddings ffn weights normalization parameters output projection positional parameters where applicable then: \nabla_\theta l is computed. finally: \boxed{ \theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l } the model has learned a little. then we repeat this billions of times. 0.4.35 the four equations you now need to own derivative \boxed{ \frac{df}{dx} } “how does f change with x ?” gradient \boxed{ \nabla_\theta l = \left[ \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_n} \right]^t } “how does loss change with every parameter?” chain rule \boxed{ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \frac{du}{dx} } “how do local changes combine through a chain of operations?” gradient descent \boxed{ \theta_{\text{new}} = \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l } “how do we actually change the parameters?” 0.4.36 the master picture you now have the mathematical story from beginning to end: forward ↓ input x ↓ q = xwq k = xwk v = xwv ↓ qkᵀ ↓ scale + mask ↓ softmax ↓ attention weights a ↓ av ↓ transformer blocks ↓ logits z ↓ softmax ↓ probabilities p ↓ cross-entropy ↓ loss l ↑ backward │ chain rule │ backprop │ gradients ∇l │ optimizer │ └──── θ ← θ - η∇l this is the entire training mechanism in one picture. raschka's treatment of automatic differentiation specifically ties together computational graphs, partial derivatives, gradients, chain rule, backpropagation, and parameter updates in precisely this training context. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.4.37 one important correction to a common mental model backpropagation does not mean: "the model runs backward and generates the sentence backward." it has nothing to do with reversing language. it means: the model's mathematical computation graph is traversed backward to calculate derivatives of the loss with respect to earlier quantities and parameters. 0.4.38 another common mistake don't think: \boxed{\text{backpropagation}=\text{gradient descent}} they are related, but different. backpropagation computes: \nabla_\theta l gradient descent uses that gradient: \theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l so: \boxed{ \text{backpropagation} \rightarrow \text{gradient} } \boxed{ \text{optimizer} \rightarrow \text{parameter update} } 0.4.39 connection to adam in modern transformers, the optimizer is commonly more sophisticated than plain gradient descent. instead of simply: \theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l optimizers such as adam maintain statistics of gradients and adapt updates. but the fundamental input to the optimizer is still: \boxed{\nabla_\theta l} so even when we later study adam/adamw, this lesson remains the foundation. 0.4.40 what comes next? we've now completed the core calculus needed to understand training mechanics. the remaining mathematical foundation we should add before starting the transformer itself is: \boxed{\text{expectation and weighted averages}} this is deceptively important because the exact concept will reappear in: \text{attention} \rightarrow \text{probabilistic modeling} \rightarrow \text{reinforcement learning} \rightarrow \text{policy objectives} in particular, an expression such as: e_{x\sim p}[f(x)] is the mathematical language for: "take an average, weighted according to a probability distribution." that will make the later rl formulas much less mysterious. master check — step 0.4 before moving on, make sure you can answer these. q1. what is the conceptual difference between a derivative and a partial derivative? q2. what does the gradient contain? q3. if: l(w)=w^2 what is: \frac{dl}{dw} ? q4. if w=5 and the gradient is 10 , which direction should gradient descent move w ? q5. what does the learning rate \eta control? q6. apply the chain rule to: u=x^2,\qquad y=3u and find: \frac{dy}{dx} q7. what is the difference between forward pass and backward pass ? q8. why is backpropagation essentially the chain rule applied through a computation graph? q9. what is the difference between: \text{backpropagation} and: \text{gradient descent} ? q10. most important: explain how a single transformer parameter such as w_q can ultimately receive a gradient from the final next-token loss. grounding for this step the calculus/backpropagation explanation is grounded primarily in the supplied hands-on machine learning material for partial derivatives, gradients, and gradient descent, and sebastian raschka's build a large language model (from scratch) for computational graphs, automatic differentiation, and backpropagation. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs) 0.5.5 why do we need f(x) ? because often we don't want the expectation of x itself. we may want: e[x^2] or: e[|x|] or: e[\log x] or: e[r] or: e[a(x)] the general form handles all of these:  oxed{ e[f(x)] = \sum_xp(x)f(x) } 0.5.6 numerical example with f(x)=x^2 use: x= \{1,2,3\} with: p=[0.2,0.5,0.3] first: e[x] = 1(0.2)+2(0.5)+3(0.3) =2.1 now: e[x^2] = 1^2(0.2)+2^2(0.5)+3^2(0.3) =0.2+2+2.7  oxed{e[x^2]=4.9} notice: e[x^2]
eq(e[x])^2 here: (e[x])^2=2.1^2=4.41 while: e[x^2]=4.9 this distinction will become important when we study variance . 0.5.7 expectation and probability distributions suppose: p=[0.1,0.2,0.7] and values: x=[2,5,10] then: e[x] = 0.1(2)+0.2(5)+0.7(10) =0.2+1+7  oxed{e[x]=8.2} so the probability distribution acts as the weighting mechanism. this is a recurring pattern throughout machine learning:  oxed{ 	ext{distribution} ightarrow 	ext{weights} ightarrow 	ext{weighted average} } 0.5.8 this should immediately remind you of attention remember: a=\operatorname{softmax}(s) each row of a contains weights: a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n such that: a_i\ge0 and: \sum_i a_i=1 then attention computes:  oxed{ o=\sum_i a_iv_i } that is mathematically a weighted average of the value vectors. for one query: o= a_1v_1+a_2v_2+\cdots+a_nv_n this is extremely closely related to expectation: e[v] = \sum_ip(i)v_i so a powerful mental model is:  oxed{ 	ext{attention output} \approx 	ext{expectation of values under the attention distribution} } the supplied attention handbook describes attention as a weighted combination of values, with softmax turning scores into normalized weights and av producing the output. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) 0.5.9 concrete attention example suppose there are three value vectors: v_1=  egin{bmatrix} 1\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad v_2=  egin{bmatrix} 0\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad v_3=  egin{bmatrix} 3\ 1 \end{bmatrix} and attention weights: a=[0.2,0.5,0.3] then: o = 0.2v_1+0.5v_2+0.3v_3 compute the first component: 0.2(1)+0.5(0)+0.3(3) = 1.1 second component: 0.2(0)+0.5(2)+0.3(1) = 1.3 therefore:  oxed{ o=  egin{bmatrix} 1.1\ 1.3 \end{bmatrix} } the attention mechanism has effectively computed: "take the expected value representation under the distribution of attention weights." that's an excellent mathematical interpretation. 0.5.10 but attention weights are not literally an event probability be precise here. we can mathematically treat: [a_1,\ldots,a_n] as a normalized distribution over positions. that allows us to use expectation-like language. but that does not mean: "there is a real-world random event where token 2 occurs with probability 0.5." these are learned coefficients used for aggregation. the attention handbook explicitly distinguishes normalized attention weights from stronger claims about semantic interpretation or explanation. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) 0.5.11 expectation of a constant if: x=c always, then: e[x]=c example: x=5 with probability 1. then: e[x]=1(5)=5 so:  oxed{e[c]=c} 0.5.12 linearity of expectation one of the most useful properties is:  oxed{ e[ax+by] = ae[x]+be[y] } for constants a,b . and more generally:  oxed{ e[x+y]=e[x]+e[y] } this is true even when x and y are not independent. that is a very useful fact in probability and reinforcement learning. 0.5.13 numerical example suppose: e[x]=4 e[y]=7 find: e[3x+2y+5] by linearity: e[3x+2y+5] = 3e[x]+2e[y]+5 =3(4)+2(7)+5 =12+14+5  oxed{31} no need to enumerate every possible combination of x and y . 0.5.14 why linearity is so useful in machine learning suppose we have many token losses: l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_n and define: l= rac1n\sum_tl_t we can reason about their expected value using linearity. similarly, in rl we may have total reward: r=r_1+r_2+\cdots+r_t and expectation can be decomposed: e[r] = e[r_1]+\cdots+e[r_t] this becomes very useful when reasoning about returns and policy objectives. 0.5.15 expected reward now enter reinforcement learning. suppose an agent can produce three possible trajectories: trajectory probability reward 	au_1 0.2 10 	au_2 0.5 4 	au_3 0.3 -2 expected reward: e[r] = 0.2(10)+0.5(4)+0.3(-2) =2+2-0.6  oxed{e[r]=3.4} the agent's objective is not: "always get the reward of the single best trajectory." it is often formulated as: maximize expected reward under the policy. your supplied reasoning-model material introduces the policy objective in exactly this expectation form, and the master cheatsheet records:  oxed{ j(	heta)=e_{	au\sim\pi_	heta}[r(	au)] } . (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch); master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) 0.5.16 why the subscript 	au\sim\pi_	heta ? this notation: e_{	au\sim\pi_	heta}[r(	au)] means: take trajectories 	au generated according to policy \pi_	heta , and average their rewards. so: 	au = trajectory / generated response \pi_	heta = policy parameterized by 	heta r(	au) = reward of trajectory e = average weighted according to the policy's distribution over trajectories this is why expectation is fundamental to rl. 0.5.17 llm as a probability policy for an llm: \pi_	heta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}) means: probability of choosing token y_t , given the prompt and previous generated tokens. so the model's token probability distribution becomes an rl policy . the supplied master cheatsheet makes this explicit: s_t=(x,y_{<t}) a_t=y_t \pi_	heta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}) . (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) therefore: llm probability distribution ↓ policy πθ ↓ generate actions/tokens ↓ trajectory τ ↓ reward ↓ expected reward e[r] 0.5.18 conditional expectation now we need another concept. sometimes the expected value changes depending on known information. for example: what is the expected reward given the current state ? this is:  oxed{ e[x\mid y=y] } called conditional expectation . in a discrete case:  oxed{ e[x\mid y=y] = \sum_x xp(x=x\mid y=y) } the important idea is: first restrict the distribution using the known condition, then calculate the weighted average. 0.5.19 simple example suppose today's weather y is known to be rainy. possible temperature x : temperature p(x\mid rain) 15 0.2 20 0.5 25 0.3 then: e[x\mid rain] = 15(0.2)+20(0.5)+25(0.3) =3+10+7.5  oxed{e[x\mid rain]=20.5} we did not use the unconditional temperature distribution. we used: p(x\mid rain) 0.5.20 why conditional expectation matters for llms an llm constantly computes conditional distributions. for next-token prediction: p(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}) the model is essentially saying: given this context, what is the distribution over possible next tokens? then we can conceptually calculate expected quantities under that distribution. this same conditioning structure appears in: \pi_	heta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}) during rl. so expectation and conditional probability are naturally connected. 0.5.21 from token-level expectation to sequence-level expectation suppose the model generates a sequence: y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_t the probability of that sequence is: p_	heta(y_{1:t}\mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^{t} p_	heta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}) the model samples sequences according to this distribution. then rl can evaluate: e_{y\sim\pi_	heta}[r(y)] so:  oxed{ 	ext{token probabilities} ightarrow 	ext{sequence distribution} ightarrow 	ext{expected reward} } that is the mathematical bridge into rl. 0.5.22 variance expectation tells us the center of a distribution. but it doesn't tell us how spread out it is. for that we use variance.  oxed{ \operatorname{var}(x) = e[(x-e[x])^2] } your supplied lecture material uses this exact expectation-based definition when discussing bias-variance. (source: 5. linear regression) 0.5.23 why square the difference? suppose: e[x]=10 and outcomes are: 8,\;10,\;12 the deviations are: -2,\;0,\;+2 if we simply averaged deviations:  rac{-2+0+2}{3}=0 we would incorrectly conclude there is no spread. so we square: (-2)^2=4 0^2=0 2^2=4 which gives a positive measure of spread. 0.5.24 standard deviation variance is in squared units. so we often take the square root:  oxed{ \sigma_x=\sqrt{\operatorname{var}(x)} } this returns the spread to the same units as x . 0.5.25 why does variance matter for our later rl lessons? because rl training estimates expectations from sampled trajectories. sampling introduces noise. we therefore care about:  oxed{	ext{variance of the gradient estimate}} this motivates concepts such as: baselines advantage functions group normalization ppo stabilization grpo's relative normalization your master cheatsheet explicitly notes that the advantage subtracts a baseline to reduce variance under standard conditions, and grpo normalizes group rewards using their standard deviation. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) so today's simple expectation/variance lesson directly prepares us for grpo. 0.5.26 expected return in rl suppose an agent receives rewards: r_1,r_2,r_3,\ldots a discounted return is:  oxed{ g_t= \sum_{k=0}^{t-t-1} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1} } where: 0\le\gamma\le1 and \gamma determines how much future rewards are discounted. your master cheatsheet includes exactly this return definition. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) then rl often cares about: e[g_t] or expected cumulative reward. so expectation is now appearing again. 0.5.27 why discounting? suppose: \gamma=0.9 and future rewards are: 10,\;10,\;10 then: g = 10+ 0.9(10)+ 0.9^2(10) = 10+9+8.1  oxed{g=27.1} the later rewards still matter, but less. this gives a way to encode the idea: near-term consequences matter more than very distant consequences. we will derive rl returns much more rigorously later; for now the key point is that expectation will be applied over these returns. 0.5.28 monte carlo estimation of expectation here is another concept you absolutely need. suppose: e[x] is difficult to calculate exactly. we can sample: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n and estimate:  oxed{ e[x] \approx  rac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i } this is the sample mean . for example, suppose rewards from five sampled responses are: [8,6,10,4,7] then estimated expected reward: \hat e[r] =  rac{8+6+10+4+7}{5} =  rac{35}{5}  oxed{\hat e[r]=7} this is how sampled rollouts become useful in rl. 0.5.29 this is exactly the bridge to policy gradients the rl slides explain the key difficulty: we want to optimize an expectation over sampled outputs, but directly differentiating through a discrete token sample is not available. they then use the score-function identity:  oxed{
