transformer gradients this is the last mathematical foundation step before we start the transformer itself. so far we learned: \frac{dl}{dw} for a scalar parameter. but a transformer does not have scalar parameters. it has matrices and tensors such as: w_q,\;w_k,\;w_v,\;w_o,\;w_1,\;w_2 and activations such as: x,q,k,v,a,o therefore we need to understand: what does it mean to differentiate a scalar loss with respect to a matrix? correction: tensor parameters contain scalar entries; scalar scale parameters can also exist. matrix calculus generalizes scalar differentiation. complete grounded review 0.6.1 first: the key idea suppose: l=f(w) where l is a scalar but w is a matrix. for example: w= \begin{bmatrix} w_{11}&w_{12}\\ w_{21}&w_{22} \end{bmatrix} then w actually contains four parameters: w_{11},w_{12},w_{21},w_{22} therefore the gradient must contain four derivatives: \boxed{ \nabla_w l= \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{11}}& \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{12}}\\ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{21}}& \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{22}} \end{bmatrix} } so: a matrix gradient has the same shape as the matrix parameter. this is the mental model we will use throughout transformers. 0.6.2 why this matters for transformers remember: q=xw_q from our earlier lessons. the book implements attention through matrix multiplication, including operations such as qk^t and then softmax normalization. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) suppose the final loss is: l we eventually need: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} } because w_q is a learnable parameter. the chain is: w_q \rightarrow q \rightarrow qk^t \rightarrow a \rightarrow o \rightarrow \text{transformer} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow l so the gradient must travel backward through matrix operations . 0.6.3 start with a scalar example suppose: y=wx and: x=3 then: y=3w therefore: \frac{\partial y}{\partial w}=3 simple. now let's increase the number of parameters. 0.6.4 vector parameter suppose: \mathbf w= \begin{bmatrix} w_1\\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} and: l=w_1^2+3w_2^2 then: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_1}=2w_1 and: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_2}=6w_2 therefore: \boxed{ \nabla_{\mathbf w}l= \begin{bmatrix} 2w_1\\ 6w_2 \end{bmatrix} } again: \boxed{ \text{gradient shape}=\text{parameter shape} } 0.6.5 matrix parameter now: w= \begin{bmatrix} w_{11}&w_{12}\\ w_{21}&w_{22} \end{bmatrix} suppose: l= w_{11}^2 + 2w_{12}^2 + 3w_{21}^2 + 4w_{22}^2 then: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{11}}=2w_{11} \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{12}}=4w_{12} \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{21}}=6w_{21} \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_{22}}=8w_{22} thus: \boxed{ \nabla_wl= \begin{bmatrix} 2w_{11}&4w_{12}\\ 6w_{21}&8w_{22} \end{bmatrix} } nothing magical happened. we simply differentiated every element . 0.6.6 the crucial idea: scalar loss, many parameters a neural network normally has: \boxed{ l\in\mathbb r } but: \theta can contain millions or billions of parameters. conceptually: \theta= \{\theta_1,\theta_2,\ldots,\theta_n\} the gradient is: \nabla_\theta l = \left[ \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta_n} \right] when those parameters are arranged into matrices/tensors, the gradients are arranged into corresponding matrices/tensors. 0.6.7 a very important notation distinction you may encounter: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} and: \nabla_wl for our purposes, both mean: the collection of partial derivatives of the scalar loss with respect to every element of w . so you can mentally read: \boxed{ \nabla_wl = \text{"how should every element of w change?"} } 0.6.8 now the important case: matrix multiplication consider: y=xw where: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} and: w\in\mathbb r^{d\times m} therefore: y\in\mathbb r^{n\times m} this is exactly the type of operation used throughout a transformer. for example: q=xw_q 0.6.9 let's make it tiny take: x= \begin{bmatrix} x_1&x_2 \end{bmatrix} and: w= \begin{bmatrix} w_1\\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} then: y=xw is: y=x_1w_1+x_2w_2 suppose: l=\frac12(y-t)^2 we want: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} 0.6.10 first derivative start with: l=\frac12(y-t)^2 therefore: \frac{\partial l}{\partial y}=y-t now: y=x_1w_1+x_2w_2 so: \frac{\partial y}{\partial w_1}=x_1 and: \frac{\partial y}{\partial w_2}=x_2 by the chain rule: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial w_1} therefore: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_1} = (y-t)x_1 similarly: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_2} = (y-t)x_2 thus: \boxed{ \nabla_wl = (y-t) \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} } or: \boxed{ \nabla_wl=x^t\frac{\partial l}{\partial y} } this is the basic pattern behind gradients of linear layers. 0.6.11 the beautiful pattern forward: \boxed{ y=xw } backward: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = x^t \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} } and: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial y}w^t } these formulas are extremely useful. don't memorize them blindly. understand the principle: the backward pass reverses the matrix multiplication while preserving compatible dimensions. 0.6.12 check the dimensions suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} and: w\in\mathbb r^{d\times m} then: y=xw has: y\in\mathbb r^{n\times m} now: \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} \in \mathbb r^{n\times m} for: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = x^t \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} we have: x^t\in\mathbb r^{d\times n} and: \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} \in\mathbb r^{n\times m} therefore: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} \in\mathbb r^{d\times m} } exactly the same shape as w . that shape check is one of the best ways to catch errors. 0.6.13 apply this directly to q=xw_q suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} w_q\in\mathbb r^{d\times d_k} then: q=xw_q and: q\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k} during backpropagation: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} = x^t \frac{\partial l}{\partial q} shapes: x^t: d\times n \frac{\partial l}{\partial q}: n\times d_k therefore: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} : d\times d_k } which matches: w_q:d\times d_k perfect. 0.6.14 but where does \partial l/\partial q come from? this is where the chain rule returns. we have: q \rightarrow qk^t \rightarrow \frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow a \rightarrow av \rightarrow l therefore: \frac{\partial l}{\partial q} is itself obtained by backpropagating through all those operations. so: \boxed{ w_q \rightarrow q \rightarrow s \rightarrow a \rightarrow o \rightarrow l } and the backward path is: \boxed{ l \rightarrow o \rightarrow a \rightarrow s \rightarrow q \rightarrow w_q } 0.6.15 matrix multiplication in attention recall: s=qk^t where: q,k\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k} therefore: k^t\in\mathbb r^{d_k\times n} and: s\in\mathbb r^{n\times n} the book explicitly constructs all pairwise attention scores using matrix multiplication qk^t . (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) each element is: \boxed{ s_{ij}=q_i^tk_j } so: row i asks: how compatible is query q_i with every key? 0.6.16 why qk^t produces n\times n this is worth understanding deeply. suppose: n=4 tokens and: d_k=3 then: q= 4\times3 and: k= 4\times3 therefore: k^t= 3\times4 thus: qk^t: (4\times3)(3\times4) = 4\times4 the resulting matrix contains: 4\times4=16 pairwise query-key scores. 0.6.17 now add scaling attention uses: s= \frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}} then: a=\operatorname{softmax}(s) then: o=av the book explains this progression from dot-product scores to scaled softmax attention weights and then weighted value aggregation. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.6.18 what happens during backward propagation? suppose: l=l(o) we first obtain: \frac{\partial l}{\partial o} then propagate through: o=av giving gradients for: a and: v then propagate through: a=\operatorname{softmax}(s) giving: \frac{\partial l}{\partial s} then: s=\frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}} gives gradients for: q and: k finally: q=xw_q gives: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} this is the exact computational chain we needed matrix calculus to understand. 0.6.19 a complete gradient dependency map forward ↓ x ──→ wq ──→ q ─────────────┐ │ x ──→ wk ──→ k ──→ kᵀ ─────┤ ↓ qkᵀ ↓ / √dₖ ↓ softmax ↓ a │ x ──→ wv ──→ v ─────────────┤ ↓ av ↓ transformer... ↓ loss backward ↑ ∂l/∂loss ↑ ... ↑ ∂l/∂o ↙ ↘ ∂l/∂a ∂l/∂v ↑ ↑ softmax wv ↑ ∂l/∂s ↙ ↘ ∂l/∂q ∂l/∂k ↑ ↑ wq wk this is what "the transformer learns" mathematically means. 0.6.20 numerical example: gradient of a matrix let's make a tiny linear layer: x= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4 \end{bmatrix} and: w= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} then: y=xw=x suppose the target is: t= \begin{bmatrix} 2&1\\ 4&3 \end{bmatrix} and define: l=\frac12\sum_{ij}(y_{ij}-t_{ij})^2 then: y-t= \begin{bmatrix} -1&1\\ -1&1 \end{bmatrix} therefore: \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} = \begin{bmatrix} -1&1\\ -1&1 \end{bmatrix} now: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = x^t \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} we have: x^t= \begin{bmatrix} 1&3\\ 2&4 \end{bmatrix} therefore: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = \begin{bmatrix} 1&3\\ 2&4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1&1\\ -1&1 \end{bmatrix} giving: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = \begin{bmatrix} -4&4\\ -6&6 \end{bmatrix} } notice the shape: 2\times2 same as w . 0.6.21 why does the gradient depend on the input? look at: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w} = x^t\frac{\partial l}{\partial y} } this tells us something important. a weight doesn't learn in isolation. its update depends on: the input that passed through it how wrong the output was so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{weight gradient} = \text{input} \times \text{error signal} } this is a very useful intuition for neural networks. 0.6.22 tensor calculus: why a transformer makes this bigger in a real transformer, we don't just have: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} we usually have batches: \boxed{ x\in\mathbb r^{b\times n\times d} } where: b = batch size n = sequence length d = hidden dimension then attention may have: q,k,v \in \mathbb r^{b\times h\times n\times d_k} where: h = number of heads d_k = dimension per head raschka's implementation similarly uses batched tensor shapes involving batch, heads, tokens, and head dimension. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.6.23 does the mathematics change? no. the fundamental principle is still: \boxed{ \text{differentiate every element and propagate the chain rule} } the only difference is that there are many dimensions and repeated operations. pytorch's automatic differentiation handles this bookkeeping. 0.6.24 why automatic differentiation is so important imagine manually calculating: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} for a 70-billion-parameter model. obviously impossible by hand. instead, the framework constructs a computation graph and automatically applies the chain rule. conceptually: forward operations ↓ computation graph ↓ loss ↓ automatic differentiation ↓ gradients for tensors ↓ optimizer ↓ updated parameters this is why understanding the mathematics is important even though we don't manually derive every gradient in code. 0.6.25 jacobian — one more concept we need one more piece of vocabulary. suppose: \mathbf y=f(\mathbf x) where both are vectors: \mathbf x\in\mathbb r^n and: \mathbf y\in\mathbb r^m then the jacobian is: \boxed{ j= \frac{\partial\mathbf y}{\partial\mathbf x} } containing all derivatives: j_{ij} = \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j} so: j\in\mathbb r^{m\times n} 0.6.26 example of a jacobian let: y_1=x_1^2+x_2 y_2=x_1x_2 then: \frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_1}=2x_1 \frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_2}=1 \frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_1}=x_2 \frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_2}=x_1 therefore: \boxed{ j= \begin{bmatrix} 2x_1&1\\ x_2&x_1 \end{bmatrix} } you do not need to manually calculate jacobians throughout our transformer course. but you need to understand: a jacobian describes how a vector of outputs changes with respect to a vector of inputs. 0.6.27 why don't we usually see giant jacobian matrices in pytorch? because explicitly constructing them would often be extremely inefficient. for neural networks we usually care about: \frac{\partial l}{\partial\theta} where: l is a scalar. automatic differentiation can compute the needed vector-jacobian products efficiently without materializing every possible derivative. this is one reason reverse-mode autodiff is so useful for neural-network training. 0.6.28 scalar → vector → matrix → tensor you should now have this hierarchy: scalar ↓ derivative ↓ vector ↓ gradient ↓ matrix ↓ matrix gradient / jacobian ↓ tensor ↓ automatic differentiation the underlying idea never changes: \boxed{ \text{how does the loss change when this quantity changes?} } 0.6.29 the transformer version now we can finally understand the mathematical meaning of: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} } it means: for every element of w_q , how much would the final loss change if that element were changed slightly, while accounting for all downstream computations? and similarly: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_k} means: how does every element of the key projection affect the final loss? and: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_v} means: how does every element of the value projection affect the final loss? 0.6.30 why the gradient has the same shape as the parameter suppose: w_q\in\mathbb r^{768\times64} then there are: 768\times64=49,152 individual parameters. therefore: \boxed{ \nabla_{w_q}l\in\mathbb r^{768\times64} } there is one gradient value corresponding to every parameter. then the optimizer performs: w_q \leftarrow w_q-\eta\nabla_{w_q}l element by element. 0.6.31 one complete numerical mini-example suppose: w_q= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4 \end{bmatrix} and suppose backpropagation produces: \nabla_{w_q}l= 0.01&0.03 \end{bmatrix} giving: \boxed{ w_q^{new} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.98&2.05\\ 2.99&3.97 \end{bmatrix} } that is literally a tiny piece of what happens during transformer training. 0.6.32 the entire transformer training mathematics now we can finally connect everything . forward input: x projection: q=xw_q k=xw_k v=xw_v attention scores: s=\frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}} causal masking: s'=s+m attention distribution: a=\operatorname{softmax}(s') attention output: o=av transformer layers: o \rightarrow \text{residual/normalization/ffn/etc.} output: z probability: p=\operatorname{softmax}(z) loss: \nabla_{w_q}l \nabla_{w_k}l \nabla_{w_v}l and gradients for every other learnable parameter. update \boxed{ \theta \leftarrow \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l } this is the complete mathematical skeleton of independent depth scoring pending. step 1.1 — what exactly is a language model? plan node: i1 · chat order #8 we have finished the mathematical foundation. now we move from mathematics → the actual objective of an llm . this is the most important conceptual transition in the whole course because almost everything that comes later—transformer attention, decoding, fine-tuning, rl, grpo, reasoning models—builds on this basic objective. your transformer slides explicitly define the training goal as predicting the probability of the next token given all previous tokens . raschka's book gives the same foundation from the llm perspective: an llm is trained on large amounts of text, with parameters optimized to predict the next word/token and thereby learn context, structure, and relationships in language. 1.1.1 first: what is a language model? imagine that i give you: the cat is sitting on the what should come next? possible tokens might be: \{\text{mat},\text{floor},\text{chair},\text{roof},...\} a language model does not simply say: "the answer is mat." instead, its fundamental output is a probability distribution : p(x_{t+1}\mid x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_t) for example: next token probability mat 0.55 floor 0.20 chair 0.10 roof 0.01 ... ... so: a language model is fundamentally a function that maps previous tokens to a probability distribution over possible next tokens. that is the central idea. 1.1.2 why "language model" instead of "next-token predictor"? because predicting the next token lets us model the probability of an entire sequence . suppose: x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4 is i love machine learning the model wants to assign a probability to the whole sequence: p(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4) but directly learning a probability for every possible complete sentence would be absurdly difficult. there are an enormous number of possible sequences. so we use the chain rule of probability . 1.1.3 the chain rule the chain rule says: p(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_t) = \prod_{t=1}^{t}p(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}) we usually write: p(x_{1:t}) = \prod_{t=1}^{t} p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) where x_{<t} = (x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}) means: all tokens before position t . your transformer slides explicitly use this autoregressive factorization. 1.1.4 let's understand this equation slowly take: i love deep learning let x_1=\text{i} x_2=\text{love} x_3=\text{deep} x_4=\text{learning} then: p(\text{i, love, deep, learning}) becomes p(\text{i}) \cdot p(\text{love}\mid\text{i}) \cdot p(\text{deep}\mid\text{i,love}) \cdot p(\text{learning}\mid\text{i,love,deep}) this is incredibly important. the model doesn't need to learn: "what is the probability of this entire sentence?" instead, it learns a sequence of next-token predictions. that is what makes language modeling tractable. 1.1.5 why is this called "autoregressive"? because every prediction depends on what came before. at position t : p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) the model uses the previous tokens to predict the current token. so information flows: x_1 \rightarrow x_2 \rightarrow x_3 \rightarrow x_4 \rightarrow \cdots conceptually: "i" ↓ "i love" ↓ "i love deep" ↓ "i love deep learning" at generation time, the newly generated token becomes part of the context for the next prediction. that is why it is called autoregressive : the model uses its own previous outputs as part of the input for future outputs. 1.1.6 the crucial distinction: training vs generation this is one of the things you must understand before going further. during training suppose the training text is: i love deep learning we already know the complete sequence. so we can create: input: i love deep target: love deep learning the model performs many next-token predictions simultaneously. conceptually: i → predict love i love → predict deep i love deep → predict learning the future tokens are known to us because this is training data. but the model is prevented from looking at them when computing the prediction . that is where causal masking will become essential in step 1.8. the slides explicitly connect causal masking with the next-token training objective. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) 1.1.7 during generation now imagine that the user gives: i love the model predicts: p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2) suppose it chooses: deep now the input becomes: i love deep then it predicts: p(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3) suppose it chooses: learning now: i love deep learning this continues one token at a time. raschka's generation procedure describes exactly this loop: encode the prompt, run the model, select a next token, append it to the sequence, and repeat. 1.1.8 the most important picture so far think of an llm as this pipeline: text ↓ tokens ↓ token ids ↓ embeddings ↓ transformer ↓ logits ↓ softmax ↓ next-token probabilities the transformer is not itself the probability distribution . it produces representations and ultimately logits . then softmax converts those logits into probabilities. the slides explicitly separate: logits, softmax, probability assigned to the actual token, sequence loss. 1.1.9 what are logits? suppose the vocabulary contains only five tokens: v=\{\text{cat},\text{dog},\text{car},\text{tree},\text{book}\} the model might produce: z= \begin{bmatrix} 2.5\\ 1.2\\ 0.1\\ -1.0\\ 0.4 \end{bmatrix} these are logits . they are raw scores. they are not probabilities . notice: they can be negative, they do not sum to 1, they do not need to lie between 0 and 1. 1.1.10 why do we need softmax? we want: p(\text{cat}),p(\text{dog}),\ldots such that: p_i\geq0 and \sum_i p_i=1 so we apply: \operatorname{softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}} {\sum_j e^{z_j}} therefore: z \rightarrow \operatorname{softmax}(z) \rightarrow p where p is a probability distribution. your slide deck explicitly describes softmax as turning the logits into a normalized distribution over the vocabulary. 1.1.11 tiny numerical example suppose: z=[2,1,0] compute exponentials: e^2\approx7.389 e^1\approx2.718 e^0=1 sum: 7.389+2.718+1=11.107 therefore: p_1=\frac{7.389}{11.107}\approx0.665 p_2=\frac{2.718}{11.107}\approx0.245 p_3=\frac{1}{11.107}\approx0.090 so: p\approx[0.665,0.245,0.090] and: 0.665+0.245+0.090\approx1 now we have an actual distribution. 1.1.12 from probability to loss suppose the correct next token is token 1. the model assigned: p(x_t\mid x_{<t})=0.665 how should we measure whether this was good? we use negative log-likelihood: l_t=-\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) thus: l_t=-\log(0.665) l_t\approx0.408 smaller is better. imagine two models model a: p(\text{correct token})=0.9 then: -\log(0.9)\approx0.105 model b: p(\text{correct token})=0.1 then: -\log(0.1)\approx2.303 so: correct probability ↑ → loss ↓ correct probability ↓ → loss ↑ this is exactly why the loss teaches the model to increase the probability of the correct token. 1.1.13 sequence loss for a sequence of t tokens: l = -\frac{1}{t} \sum_{t=1}^{t} \log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) this is the average negative log-likelihood across the sequence. your transformer slide gives this sequence-level objective directly. this equation connects everything we have learned: \boxed{ \text{next-token probability} \rightarrow \text{log probability} \rightarrow \text{negative log likelihood} \rightarrow \text{loss} } 1.1.14 why does log appear? recall: p(x_{1:t}) = \prod_{t=1}^{t}p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) suppose: p_1=0.8,\quad p_2=0.7,\quad p_3=0.9 then: p(x_{1:3}) = 0.8\times0.7\times0.9 = 0.504 for long sequences, multiplying hundreds or thousands of numbers below 1 can become numerically tiny. use logarithms: \log p(x_{1:t}) = \sum_{t=1}^{t} \log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) so: \boxed{ \log\left(\prod_t p_t\right) = \sum_t\log p_t } this is one of the reasons log-probabilities are so important later in: decoding, sequence scoring, knowledge distillation, rl, grpo, reasoning models. 1.1.15 cross-entropy connection earlier we learned: h(p,q) = -\sum_i p_i\log q_i for a one-hot target, suppose the correct token is k . then: p_k=1 and all other entries are zero. so: h(p,q) = -\log q_k that is exactly the next-token loss: l_t=-\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) therefore: next-token language-model training is a cross-entropy classification problem applied at every token position. this is a major conceptual connection. the model is effectively performing: at every position: "which of the |v| vocabulary tokens is correct next?" so if: |v|=50,257 the model performs a 50,257-way classification at every position. raschka's gpt implementation has a final linear layer whose output dimension equals the vocabulary size, producing logits for every vocabulary token. 1.1.16 what exactly does the transformer predict? suppose: b=2 batch size, t=5 sequence length, d=768 hidden dimension, and |v|=50,257 vocabulary size. after embeddings: x\in\mathbb r^{2\times5\times768} after the transformer: h\in\mathbb r^{2\times5\times768} then the output projection maps: 768\rightarrow50,257 giving: z\in\mathbb r^{2\times5\times50,257} this means: batch 1 ├── position 1 → 50,257 logits ├── position 2 → 50,257 logits ├── position 3 → 50,257 logits ├── position 4 → 50,257 logits └── position 5 → 50,257 logits batch 2 ├── position 1 → 50,257 logits ... raschka's gpt implementation shows the same architectural progression: token embeddings + positional embeddings → transformer blocks → final normalization → vocabulary projection → logits. 1.1.17 why are there logits at every position? this is a subtle but very important point. suppose our input is: i love deep learning we can construct: input target i love i love deep i love deep learning therefore, every position produces a prediction. in matrix form: z= \begin{bmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ z_3\\ z_4 \end{bmatrix} where each: z_t\in\mathbb r^{|v|} so the model simultaneously produces: p(x_2|x_1) p(x_3|x_1,x_2) p(x_4|x_1,x_2,x_3) and so on. this is why training can be highly parallelized across positions. 1.1.18 the input/target shift this is worth memorizing. suppose token ids are: [10, 25, 17, 42, 91] we create: input [10, 25, 17, 42] target [25, 17, 42, 91] notice: \text{target}_t=\text{input}_{t+1} so: input: 10 25 17 42 ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ target: 25 17 42 91 the model learns: 10 → 25 10,25 → 17 10,25,17 → 42 10,25,17,42 → 91 this is commonly called teacher forcing in autoregressive training. why? because during training the correct previous tokens come directly from the training sequence rather than from the model's own sampled outputs. 1.1.19 why doesn't training have to generate one token at a time? this often confuses people. generation: token 1 ↓ token 2 ↓ token 3 ↓ token 4 must be sequential because token 3 is unknown until token 2 has been generated. training is different. the whole sequence is already known: i love deep learning therefore we can feed the entire sequence into the transformer. the causal mask ensures: position 1 sees: 1 position 2 sees: 1,2 position 3 sees: 1,2,3 position 4 sees: 1,2,3,4 but never: position 2 → position 3,4 position 3 → position 4 that allows parallel computation while preserving the autoregressive objective. the attention handbook in your source set explains this distinction explicitly: causal masking permits parallel training across positions, while generation remains sequential because future generated tokens do not yet exist. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) we will derive exactly how this happens when we reach step 1.8 — causal mask . 1.1.20 what does the model actually learn? at the beginning, the model is essentially terrible. for example: "the capital of france is ___" paris → 0.003 london → 0.002 berlin → 0.002 paris → ... during training, the loss generates gradients. earlier we learned: \theta \leftarrow \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta l so the complete learning loop is: text ↓ tokens ↓ transformer ↓ logits ↓ softmax ↓ probability of correct token ↓ loss ↓ backpropagation ↓ gradients ↓ update weights ↓ repeat billions of times this connects our step 0.6 tensor calculus directly to language-model training. 1.1.21 important: the model does not store a dictionary of sentences a beginner often imagines: "the model sees 'the capital of france is paris' many times and memorizes the sentence." that is not the fundamental mechanism. the model parameters are adjusted so that, across massive numbers of contexts, the network learns statistical patterns that help predict tokens. for example: "the capital of france is" ↓ representation ↓ high score for "paris" but those predictions arise through the learned neural-network parameters and contextual computation. raschka emphasizes that the model's parameters are optimized during training to perform next-word prediction and that this objective causes the model to learn context, structure, and relationships in language. 1.1.22 the vocabulary dimension suppose: |v|=10,000 then at every position the model must output: 10,000 scores. so: z_t\in\mathbb r^{10,000} after softmax: p_t\in\mathbb r^{10,000} and: \sum_{i=1}^{10,000}p_{t,i}=1 the correct token corresponds to one position in this vector. for example: token id probability 0 0.0001 1 0.0021 2 0.0003 ... 713 0.7612 ← correct token ... 9999 0.0000 the loss looks only at the probability assigned to token 713 for this particular training example: l=-\log(0.7612) 1.1.23 training tensor shapes — memorize this for a decoder-only language model: token ids \boxed{[b,t]} where: b = batch size t = sequence length embeddings \boxed{[b,t,d]} where: d = model/embedding dimension transformer output \boxed{[b,t,d]} logits \boxed{[b,t,|v|]} target ids \boxed{[b,t]} this shape progression is one of the most important pieces of practical understanding: [b, t] ↓ embedding [b, t, d] ↓ transformer [b, t, d] ↓ output projection [b, t, v] raschka's concrete gpt implementation follows this exact conceptual structure, with the final linear layer projecting each hidden representation into vocabulary-sized logits. 1.1.24 tiny pytorch example here is the core of next-token training without implementing the transformer yet: import torch import torch.nn.functional as f # -------------------------------------------------- # example logits # shape: [batch=1, sequence=4, vocab=5] # -------------------------------------------------- logits = torch.tensor([ [ [2.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.0, -1.0], # position 1 [0.2, 1.8, 0.4, 0.1, -0.5], # position 2 [0.1, 0.2, 2.5, 0.3, -0.2], # position 3 [0.0, 0.4, 0.2, 2.2, -0.1], # position 4 ] ], dtype=torch.float32) # -------------------------------------------------- # correct next-token ids # one target for each position # shape: [1, 4] # -------------------------------------------------- targets = torch.tensor([ [0, 1, 2, 3] ]) # -------------------------------------------------- # cross entropy expects: # logits -> [n, c] # targets -> [n] # -------------------------------------------------- loss = f.cross_entropy( logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.reshape(-1) ) print("loss:", loss.item()) the important transformation is: logits: [b, t, v] reshape: [b*t, v] targets: [b, t] reshape: [b*t] so pytorch effectively sees this as: "b*t classification problems, each having v possible classes" that is exactly what next-token training is. 1.1.25 now connect this to the transformer we can now understand the entire architecture before learning its internal pieces: tokens ↓ token embedding ↓ position information ↓ transformer block ├── attention └── mlp ↓ transformer block ↓ ... ↓ final hidden states ↓ linear output head ↓ logits ↓ softmax ↓ next-token distribution ↓ cross-entropy / nll ↓ backpropagation ↓ parameter update your transformer slides summarize the decoder-only architecture as blocks where attention moves information between positions, mlps process information within a position, and causal masking prevents reading the future. and the gpt implementation in your book follows the same high-level flow from token embeddings and positional embeddings through stacked transformer blocks to vocabulary logits. 1.1.26 training vs generation — final comparison training generation full target sequence is known future tokens are unknown uses shifted input/target uses current generated prefix many positions processed in parallel new tokens generated sequentially loss is computed tokens are selected/sampled backpropagation occurs usually no gradient computation goal: improve parameters goal: produce text during generation, raschka's implementation takes the logits from the last position , turns them into probabilities, chooses the next token, appends it, and repeats. this distinction will become extremely important when we study: decoding, kv caching, inference-time scaling, reasoning models. 1.1.27 one very important correction in terminology you will see both: next-word prediction and next-token prediction. for modern llms, next-token prediction is the more precise term. a token may be: word subword punctuation number part of a word special token for example, tokenization could conceptually produce: "transformers are powerful" ↓ ["transform", "ers", " are", " powerful"] the exact tokenizer determines the actual token boundaries. so the mathematical objective is: \boxed{ p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } where x_t is a token , not necessarily an entire word. 1.1.28 the big mental model at this point you should be able to explain an llm like this: an autoregressive language model receives a sequence of tokens, transforms them into contextual representations using a decoder-only transformer, produces vocabulary-sized logits for each position, converts those logits to a probability distribution over the next token, and is trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood/cross-entropy of the correct next token. that single sentence contains almost the entire mathematical backbone of the course. 1.1.29 what we have built from the previous steps notice how everything connects: step 0.1 vectors and matrices: xw step 0.5 expectation and probability: p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) step 0.6 gradients: \nabla_\theta l step 1.1 language modeling: p(x_{1:t}) = \prod_tp(x_t\mid x_{<t}) and l = -\frac1t \sum_t \log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) so the mathematical chain is now: \boxed{ \text{linear algebra} \rightarrow \text{probability} input is: i love transformers a neural network performs mathematical operations such as: xw qk^t \operatorname{softmax}(z) these require numerical representations. but the string "i" "love" "transformers" is categorical data. there is no meaningful operation such as: \text{"love"}\times 2.7 so we need to convert the language into numbers. raschka explicitly introduces embeddings for this reason: raw text is categorical, whereas neural networks need continuous-valued numerical representations. 1.2.2 stage 1 — tokenization the first question is: how should we split text into units? these units are called tokens . for example: "the cat is sleeping." could conceptually become: ["the", "cat", "is", "sleeping", "."] now the text is no longer one large string. it is a sequence: x_1=\text{"the"} x_2=\text{"cat"} x_3=\text{"is"} x_4=\text{"sleeping"} x_5=\text{"."} raschka first demonstrates a simple tokenizer that separates words and punctuation. 1.2.3 token does not necessarily mean word this distinction is extremely important. a token can be: a complete word, part of a word, punctuation, whitespace-related representation, a special symbol. for example, a modern tokenizer might represent: "unbelievable" as something conceptually like: ["un", "believ", "able"] the exact result depends on the tokenizer. therefore, in all of our mathematics: x_t means a token , not necessarily a whole word. this is why modern llm literature almost always says: next-token prediction rather than strictly next-word prediction. 1.2.4 why not use one token for every possible word? suppose english contains millions of possible word forms. then a word-level vocabulary would become enormous. worse, consider: play played playing playful player players many of these share useful structure. and new words can appear. for example: quantization-aware or a person's unusual name. a tokenizer that can break unknown words into reusable smaller pieces is more flexible. this motivates subword tokenization , including bpe. raschka's book first builds intuition using a simple word/punctuation tokenizer and then transitions to byte-pair encoding. 1.2.5 stage 2 — token ids the transformer still does not want strings. so we create a vocabulary: v=\{v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_{|v|-1}\} and assign each token a unique integer. for example: token id "i" 17 "love" 42 "transformers" 815 "." 9 then: "i love transformers ." becomes: [17, 42, 815, 9] these are token ids . raschka's vocabulary construction explicitly maps each unique token to a unique integer id. 1.2.6 why integer ids? notice something subtle. we don't claim: 42 > 17 means "love" is somehow mathematically greater than "i" . the integer is simply an index . think: 17 → row 17 42 → row 42 815 → row 815 the numerical value itself has no semantic meaning. this is why it would be wrong to simply feed token ids directly into the transformer as though: i = 17 love = 42 transformers = 815 were meaningful continuous features. the next stage fixes this. 1.2.7 stage 3 — the embedding matrix we introduce a learnable matrix: \boxed{ w_e\in\mathbb r^{|v|\times d} } where: |v| = vocabulary size d = embedding dimension suppose: |v|=6 and d=3 then: w_e\in\mathbb r^{6\times3} for example: w_e= \begin{bmatrix} 0.3&-0.2&0.5\\ 0.8&0.1&-0.4\\ -0.7&0.6&0.2\\ 0.4&0.9&-0.1\\ -0.5&0.2&0.8\\ 0.1&-0.8&0.3 \end{bmatrix} each row corresponds to one token. so: w_e[0] is the vector for token id 0. and: w_e[3] is the vector for token id 3. 1.2.8 embedding = lookup suppose the token sequence is: [2,3,5,1] then the embedding operation retrieves: w_e[2],w_e[3],w_e[5],w_e[1] giving: x= \begin{bmatrix} w_e[2]\\ w_e[3]\\ w_e[5]\\ w_e[1] \end{bmatrix} therefore: x\in\mathbb r^{4\times3} the key idea is: \boxed{ \text{token id} \rightarrow \text{row lookup in }w_e } raschka demonstrates this directly with a pytorch embedding layer: each token id retrieves the corresponding row of the embedding weight matrix. 1.2.9 let's do the exact numerical example suppose: w_e= \begin{bmatrix} 0.3374&-0.1778&-0.1690\\ 0.9178&1.5810&1.3010\\ 1.2753&-0.2010&-0.1606\\ -0.4015&0.9666&-1.1481\\ -1.1589&0.3255&-0.6315\\ -2.8400&-0.7849&-1.4096 \end{bmatrix} this is essentially the small example used in raschka's book. suppose: \text{input ids}=[2,3,5,1] then: id 2 w_e[2] = [1.2753,-0.2010,-0.1606] id 3 w_e[3] = [-0.4015,0.9666,-1.1481] id 5 w_e[5] = [-2.8400,-0.7849,-1.4096] id 1 w_e[1] = [0.9178,1.5810,1.3010] so: x= \begin{bmatrix} 1.2753&-0.2010&-0.1606\\ -0.4015&0.9666&-1.1481\\ -2.8400&-0.7849&-1.4096\\ 0.9178&1.5810&1.3010 \end{bmatrix} and: \boxed{x\in\mathbb r^{4\times3}} the book gives this exact lookup behavior and resulting 4\times3 matrix example. 1.2.10 why are these vectors random initially? this is extremely important. at the beginning, the embedding matrix is generally initialized from small random values. so initially, there is no reason for: cat to have a useful relationship with: dog the model has to learn those representations. raschka explicitly states that the embedding weights are initialized and later optimized as part of llm training. so: w_e^{(0)} is the initial embedding matrix. after training: w_e^{(*)} is the learned embedding matrix. 1.2.11 the embeddings are trainable parameters this connects directly to our step 0.6 on gradients. suppose: w_e\in\mathbb r^{|v|\times d} the loss is: l backpropagation calculates: \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_e} then gradient descent updates it: w_e \leftarrow w_e-\eta\frac{\partial l}{\partial w_e} so the embedding matrix is not a fixed dictionary. it is a learned part of the neural network . the transformer slides also emphasize that w_e is learned end-to-end using the same next-token loss used for the rest of the model. 1.2.12 one-hot encoding connection there is another mathematically beautiful way to understand embedding lookup. suppose the vocabulary contains 5 tokens and token id is 2. one-hot encoding gives: e_2= [0,0,1,0,0] now multiply: e_2w_e where: e_2\in\mathbb r^{1\times5} and w_e\in\mathbb r^{5\times d} then: e_2w_e=w_e[2] because the one-hot vector selects exactly one row. therefore: \boxed{ \text{embedding lookup} \equiv \text{one-hot vector}\times w_e } conceptually. but explicitly creating a giant one-hot vector is wasteful. so frameworks use an efficient lookup operation. raschka explains this equivalence directly. 1.2.13 why embeddings are better than raw ids suppose: cat = 100 dog = 101 car = 102 the integer ids suggest: 101-100=1 but this difference has no semantic interpretation. after embedding: e(\text{cat})=[0.7,0.2,-0.1,\ldots] e(\text{dog})=[0.65,0.25,-0.05,\ldots] e(\text{car})=[-0.4,0.8,0.9,\ldots] now the geometry of the vectors can encode useful relationships. for example: \cos(e(\text{cat}),e(\text{dog})) could be relatively high. this idea connects directly to our earlier discussion of vectors and dot products. 1.2.14 but there is an important modern-lm nuance a token embedding by itself is not necessarily contextual . consider: bank in: i deposited money in the bank. and: we sat beside the river bank. the initial embedding lookup for "bank" is the same token vector. but after passing through the transformer, the representations can differ because the surrounding context is different. so think: \boxed{ \text{token embedding} = \text{initial representation} } while: \boxed{ \text{transformer hidden state} = \text{contextual representation} } this distinction becomes crucial when we reach self-attention. raschka distinguishes the learned input embeddings from contextualized representations produced later by the transformer. 1.2.15 where bpe enters now we return to the tokenization question. a simple word tokenizer has a problem with rare or unseen words. suppose our vocabulary has: play playing played but encounters: playfulness a word-level tokenizer may not know that whole word. bpe instead works with smaller reusable units. conceptually: playfulness ↓ play + ful + ness the exact segmentation is determined by the learned tokenizer vocabulary/merges. raschka's book explains that gpt-family models use bpe-style tokenization and presents bpe after the simpler tokenizer. 1.2.16 the main idea behind bpe you don't need to memorize the implementation yet. understand the intuition first. start with smaller pieces. suppose the data contains: low lower lowest the tokenizer notices frequent pieces such as: l o w e r s t and repeatedly merges frequent neighboring pieces. for example, conceptually: l+o\rightarrow lo lo+w\rightarrow low low+e\rightarrow lowe and so on. the final tokenizer vocabulary contains reusable subword units. this gives a compromise: \boxed{ \text{character-level flexibility} \quad+\quad \text{word-level efficiency} } raschka notes that gpt-2 and gpt-3 and the original chatgpt model used bpe tokenization, and uses tiktoken to demonstrate it. 1.2.17 why subwords are so useful imagine we encounter: unbelievability a word-level tokenizer may treat it as one unknown item. a subword tokenizer can potentially decompose it into reusable components. that means the model can represent previously unseen combinations using pieces it has already encountered. this is particularly important for: rare words, names, technical terminology, morphology, new combinations. 1.2.18 special tokens the tokenizer can also contain tokens whose purpose is structural rather than linguistic. the book discusses: bos beginning of sequence. [\text{bos},x_1,x_2,\ldots] eos end of sequence. [x_1,x_2,\ldots,\text{eos}] pad used to make sequences in a batch the same length. for example: sequence a: [i, like, ai] sequence b: [i, really, like, ai] after padding: [i, like, ai, pad] [i, really, like, ai] the book also discusses <|endoftext|> and how special-token handling depends on the tokenizer/model. the important lesson is: not every token represents ordinary natural-language content. some tokens help the model structure sequences. 1.2.19 complete representation pipeline let's put everything together. take: "i love ai." stage 1 — raw text \text{"i love ai."} stage 2 — tokenization conceptually: [\text{"i"},\text{"love"},\text{"ai"},\text{"."}] stage 3 — token ids suppose: [17,42,815,9] stage 4 — embedding lookup x= \begin{bmatrix} w_e[17]\\ w_e[42]\\ w_e[815]\\ w_e[9] \end{bmatrix} therefore: x\in\mathbb r^{4\times d} stage 5 now this matrix enters the transformer. but there's a problem. the transformer currently sees: vector vector vector vector how does it know which vector is first, second, third, fourth? this brings us to the next concept: \boxed{\text{position}} 1.2.20 batch shapes suppose: b=2 t=5 d=768 then: token ids \boxed{[2,5]} embeddings \boxed{[2,5,768]} interpretation: 2 sequences × 5 tokens each × 768 numbers per token for example: token ids [b,t] 5 tokens ┌─────────────┐ b=2│ 17 42 81 9 5│ │ 23 11 72 4 8│ └─────────────┘ after embedding: [b,t,d] 2 × 5 × 768 each integer has been replaced by a 768-dimensional vector. 1.2.21 executable pytorch example let's reproduce the central idea ourselves. import torch import torch.nn as nn # --------------------------------------------------------- # configuration # --------------------------------------------------------- vocab_size = 6 embedding_dim = 3 # --------------------------------------------------------- # input token ids # four tokens # --------------------------------------------------------- input_ids = torch.tensor([2, 3, 5, 1]) # --------------------------------------------------------- # create learnable embedding table # shape = [vocab_size, embedding_dim] # [6, 3] # --------------------------------------------------------- embedding = nn.embedding( num_embeddings=vocab_size, embedding_dim=embedding_dim ) print("embedding matrix:") print(embedding.weight) print("\nembedding matrix shape:") print(embedding.weight.shape) # --------------------------------------------------------- # lookup embeddings # --------------------------------------------------------- output = embedding(input_ids) print("\ninput ids:") print(input_ids) print("\noutput embeddings:") print(output) print("\noutput shape:") print(output.shape) expected shape: embedding matrix: [6, 3] input ids: [4] output: [4, 3] so: [4] \rightarrow [4,3] 1.2.22 batch example now: import torch import torch.nn as nn vocab_size = 10000 embedding_dim = 768 # two sequences, five tokens each input_ids = torch.tensor([ [10, 25, 17, 42, 91], [13, 81, 5, 72, 6] ]) embedding = nn.embedding( num_embeddings=vocab_size, embedding_dim=embedding_dim ) x = embedding(input_ids) print("input shape :", input_ids.shape) print("output shape:", x.shape) the shapes are: input: [2, 5] embedding: [10000, 768] output: [2, 5, 768] mathematically: \boxed{ [b,t] \rightarrow [b,t,d] } this is the tensor that will enter the transformer. 1.2.23 why is the embedding matrix so large? this is a useful parameter-count connection. if: |v|=50,000 and: d=4,096 then: \text{parameters in }w_e = 50,000\times4,096 =204,800,000 so the embedding table alone contains about: \boxed{205\text{ million parameters}} this is why vocabulary size and hidden dimension matter substantially in model size. 1.2.24 a crucial distinction: token ids vs embeddings vs hidden states do not mix these three. token id 17 a discrete integer index. token embedding [0.32,-0.81,0.14,\ldots] a learned vector from w_e . contextual hidden state h_t = [0.71,0.12,-0.35,\ldots] after transformer processing. so: id ↓ lookup embedding ↓ transformer contextual hidden state this distinction will be essential for understanding q/k/v. 1.2.25 where the learning happens the complete forward path is now: \text{text} \rightarrow \text{token ids} \rightarrow w_e \rightarrow x \rightarrow \text{transformer} \rightarrow h \rightarrow z \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow p \rightarrow l during backpropagation: l \rightarrow z \rightarrow h \rightarrow x \rightarrow w_e so the embedding table itself receives gradients. that means the model learns: "what numerical representation should this token have so that, together with the rest of the network, next-token prediction improves?" that is much deeper than simply assigning fixed meanings to words. 1.2.26 source mapping for this step, the primary grounding is: transformer slides: explicitly show tokens being converted into embeddings through w_e\in\mathbb r^{|v|\times d} and describe w_e as learned end-to-end through the next-token objective. raschka, chapter 2: provides the detailed progression: \text{raw text} \rightarrow \text{tokens} \rightarrow \text{token ids} \rightarrow \text{special tokens} \rightarrow \text{bpe} \rightarrow \text{embedding vectors} and gives executable python/pytorch examples for these stages. 1.2.27 the mental model you should now have memorize this pipeline conceptually, not just mechanically: tokenization raw text ──────────────────────────→ tokens │ ▼ token ids │ ▼ embedding lookup │ ▼ vectors in r^d │ ▼ transformer or mathematically: \boxed{ x_t \in\{0,\ldots,|v|-1\} } then: \boxed{ e_t=w_e[x_t] } then for a sequence: \boxed{ x\in\mathbb r^{t\times d} } and for a batch: \boxed{ x\in\mathbb r^{b\times t\times d} } 1.2.28 one more important connection look back at step 0.1. we learned: x\in\mathbb r^{t\times d} and: q=xw_q now we know where x actually comes from. it is not magical . it comes from: \boxed{ \text{text} \rightarrow \text{token ids} \rightarrow \boxed{w_e\text{ lookup}} \rightarrow x } therefore the beginning of the transformer computation is: x \rightarrow q=xw_q x \rightarrow k=xw_k x \rightarrow v=xw_v and now we are ready to answer the understanding_attention_handbook_01 ; transformers-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 1.3 — position: how does a transformer know word order? plan node: i1 · chat order #10 we now have: \text{text} \rightarrow \text{tokens} \rightarrow \text{token ids} \rightarrow \text{token embeddings} at this point, however, there is a fundamental problem: the token embedding tells us what the token is, but not where it occurs. this is exactly the issue identified in the transformer slides: self-attention by itself does not tell the model that token 3 comes after token 2, so position information must be injected. (source: transformers-slides) raschka's chapter 2.8 makes the same point: the same token id always receives the same embedding regardless of where it occurs in the sequence. 1.3.1 the problem suppose we have: \text{a dog bites a man} and: \text{a man bites a dog} the tokens are the same: a dog bites a man versus a man bites a dog but the order is different. and order changes the meaning. so the model needs two kinds of information: \boxed{\text{what token is this?}} and \boxed{\text{where is this token?}} the token embedding answers the first. positional information answers the second. 1.3.2 why token embeddings alone are not enough suppose: e(\text{dog})= [0.2,0.7,-0.1,\ldots] whenever token "dog" appears, the lookup table gives exactly this same vector. for example: position 1: dog → [0.2, 0.7, -0.1, ...] position 5: dog → [0.2, 0.7, -0.1, ...] the embedding layer doesn't inherently know whether the dog is: first, third, fifth, tenth. raschka explicitly illustrates this: the same token id produces the same vector regardless of its position. so we need to add another signal. 1.3.3 the simplest solution: add a position vector suppose the sequence length is: t=4 and embedding dimension: d=3 our token embeddings might be: x_{\text{token}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7&0.1&0.2\\ 0.4&0.9&0.3\\ 0.8&0.2&0.5\\ 0.1&0.6&0.7 \end{bmatrix} create a positional embedding matrix: p = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1&0.0&0.2\\ 0.0&0.2&0.1\\ 0.2&0.1&0.0\\ 0.3&0.0&0.1 \end{bmatrix} then simply add: \boxed{ x=x_{\text{token}}+p } giving: x= \begin{bmatrix} 0.8&0.1&0.4\\ 0.4&1.1&0.4\\ 1.0&0.3&0.5\\ 0.4&0.6&0.8 \end{bmatrix} now the representation contains: \text{token information}+\text{position information} the transformer slides give precisely this conceptual operation: \boxed{x\leftarrow x+p} where p has the same shape as the token representation matrix. (source: transformers-slides) raschka's implementation also uses addition of token and positional embeddings. 1.3.4 why addition? a natural question is: why add instead of concatenate? we could theoretically do: [x_{\text{token}};p] which would give: d+d=2d dimensions. but then every following layer would need to process twice as many dimensions. addition keeps: \boxed{\text{model width}=d} so the existing transformer architecture can process the result without changing its width. the positional vector has the same dimension as the token embedding: p_t\in\mathbb r^d and therefore: x_t=e_t+p_t is also: x_t\in\mathbb r^d raschka explicitly notes that positional vectors have the same dimensionality as token embeddings so they can be added directly. 1.3.5 shape mathematics suppose: b=8 t=128 d=768 then: token embeddings x_{\text{token}}\in\mathbb r^{8\times128\times768} positional embeddings for absolute learned positional embeddings: p\in\mathbb r^{128\times768} pytorch broadcasts p across the batch: [8,128,768] + [128,768] becomes: \boxed{[8,128,768]} final input \boxed{ x=x_{\text{token}}+p \in\mathbb r^{8\times128\times768} } raschka gives essentially this exact pattern with a batch of 8 sequences, 4 tokens per sequence, and 256-dimensional embeddings. 1.3.6 absolute vs relative position now we reach an important distinction. there are two broad approaches. absolute positional information ask: what is the exact position of this token? for example: 0,1,2,3,4,\ldots position 0 has one positional vector. position 1 has another. position 2 has another. so: p_0,p_1,p_2,\ldots raschka describes this as assigning a unique embedding to each position and adding it to the token embedding. relative positional information instead of asking: "what is your absolute position?" we care about: "how far are you from the other token?" for example: the cat sat on the mat when "mat" attends to "cat" : \text{distance}=4 it may be more useful for the model to understand this relationship than to simply know: "mat" is at position 6. raschka explains relative positional approaches in terms of the distance between tokens. 1.3.7 why relative position can be attractive imagine training sequences mostly have lengths around 100. an absolute-position scheme learns: p_0,\ldots,p_{99} but what if inference gives a sequence of length 500? absolute position representations can become problematic depending on the implementation and training regime. relative approaches can focus more naturally on relationships such as: j-i rather than exact positions. raschka notes the potential advantage of relative position methods for generalizing to different sequence lengths. 1.3.8 learned absolute positional embeddings this is the simplest version to understand and the one implemented in raschka's gpt-from-scratch chapter. we create: p\in\mathbb r^{t_{\max}\times d} and treat p as a learnable parameter. for example: p= \begin{bmatrix} p_0\\ p_1\\ p_2\\ \vdots\\ p_{t_{\max}-1} \end{bmatrix} each: p_i\in\mathbb r^d is learned during training. so: x_t=e(x_t)+p_t this means the same token gets different final initial representations depending on where it occurs. for "cat" : e(\text{cat})+p_2 is different from: e(\text{cat})+p_8 raschka's pytorch implementation creates a positional embedding layer and uses: torch.arange(context_length) to retrieve the position vectors. 1.3.9 exact pytorch implementation the core implementation is surprisingly small: import torch import torch.nn as nn batch_size = 2 seq_len = 5 embedding_dim = 8 # token ids input_ids = torch.tensor([ [1, 4, 7, 2, 9], [3, 5, 8, 6, 0] ]) # token embedding table token_embedding = nn.embedding( num_embeddings=10, embedding_dim=embedding_dim ) # position embedding table position_embedding = nn.embedding( num_embeddings=seq_len, embedding_dim=embedding_dim ) # token embeddings token_embeddings = token_embedding(input_ids) # positions: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] positions = torch.arange(seq_len) # positional embeddings position_embeddings = position_embedding(positions) # add token + position x = token_embeddings + position_embeddings print("token ids: ", input_ids.shape) print("token embeddings: ", token_embeddings.shape) print("position embeddings:", position_embeddings.shape) print("final input x: ", x.shape) shapes: token ids [2, 5] token embeddings [2, 5, 8] positions [5] position embeddings [5, 8] final x [2, 5, 8] so: \boxed{ [ b,t] \rightarrow [b,t,d] + [t,d] \rightarrow [b,t,d] } this follows the positional-embedding procedure shown in raschka's implementation. 1.3.10 but what did the original transformer do? now an important historical distinction. the original transformer used sinusoidal positional encodings rather than learned position vectors. the standard equations are: \boxed{ pe_{(pos,2i)} = \sin \left( \frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}} \right) } and \boxed{ pe_{(pos,2i+1)} = \cos \left( \frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}} \right) } here: pos = token position i = dimension index d_{\text{model}} = model dimension your deepseek book explains this construction as using smooth sine/cosine waves at different frequencies, replacing crude discrete position encodings with continuous signals. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1.3.11 why sine and cosine? this formula looks scary: \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right) but the underlying idea is simple. we want every position to generate a distinctive pattern. so imagine several waves: dimension 1: ~~~~~ very fast dimension 2: ~~~~ fast dimension 3: ~~~ medium dimension 4: ~~ slower dimension 5: ~ very slow each dimension changes at a different frequency. thus position 10 and position 11 produce slightly different patterns, while position 10 and position 100 produce much more different patterns. the deepseek book explains exactly this multi-frequency intuition. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1.3.12 small numerical example take: d_{\text{model}}=4 and position: pos=1 for dimension 2i=0 : pe(1,0) = \sin(1) \approx0.8415 for dimension 2i+1=1 : pe(1,1) = \cos(1) \approx0.5403 for the next pair, the denominator becomes larger: 10000^{2/4}=100 so: pe(1,2)=\sin(0.01)\approx0.0100 pe(1,3)=\cos(0.01)\approx0.99995 so approximately: pe_1 = [0.8415,0.5403,0.0100,0.99995] another position, say pos=2 , produces another vector: pe_2 = [\sin2,\cos2,\sin0.02,\cos0.02] hence the position is encoded as a pattern across dimensions. 1.3.13 the beautiful part of sinusoidal encoding the low-frequency dimensions change slowly. the high-frequency dimensions change rapidly. so together they provide: \boxed{ \text{fine positional information} + \text{coarse positional information} } think of it like having multiple clocks running at different speeds. one clock distinguishes nearby positions. another captures broader location. another changes even more slowly. the deepseek book's discussion specifically emphasizes this multi-frequency structure. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1.3.14 learned absolute vs sinusoidal now keep these distinct. method position representation learned? learned absolute one vector per position yes sinusoidal sine/cosine functions no relative methods position relationships/distances depends rope rotates q/k by position learned projections + fixed rotational structure raschka's book, in its gpt-from-scratch implementation, uses learned absolute positional embeddings. the original transformer used sinusoidal encodings. your transformer slides then point out an important modern development: rope (rotary position embedding). (source: transformers-slides) 1.3.15 rope — the modern direction we will study rope more deeply later, but you should understand the core idea now. instead of doing: x=e+p rope modifies the query and key vectors according to their positions. for a simplified 2d pair: r_m(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(m\theta)&-\sin(m\theta)\\ \sin(m\theta)&\cos(m\theta) \end{bmatrix} then: q_m=r_mq and: k_n=r_nk the important mathematical consequence is: q_m^tk_n becomes dependent on the relative displacement: n-m the attention handbook in your source set derives this relationship explicitly. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) so rope gives attention a way to incorporate positional relationships inside the q/k interaction . 1.3.16 why this is different from adding p compare: learned absolute position \boxed{ x_t=e_t+p_t } position is injected into the representation. rope \boxed{ q_t\rightarrow r_tq_t,\qquad k_t\rightarrow r_tk_t } position is incorporated directly into the attention compatibility calculation. this distinction becomes extremely important when we study the actual attention equation. correction: causal attention already has a position-dependent access pattern; lack of explicit positional embeddings does not make every causal decoder strictly permutation-equivariant. position encoding and eligibility remain distinct. complete grounded review 1.3.17 a subtle but important point: causal mask ≠ positional encoding do not confuse these. a causal mask says: you are not allowed to look at future positions. for example: position 4 can see: 1 2 3 4 but cannot see: 5 6 7 that provides a directional constraint . but it does not fully tell the model: "token 4 is exactly four positions after token 0." the attention handbook explicitly distinguishes these: a causal mask imposes directional ordering constraints, but does not itself provide a rich representation of position or distance. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) so: \boxed{ \text{causal mask} \neq \text{positional encoding} } this will save you from a very common interview mistake. 1.3.18 why position matters for attention we are now ready to connect position to what comes next. without positional information: x= \begin{bmatrix} e_{\text{cat}}\\ e_{\text{sat}}\\ e_{\text{here}} \end{bmatrix} self-attention computes interactions between these representations. but if you permute the rows, plain self-attention without position-dependent information treats the operation symmetrically with respect to that permutation: the outputs permute along with the inputs. the attention handbook describes this as permutation equivariance . (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) that's the mathematical reason position must be injected. 1.3.19 the full input representation now previously: x_t=e(x_t) now: \boxed{ x_t=e(x_t)+p_t } or, for the complete sequence: \boxed{ x=x_{\text{token}}+x_{\text{position}} } therefore: token id ↓ token embedding + position information ↓ position-aware representation ↓ transformer this is the complete input to the attention mechanism in the learned-absolute-position formulation. 1.3.20 connecting all three steps we now have: step 1.1 — language model p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) step 1.2 — token representation x_t \rightarrow \text{token id} \rightarrow e(x_t) step 1.3 — position e(x_t) \rightarrow e(x_t)+p_t therefore: \boxed{ \text{text} \rightarrow \text{tokens} \rightarrow \text{ids} \rightarrow \text{token embeddings} \rightarrow \text{position-aware embeddings} \rightarrow \text{attention} } and now we can finally understand the heart of the transformer. 1.3.21 the next question suppose we have: the animal didn't cross the road because it was tired. when processing: it the model should probably look strongly at: animal rather than: road so we need a mechanism that answers: for the current token, which other tokens are relevant, and by how much? that mechanism is self-attention . and this is where our earlier mathematical concepts suddenly become useful: \boxed{ q=xw_q } \boxed{ k=xw_k } \boxed{ v=xw_v } followed by: \boxed{ s=qk^t } then: \boxed{ a=\operatorname{softmax} \left( \frac{s}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) } and: \boxed{ o=av } we already saw these equations abstractly in the mathematical foundation. now we are going to derive why every single one of them exists . step 1.3 master check before moving to self-attention, make sure these are clear: q1. why does: e(\text{"cat"}) remain the same whether "cat" occurs at position 1 or position 10? retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 1.4 — the residual stream plan node: i1 · chat order #11 we now know how the model creates a position-aware representation: \text{text} \rightarrow \text{tokens} \rightarrow \text{ids} \rightarrow \text{token embeddings} \rightarrow \text{position information} so we have a matrix: x\in\mathbb r^{t\times d} or, with a batch: x\in\mathbb r^{b\times t\times d} the next question is: what happens to this representation as it passes through 12, 24, 48, or hundreds of transformer blocks? the answer is the residual stream . your transformer slides make this the central organizing idea of the architecture: attention and mlp sublayers read from the stream and write their updates back into it additively. 1.4.1 first, what is a "stream"? suppose we have: the cat is sleeping ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ d d d d each token has a d -dimensional vector. so for one sequence: x= \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3\\ x_4 \end{bmatrix} \in\mathbb r^{4\times d} think of every row as a lane . token 1 ───────────────────────── lane 1 token 2 ───────────────────────── lane 2 token 3 ───────────────────────── lane 3 token 4 ───────────────────────── lane 4 the collection of these d -dimensional representations is the residual stream . the important idea from your slide is: attention moves information between lanes; mlps process information within a lane. this is an extremely useful mental model. 1.4.2 why do we need a residual stream? imagine a transformer block simply did: x_{\text{new}}=f(x) where f is some complicated neural network. then every layer would completely replace the previous representation. with many layers: x_1=f_1(x_0) x_2=f_2(x_1) x_3=f_3(x_2) and eventually: x_l=f_l(\cdots f_2(f_1(x_0))) this creates a long chain of transformations. training becomes harder because gradients have to flow through all those transformations. residual connections instead make the layer say: "keep what you already know, and add an update." so: \boxed{ x_{\text{new}}=x+f(x) } this is the core residual idea. 1.4.3 the most important equation of this step your slides use: \boxed{ x\leftarrow x+\operatorname{attn}(\operatorname{norm}(x)) } and then: \boxed{ x\leftarrow x+\operatorname{mlp}(\operatorname{norm}(x)) } for the entire sequence: \boxed{ x\leftarrow x+\operatorname{attn}(\operatorname{norm}(x)) } \boxed{ x\leftarrow x+\operatorname{mlp}(\operatorname{norm}(x)) } notice the structure: old representation + new information ↓ new representation that is the residual stream. 1.4.4 why is it called "residual"? suppose we want the layer to produce some ideal transformation: h(x) instead of forcing the layer to learn h(x) directly, write: h(x)=x+f(x) therefore: f(x)=h(x)-x so the neural network only has to learn: \boxed{ \text{what should i add to the current representation?} } that difference: h(x)-x is the residual . hence the name: residual connection / residual block. correction: residual addition includes the old vector algebraically but may cancel it; it does not preserve it as a separately recoverable record. complete grounded review 1.4.5 tiny numerical example suppose one token has representation: x= [2,4,1] the attention sublayer generates: a= [0.5,-1,2] residual addition gives: x' = x+a so: x' = [2.5,3,3] the original information was not discarded. it remains: [2,4,1] and attention contributed: [0.5,-1,2] therefore: \boxed{ \text{new representation} = \text{old representation} + \text{attention update} } 1.4.6 now add the mlp the mlp produces another update: m=[-0.2,0.4,0.8] then: x''=x'+m giving: x''= [2.3,3.4,3.8] so the block has done: x \rightarrow x+a \rightarrow x+a+m therefore: \boxed{ x_{\text{out}} = x_{\text{in}} + a + m } this is the simplest way to understand the residual stream. 1.4.7 the stream across many layers now suppose there are l blocks. let: r_0 be the representation entering the first block. for block 1: r_1 = r_0+a_1+m_1 for block 2: r_2 = r_1+a_2+m_2 substitute: r_2 = r_0+a_1+m_1+a_2+m_2 continue through l blocks: \boxed{ r_l = r_0+ \sum_{\ell=1}^{l}a_\ell+ \sum_{\ell=1}^{l}m_\ell } conceptually, the residual stream contains: \boxed{ \text{initial embedding} + \text{many learned updates} } this matches the slide's description that the final representation is the embedding plus the contributions written by the sublayers. 1.4.8 what does attention write? attention performs: \operatorname{attn}(x) and produces an update for each position. why is this described as: moving information between lanes ? because token i 's new representation can incorporate information from token j . for example: "the animal didn't cross the road because it was tired." ↑ ↑ └──── attention ────────┘ a token's representation can receive information from other token positions. so attention performs cross-token communication . 1.4.9 what does the mlp write? the mlp acts independently on each token position. for token i : m_i=\operatorname{mlp}(x_i) it can transform the information stored in that token's vector. so: attention: token 1 ↔ token 2 ↔ token 3 ↔ token 4 mlp: token 1 → transformation token 2 → transformation token 3 → transformation token 4 → transformation the mlp doesn't itself perform the cross-position mixing that attention does. this is why your slide summarizes the division of labor as: \boxed{ \text{attention = between positions} } \boxed{ \text{mlp = within a position} } 1.4.10 why must the dimensions match? we want: x+f(x) addition is only possible when the shapes match. suppose: x\in\mathbb r^d then: f(x)\in\mathbb r^d and therefore: x+f(x)\in\mathbb r^d for a sequence: x\in\mathbb r^{t\times d} and: f(x)\in\mathbb r^{t\times d} so: x+f(x)\in\mathbb r^{t\times d} for a batch: x\in\mathbb r^{b\times t\times d} and the branch must return: \mathbb r^{b\times t\times d} this is why transformer blocks preserve the model width. raschka's implementation demonstrates that a transformer block can take: [2,4,768] and return: [2,4,768]. 1.4.11 why does preserving the shape matter? suppose: d=768 then every block can accept and return: [b,t,768] so we can simply do: embedding ↓ block 1 ↓ block 2 ↓ block 3 ↓ ... ↓ block l without changing the dimensionality between blocks. raschka explicitly notes that preserving the input dimensions makes the transformer architecture stackable and scalable. 1.4.12 the gradient problem now we get to the main reason residual connections are important . suppose a layer is simply: y=f(x) then by the chain rule: \frac{\partial l}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} across many layers, gradients involve repeated multiplication: \frac{\partial l}{\partial x_0} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial x_l} j_lj_{l-1}\cdots j_1 where j_i is the jacobian of layer i . if these jacobians tend to shrink gradients, the gradient can become extremely small. that is the vanishing-gradient problem . raschka explicitly introduces shortcut/residual connections as a mechanism to mitigate this issue in deep networks. correction: i+j_f supplies an identity gradient route, but j_f=-i can cancel it. residuals do not guarantee nonvanishing gradients. complete grounded review 1.4.13 what changes with a residual connection? now: y=x+f(x) differentiate: \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = i+\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x} the key term is: \boxed{i} the identity matrix. that means there is a direct gradient pathway. so: \frac{\partial l}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial l}{\partial y} \left( i+j_f \right) the network does not have to rely entirely on: j_f to transmit the gradient. there is an identity route. 1.4.14 the simplest scalar demonstration suppose: f(x)=0.1x without residual connection: y=0.1x so: \frac{dy}{dx}=0.1 after 20 such layers: (0.1)^{20}=10^{-20} that is extremely small. now use a residual connection: y=x+0.1x=1.1x so: \frac{dy}{dx}=1.1 after 20 layers: 1.1^{20}\approx6.73 this example is deliberately simplified. real transformer jacobians are much more complicated, and residual connections do not mathematically guarantee that gradients can never vanish. the important point is that the identity pathway makes gradient propagation much easier. raschka's experimental example shows exactly the intended training effect: gradient magnitudes across earlier layers remain substantially more stable with shortcut connections than without them. 1.4.15 this also helps the forward pass residual connections are not only useful during backpropagation. they also make each block behave like: \boxed{ \text{current representation} + \text{learned refinement} } rather than: \text{completely replace representation} so one way to think about depth is: layer 0: "here is my initial understanding." layer 1: "let me add information about relationships." layer 2: "let me refine those relationships." layer 3: "let me add another feature." ... layer l: "here is the final contextual representation." that is an intuition, not a literal claim that every layer learns one clean human-interpretable feature. 1.4.16 pre-norm architecture in your slides your transformer slides use: \boxed{ x' = x+\operatorname{attn}(\operatorname{norm}(x)) } then: \boxed{ y = x'+\operatorname{mlp}(\operatorname{norm}(x')) } this is commonly called a pre-normalization arrangement because normalization occurs before the sublayer. your slide's exact decoder-block summary is: y=x+\operatorname{mha}(\operatorname{norm}(x),\text{causal mask}) followed by: h=\; y+\operatorname{ffn}(\operatorname{norm}(y)). this ordering matters. we will study layernorm/rmsnorm later as its own topic, but for now understand the flow. 1.4.17 one complete transformer block let the input residual stream be: x^{(\ell)} step 1 — normalize \tilde x^{(\ell)} = \operatorname{norm}(x^{(\ell)}) step 2 — attention a^{(\ell)} = \operatorname{attention}(\tilde x^{(\ell)}) step 3 — residual addition x'^{(\ell)} = x^{(\ell)}+a^{(\ell)} step 4 — normalize again \tilde x'^{(\ell)} = \operatorname{norm}(x'^{(\ell)}) step 5 — mlp m^{(\ell)} = \operatorname{mlp}(\tilde x'^{(\ell)}) step 6 — second residual addition \boxed{ x^{(\ell+1)} = x'^{(\ell)}+m^{(\ell)} } so the block is: x │ ├───────────────┐ │ │ norm │ ↓ │ attention │ ↓ │ + <─────────────┘ │ ├───────────────┐ │ │ norm │ ↓ │ mlp │ ↓ │ + <─────────────┘ │ ↓ y that is the basic unit that gets repeated. 1.4.18 sequence-level view now use: x\in\mathbb r^{t\times d} the attention branch: \operatorname{attention}(x) \in\mathbb r^{t\times d} so: x+\operatorname{attention}(x) \in\mathbb r^{t\times d} then mlp: \operatorname{mlp}(x') \in\mathbb r^{t\times d} and: x'+\operatorname{mlp}(x') \in\mathbb r^{t\times d} therefore a block performs: \boxed{ t\times d \rightarrow t\times d } it changes the contents , not the shape. 1.4.19 the residual stream is shared across the architecture this is an important conceptual phrase from your slides: every block reads from and writes back into the same residual stream. imagine: embedding + position ↓ residual stream ↓ ┌───────────────┐ │ transformer 1 │ └───────────────┘ ↓ residual stream ↓ ┌───────────────┐ │ transformer 2 │ └───────────────┘ ↓ residual stream ↓ ... ↓ ┌───────────────┐ │ transformer l │ └───────────────┘ ↓ final stream the model is not creating an entirely separate representation space for each block. the same-width stream is repeatedly refined. 1.4.20 why this matters for interpretability you will later encounter statements such as: "the residual stream contains information." that is because the architecture literally accumulates contributions there. for example, conceptually: r_l = r_0 + \delta_{\text{attn},1} + \delta_{\text{mlp},1} + \cdots + \delta_{\text{attn},l} + \delta_{\text{mlp},l} this gives a useful way to think about the transformer: each sublayer writes an update into a shared representation. we should not overinterpret this as saying every update corresponds to one human-readable concept. the mathematical structure is what is guaranteed. 1.4.21 connection to the output after all blocks: h=x^{(l)} then the final representation is normalized and projected into vocabulary space: z = \operatorname{norm}(h)w_u where: w_u\in\mathbb r^{d\times|v|} and: z\in\mathbb r^{t\times|v|} your slides explicitly describe this as taking the final residual-stream representation and projecting it back to vocabulary space for next-token prediction. so the entire journey is now: \boxed{ \text{embedding} \rightarrow \text{residual updates} \rightarrow \text{final residual stream} \rightarrow \text{logits} } 1.4.22 simple pytorch residual block let's implement the core idea without attention details yet. import torch import torch.nn as nn class residualblock(nn.module): def __init__(self, d_model): super().__init__() self.norm = nn.layernorm(d_model) self.branch = nn.sequential( nn.linear(d_model, d_model), nn.gelu(), nn.linear(d_model, d_model) ) def forward(self, x): # save the original residual stream residual = x # transform a normalized copy update = self.branch(self.norm(x)) # write the update back into the stream x = residual + update return x # example x = torch.randn(2, 5, 8) block = residualblock(d_model=8) y = block(x) print("input shape :", x.shape) print("output shape:", y.shape) output shape: input shape : torch.size([2, 5, 8]) output shape: torch.size([2, 5, 8]) notice: \boxed{ [2,5,8]\rightarrow[2,5,8] } the branch changes the information, while the residual addition preserves the stream dimensions. raschka's actual transformer block follows this same residual-addition idea, storing shortcut = x , applying normalization and the sublayer, then adding the original input back. 1.4.23 a very common mistake do not think: "residual connection means we skip the layer." not exactly. the branch is still computed. we do: f(x) and then: x+f(x) so the layer is not skipped in the forward computation. what is provided is an alternative path for both representation flow and gradients. that is why the book calls them shortcut/skip connections. 1.4.24 another common mistake do not confuse: \boxed{\text{residual stream}} with: \boxed{\text{residual connection}} they are related but conceptually different. residual stream the evolving representation: x^{(0)},x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(l)} residual connection the addition operation: x_{\text{out}}=x_{\text{in}}+f(x_{\text{in}}) the stream is the thing being carried through the network . the residual connection is the mechanism used to update it . 1.4.25 where we are now we have now constructed: \boxed{ \text{tokens} \rightarrow \text{token ids} \rightarrow \text{embeddings} \rightarrow \text{position} \rightarrow \text{residual stream} } inside a block: \boxed{ x \rightarrow \operatorname{norm}(x) \rightarrow \operatorname{attention} \rightarrow +x \rightarrow \operatorname{norm} \rightarrow \operatorname{mlp} \rightarrow +x } the only major piece we haven't yet opened is the attention mechanism itself . and now we can finally introduce it properly. 1.4.26 why q, k, v are the next step suppose the residual stream contains: x= \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3\\ x_4 \end{bmatrix} we want token i to ask: which other tokens are relevant to me? for this, the transformer creates three different views of the same representation: \boxed{ q=xw_q } \boxed{ k=xw_k } \boxed{ v=xw_v } then: query = what this token is looking for key = what each token offers for matching value = what information each token can provide and the similarity computation: \boxed{ qk^t } creates all pairwise token-to-token relevance scores. we are now at the exact point where the mathematics from step 0.1 becomes the core transformer mechanism. step 1.4 master check make sure you can explain these without looking back. q1. what exactly is the residual stream? q2. why do
