claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 2.4 — top-p / nucleus sampling plan node: i2 · chat order #24 we have now seen: \boxed{\text{greedy}} \boxed{\text{beam search}} \boxed{\text{temperature}} \boxed{\text{top-k sampling}} the problem with top-k was: k is fixed. whether the model is extremely confident or highly uncertain, we always keep exactly k candidates. top-p solves this by making the candidate set adaptive to the probability distribution . your decoding slides define top-p, also called nucleus sampling , as truncating by cumulative probability rather than by count . (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.4.1 the core idea suppose the model predicts: p= [0.50,0.20,0.15,0.08,0.04,0.03]. instead of saying: "keep the top 3." we say: "keep enough of the most probable tokens so that their cumulative probability reaches at least p ." for example: p=0.90. accumulate: 0.50 then: 0.50+0.20=0.70 then: 0.70+0.15=0.85 then: 0.85+0.08=0.93. we have crossed 0.90 . therefore the nucleus is: \boxed{ \{1,2,3,4\} } containing 4 tokens. notice: \boxed{k\text{ is not specified}.} the distribution itself determines how many tokens survive. 2.4.2 why do we need top-p? recall the weakness of top-k. consider two distributions. distribution a — very confident [0.90,0.05,0.02,0.01,0.01,0.01] distribution b — uncertain [0.20,0.18,0.17,0.15,0.12,0.10,0.08] suppose: k=3. top-k gives: a [0.90,0.05,0.02] b [0.20,0.18,0.17] but in b, many additional tokens are also plausible. top-p adapts automatically. so: \boxed{ \text{top-k adapts to rank count} } while: \boxed{ \text{top-p adapts to probability mass}. } 2.4.3 definition let the token probabilities be sorted in descending order: q_{(1)}\ge q_{(2)}\ge\cdots\ge q_{(v)}. for a chosen threshold: p\in(0,1], we find the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least p . formally: \boxed{ v^{(p)} = \arg\min_{s} \left\{ |s|: \sum_{v\in s}q(v)\ge p \right\} } with the tokens selected from highest probability downward. the slide expresses the same idea as the smallest set satisfying the cumulative-probability condition. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.4.4 the most important phrase memorize this: \boxed{ \text{top-p = smallest set whose cumulative probability }\ge p } that one sentence solves most conceptual questions. 2.4.5 step-by-step algorithm given the model probabilities: q_1,q_2,\ldots,q_v step 1 sort tokens by probability: q_{(1)}\ge q_{(2)}\ge\cdots\ge q_{(v)}. step 2 compute cumulative sums: c_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j}q_{(i)}. step 3 find the first j such that: c_j\ge p. step 4 keep those j tokens. step 5 remove the rest. step 6 renormalize probabilities over the retained tokens. so: \boxed{ \text{sort} \rightarrow \text{cumulative sum} \rightarrow \text{stop at }p \rightarrow \text{filter} \rightarrow \text{renormalize} \rightarrow \text{sample} } 2.4.6 why do we sort? because top-p wants the most probable tokens first . suppose: p=[0.10,0.50,0.05,0.35]. we must sort: [0.50,0.35,0.10,0.05]. otherwise a random ordering could cause us to include low-probability tokens before high-probability ones. so: \boxed{ \text{top-p operates on probabilities ordered from largest to smallest}. } correction: the four displayed france probabilities sum .9667 and are an excerpt; missing tail mass .0333 exists. their nucleus prefix computation is valid without pretending the four form the whole vocabulary. complete grounded review 2.4.7 exact slide example your decoding slides use: p=0.90 with the probability distribution: token probability france 0.8062 europe 0.0662 the 0.0542 a 0.0401 the tokens are already sorted. now calculate the cumulative probability. after france 0.8062 after europe 0.8062+0.0662 = 0.8724 still below: 0.90. after the 0.8724+0.0542 = 0.9266. now: 0.9266\ge0.90. so we stop. the nucleus is: \boxed{ \{\text{france},\text{europe},\text{the}\} } and the token a is removed. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.4.8 the nucleus does not need to sum exactly to p this is a very important exam point. we wanted: p=0.90. but our cumulative probability became: 0.9266. not: 0.9000. why? because we cannot usually include a fraction of a token. therefore top-p takes the smallest complete set that crosses the threshold. so: \boxed{ \text{cumulative probability can exceed }p. } it does not have to equal p . 2.4.9 renormalization after filtering we retain: [0.8062,0.0662,0.0542]. their sum is: 0.9266. but probabilities must sum to 1. therefore: p'_i=\frac{p_i}{0.9266}. for france: p'(\text{france}) = \frac{0.8062}{0.9266} \approx0.8701. for europe: p'(\text{europe}) = \frac{0.0662}{0.9266} \approx0.0714. for the: p'(\text{the}) = \frac{0.0542}{0.9266} \approx0.0585. thus: \boxed{ [0.8701,\;0.0714,\;0.0585,\;0]. } these are the renormalized values shown on the slide. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.4.10 why renormalization is necessary before filtering: \sum_ip_i=1. after filtering: \sum_{i\in nucleus}p_i=0.9266. but sampling requires: \sum_ip_i'=1. therefore: \boxed{ p_i'= \frac{p_i} {\sum_{j\in nucleus}p_j} } for retained tokens. the removed tokens receive: \boxed{0}. 2.4.11 a complete top-p example suppose: p= [0.40,0.25,0.15,0.10,0.06,0.04]. let: p=0.80. calculate cumulative probabilities. token probability cumulative a 0.40 0.40 b 0.25 0.65 c 0.15 0.80 we have reached: 0.80. therefore: \boxed{ nucleus=\{a,b,c\} } and retained mass is: 0.80. renormalize: p'(a)=\frac{0.40}{0.80}=0.50 p'(b)=\frac{0.25}{0.80}=0.3125 p'(c)=\frac{0.15}{0.80}=0.1875. thus: \boxed{ [0.50,0.3125,0.1875,0,0,0]. } interesting: this happens to be exactly the same numerical result as our earlier top-k example with k=3 , but for a very different reason. 2.4.12 top-k and top-p can sometimes produce the same result suppose: p=[0.40,0.25,0.15,0.10,0.06,0.04] and: k=3. top-k keeps: a,b,c. now choose: p=0.80. top-p also keeps: a,b,c. therefore both methods produce the same candidate set. but this does not mean they are the same algorithm. 2.4.13 the critical difference suppose: p= [0.60,0.20,0.10,0.05,0.03,0.02]. use: p=0.90. cumulative: 0.60 0.60+0.20=0.80 0.80+0.10=0.90. so top-p keeps: \boxed{3} tokens. now suppose the distribution changes to: p= [0.30,0.25,0.20,0.15,0.07,0.03]. again: p=0.90. cumulative: 0.30 0.55 0.75 0.90. now it keeps: \boxed{4} tokens. same p , different number of candidates. that is the defining advantage. 2.4.14 top-p is adaptive we can state the key idea mathematically: \boxed{ |v^{(p)}| \text{ depends on the shape of the probability distribution}. } for a sharp distribution: |v^{(p)}| can be small. for a flat distribution: |v^{(p)}| can be large. this is why nucleus sampling is often described as an adaptive candidate set . 2.4.15 sharp distribution example suppose: p=[0.85,0.08,0.03,0.02,0.01,0.01]. take: p=0.90. cumulative: 0.85 0.85+0.08=0.93. so only: \boxed{2} tokens are retained. 2.4.16 flat distribution example suppose: p= [0.15,0.14,0.13,0.12,0.11,0.10,0.09,0.08,0.08]. take: p=0.90. cumulative: 0.15 0.29 0.42 0.54 0.65 0.75 0.84 0.92. so top-p retains: \boxed{8} tokens. notice how dramatically the candidate count changed. 2.4.17 this is why top-p is different from top-k top-k: \boxed{|s|=k} top-p: \boxed{ \sum_{i\in s}p_i\ge p } with s chosen minimally. therefore: \boxed{ \text{top-k asks "how many?"} } while: \boxed{ \text{top-p asks "how much probability mass?"} } this is probably the single most important comparison for this section. 2.4.18 what does p=0.90 actually mean? it does not mean: keep exactly 90% of the vocabulary. it means: keep the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose total probability mass is at least 90%. for example, if vocabulary size is: 50,000, top-p might retain: 5 tokens in one context and: 500 in another. so: \boxed{ p\text{ is a probability-mass threshold, not a vocabulary percentage}. } 2.4.19 very important: top-p uses probabilities top-k can be naturally described using logits because selecting the largest logits gives the same ranking as selecting the largest probabilities. but top-p requires cumulative probability mass . so the clean conceptual pipeline is: \boxed{ z \rightarrow softmax \rightarrow sort probabilities \rightarrow cumulative sum \rightarrow top-p filter \rightarrow renormalize \rightarrow sample } the source slide describes top-p directly using the probability distribution. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.4.20 where does temperature fit? recall temperature: q_i(t) = \frac{e^{z_i/t}} {\sum_j e^{z_j/t}}. top-p is usually applied to the resulting probability distribution. so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{temperature} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{top-p} \rightarrow \text{renormalize} \rightarrow \text{sample} } the precise implementation ordering can vary, but the mathematical role is clear: temperature changes the distribution; top-p chooses the probability-mass nucleus. for exam questions, follow the ordering specified in the question/source. 2.4.21 temperature can change the top-p candidate set this is different from top-k. for positive t , temperature preserves the ranking. but it changes the probability values. since top-p depends on cumulative probability , temperature can therefore change how many tokens are needed to reach p . this is an important distinction: \boxed{ \text{temperature does not change top-k membership} } but: \boxed{ \text{temperature can change top-p membership}. } why? because top-k only cares about ranking. top-p cares about cumulative probabilities. 2.4.22 numerical demonstration suppose: z=[4,3,2,1]. take: p=0.90. at: t=1, the softmax probabilities are approximately: [0.6439,0.2369,0.0871,0.0321]. cumulative: 0.6439 0.8808 0.9679. so top-p =0.90 needs: \boxed{3} tokens. now increase temperature: t=2. scaled logits: [2,1.5,1,0.5]. the distribution becomes flatter. approx: [0.4551,0.2760,0.1674,0.1015]. cumulative: 0.4551 0.7311 0.8985 1.0000. notice: 0.8985<0.90. so top-p now needs: \boxed{4} tokens. that is a very important numerical fact. 2.4.23 compare with top-k on the same example for: z=[4,3,2,1] and: k=3, top-k always retains: \boxed{3} tokens, regardless of whether temperature is 1 or 2. top-p with: p=0.90 changed from: 3 to: 4. so: \boxed{ \text{top-p adapts to temperature-induced distribution changes}. } 2.4.24 the renormalization formula let the nucleus be: v^{(p)}. then: \boxed{ q'(v)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{q(v)} {\sum_{u\in v^{(p)}}q(u)}, &v\in v^{(p)}\\[8pt] 0, &\text{otherwise} \end{cases} } this is exactly the mathematical structure displayed in the decoding slide. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.4.25 why does the source say "nucleus"? the retained tokens collectively form a high-probability core of the distribution. that core is called the: \boxed{\text{nucleus}}. instead of exploring the entire vocabulary, sampling occurs inside this high-probability region. 2.4.26 complete example with p=0.75 suppose: p=[0.35,0.20,0.15,0.12,0.10,0.08]. we want: p=0.75. cumulative: 0.35 0.55 0.70 0.82. therefore stop after token 4. the nucleus: \boxed{ \{1,2,3,4\} } retained mass: 0.82. renormalized: p'_1=\frac{0.35}{0.82}\approx0.4268 p'_2=\frac{0.20}{0.82}\approx0.2439 p'_3=\frac{0.15}{0.82}\approx0.1829 p'_4=\frac{0.12}{0.82}\approx0.1463. therefore: \boxed{ p'\approx [0.4268,0.2439,0.1829,0.1463,0,0] } check: 0.4268+0.2439+0.1829+0.1463 \approx1. 2.4.27 what if p=1 ? suppose: p=1. then we need all probability mass. therefore: \boxed{ v^{(1)}=v } and top-p filtering does nothing. so: \boxed{ p=1\rightarrow\text{ordinary sampling}. } 2.4.28 what happens as p gets smaller? smaller p : \boxed{\text{smaller candidate set}} usually. larger p : \boxed{\text{larger candidate set}} usually. for example: p=0.50 might keep 1–3 tokens. p=0.90 might keep 3–10 tokens. p=0.99 could keep many tokens. the exact count depends on the distribution. 2.4.29 important exam trap — "at least" the definition says: \boxed{ \text{cumulative probability }\ge p } not: =p. therefore: suppose: p=[0.51,0.30,0.10,0.09] and: p=0.80. cumulative: 0.51 0.81. therefore we stop after token 2. even though: 0.81\neq0.80. answer: \boxed{2\text{ tokens}} not 3. 2.4.30 important exam trap — don't stop before crossing suppose: p=[0.45,0.25,0.20,0.10] and: p=0.90. cumulative: 0.45 0.70 0.90. we stop exactly at token 3. but if: p=[0.45,0.25,0.19,0.11], then: 0.45+0.25+0.19 = 0.89. still insufficient. so we must include token 4: 0.89+0.11=1. thus the nucleus contains all 4 tokens. 2.4.31 important exam trap — sort first suppose: p=[0.1,0.5,0.2,0.2]. for: p=0.70, you must sort: [0.5,0.2,0.2,0.1]. cumulative: 0.5 0.7. therefore 2 tokens survive. if you accumulate in original order: 0.1+0.5+0.2=0.8, you might incorrectly say 3 tokens. so: \boxed{ \text{never perform top-p cumulative selection without sorting by probability.} } 2.4.32 top-k vs top-p — the definitive comparison property top-k top-p selection basis rank cumulative probability candidate count fixed k variable needs sorting? conceptually yes yes probability threshold? no yes adapts to uncertainty? limited yes k=v ordinary sampling — p=1 — ordinary sampling the key formulas are: top-k \boxed{|s|=k} top-p \boxed{ \min |s| \quad \text{s.t. } \sum_{i\in s}p_i\ge p } 2.4.33 a very powerful mental model imagine 100,000 vocabulary tokens. top-k says: "give me the best 50." no matter what the model thinks. top-p says: "give me enough of the best tokens to cover 90% of the probability mass." thus the second strategy asks the model's uncertainty to determine the candidate count. 2.4.34 connection to temperature now the whole picture becomes: low temperature distribution becomes sharp. top-p nucleus often becomes: \boxed{\text{small}} because a few tokens contain most of the probability. high temperature distribution becomes flatter. top-p nucleus often becomes: \boxed{\text{larger}} because more tokens are needed to reach the same probability mass. this is one reason temperature and top-p interact strongly. 2.4.35 top-p + sampling suppose after top-p we obtain: p'=[0.70,0.20,0.10]. top-p does not mean: \text{choose }0.70\text{ token}. instead we sample: y_t\sim p'. so: \boxed{ 70\%\rightarrow\text{first token} } 20\%\rightarrow\text{second} 10\%\rightarrow\text{third}. this maintains stochasticity. 2.4.36 top-p does not mean "top probability" another common misunderstanding: \boxed{ \text{top-p}\neq\text{pick the single token with highest probability}. } that would be greedy decoding. instead: \boxed{ \text{top-p defines the allowed candidate set}. } sampling then chooses from that set. 2.4.37 complete decoding pipeline we can now write the full process: \boxed{ \text{context} \rightarrow \text{transformer} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{temperature} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{top-p filtering} \rightarrow \text{renormalization} \rightarrow \text{sampling} \rightarrow \text{next token} } then: \boxed{ \text{append token} \rightarrow \text{run again}. } 2.4.38 numerical exam — level 1 given: p=[0.50,0.20,0.15,0.10,0.05] and: p=0.80. cumulative: 0.50 0.70 0.85. therefore: \boxed{3\text{ tokens}} are retained. retained mass: 0.85. renormalized: \boxed{ [0.5882,0.2353,0.1765,0,0]. } 2.4.39 numerical exam — level 2 given: p=[0.31,0.28,0.18,0.12,0.07,0.04] and: p=0.75. cumulative: 0.31 0.59 0.77. so retain: \boxed{3}. renormalization denominator: 0.77. therefore: p'_1=\frac{0.31}{0.77}\approx0.4026 p'_2=\frac{0.28}{0.77}\approx0.3636 p'_3=\frac{0.18}{0.77}\approx0.2338. thus: \boxed{ [0.4026,0.3636,0.2338,0,0,0]. } 2.4.40 numerical exam — level 3 given: p=[0.22,0.19,0.17,0.13,0.11,0.10,0.08]. take: p=0.80. cumulative: 0.22 0.41 0.58 0.71 0.82. thus: \boxed{5} tokens survive. renormalization denominator: 0.82. therefore: p' = \left[ \frac{0.22}{0.82}, \frac{0.19}{0.82}, \frac{0.17}{0.82}, \frac{0.13}{0.82}, \frac{0.11}{0.82} \right] \boxed{ \approx[0.2683,0.2317,0.2073,0.1585,0.1341]. } 2.4.41 numerical exam — level 4: compare two distributions use: p=0.90. distribution a [0.80,0.10,0.05,0.03,0.02] cumulative: 0.80 0.90 therefore: \boxed{2\text{ tokens}} survive. distribution b [0.30,0.25,0.20,0.10,0.08,0.07] cumulative: 0.30 0.55 0.75 0.85 0.93. therefore: \boxed{5\text{ tokens}} survive. same: p=0.90, different nucleus size. that is the core adaptive property of top-p. 2.4.42 numerical exam — level 5: temperature + top-p suppose the logits are: z=[4,3,2,1]. use: t=2,\qquad p=0.90. step 1 — temperature z/t=[2,1.5,1,0.5]. step 2 — softmax approximately: p=[0.4551,0.2760,0.1674,0.1015]. step 3 — sort already sorted. step 4 — cumulative 0.4551 0.7311 0.8985 1.0000. since: 0.8985<0.90, we must include the fourth token. thus: \boxed{ \text{nucleus size}=4. } this is exactly the sort of multi-step numerical question worth practicing because it combines: \boxed{ \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{temperature} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{cumulative probability} \rightarrow \text{top-p}. } 2.4.43 exam-level conceptual question question why can temperature change the top-p candidate set but not the positive-temperature top-k candidate set? answer for t>0 , temperature divides every logit by the same positive number, so ranking does not change: z_i>z_j \rightarrow \frac{z_i}{t}>\frac{z_j}{t}. therefore top-k membership remains unchanged. however, temperature changes the probability magnitudes after softmax. since top-p depends on the cumulative probability mass, changing those probabilities can change how many tokens are required to cross p . hence: \boxed{ \text{top-k depends on ranking} } while: \boxed{ \text{top-p depends on probability mass}. } 2.4.44 exam-level conceptual question why is top-p usually more adaptive than top-k? because the candidate count is not fixed. top-p chooses: \boxed{ \text{the smallest candidate set that covers a chosen probability mass}. } therefore the number of candidates can increase when the distribution becomes flatter and decrease when it becomes sharper. 2.4.45 another important connection — entropy we previously introduced entropy: h(p)=-\sum_ip_i\log p_i. high entropy means the distribution is relatively spread out. low entropy means it is concentrated. therefore, intuitively: \boxed{ \text{high entropy} \rightarrow \text{top-p may need more tokens} } while: \boxed{ \text{low entropy} \rightarrow \text{top-p may need fewer tokens}. } this is not an explicit additional formula in the decoding slide, but it follows directly from the cumulative-probability definition. 2.4.46 top-k and top-p together they can both be applied. for example: k=50 and: p=0.90. conceptually: limit to a maximum candidate pool with top-k. within that distribution, apply the nucleus threshold. sample. the exact order and implementation depend on the decoding system, so in an exam or source-specific question we should follow the stated procedure rather than assume a universal implementation. 2.4.47 what the slides recommend your decoding slides summarize the typical use cases as: tasks with one/few correct outputs → beam search is often used; tasks with many valid outputs such as chat, stories, brainstorming → temperature + top-k and/or top-p; exact reproducibility → greedy decoding. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) so top-p is part of the stochastic decoding family , not a replacement for beam search in every task. 2.4.48 the three most important equations so far temperature \boxed{ q_i(t)= \frac{e^{z_i/t}} {\sum_j e^{z_j/t}} } top-k \boxed{ s_k=\text{indices of the }k\text{ largest logits} } and: \boxed{ z_i'= -\infty \quad\text{for }i\notin s_k. } top-p \boxed{ v^{(p)} = \text{smallest set such that } \sum_{v\in v^{(p)}}q(v)\ge p. } these three equations represent three different controls: \boxed{ t=\text{reshape} } \boxed{ k=\text{fixed count} } \boxed{ p=\text{probability mass}. } 2.4.49 master comparison think of the decoder asking three different questions: temperature how sharply should i distribute probability? top-k how many of the highest-ranked candidates am i allowed to consider? top-p how much total probability mass should my candidate set contain? that is the conceptual foundation. 2.4.50 final numerical checklist for top-p when you see a top-p numerical in the exam, immediately do: \boxed{1.\ \text{sort probabilities descending}} \boxed{2.\ \text{compute cumulative sum}} \boxed{3.\ \text{stop at the first cumulative}\ge p} \boxed{4.\ \text{discard the rest}} \boxed{5.\ \text{renormalize}} \boxed{6.\ \text{sample from the new distribution}} do not stop merely because you are "close" to p . you stop only when: \boxed{\text{cumulative}\ge p}. 2.4.51 the whole decoding family we've built we can now see the progression clearly: \boxed{ \text{greedy} } choose: \arg\max_i p_i. then: \boxed{ \text{sampling} } choose randomly according to p . then: \boxed{ \text{temperature} } reshape p . then: \boxed{ \text{top-k} } remove everything except a fixed number of top candidates. then: \boxed{ \text{top-p} } remove everything outside an adaptive probability-mass nucleus. this builds the conceptual bridge to the next decoding topics. step 2.4 — one-page memory map \boxed{ \text{logits} } ↓ \boxed{\text{temperature}} z_i\rightarrow z_i/t ↓ \boxed{\text{softmax}} p_i=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} ↓ top-k \boxed{ \text{keep exactly }k\text{ highest} } ↓ top-p \boxed{ \text{keep smallest set with cumulative mass }\ge p } ↓ \boxed{\text{renormalize}} ↓ \boxed{\text{sample}} what you should now be able to answer without hesitation, you should be able to explain: \boxed{ \text{why top-p was introduced} } \boxed{ \text{how to calculate the nucleus} } \boxed{ \text{why cumulative probability can exceed }p } \boxed{ \text{why renormalization is required} } \boxed{ \text{why top-p has a variable candidate count} } \boxed{ \text{why temperature can alter top-p membership} } and especially: \boxed{ \text{top-k = fixed count} \qquad \text{top-p = cumulative probability mass} }

beam search operates on candidate sequences, while temperature/top-k/top-p operate on the next-token distribution. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) 2.5.1 first: what does the llm actually produce? suppose the current context is: the weather today is the transformer does not directly output: sunny instead, the final layer produces logits: \boxed{ z\in\mathbb{r}^{|v|} } where every vocabulary token has one logit. for example: token logit bright 3.0 sunny 2.5 cold 1.5 rainy 0.2 pizza -2.0 then: p=\operatorname{softmax}(z). the resulting distribution might be: p=[0.50,0.35,0.10,0.04,0.01]. this distribution is the raw decision space. everything we have studied is a different way of deciding what happens next. 2.5.2 the critical question at this point ask: do i want to choose one token immediately, or do i want to search through several possible future sequences? that separates the decoding world into two major families. family a — immediate next-token selection \boxed{ \text{greedy / sampling / temperature / top-k / top-p} } these operate primarily on the current next-token distribution. family b — sequence-level search \boxed{ \text{beam search} } beam search keeps multiple partial sequences alive and explores future continuations. this distinction is extremely important. 2.5.3 greedy decoding greedy decoding chooses: \boxed{ y_t=\arg\max_v p(y_t=v\mid y_{<t},x) } suppose: p= [0.50,0.35,0.15]. greedy chooses the: \boxed{0.50} token. then the token is appended. then the model runs again. so: context ↓ model ↓ probabilities ↓ argmax ↓ next token ↓ append ↓ repeat the source emphasizes that this is efficient and deterministic, but myopic: it optimizes the immediate decision rather than the overall sequence. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.4 why greedy can fail your slides give this exact idea with: p(\text{bright})=0.50 and: p(\text{sunny})=0.35. greedy says: \text{bright}. but suppose: p(\text{outside}\mid\text{bright})=0.50 while: p(\text{outside}\mid\text{sunny})=0.95. then: bright sequence p(\text{bright outside}) = 0.50\times0.50 = 0.25. sunny sequence p(\text{sunny outside}) = 0.35\times0.95 = 0.3325. therefore: \boxed{ 0.3325>0.25. } so the globally better sequence starts with the token that greedy rejected. the source explicitly uses this example to demonstrate greedy's myopia. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.5 sequence probability for a generated sequence: y=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_t), the probability is: \boxed{ p(y|x) = \prod_{t=1}^{t} p(y_t|y_{<t},x) } this comes from the chain rule. because multiplying many probabilities quickly creates very tiny values, we usually take logarithms: \boxed{ \log p(y|x) = \sum_{t=1}^{t} \log p(y_t|y_{<t},x) } the master cheatsheet uses exactly this sequence scoring formulation. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) 2.5.6 why log probability is better computationally suppose: p_1=0.8,\quad p_2=0.7,\quad p_3=0.9. sequence probability: 0.8\times0.7\times0.9 = 0.504. log probability: \log(0.8)+\log(0.7)+\log(0.9). approximately: -0.2231-0.3567-0.1054 = -0.6852. the two rankings are equivalent because log is monotonic: p_a>p_b \iff \log p_a>\log p_b. so beam search can safely compare: \boxed{\log p} instead of tiny probability products. the decoding slides explicitly mention log-probabilities for avoiding numerical underflow. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.7 beam search greedy keeps: \boxed{1} partial sequence. beam search keeps: \boxed{b} partial sequences. the integer: \boxed{b=\text{beam width}} controls how many hypotheses survive. your source describes the beam process as: start with an empty sequence. expand every retained sequence. score resulting candidates using sequence probability or log-probability. keep only the best b . repeat until candidates finish. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.8 why beam search helps suppose at step 1: p(\text{bright})=0.50 p(\text{sunny})=0.35 p(\text{cold})=0.15. greedy keeps only: \boxed{\text{bright}}. beam search with: b=2 keeps: \boxed{ \text{bright},\text{sunny} } and removes: \text{cold}. now at the next step, both are expanded. this gives the second hypothesis a chance to prove itself. 2.5.9 beam search worked example using the same distributions from your slide: step 1 token probability status bright 0.50 keep sunny 0.35 keep cold 0.15 prune because: b=2. step 2 suppose: p(\text{outside}\mid\text{bright})=0.50 p(\text{today}\mid\text{bright})=0.30 p(\text{again}\mid\text{bright})=0.20. for sunny: p(\text{outside}\mid\text{sunny})=0.95 p(\text{today}\mid\text{sunny})=0.03 p(\text{again}\mid\text{sunny})=0.02. now calculate every candidate. bright branch p(\text{bright outside}) = 0.50\times0.50 = 0.25 p(\text{bright today}) = 0.50\times0.30 = 0.15 p(\text{bright again}) = 0.50\times0.20 = 0.10 sunny branch p(\text{sunny outside}) = 0.35\times0.95 = 0.3325 p(\text{sunny today}) = 0.35\times0.03 = 0.0105 p(\text{sunny again}) = 0.35\times0.02 = 0.007. top two: \boxed{ 0.3325,\;0.25 } therefore final beams: \boxed{ \text{sunny outside} } and: \boxed{ \text{bright outside}. } the source gives this exact worked example. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.10 the special case b=1 if: b=1, only one sequence survives after every step. so: \boxed{ b=1\rightarrow\text{greedy decoding} } this is one of the most useful exam facts. 2.5.11 why raw sequence probability has a problem suppose candidate a has: 2 tokens, each with probability: 0.60. then: p(a)=0.60^2=0.36. candidate b has: 4 tokens, each with probability: 0.75. then: p(b)=0.75^4 \approx0.3164. raw probability says: \boxed{a>b} because: 0.36>0.3164. but b was more confident at every individual token . this exposes a length bias. the longer sequence is forced to multiply more numbers below 1. 2.5.12 length normalization your decoding slide introduces the google nmt length-normalization formulation from wu et al. define: \boxed{ lp(y)= \frac{(5+|y|)^\alpha} {(5+1)^\alpha} } and: \boxed{ s(y)= \frac{\log p(y)} {lp(y)} } where: |y| = sequence length, \alpha = strength of the length penalty. the slide notes that the reported useful range was around: \alpha\in[0.6,0.7]. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.13 why divide by length penalty? raw log probability becomes more negative as more tokens are added. for example: \log0.6\approx-0.5108. two such tokens: 2(-0.5108)=-1.0217. four 0.75 -probability tokens: 4\log0.75 = -1.1507. raw scoring says: -1.0217>-1.1507. so a wins. but length normalization changes the score. for: \alpha=0.6, the slide gives approximately: a lp(a)\approx1.0969 s(a)=\frac{-1.0217}{1.0969} \approx-0.9314. b lp(b)\approx1.2754 s(b)=\frac{-1.1507}{1.2754} \approx-0.9022. now: \boxed{ -0.9022>-0.9314 } so b wins. that exact inversion is shown in the slide. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.14 what is length normalization really doing? think of it as saying: "don't punish a sequence solely because it contains more tokens." it does not simply divide by: |y|. instead, the slide uses a smoother length penalty: \frac{(5+|y|)^\alpha}{6^\alpha}. so it partially compensates for the systematic decrease in raw sequence probability. 2.5.15 beam search + length normalization therefore, a better beam-search scoring pipeline is: \boxed{ \text{candidate sequence} \rightarrow \log p(y) \rightarrow lp(y) \rightarrow s(y)=\frac{\log p(y)}{lp(y)} } then rank beams using: \boxed{s(y)}. 2.5.16 the big difference between beam search and top-k this distinction is essential. top-k looks at the current vocabulary distribution : p(y_t|\text{context}) and says: keep the top k next-token candidates. beam search looks at multiple partial sequences : (y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_t) and says: keep the best b sequence hypotheses. so: \boxed{ k=\text{next-token candidate count} } while: \boxed{ b=\text{sequence hypothesis count} } do not confuse k and b . 2.5.17 sampling now return to stochastic generation. sampling means: \boxed{ y_t\sim p(\cdot|y_{<t},x) } instead of: \arg\max. suppose: p=[0.6,0.3,0.1]. over many independent draws: first token appears roughly 60% of the time, second roughly 30%, third roughly 10%. this introduces diversity. the source notes that sampling can break deterministic loops and produce multiple plausible continuations. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) 2.5.18 temperature is not sampling this distinction is critical. temperature: \boxed{ z_i\rightarrow z_i/t } changes the distribution. sampling: \boxed{ y_t\sim p } actually introduces randomness. therefore: \boxed{ t=0 \rightarrow \text{greedy} } in the implementations described by your sources, while: t>0 normally means scale logits and then sample. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 2.5.19 top-k + temperature now combine: \boxed{ \text{top-k}+\text{temperature}+\text{sampling}. } this is the exact combination implemented in raschka's generation function. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) the source implementation effectively does: model ↓ last-position logits ↓ top-k filter ↓ temperature scaling ↓ softmax ↓ multinomial sampling ↓ next token then append and repeat. 2.5.20 let's follow the actual code logic the source generation function does: logits = model(idx_cond) logits = logits[:, -1, :] the second line means: we only care about the model's distribution for the next token , which corresponds to the final sequence position. then: torch.topk(...) performs top-k filtering. then: logits = logits / temperature performs temperature scaling. then: probs = torch.softmax(...) converts the filtered logits into probabilities. then: torch.multinomial(...) samples the next token. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 2.5.21 complete next-token mathematical pipeline we can write the source logic as: z_t=f_\theta(y_{<t}) then top-k masking: \tilde z_{t,i} = \begin{cases} z_{t,i},&i\in s_k\\ -\infty,&i\notin s_k \end{cases} then temperature: \hat z_{t,i} = \frac{\tilde z_{t,i}}{t} then: p(y_t=i) = \frac{e^{\hat z_{t,i}}} {\sum_j e^{\hat z_{t,j}}} then: \boxed{ y_t\sim p. } then: y_{<t+1} = (y_{<t},y_t). and repeat. 2.5.22 where does top-p fit? top-p performs a different type of filtering. instead of: |s|=k, it constructs: s_p such that: \boxed{ \sum_{i\in s_p}p_i\ge p } with s_p minimal. so a combined stochastic decoder can use: \boxed{ \text{temperature + top-k} } or: \boxed{ \text{temperature + top-p} } or, depending on the system: \boxed{ \text{top-k + top-p + temperature}. } your decoding slides recommend temperature plus top-k and/or top-p for tasks such as chat, stories, and brainstorming. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.23 repetition penalty there is another control in your master cheatsheet: \boxed{\text{repetition penalty}} the purpose is different from top-k/top-p. top-k/top-p says: remove low-ranked candidates. repetition penalty says: make already-generated tokens less attractive. your master cheatsheet summarizes the slide formulation as: \boxed{ z_i\leftarrow\frac{z_i}{\theta} \quad\text{for previously seen tokens, with }\theta>1 } before softmax. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) correction: dividing a negative repeated logit by theta>1 increases it. the supplied rule suppresses positive logits; sign-aware implementations multiply negative logits instead. complete grounded review 2.5.24 why does this reduce repetition? suppose two candidate tokens have: z_a=4 and: z_b=2. suppose a already appeared. take: \theta=2. then: z_a'=\frac42=2. while: z_b'=2. now they tie. before penalty: 4>2. after penalty: 2=2. so a's advantage has been reduced. thus: \boxed{ \theta>1 \rightarrow \text{previously seen tokens receive reduced logits under this slide formulation}. } 2.5.25 repetition penalty vs top-k these solve different problems. repetition penalty changes the score of certain tokens based on history . top-k changes which tokens remain eligible based on current rank . top-p changes which tokens remain eligible based on current probability mass . therefore: \boxed{ \text{history-based control} \neq \text{distribution truncation}. } 2.5.26 a full combined numerical let's create an exam-style question. suppose the current logits are: z=[5,4,2,0]. token 1 has already appeared. use: \theta=2, t=2, k=3. we will follow the conceptual order: \text{repetition penalty} \rightarrow \text{top-k} \rightarrow \text{temperature} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{sample}. step 1 — repetition penalty token 1: 5/2=2.5. other logits unchanged: 4,\;2,\;0. thus: z'=[2.5,4,2,0]. step 2 — top-3 the top three are: 4,\;2.5,\;2. so: z''=[2.5,4,2,-\infty]. step 3 — temperature divide by: t=2. [1.25,2,1,-\infty]. step 4 — softmax subtract the max 2: [-0.75,0,-1]. exponentials: [e^{-0.75},1,e^{-1}] \approx[0.4724,1,0.3679]. total: 1.8403. therefore: p_1\approx0.2567 p_2\approx0.5434 p_3\approx0.1999 p_4=0. final distribution: \boxed{ [0.2567,\;0.5434,\;0.1999,\;0]. } this example shows three different mechanisms acting sequentially. 2.5.27 what if we had no repetition penalty? original: z=[5,4,2,0]. top 3: [5,4,2,-\infty]. temperature t=2 : [2.5,2,1,-\infty]. softmax: \approx[0.5465,0.3315,0.1220,0]. with repetition penalty: [0.2567,0.5434,0.1999,0]. the previously seen first token loses its dominance. that is exactly what the penalty is intended to do. 2.5.28 important caveat about repetition penalty the exact repetition-penalty implementation can vary across libraries and systems. for this course, use the formulation given in your supplied slides/cheatsheet: \boxed{ z_i/\theta,\qquad \theta>1 } for previously seen tokens. do not silently substitute another library's exact variant into a source-specific numerical question. 2.5.29 now the entire decoding decision tree suppose the model produces: \boxed{z\in\mathbb{r}^{|v|}}. you need to decide what the task requires. case 1 — exact reproducibility use: \boxed{\text{greedy}} as the deterministic baseline. your slides explicitly associate greedy decoding with debugging/evaluation when exact reproducibility is desired. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) case 2 — need a strong sequence among a few plausible outputs use: \boxed{\text{beam search}} often with: \boxed{\text{length normalization}}. the slides associate this with translation, summarization, and code-style tasks where there may be one or a few good outputs. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) case 3 — many valid outputs use: \boxed{ \text{sampling} } possibly with: \boxed{\text{temperature + top-k/top-p}}. this is the slide's recommendation for chat, stories, and brainstorming. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.30 the most important conceptual split memorize this diagram: llm logits │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ │ │ next-token control sequence search │ │ ┌───────┼─────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ greedy temperature top-k/p beam search │ │ sampling length normalization this is the clean mental model for the whole decoding chapter. 2.5.31 numerical comparison — greedy vs beam suppose: step 1 p(a)=0.6,\qquad p(b)=0.4. step 2 p(x|a)=0.5 p(x|b)=0.95. greedy chooses a. then: p(ax)=0.6\times0.5=0.30. but: p(bx)=0.4\times0.95=0.38. so: \boxed{ b x } is better. beam width: b=2 can retain both a and b and discover this. beam width: b=1 cannot. 2.5.32 numerical comparison — top-k vs top-p suppose: p=[0.50,0.20,0.15,0.10,0.05]. top-k, k=2 retain: \boxed{2} tokens. top-p, p=0.80 cumulative: 0.50,\;0.70,\;0.85. therefore retain: \boxed{3} tokens. so: \boxed{ k=2\rightarrow2\text{ candidates} } but: \boxed{ p=0.80\rightarrow3\text{ candidates}. } 2.5.33 numerical comparison — same distribution, different p suppose: p=[0.50,0.20,0.15,0.10,0.05]. p=0.50 the first token already reaches the threshold. \boxed{1} candidate. p=0.70 first two: 0.50+0.20=0.70. \boxed{2} candidates. p=0.85 first three: 0.85. \boxed{3} candidates. p=0.95 first four: 0.95. \boxed{4} candidates. thus: \boxed{ \text{increasing }p \rightarrow \text{typically increasing candidate set}. } 2.5.34 numerical comparison — why temperature is different take logits: z=[4,3,2]. at: t=1: p\approx[0.6652,0.2447,0.0900]. at: t=2: p\approx[0.5065,0.3072,0.1863]. all three candidates still exist. so temperature does not perform hard filtering. it only redistributes mass: \boxed{ \text{temperature = soft control}. } 2.5.35 numerical comparison — top-k is hard control same distribution: [0.6652,0.2447,0.0900]. take: k=2. then: [0.6652,0.2447,0] and renormalize: \frac{0.6652}{0.9099}\approx0.7311 \frac{0.2447}{0.9099}\approx0.2689. so final: \boxed{ [0.7311,0.2689,0]. } a token has gone from: 0.09 to: \boxed{0}. that's the defining hard cutoff. 2.5.36 numerical exam — full sequence scoring suppose two candidate sequences are: a=(a_1,a_2,a_3) with probabilities: 0.8,\;0.5,\;0.9 and: b=(b_1,b_2) with probabilities: 0.7,\;0.95. compute sequence probabilities. a p(a)=0.8\times0.5\times0.9 = 0.36. b p(b)=0.7\times0.95 = 0.665. so: \boxed{b>a}. this reminds us that beam search scores complete or partial sequences jointly rather than just comparing their latest tokens. correction: ln(.665)=-.4079682383; four-decimal rounding is -.4080, rather than -.4072. complete grounded review 2.5.37 numerical exam — log probability for: p(a)=0.36 we get: \log p(a)\approx-1.0217. for: p(b)=0.665 we get: \log p(b)\approx-0.4072. since: -0.4072>-1.0217, b remains the better sequence. 2.5.38 numerical exam — length normalization suppose: |a|=2,\qquad |b|=4 and: \log p(a)=-1.0217, \log p(b)=-1.1507. take: \alpha=0.6. use: lp(y)=\frac{(5+|y|)^{0.6}}{6^{0.6}}. then approximately: lp(a)=1.0969 lp(b)=1.2754. scores: s(a)=\frac{-1.0217}{1.0969}\approx-0.9314 s(b)=\frac{-1.1507}{1.2754}\approx-0.9022. therefore: \boxed{b\text{ wins after normalization}.} this exact numerical pattern comes from the decoding slide. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.39 what an exam question might actually look like a typical mixed question could say: a model outputs logits [5,4,2,0,-1] . apply temperature t=2 , retain top-3 candidates, and sample from the resulting distribution. the correct reasoning is: step 1 select top-3: 5,4,2. step 2 mask: [5,4,2,-\infty,-\infty]. step 3 temperature: [2.5,2,1,-\infty,-\infty]. step 4 softmax: \boxed{ [0.5465,0.3315,0.1220,0,0] } approximately. step 5 sampling occurs from exactly those three tokens. this is the kind of multi-stage numerical that you should now be able to solve mechanically. 2.5.40 another mixed exam question the model probabilities are [0.55,0.20,0.10,0.08,0.07] . apply top-p with p=0.80 , then renormalize. cumulative: 0.55 0.75 0.85. therefore keep 3 tokens. normalize by: 0.85. final: \boxed{ [0.6471,\;0.2353,\;0.1176,\;0,\;0]. } 2.5.41 another mixed exam question why could top-p retain 3 tokens in one context and 30 in another, even with the same p=0.9 ? because: \boxed{ p } controls cumulative probability mass rather than candidate count. a sharply concentrated distribution reaches 0.9 quickly. a flat distribution requires many tokens to reach 0.9. 2.5.42 another mixed exam question which strategy is better when exact reproducibility is required? from your slides: \boxed{\text{greedy decoding}} because it is deterministic. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.43 another mixed exam question which strategy is more appropriate when many different outputs can be valid? the source guidance is: \boxed{ \text{sampling with temperature + top-k/top-p} } for tasks such as chat, storytelling, and brainstorming. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.44 another mixed exam question why is beam search often paired with length normalization? because: \boxed{ \text{raw sequence probability decreases as more token probabilities are multiplied}. } without normalization, longer candidates can be unfairly penalized merely because they contain more factors below 1. the source explicitly motivates the length penalty this way. (source: decoding-sampling-slides) 2.5.45 one subtle but very important distinction you should now distinguish: model quality the model produces: p(y_t|y_{<t},x). decoder policy the decoder decides: \boxed{\text{what to do with that distribution}.} therefore: \boxed{ \text{decoder }\neq\text{ model}. } the same model can generate very different outputs depending on: t,\;k,\;p,\;b, and other decoding controls. 2.5.46 complete pipeline for deterministic decoding greedy \boxed{ z \rightarrow \arg\max \rightarrow y_t } no stochastic sampling. 2.5.47 complete pipeline for stochastic decoding temperature + top-k \boxed{ z \rightarrow topk \rightarrow z/t \rightarrow softmax \rightarrow multinomial \rightarrow y_t } raschka's generation code directly implements this form. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 2.5.48 complete pipeline for nucleus sampling \boxed{ z \rightarrow temperature \rightarrow softmax \rightarrow sort \rightarrow cumulative\ sum \rightarrow topp \rightarrow renormalize \rightarrow sample } 2.5.49 complete pipeline for beam search \boxed{ z_1 \rightarrow \text{candidate sequences} \rightarrow \text{score} \rightarrow \text{prune} \rightarrow z_2 \rightarrow \text{expand again} \rightarrow\cdots } with: \boxed{ s(y)=\log p(y)/lp(y) } when length normalization is used. 2.5.50 your decoding master table method works on deterministic? main control greedy current distribution yes highest probability sampling current distribution no random draw temperature distribution depends on sampling sharpness top-k current distribution depends on sampling fixed candidate count top-p current distribution depends on sampling probability mass beam search partial sequences usually yes beam width b length normalization sequence score — correct length bias repetition penalty history-conditioned logits depends on decoder reduce repetition the first six are directly covered by the supplied decoding material; repetition penalty is also summarized in the master cheatsheet. (source: decoding-sampling-slides; master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) 2.5.51 the five numerical patterns you must master at this point, your exam preparation should automatically recognize these five patterns. pattern 1 — temperature z\rightarrow z/t\rightarrow softmax. pattern 2 — top-k \text{rank}\rightarrow\text{keep }k\rightarrow-\infty\rightarrow softmax. pattern 3 — top-p \text{sort probabilities}\rightarrow \text{cumulative}\rightarrow \ge p\rightarrow \text{renormalize}. pattern 4 — beam \text{expand}\rightarrow \text{multiply/log-sum}\rightarrow \text{keep top }b. pattern 5 — length normalization \boxed{ s(y)= \frac{\log p(y)} {(5+|y|)^\alpha/6^\alpha} } 2.5.52 exam trap summary trap 1 top-k is not : \text{top }k\%\text{ vocabulary}. it is: \boxed{k\text{ tokens}}. trap 2 top-p is not : p\%\text{ vocabulary}. it is: \boxed{\text{probability mass }p}. trap 3 top-p cumulative sum does not have to equal exactly p . it must first become: \boxed{\ge p}. trap 4 temperature does not remove tokens. \boxed{ t=\text{distribution reshape} } trap 5 top-k does not choose the final token. it restricts the sampling set. trap 6 beam width b is not top-k k . \boxed{ b=\text{number of sequences} } \boxed{ k=\text{number of next-token candidates} } trap 7 raw sequence probability and length-normalized score are not the same. 2.5.53 final mental model think of the model as saying: "here are the possibilities." then the decoder asks: greedy which one is best right now? sampling let's draw one according to the probabilities. temperature how sharply should i favor the likely choices? top-k only let the best k choices participate. top-p let enough high-probability choices participate to cover probability mass p . beam keep several possible futures alive and compare their sequence scores. length normalization don't let sequence length unfairly dominate beam scoring. repetition penalty reduce the attractiveness of tokens that have already appeared. that is the complete conceptual map. 2.5.54 numerical master test before leaving decoding, these are the kinds of questions you should be able to solve. q1. given logits and t , calculate softmax. q2. given logits and k , identify the retained candidates and calculate the filtered softmax. q3. given probabilities and p , construct the nucleus and renormalize. q4. given two candidate sequences, calculate: p(y) and: \log p(y). q5. compare two beam candidates using: lp(y) and: s(y). q6. explain why: b=1 reduces beam search to greedy. q7. explain why positive temperature preserves ranking. q8. explain why temperature can change top-p membership. q9. combine: \text{repetition penalty + top-k + temperature + softmax}. q10. given a task description, choose: \boxed{\text{greedy / beam / sampling / top-k / top-p}} and justify the choice. 2.5.55 decoding section status at this point we have covered: \boxed{\text{2.1 decoding basics}} \boxed{\text{2.2 temperature}} \boxed{\text{2.3 top-k}} \boxed{\text{2.4 top-p}} \boxed{\text{2.5 combined decoding + beam scoring + length normalization + repetition control}} the supplied decoding slides explicitly present these methods together as a family of alternative decoding strategies and emphasize that there is no single best decoder for every task . """small deterministic decoding examples; python standard library only.""" import math def softmax(logits, temperature=1.0): if not logits or not all(math.isfinite(z) for z in logits): raise valueerror('logits must be a nonempty finite vector.') if not math.isfinite(temperature) or temperature <= 0: raise valueerror('use an explicit greedy branch for temperature zero.') scaled = [z / temperature for z in logits] peak = max(scaled) values = [math.exp(z - peak) for z in scaled] return [v / sum(values) for v in values] def renormalize(p, indices): total = sum(p[i] for i in indices) if not total: raise valueerror('the retained set must have positive mass.') return [p[i] / total if i in indices else 0.0 for i in range(len(p))] def validate_probabilities(p): if not p or not all(math.isfinite(x) and x >= 0 for x in p): raise valueerror('probabilities must be nonempty, finite, and nonnegative.') if not math.isclose(sum(p), 1.0, abs_tol=1e-9): raise valueerror('probabilities must sum to one.') def min_p(p, base): validate_probabilities(p) if not 0 < base <= 1: raise valueerror('base must be in (0, 1].') threshold = base * max(p) keep = [i for i, prob in enumerate(p) if prob >= threshold] return threshold, keep, renormalize(p, keep) def top_p(p, target): validate_probabilities(p) if not 0 < target <= 1: raise valueerror('target must be in (0, 1].') keep, total = [], 0.0 for i in sorted(range(len(p)), key=lambda i: (-p[i], i)): keep.append(i) total += p[i] if total >= target: break return keep, renormalize(p, keep) def repetition_penalty(logits, seen, penalty): if penalty <= 0: raise valueerror('penalty must be positive.') return [(z / penalty if z >= 0 else z * penalty) if i in seen else z for i, z in enumerate(logits)] def main(): # toy distributions, chosen to make every retained token inspectable. peaked = [0.80, 0.07, 0.05, 0.04, 0.03, 0.01] flat = [0.22, 0.20, 0.18, 0.16, 0.14, 0.10] assert min_p(peaked, 0.1)[1] == [0] assert len(min_p(flat, 0.1)[1]) == 6 assert len(top_p(peaked, 0.9)[0]) == 3 assert len(top_p(flat, 0.9)[0]) == 5 tied = [0.5, 0.5] assert min_p(tied, 1.0)[1] == [0, 1] logits = [1.2, 0.8, 2.0, 0.3] before, after = softmax(logits), softmax(repetition_penalty(logits, {1}, 1.5)) assert after[1] < before[1] assert repetition_penalty([-2.0, 1.0], {0}, 1.5)[0] == -3.0 p = [0.7, 0.2, 0.1] entropy = -sum(x * math.log(x) for x in p) typical_order = sorted(range(len(p)), key=lambda i: abs(-math.log(p[i]) - entropy)) print('min-p peaked:', min_p(peaked, 0.1)) print('min-p flat:', min_p(flat, 0.1)) print('cat probability:', round(before[1], 4), '->', round(after[1], 4)) print('typicality order:', typical_order, 'entropy:', round(entropy, 4)) if __name__ == '__main__': (source: peft-slides) 3.1.1 start with a pretrained llm suppose we have a pretrained model: f_	heta(x) where: 	heta=\{w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_l\} represents all learned parameters. the model has already learned general language structure from large-scale pretraining. for example, imagine a pretrained llm understands: grammar, syntax, general facts, language patterns, long-range dependencies. now we want to specialize it for:  oxed{	ext{medical classification}} or:  oxed{	ext{spam detection}} or:  oxed{	ext{instruction following}}. we have a smaller task-specific dataset: d=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}. 3.1.2 what does fine-tuning actually do? during fine-tuning, we calculate the task loss:  oxed{ l(	heta) } and use backpropagation to determine how each parameter should change. for a parameter matrix w :  oxed{ \delta w } represents the desired update. ordinary gradient descent is conceptually:  oxed{ w' = w-\eta
abla_w l } where: w = pretrained weights, l = loss, 
abla_w l = gradient of the loss with respect to w , \eta = learning rate, w' = updated weight matrix. so full fine-tuning means:  oxed{ 	ext{every trainable weight gets updated}. } 3.1.3 the important problem suppose the llm contains: 7	ext{ billion parameters}. full fine-tuning says:  oxed{ 	ext{train all 7 billion}. } even though the task-specific dataset may be relatively small. this creates a huge computational and storage burden. the peft slides specifically motivate peft because storing and updating gradients for every parameter of a multi-billion-parameter model can make fine-tuning impractical on a single consumer gpu. (source: peft-slides) 3.1.4 what does "trainable" actually mean? a parameter is trainable if:  oxed{ 	ext{gradient is computed for it and optimizer can update it}. } for full fine-tuning:  oxed{ 	ext{almost/all pretrained parameters are trainable}. } for peft:  oxed{ 	ext{most pretrained parameters are frozen} } and only a small set is trained. the peft slides describe this as often training under 1% of the model's parameters while keeping the rest frozen. (source: peft-slides) 3.1.5 frozen vs trainable imagine: 	heta= \{w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4,w_5\}. full fine-tuning w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4,w_5 all update. peft we might have: w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4,w_5 frozen and introduce a small trainable component: \phi. then:  oxed{ 	heta_{	ext{base}} 	ext{ is frozen} } while:  oxed{ \phi 	ext{ is trainable}. } the model becomes conceptually: f_{	heta,\phi}(x) where:  oxed{ 	heta=	ext{large frozen base} } and:  oxed{ \phi=	ext{small trainable adaptation}. } 3.1.6 why not simply train a smaller model? this is an important conceptual question. suppose you already have a powerful pretrained model. its millions or billions of parameters contain useful general knowledge. the peft idea is: don't throw away that pretrained knowledge or rebuild it from scratch. keep the base model and learn a small task-specific modification. so we want:  oxed{ 	ext{retain general knowledge} + 	ext{learn small task-specific change}. } this is the fundamental motivation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. 3.1.7 the four peft families in your slides your peft slides divide peft methods into four families. (source: peft-slides) 1. additive introduce new trainable modules. example:  oxed{	ext{adapters}} the original model remains mostly frozen, while a small bottleneck module is trained. 2. selective train only a subset of existing parameters. example:  oxed{	ext{bitfit}} where only bias terms are trained. 3. reparameterization represent the weight update in a compressed form. example:  oxed{	ext{lora}} this is our main focus. 4. soft-prompt add trainable vectors to the input or activations. examples:  oxed{	ext{prompt tuning}} and:  oxed{	ext{prefix tuning}}. the important point is that all four share the same broad goal:  oxed{ 	ext{adapt the model without updating the full base model}. } 3.1.8 full fine-tuning vs peft let's make the contrast mathematically. suppose the model has: n_	heta parameters. full fine-tuning trainable parameters:  oxed{ n_{	ext{train}}=n_	heta } peft trainable parameters:  oxed{ n_{	ext{train}}\ll n_	heta. } often:  oxed{ n_{	ext{train}}<1\%	imes n_	heta } according to the peft lecture's characterization. (source: peft-slides) 3.1.9 numerical example — 7b model suppose: n_	heta=7,000,000,000. for full fine-tuning:  oxed{ 7,000,000,000 } parameters are trainable. now suppose a peft method trains: 0.1\% of the model. calculate: 7,000,000,000	imes0.001 = 7,000,000. so:  oxed{ 7	ext{ million trainable parameters} } instead of:  oxed{ 7	ext{ billion}. } reduction factor:  rac{7,000,000,000}{7,000,000} =  oxed{1000}. so the trainable parameter count is reduced by:  oxed{1000	imes}. 3.1.10 important: fewer trainable parameters does not mean smaller base model this is a common misconception. suppose: n_	heta=7b. and: n_{	ext{adapter}}=7m. the model is still fundamentally a:  oxed{7b	ext{-parameter base model}}. we are just training:  oxed{7m} additional/task-specific parameters. so:  oxed{ 	ext{parameter-efficient training} 
eq 	ext{parameter-free inference}. } 3.1.11 what is actually saved? peft reduces the amount of trainable state . the peft slides emphasize that full fine-tuning requires gradients and optimizer-related training state for the full parameter set, while peft keeps most pretrained weights untouched. (source: peft-slides) so the major benefit is:  oxed{ 	ext{less training memory and computation}. } it also makes it much easier to create multiple task-specific versions. 3.1.12 multiple customers example imagine we have one base model: w_0. suppose we want specialized versions for: 	ext{customer a} 	ext{customer b} 	ext{customer c}. full fine-tuning we might store: w_a w_b w_c. each is a complete model copy. peft instead, keep: w_0 once, and store: \phi_a,\quad\phi_b,\quad\phi_c. then: f_a=f(w_0,\phi_a) f_b=f(w_0,\phi_b) f_c=f(w_0,\phi_c). the raschka appendix specifically highlights this advantage: keeping lora matrices separate allows multiple customized versions without storing multiple complete llm copies. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) this becomes extremely useful in multi-customer or multi-task deployment. 3.1.13 numerical example — storage suppose: w_0=7b	ext{ parameters}. imagine a specialized adapter contains: 10m trainable parameters. if we use 16-bit values: 2	ext{ bytes/parameter}. full model 7b	imes2 = 14b	ext{ bytes}. approximately:  oxed{14	ext{ gb}} using decimal gb. adapter 10m	imes2 = 20m	ext{ bytes} approximately:  oxed{20	ext{ mb}}. this illustrates why task-specific adapter storage can be dramatically smaller. this storage comparison is a derived numerical illustration; the supplied sources establish the architectural advantage, not this particular 7b/10m example. 3.1.14 but why should a tiny update be enough? this is the key question. suppose a weight matrix is: w\in\mathbb{r}^{d	imes d_{	ext{out}}}. full fine-tuning learns: \delta w with: d	imes d_{	ext{out}} free entries. that is potentially a huge number of independent changes. peft asks: do we actually need arbitrary changes in every direction? lora's answer is:  oxed{	ext{perhaps not}.} many task-specific adaptations may be approximated using a much smaller number of effective directions. that brings us directly to:  oxed{	ext{rank}} and:  oxed{	ext{low-rank updates}}. 3.1.15 before lora, we need rank your peft slides explicitly introduce rank before lora. (source: peft-slides) for a matrix: m, the rank is:  oxed{ 	ext{number of linearly independent rows} } which is equivalently the number of linearly independent columns. your source emphasizes the idea as: how much genuinely new information the matrix contains. a row that is merely a multiple or linear combination of existing rows does not add a new independent direction. (source: peft-slides) 3.1.18 why is rank relevant to fine-tuning? suppose: w_0 is a pretrained matrix. full fine-tuning gives: w'=w_0+\delta w. here: \delta w could be a full-rank matrix. lora instead tries to constrain:  oxed{ \delta w } to have low rank. conceptually:  oxed{ 	ext{full update} ightarrow 	ext{potentially huge number of directions} } versus:  oxed{ 	ext{low-rank update} ightarrow 	ext{small number of important directions}. } raschka describes lora precisely as restricting model adjustments to a lower-dimensional subspace and aiming to capture influential directions of the weight changes. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 3.2.7 a tiny numerical example let's use something we can calculate by hand. take: b= \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} and: a= \begin{bmatrix} 3&4&5 \end{bmatrix}. shapes: b:2\times1 a:1\times3. therefore: ba has shape: 2\times3. calculate: ba= \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3&4&5 \end{bmatrix}. multiply each element of b by the whole row a : \boxed{ ba= \begin{bmatrix} 3&4&5\\ 6&8&10 \end{bmatrix} } notice something: r_2=2r_1. therefore: \boxed{ \operatorname{rank}(ba)=1. } and that is exactly what we expected because: r=1. 3.2.8 why rank cannot exceed r this is the mathematical heart of lora. we have: b\in\mathbb{r}^{d\times r} and: a\in\mathbb{r}^{r\times d_{\text{out}}}. their product passes information through an r -dimensional intermediate space. therefore: \boxed{ \operatorname{rank}(ba)\le r. } this relationship appears explicitly in your master mathematical cheatsheet. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs) so if: r=4, the update can have rank at most: \boxed{4}. it cannot become rank 5, 100, or 4096. 3.2.9 why does this save parameters? the full matrix contains: d\,d_{\text{out}} parameters. the factors contain: dr for b , and: rd_{\text{out}} for a . therefore: \boxed{ n_{\text{lora}} = dr+rd_{\text{out}} = r(d+d_{\text{out}}) } as given in the master cheatsheet. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs) 3.2.10 derive the parameter formula yourself suppose: b\in\mathbb{r}^{d\times r}. number of entries: d\times r. suppose: a\in\mathbb{r}^{r\times d_{\text{out}}}. number of entries: r\times d_{\text{out}}. add: dr+rd_{\text{out}}. factor r : \boxed{ r(d+d_{\text{out}}). } that is why you do not need to memorize where it comes from. 3.2.11 numerical parameter count suppose: d=1024, \qquad d_{\text{out}}=1024, \qquad r=8. full update: 1024\times1024 = \boxed{1,048,576}. lora: 8(1024+1024) =8(2048) =\boxed{16,384}. reduction: \frac{1,048,576}{16,384} = \boxed{64}. so lora uses: \boxed{64\times} fewer trainable parameters for this matrix. 3.2.12 why the reduction becomes huge when r\ll d for a square matrix: d_{\text{out}}=d. then: n_{\text{full}}=d^2 and: n_{\text{lora}}=2dr. therefore: \text{reduction factor} = \frac{d^2}{2dr} = \boxed{\frac{d}{2r}}. so if: d=4096,\quad r=8, then: \frac{4096}{16} = \boxed{256}. this is the exact example from your peft lecture. (source: peft-slides) 3.2.13 now look at the forward pass this is where the matrix factorization becomes even more intuitive. we have: h = x\left(w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba\right). by the distributive law: \boxed{ h=xw_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}xba. } we can associate the multiplications as: \boxed{ h=xw_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb)a. } this is computationally useful because: x first passes through the small matrix b , then through a . 3.2.14 shape of the forward pass suppose: x\in\mathbb{r}^{n\times d}. then: b\in\mathbb{r}^{d\times r}. so: xb has shape: \boxed{ n\times r. } then: a\in\mathbb{r}^{r\times d_{\text{out}}}. therefore: (xb)a has shape: \boxed{ n\times d_{\text{out}}. } exactly what we need to add to: xw_0. 3.2.15 tiny forward numerical let's take: x= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2 \end{bmatrix} so: x:1\times2. take: b= \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} so: b:2\times1. and: a= \begin{bmatrix} 3&4 \end{bmatrix} so: a:1\times2. first: xb = [1\;\;2] \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = 1+4 = [5]. then: (xb)a = [5] \begin{bmatrix} 3&4 \end{bmatrix} = \boxed{ [15,\;20]. } so a low-rank transformation has converted a 2-dimensional input into a 2-dimensional output through: \boxed{2\rightarrow1\rightarrow2}. 3.2.16 compare direct full update a full update could have been: \delta w= \begin{bmatrix} a&b\\ c&d \end{bmatrix}. then: x\delta w could produce any arbitrary 2-dimensional output. with rank-1 lora: \delta w=ba, the update is restricted to a rank-1 structure. so lora trades: \boxed{\text{full flexibility}} for: \boxed{\text{parameter efficiency}}. that is the fundamental tradeoff. 3.2.17 why can a low-rank update still be useful? this is the intuition emphasized in the raschka appendix: lora assumes task-specific changes can often be captured effectively in a lower-dimensional subspace, allowing the model to focus on influential directions rather than learning an unrestricted update for every weight. so the base model already contains a large amount of useful structure. the task-specific adaptation does not necessarily need to redesign everything. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{large pretrained knowledge} + \text{small task-specific correction} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{rewrite the entire model}. } 3.2.18 a crucial point: ba is large, even though a and b are small this often confuses students. suppose: b=4096\times8 and: a=8\times4096. both are relatively small. but their product: ba is: 4096\times4096. so: \boxed{ ba\text{ has the full weight shape}. } the savings come because we store and train a and b rather than storing a free full-rank \delta w . we do not need to maintain ba as a separate trainable parameter matrix. 3.2.19 think of ba as an implicit matrix instead of learning: \delta w= \begin{bmatrix} \text{millions of independent values} \end{bmatrix}, we learn: b,\;a. then: \boxed{ \delta w=ba } is generated from those factors. that is why this is called a reparameterization approach in the peft taxonomy. (source: peft-slides) 3.2.20 why the rank is a capacity knob consider: r=1. then: \operatorname{rank}(\delta w)\le1. very restrictive. now: r=8. then: \operatorname{rank}(\delta w)\le8. more expressive. now: r=64. then: \operatorname{rank}(\delta w)\le64. more expressive again, but more trainable parameters. thus: \boxed{ r\uparrow \rightarrow \text{capacity}\uparrow } and: \boxed{ r\uparrow \rightarrow \text{trainable parameters}\uparrow. } the source explicitly describes r as the balance between adaptability and efficiency. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 3.2.21 numerical — rank vs parameter count take: d=d_{\text{out}}=4096. then: n_{\text{lora}}=8192r. r trainable parameters 1 8,192 2 16,384 4 32,768 8 65,536 16 131,072 32 262,144 64 524,288 so doubling rank doubles parameter count. 3.2.22 numerical — maximum rank suppose: b\in\mathbb{r}^{100\times4} and: a\in\mathbb{r}^{4\times200}. then: ba\in\mathbb{r}^{100\times200}. what is the maximum possible rank? because: \boxed{r=4}, we have: \boxed{ \operatorname{rank}(ba)\le4. } even though the resulting matrix contains: 100\times200=20,000 entries, its rank can be at most 4. this is the essence of low-rank structure. 3.2.23 numerical — can a rank-2 update be full rank? suppose: \delta w=ba with: b\in\mathbb{r}^{100\times2} and: a\in\mathbb{r}^{2\times100}. then: \operatorname{rank}(\delta w)\le2. but a 100\times100 full-rank matrix has rank: 100. therefore: \boxed{ \text{no. a rank-2 lora update cannot be full rank}. } 3.2.24 rank is not the number of parameters this is an important exam trap. suppose: ba\in\mathbb{r}^{4096\times4096} with: r=8. then the matrix contains: 16,777,216 entries. but: \operatorname{rank}(ba)\le8. so: \boxed{ \text{matrix size}\neq\text{matrix rank}. } and: \boxed{ \text{rank}\neq\text{number of trainable parameters}. } they are different concepts. 3.2.25 now introduce the scaling factor \alpha your peft slides use: \boxed{ w'=w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba } rather than simply: w_0+ba. why? because we want a way to control the strength of the lora contribution . the source describes \alpha as a fixed scaling factor controlling how strongly the adaptation affects the original layer output. (source: peft-slides; build a large language model (from scratch)) 3.2.26 what does \alpha/r do? define: \boxed{ s=\frac{\alpha}{r}. } then: w'=w_0+sba. so: s simply controls the magnitude of the low-rank update. for example: r=8,\quad\alpha=16 gives: \boxed{ \frac{\alpha}{r}=2. } therefore: w'=w_0+2ba. 3.2.27 why divide by r ? the source formulation uses the normalized scaling: \frac{\alpha}{r}. conceptually, this separates: the chosen rank r , the desired adaptation scale \alpha . this lets the rank control capacity while \alpha separately controls update strength. we should therefore distinguish: \boxed{ r=\text{capacity/number of low-rank directions} } from: \boxed{ \alpha=\text{scale of the lora contribution}. } 3.2.28 numerical example with scaling suppose: b= \begin{bmatrix} 1\\2 \end{bmatrix} and: a= \begin{bmatrix} 3&4 \end{bmatrix}. we already found: ba= \begin{bmatrix} 3&4\\ 6&8 \end{bmatrix}. take: r=1,\quad\alpha=2. then: \frac{\alpha}{r}=2. therefore: \frac{\alpha}{r}ba = 2 \begin{bmatrix} 3&4\\ 6&8 \end{bmatrix} = \boxed{ \begin{bmatrix} 6&8\\ 12&16 \end{bmatrix}. } so the scaling factor simply amplifies the low-rank update. correction: the lecture page6 uses a=[1,2], not the inherited a=[1,1]. with inherited w0=[[2,0],[1,1],[1,2]], x=[1,1,1], a=[1,1], b=[1,1,0]ᵀ, s2, the derived output[8,7] is correct for those toy matrices but must not be called the slide’s exact example. the slide page6 has a different displayed w0 and output[7,12]; its separate and merged paths should be checked using that exact source matrix. complete grounded review 3.2.29 source numeric example the peft slide gives a complete numerical example with: d=3,\quad d_{\text{out}}=2,\quad r=1,\quad\alpha=2. it uses: w_0= \begin{bmatrix} 2&0\\ 1&1\\ 1&2 \end{bmatrix}, b= \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, and: a= \begin{bmatrix} 1&1 \end{bmatrix}. therefore: ba= \begin{bmatrix} 1&1\\ 1&1\\ 0&0 \end{bmatrix}. the merged weight is: w' = w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba. since: \frac{\alpha}{r}=2, we get: w' = \begin{bmatrix} 2&0\\ 1&1\\ 1&2 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1&1\\ 1&1\\ 0&0 \end{bmatrix} = \boxed{ \begin{bmatrix} 4&2\\ 3&3\\ 1&2 \end{bmatrix}. } this is the concrete lora factorization example in your peft slides. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) so in raschka code: x @ a @ b while in the slide notation: xba. these are notation differences, not conceptual differences . for your exam, follow the notation used by the question. 3.2.32 separate computation vs merged computation lora can be viewed in two mathematically equivalent ways. separate form \boxed{ h=xw_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb)a } merged form first construct: \boxed{ w'=w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba } then: \boxed{ h=xw'. } by distributivity: x\left(w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba\right) = xw_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}xba. therefore they produce the same result. the peft slide explicitly demonstrates this equivalence numerically. (source: peft-slides) 3.2.33 why is this useful? it means after training, we can merge: \frac{\alpha}{r}ba into: w_0. then inference can simply use: \boxed{ w' } instead of maintaining a separate lora branch. your peft lecture describes this as allowing the lora update to be merged into the pretrained weights, producing zero additional inference latency from maintaining a separate lora computation path. (source: peft-slides) correction: slide convention b: d×r, a: r×out and book convention a: d×r, b: r×out reverse names. book zero-initializes its output factorb; slides zero-initialize their input factorb. both preserve zero initial update, but first nonzero factor gradient changes accordingly; do not mix the convention names. complete grounded review 3.2.34 why is initialization important? your source says: b is initialized to zero, while the other factor is initialized with small/random values. therefore initially: ba=0. hence: w' = w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}(0) = w_0. so at the beginning of lora training: \boxed{ \text{adapted model behaves exactly like the pretrained model}. } this is a very important design choice. raschka explicitly explains that zero-initializing b makes the initial lora contribution zero. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 3.2.35 why not initialize both randomly? suppose both a and b were random. then: ba\neq0 in general. so the model would begin training from: w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba rather than: w_0. the source's design instead gives: \boxed{ \delta w=0 } at initialization. this preserves the pretrained model's behavior at the start. 3.2.36 numerical initialization check suppose: a= \begin{bmatrix} 0.5&-0.2\\ 0.1&0.4 \end{bmatrix} but: b= \begin{bmatrix} 0&0\\ 0&0\\ 0&0 \end{bmatrix}. then: ba=0. therefore: w'=w_0. no matter what a is initially, zero b guarantees: \boxed{\delta w=0}. 3.2.37 training then changes the factors during training, gradients update a and b . eventually: a\neq a_0 and: b\neq0. therefore: ba\neq0. now: \boxed{ w'\neq w_0. } the task-specific knowledge is encoded in the learned low-rank update. 3.2.38 why freeze w_0 ? this is essential. if: w_0 were also trainable, then we would lose much of the parameter-efficiency advantage. lora therefore uses: \boxed{ w_0:\text{frozen} } and: \boxed{ a,b:\text{trainable}. } your peft slides explicitly frame lora as leaving pretrained weights frozen while only the low-rank matrices are trained. \boxed{w_0} pretrained base knowledge. \boxed{a,b} trainable adaptation factors. \boxed{r} low-rank bottleneck / adaptation capacity / parameter count. \boxed{\alpha} strength of the lora contribution. \boxed{\alpha/r} actual scaling applied to the low-rank update in this formulation. 3.2.45 the most important equation of this step everything comes back to: \boxed{ w'=w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba } with: \boxed{ b\in\mathbb{r}^{d\times r}, \qquad a\in\mathbb{r}^{r\times d_{\text{out}}}, \qquad r\ll d,d_{\text{out}}. } then: \boxed{ \operatorname{rank}(ba)\le r. } and: \boxed{ n_{\text{trainable}} = r(d+d_{\text{out}}). } these are the three formulas you should be able to reconstruct from the matrix shapes. 3.2.46 master mental model think of lora as: pretrained weight w0 │ │ frozen │ ├─────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ xw0 lora │ x → b → a │ n × r │ n × dout │ α / r scale │ └─────── add ───┘ │ ▼ h or mathematically: \boxed{ \text{base path}=xw_0 } \boxed{ \text{lora path}=\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb)a } \boxed{ h=\text{base path}+\text{lora path}. } 3.2.47 what you should now be able to derive without memorizing, you should now be able to derive: shape of the update (d\times r)(r\times d_{\text{out}}) \rightarrow d\times d_{\text{out}}. parameter count dr+rd_{\text{out}} = r(d+d_{\text{out}}). rank bound \operatorname{rank}(ba)\le r. forward pass xw_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb)a. initialization b=0 \rightarrow ba=0 \rightarrow w'=w_0. merge w'=w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba. these are the core mechanics supported by the peft lecture and raschka's lora appendix.
