(source: peft-slides) 3.3.1 first recall the transformer attention block from our earlier transformer lessons: x\in\mathbb{r}^{n\times d}. we calculate: q=xw_q k=xw_k v=xw_v. then: s=\frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}} followed by: a=\operatorname{softmax}(s+m) and: o=av. finally, multi-head attention applies the output projection: \boxed{ \operatorname{mha}(x)=\operatorname{concat}(\text{heads})w_o. } these projection matrices are part of the standard transformer mathematical structure. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 3.3.2 there are four important attention matrices so one transformer attention module contains: \boxed{w_q} \boxed{w_k} \boxed{w_v} \boxed{w_o}. they have different jobs. w_q creates queries: q=xw_q. w_k creates keys: k=xw_k. w_v creates values: v=xw_v. w_o projects the concatenated head outputs back into the model dimension. 3.3.3 now apply lora instead of directly changing: w_q, we can write: \boxed{ w_q' = w_q+ \frac{\alpha}{r}b_qa_q. } similarly: \boxed{ w_k' = w_k+ \frac{\alpha}{r}b_ka_k } \boxed{ w_v' = w_v+ \frac{\alpha}{r}b_va_v } and: \boxed{ w_o' = w_o+ \frac{\alpha}{r}b_oa_o. } so the original attention becomes a frozen base path plus trainable low-rank corrections . 3.3.4 what does the forward pass now look like? originally: q=xw_q. with lora: q=xw_q'. substitute: q = x\left(w_q+\frac{\alpha}{r}b_qa_q\right). therefore: \boxed{ q=xw_q+\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb_q)a_q. } exactly the same idea we derived in step 3.2. likewise: \boxed{ k=xw_k+\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb_k)a_k } and: \boxed{ v=xw_v+\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb_v)a_v. } then attention proceeds normally. 3.3.5 the important insight lora does not replace attention. it does not change: qk^t or: \operatorname{softmax} or: av. instead, it changes how the model constructs the projections feeding attention . so: original transformer x │ ├── wq ──> q ├── wk ──> k └── wv ──> v │ ▼ attention │ ▼ wo becomes: lora transformer frozen wq x ───────────────┐ ├──> q lora ────┘ frozen wk x ───────────────┐ ├──> k lora ────┘ frozen wv x ───────────────┐ ├──> v lora ────┘ attention │ ▼ frozen wo │ + lora │ ▼ output 3.3.6 why are these good places to adapt? the attention projections determine the representations used to decide: what information should interact with what other information? recall: qk^t determines compatibility. so changing: w_q,w_k can change the attention relationships. changing: w_v changes the content being transported. changing: w_o changes how the resulting head information is recombined. thus, even though the lora matrices are small, they sit at important transformation points inside the network. the supplied peft material directly demonstrates the attention-projection application; broader claims about why these are universally optimal target modules are not established by the slide itself, so we should not treat that as a source-derived guarantee. 3.3.7 let's do the full attention computation suppose: x\in\mathbb{r}^{n\times d}. with lora: w_q' = w_q+\frac{\alpha}{r}b_qa_q. then: q=xw_q'. similarly: k=xw_k' and: v=xw_v'. then: \boxed{ s=\frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}} } \boxed{ a=\operatorname{softmax}(s+m) } \boxed{ o=av. } finally: \boxed{ y=ow_o' } for the simplified single-matrix representation. the attention mathematics itself has not changed. only the learned projections have received low-rank trainable updates. 3.3.8 a small numerical shape example suppose: n=8, \qquad d=16, \qquad d_k=4. for one attention projection: w_q\in\mathbb{r}^{16\times4}. take: r=2. then: b_q\in\mathbb{r}^{16\times2} and: a_q\in\mathbb{r}^{2\times4}. therefore: b_qa_q has shape: (16\times2)(2\times4) = \boxed{16\times4}. exactly the shape of: w_q. 3.3.9 parameter count for w_q original: 16\times4=64 parameters. lora: 2(16+4) = 40. so for this deliberately small example, the reduction is: \frac{64}{40}=1.6. notice something important: lora is only strongly parameter-efficient when r is much smaller than the layer dimensions. that is why the condition: \boxed{ r\ll d,d_{\text{out}} } matters. 3.3.10 now use a realistic hidden size the peft lecture uses: d=4096 and: r=8. for a square attention projection: w_q\in\mathbb{r}^{4096\times4096}. full parameter count: 4096^2 = \boxed{16,777,216}. lora parameter count: 8(4096+4096) = 8(8192) = \boxed{65,536}. this is the source's exact numerical example. (source: peft-slides) 3.3.11 reduction for one projection \frac{16,777,216}{65,536} = \boxed{256}. so instead of training: 16.78\text{ million} parameters for one projection, we train: 65,536. the reduction is: \boxed{256\times}. 3.3.12 but one transformer layer has four projections the source applies lora to: \boxed{ w_q,w_k,w_v,w_o. } so there are: 4 such matrices. each requires: 65,536 lora parameters. therefore: 4\times65,536 = \boxed{262,144} trainable parameters per layer. 3.3.13 now 32 transformer layers suppose: l=32. then: 32\times262,144 = \boxed{8,388,608}. therefore: \boxed{ 8,388,608 } lora parameters are trainable across all four attention projections of all 32 layers. this exact full-model calculation appears in your peft lecture. (source: peft-slides) 3.3.14 compare against the full model the source's model is described as: \boxed{6.74b} total parameters. lora trains: 8,388,608. calculate the fraction: \frac{8,388,608}{6.74\times10^9}. approximately: 0.001244. as a percentage: 0.1244\%. so: \boxed{ \approx0.124\% } of the model parameters are trained. the remaining approximately: \boxed{99.876\%} are frozen under this setup. this is the exact percentage highlighted by the peft lecture. (source: peft-slides) 3.3.15 this is the key full-model numerical memorize the derivation , not just the answer. given: d=4096, \quad r=8, \quad l=32. one projection: r(2d) = 8(8192) = 65,536. four projections: 4(65,536) = 262,144. 32 layers: 32(262,144) = \boxed{8,388,608}. therefore: \boxed{ 8.39\text{ million trainable parameters}. } 3.3.16 exam question a 32-layer transformer has hidden size 4096 . lora rank is 8 . lora is applied to w_q,w_k,w_v,w_o in every layer. how many trainable lora parameters are introduced? step 1 — one projection 8(4096+4096) = 65,536. step 2 — four projections 4(65,536) = 262,144. step 3 — 32 layers 32(262,144) = \boxed{8,388,608}. 3.3.17 exam question — what if rank doubles? suppose: r=16 instead of: r=8. because: n_{\text{lora}}\propto r, the number doubles: 8,388,608\times2 = \boxed{16,777,216}. so: \boxed{ r\uparrow2\times \rightarrow n_{\text{trainable}}\uparrow2\times. } 3.3.18 exam question — what if layers double? suppose: l=64 instead of 32, with everything else unchanged. since: n\propto l, we get: 8,388,608\times2 = \boxed{16,777,216}. therefore: \boxed{ n_{\text{lora}}\propto lr } when the target dimensions and number of target matrices per layer remain fixed. 3.3.19 general full-model formula suppose: l = number of layers, m = number of targeted matrices per layer, each matrix has dimensions d\times d_{\text{out}} , lora rank r . then: \boxed{ n_{\text{lora,total}} = l\,m\,r(d+d_{\text{out}}). } for the source example: l=32 m=4 r=8 d=d_{\text{out}}=4096. therefore: 32\times4\times8(4096+4096) = \boxed{8,388,608}. this formula is one of the most useful exam formulas from this section. 3.3.20 important: number of heads does not appear here you might ask: "the transformer has multiple attention heads. why didn't we multiply by the number of heads?" because in the standard combined projection representation: w_q\in\mathbb{r}^{d\times d} already produces the projections for all heads. for example: d=4096. if: h=32, then each head might have: d_h=\frac{4096}{32}=128. but the combined w_q is still: 4096\times4096. so you do not multiply its parameter count by 32 again. this is an important exam trap. 3.3.21 let's see why the combined projection produces: q=xw_q. suppose: x:n\times4096 and: w_q:4096\times4096. then: q:n\times4096. afterward, reshape: n\times4096 into: 32\times n\times128. so the head separation happens after the projection. therefore: \boxed{ w_q\text{ already contains all head projections}. } 3.3.22 connection to our earlier mha lesson previously we learned: d_h=\frac{d}{h}. for: d=4096,\quad h=32, we get: d_h=128. the q tensor can be viewed as: q\in\mathbb{r}^{n\times32\times128} or, depending on convention: 32\times n\times128. but the lora target matrix before reshaping is: \boxed{ w_q:4096\times4096. } this connects the lora lesson directly back to the transformer mathematics we already completed. 3.3.23 what about w_o ? after attention: \text{concat(head}_1,\ldots,\text{head}_h) returns to model width: n\times d. then: w_o\in\mathbb{r}^{d\times d} projects it. so for: d=4096, we again have: 4096\times4096. therefore w_o receives exactly the same lora parameter count in the source's simplified model: \boxed{65,536}. 3.3.24 full one-layer picture for one transformer layer: x │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ │ │ │ wq wk wv │ │ │ +lora +lora +lora │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ q k v \ │ / \ │ / attention │ ▼ concat heads │ wo +lora │ ▼ attention output so lora is attached to the linear projections, while the attention operation itself remains the same. 3.3.25 does lora change the causal mask? no. the causal mask is still: m_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0,&j\le i\\ -\infty,&j>i. \end{cases} lora changes the learned projections: w_q,w_k,w_v,w_o. it does not remove the autoregressive constraint. therefore: \boxed{ \text{lora adaptation}\neq\text{change to causal masking}. } the attention mathematics remains: a= \operatorname{softmax} \left( \frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}}+m \right). 3.3.26 does lora change the softmax? again: \boxed{\text{no.}} the ordinary attention calculation remains. lora changes: q,\ k,\ v through their projections. then the usual: qk^t and softmax operate on those adapted representations. 3.3.27 does lora change the transformer architecture? at the conceptual level: \boxed{ \text{no major architectural redesign is required.} } you have: \text{same transformer} + \text{small trainable low-rank branches}. this is why peft is attractive: the pretrained architecture remains largely intact. 3.3.28 lora training flow now imagine training. step 1 load pretrained model: w_0. step 2 freeze: w_0. step 3 insert lora factors: a,b. step 4 initialize them according to the lora scheme. step 5 run forward pass: xw_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}(xb)a. step 6 calculate task loss: l. step 7 backpropagate. gradients update: \boxed{a,b} but not: \boxed{w_0}. 3.3.29 which parameters receive gradients? for full fine-tuning: \nabla_{w_0}l\neq0 and optimizer updates w_0 . for lora: \boxed{ w_0\text{ frozen} } so it is not updated. instead: \boxed{ \nabla_a l,\nabla_b l } are used to train the adapters. this is where the huge reduction in trainable state comes from. 3.3.30 a critical training-memory point suppose: n_{\text{base}}=6.74b but: n_{\text{lora}}=8.39m. the base model still has to exist in memory for the forward pass. so do not conclude: "only 8.39m parameters exist during training." no. rather: \boxed{ 6.74b\text{ base parameters exist, but only }8.39m\text{ are trainable in this example}. } this distinction becomes especially important when we reach: \boxed{\text{quantization + qlora}} because quantization then attacks the memory footprint of the frozen base model itself. 3.3.31 why this leads naturally to qlora we now have two different problems: lora solves \boxed{ \text{too many trainable parameters}. } but the frozen model can still be enormous. quantization solves \boxed{ \text{large memory footprint of model weights}. } therefore the natural combination is: \boxed{ \text{quantized frozen base} + \text{trainable lora adapters}. } that will become qlora later. do not jump there yet—we first need to complete the lora mechanics. 3.3.32 exam numerical — full attention adapter count given: l=24 d=2048 r=16 and lora on: w_q,w_k,w_v,w_o. one projection: 16(2048+2048) = 16(4096) = 65,536. four: 4(65,536) = 262,144. 24 layers: 24(262,144) = \boxed{6,291,456}. 3.3.33 exam numerical — percentage suppose the base model has: 3.2b parameters. suppose lora trains: 6,291,456. percentage: \frac{6,291,456}{3.2\times10^9}\times100 \approx \boxed{0.1966\%}. so approximately: \boxed{0.20\%} of the parameters are trainable. 3.3.34 exam trap — four projections if the question says: apply lora to all four attention projections. you multiply by: \boxed{4}. if it says: apply lora only to w_q and w_v . you multiply by: \boxed{2}. if it says only: w_q, multiply by: \boxed{1}. so always identify: \boxed{ m=\text{number of target matrices per layer}. } then: n=lmr(d+d_{\text{out}}). 3.3.35 exam trap — do not multiply by sequence length the lora parameter count: lmr(d+d_{\text{out}}) does not depend on: n=\text{sequence length}. why? because the trainable matrices are model parameters. the sequence length changes the amount of computation/activation processing, but it does not create new copies of w_q . therefore: \boxed{ n_{\text{lora parameters}}\neq f(n). } 3.3.36 exam trap — do not multiply by batch size similarly: b=\text{batch size} does not multiply the number of lora parameters. the same lora matrices are shared across every example in the batch. therefore: \boxed{ n_{\text{lora parameters}} \text{ is independent of batch size}. } lora rank. \boxed{n} = sequence length. do not substitute one for another. for example: d=4096, \quad h=32, \quad d_h=128, \quad r=8, \quad n=2048. all five numbers have completely different meanings. peft-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 3.5 — quantization → qlora plan node: i4 · chat order #30 we have reached the natural next step. with ordinary lora, we solved: \boxed{\text{“how do i train only a tiny fraction of the parameters?”}} but a second problem remains: \boxed{\text{“how do i fit the huge frozen base model itself into gpu memory?”}} that is the problem quantization addresses. the supplied quantization slides build the foundation using int8/int4, scaling, dequantization, block-wise quantization, outliers, clipping, calibration, gptq, and qat. the peft slides explicitly place qlora after lora , and the original qlora paper then combines 4-bit quantization with lora. (source: peft-slides) 1. first understand the problem: numbers need memory a model weight might be stored as fp32. each fp32 value uses: 32\text{ bits}=4\text{ bytes}. suppose we have: 1,000,000,000 weights. fp32 memory: 1\times10^9\times4 = 4\times10^9\text{ bytes} approximately: \boxed{4\text{ gb}} just for the weights. now use 16-bit precision: 2\text{ bytes/weight} so: \boxed{2\text{ gb}}. now use 8-bit: 1\text{ byte/weight} so: \boxed{1\text{ gb}}. now 4-bit: \frac{4}{8}=0.5\text{ bytes/weight} so approximately: \boxed{0.5\text{ gb}}. this is the fundamental attraction of quantization. 2. what is quantization? the quantization slides define the basic idea as taking a representation containing more information and discretizing it into one containing less information. the classic example is converting fp32 values to int8. (source: quantization-slides) conceptually: \boxed{ \text{many possible real values} \longrightarrow \text{small finite set of representable values} } for example: fp32 1.384729 1.392814 1.401294 1.417382 ... millions of possible values becomes something like: int8 ... -3 -2 -1 0 1 2 3 ... the price: \boxed{\text{less memory + less numerical precision}} the challenge is to lose as little useful information as possible. 3. why can't we simply throw away decimal values? suppose the original weights are: [0.91,\ 0.87,\ 0.82,\ -0.76]. if we simply round: [1,\ 1,\ 1,\ -1] we destroy a lot of information. so quantization needs a mapping . we want: \boxed{\text{real value}} \rightarrow \boxed{\text{small integer/code}} and later: \boxed{\text{code}} \rightarrow \boxed{\text{approximate real value}}. that is why quantization has two directions: \boxed{\text{quantize}} and \boxed{\text{dequantize}}. 4. int8 gives us a finite grid the quantization slides describe signed int8 as a grid of 256 evenly spaced integer codes, with the symmetric quantization scheme using: -127,\ldots,0,\ldots,127. there is no decimal-point concept built into int8; the quantization scale determines how the real-valued tensor maps onto that grid. (source: quantization-slides) think of this as: real number line ----|----|----|----|----|----> -10 -5 0 5 10 ↓ scaling int8 grid -127 ... -64 ... 0 ... 64 ... 127 the key is: \boxed{\text{scale determines how much one integer step means}} 5. symmetric quantization this is the first formula you absolutely need. suppose a tensor is: x=[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n]. find the largest absolute magnitude: \boxed{ \alpha=\max_i |x_i| } for b -bit symmetric quantization, the quantization slides define the positive integer limit as: q_{\max}=2^{b-1}-1. then the scale is: \boxed{ s=\frac{q_{\max}}{\alpha} } and quantization is: \boxed{ x_q=\operatorname{round}(sx) } while dequantization is: \boxed{ x_{\text{deq}}=\frac{x_q}{s} } the supplied slides give exactly this formulation. (source: quantization-slides) 6. why multiply by s ? this is the part students often memorize without understanding. suppose: \alpha=10.8 and int8 symmetric range is: [-127,127]. we want: 10.8\rightarrow127. therefore: s=\frac{127}{10.8} \approx11.76. so: 10.8\times11.76\approx127. and: 5.47\times11.76\approx64.33. thus: 5.47\rightarrow64. the slides use exactly this worked example. (source: quantization-slides) so the scale is essentially answering: “how many integer units should represent one real-valued unit?” 7. full numerical example take: x=[5.47,\ 3.08,\ -7.59,\ 0,\ -1.95,\ -4.57,\ 10.8]. largest magnitude: \alpha=10.8. for int8: q_{\max}=127. therefore: s=\frac{127}{10.8} \approx11.76. now: 5.47(11.76)\approx64.33 so: x_q=64. for 3.08 : 3.08(11.76)\approx36.22 so: x_q=36. for -7.59 : -7.59(11.76)\approx-89.26 so: x_q=-89. and: 10.8(11.76)=127 so: x_q=127. therefore: \boxed{ x_q=[64,36,-89,0,-23,-54,127] } the slides show these values explicitly. (source: quantization-slides) 8. dequantization now suppose the stored value is: 64. recover an approximation: x_{\text{deq}}=\frac{64}{11.76} \approx5.44. original: 5.47. so quantization introduced: |5.47-5.44| = \boxed{0.03}. likewise: 36/11.76\approx3.06. so the error is: |3.08-3.06| = 0.02. the supplied worked example shows these reconstruction errors. (source: quantization-slides) 9. where did the error come from? notice something very important. before rounding: 5.47(11.76)=64.33. after rounding: 64. the information loss happens at: \boxed{\operatorname{round}(\cdot)} not during ordinary multiplication or division. that is precisely how the slides frame the symmetric quantization process: the rounding step is the information-losing step. (source: quantization-slides) this gives the important chain: x \rightarrow sx \rightarrow \boxed{\operatorname{round}} \rightarrow x_q \rightarrow \frac{x_q}{s}. 10. exam numerical: quantization suppose: x=2.4 and s=10. then: sx=24. so: x_q=\operatorname{round}(24)=24. dequantize: x_{\text{deq}}=\frac{24}{10}=2.4. error: \boxed{0}. now instead: x=2.43. then: sx=24.3 and: x_q=24. therefore: x_{\text{deq}}=2.4. error: |2.43-2.4| = \boxed{0.03}. 11. why symmetric quantization can be bad now imagine: x=[0.1,\ 0.2,\ 0.3,\ 100]. the maximum absolute value is: 100. so the entire scale is determined by 100. for int8: s=\frac{127}{100}=1.27. now: 0.1(1.27)=0.127 and: 0.2(1.27)=0.254. both round to: 0. so several meaningful small values collapse to the same code. this is the outlier problem . the supplied slides explicitly demonstrate that a single extreme value can ruin the precision available to the rest of the tensor. (source: quantization-slides) 12. block-wise quantization solves much of this instead of using one scale for the entire tensor: x\rightarrow1\text{ scale} split it into blocks: x= \underbrace{b_1}_{\text{scale }s_1} \underbrace{b_2}_{\text{scale }s_2} \underbrace{b_3}_{\text{scale }s_3} \cdots then each block gets its own scale. the qlora paper formalizes this as flattening the tensor and dividing it into contiguous blocks, each independently quantized with its own quantization constant. this is extremely important because an outlier in block 1 does not necessarily ruin the precision of block 2. 13. tiny block-wise example suppose: x=[0.1,0.2,0.3,100,\quad 2,3,4,5]. with one global scale, the 100 dominates. instead make blocks: b_1=[0.1,0.2,0.3,100] b_2=[2,3,4,5]. then: s_1 is based on 100, while: s_2 is based on 5. therefore the second block gets a much finer representation. this is one of the key ideas behind modern low-bit weight quantization. correction: the asymmetric multiplier must be s=(2^b-1)/(alpha-beta), as quantization-slide page 20 states. its reciprocal is incompatible with round(sx+z) and (q-z)/s. with inverse step delta, quantize as round(x/delta)+z and reconstruct as delta(q-z). include signed-code clamping and a constant-range policy. complete grounded review 14. symmetric vs asymmetric quantization symmetric quantization assumes: [-\alpha,\alpha]. but what if data looks like: [10,12,15,18,20]? it is nowhere near symmetric around zero. the slides therefore introduce asymmetric quantization , which maps the actual minimum and maximum to the full integer range and introduces a zero-point z . (source: quantization-slides) let: \beta=\min(x) and \alpha=\max(x). for b -bit integer storage: \boxed{ s= \frac{\alpha-\beta}{2^b-1} } and: \boxed{ z= \operatorname{round} \left(-s\beta\right) -2^{b-1} } under the signed convention used by the slides. the quantized value has the form: \boxed{ x_q=\operatorname{round}(sx+z) } and dequantization: \boxed{ x_{\text{deq}} = \frac{x_q-z}{s}. } the zero-point is needed because the real interval may not be centered at zero. (source: quantization-slides) 15. intuition for zero-point think of symmetric quantization as: real: -10 0 +10 |----------|-----------| integer: -127 0 127 but asymmetric quantization might need: real: +10 +15 +20 |----------|-----------| integer: -128 0 127 there is no reason the real zero has to sit at integer zero. so: \boxed{z=\text{shift}} moves the quantized grid into the correct position. 16. why qlora does not simply use int4 this is where things become interesting. if we use ordinary uniform int4, then we have only: 2^4=16 possible codes. the quantization levels are essentially uniformly spaced. but neural-network weights tend to concentrate around zero rather than being uniformly distributed. the qlora paper therefore introduces: \boxed{\text{nf4 = normalfloat 4-bit}} rather than ordinary int4 for its 4-bit weight representation. the paper describes nf4 as information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights. hugging face's documentation likewise describes nf4 as a 4-bit data type designed for normally distributed weights. 17. why nf4? imagine the weight distribution looks approximately like: /\ / \ / \ ___________/ \___________ - 0 + most weights are near zero. so we want: \boxed{\text{more quantization resolution near zero}} instead of wasting equal numbers of codes in the tails. nf4 uses 16 levels derived from quantiles of the standard normal distribution. it is therefore not the same thing as a 4-bit floating-point format with ordinary sign/exponent/mantissa fields . this distinction is important: \boxed{\text{nf4}\neq\text{ordinary fp4}} 18. what does “non-uniform levels” mean? uniform 4-bit quantization might conceptually look like: -1 -0.875 -0.75 ... 0 ... 0.75 0.875 1 every interval is equally spaced. nf4 instead places levels more densely around the high-probability central region and more sparsely in the tails. conceptually: tail center tail * * * **** ** **** * * * ^^^^^^^^^^^ more density so: \boxed{\text{same 4 bits, better allocation of representational resolution}} for the weight distribution qlora targets. 19. but how can 4-bit weights participate in matrix multiplication? this is the critical qlora trick. you store the base model's weights in 4-bit form. but you do not conceptually perform the whole neural-network computation using 4-bit arithmetic. the qlora formulation uses a low-bit storage representation and dequantizes to a higher-precision computation representation. in the paper's formulation, the stored nf4 weights are dequantized to bf16 for computation, while gradients are only needed for the lora parameters. so think: storage ↓ 4-bit nf4 weights ↓ dequantize ↓ bf16 computation ↓ forward ↓ backward ↓ update lora parameters this is the heart of qlora. 20. qlora = quantization + lora now combine the two things we learned. ordinary lora: w=w_0+\delta w with \delta w\approx ab. qlora says: what if w_0 itself is stored in 4-bit form? then: \boxed{ w_0^{\text{nf4}} } is frozen. during computation it is approximately reconstructed: \boxed{ \operatorname{dequant}(w_0^{\text{nf4}}) \rightarrow w_0^{\text{bf16}} } and the lora branch is added. the qlora paper gives the linear-layer formulation in the form y^{bf16} = x^{bf16} \operatorname{doubledequant} (c_1,c_2,w^{nf4}) + x^{bf16}l_1l_2. 21. very important: what is trainable? this is the exam-critical comparison. full fine-tuning w_0 trainable. lora w_0 frozen, a,b trainable. qlora w_0^{nf4} frozen, a,b trainable. so: \boxed{ \text{qlora does not train the 4-bit base weights} } it trains the lora adapters. the qlora paper explicitly describes gradients being propagated through the frozen quantized model into the low-rank adapters. 22. then why do gradients “pass through” the quantized model? excellent distinction. suppose: y= xw_q+xab. the loss depends on y . to calculate how a,b should change, the computational graph still needs derivatives through the operations involving w_q . but: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_q} } is not used to update the base model. so: gradient path: loss ↓ lora output ↓ a, b ← update and the gradient calculation passes through quantized base model ↓ but w0 stays frozen this is a subtle but fundamental difference between: \boxed{\text{gradient computation}} and \boxed{\text{parameter update}}. 23. why do we need double quantization? ordinary block-wise quantization needs: \text{quantized weights} + \text{scale for each block}. the scale itself is generally stored at higher precision. suppose every block contains: 64 weights. if every block requires one fp32 scale: 32\text{ bits} per 64 weights. overhead per weight: \frac{32}{64} = 0.5\text{ bits/weight}. that is surprisingly large. the qlora paper therefore introduces double quantization : quantize the quantization constants themselves. 24. double quantization concept first quantization: w \rightarrow w^{4bit} + c_2 where c_2 contains quantization constants such as scales. then: c_2 \rightarrow c_2^{k-bit} + c_1 so: original fp32 weights | | first quantization ↓ 4-bit weights + fp32 scales | | second quantization ↓ 4-bit weights + quantized scales + scale-of-scales the supplied quantization slides explicitly connect nested scale quantization to the same double-quantization idea used by qlora. (source: quantization-slides) the qlora paper reports an average saving of approximately: \boxed{0.37\text{ bits/parameter}} from double quantization. 25. numerical understanding of double quantization suppose: 64 weights share a scale. without double quantization: 64\times4=256\text{ bytes} for the 4-bit weights? careful: 4 bits = 0.5 bytes, so: 64\times0.5 = 32\text{ bytes}. and one fp32 scale: 4\text{ bytes}. thus total: 32+4=36\text{ bytes} for 64 parameters. that gives: \frac{36\times8}{64} = \boxed{4.5\text{ bits/parameter}} ignoring other metadata. so “4-bit quantization” does not necessarily mean exactly 4.000 bits/parameter once the required scale information is counted. double quantization reduces that overhead further. 26. double-quantization saving from the qlora paper the paper gives a more detailed example. for block size: 64 the fp32 second-level constants would contribute: \frac{32}{64}=0.5 bits per parameter. after quantizing those constants, the paper reports: \frac{8}{64} + \frac{32}{64\times256} = 0.127 bits per parameter. therefore the saving is: 0.5-0.127 = \boxed{0.373\text{ bits/parameter}}. this is a very good numerical question. 27. what are paged optimizers? there is one more qlora component. even when the model itself fits, training can temporarily require extra memory. this can happen from: \boxed{\text{optimizer states}} or memory spikes associated with long sequences/checkpointing. qlora therefore introduced paged optimizers , using nvidia unified memory so optimizer state can be moved between gpu and cpu memory during spikes. think: gpu memory ┌───────────────────┐ │ active tensors │ │ model computation │ └───────────────────┘ ↕ paging when needed ↕ ┌───────────────────┐ │ cpu ram │ │ optimizer states │ └───────────────────┘ so the three famous qlora ideas are: \boxed{ \text{nf4} + \text{double quantization} + \text{paged optimizers} } the original paper explicitly identifies these three innovations. 28. complete qlora architecture now put everything together. input x | ┌──────────┴──────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ quantized base lora a w0 → nf4 | │ ▼ dequantize lora b │ | ▼ ▼ bf16 base low-rank update │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ ▼ add │ ▼ transformer │ ▼ loss │ ▼ backpropagation │ ┌───────┴───────┐ ▼ ▼ frozen w0 a,b │ update the important arrows are: \boxed{ w_0:\text{stored low-bit, frozen} } and \boxed{ a,b:\text{higher precision, trainable} } 29. lora vs qlora method base weights adapter main memory idea full ft fp16/fp32 + trainable none expensive lora fp16/fp32 + frozen trainable fewer trainable parameters qlora 4-bit + frozen trainable fewer trainable params and smaller base-weight storage thus: \boxed{ \text{lora solves training-parameter memory} } while \boxed{ \text{qlora additionally attacks base-model memory} } 30. memory numerical: 7b model suppose a model has: 7\times10^9 parameters. approximate weight storage: fp32 7\times10^9\times4 \approx \boxed{28\text{ gb}} fp16 7\times10^9\times2 \approx \boxed{14\text{ gb}} int8 7\times10^9\times1 \approx \boxed{7\text{ gb}} 4-bit 7\times10^9\times0.5 \approx \boxed{3.5\text{ gb}} these are idealized raw-storage calculations and omit scales, metadata, temporary activations, kv cache, and other runtime memory. but they show why 4-bit storage is so attractive. 31. memory numerical: 65b model for: 65\times10^9 parameters: fp16 65\times10^9\times2 = 130\text{ gb} just for weights. the original qlora paper reports that conventional 16-bit fine-tuning of a 65b llama model required more than 780 gb of gpu memory, because training requires much more than just storing the weights. qlora reduced the reported fine-tuning memory requirement to below 48 gb. that distinction is crucial: \boxed{\text{weight memory}\neq\text{total training memory}} 32. why 4-bit does not mean “everything is 4-bit” this is one of the biggest exam traps. a qlora setup can have: \boxed{ \text{base storage}=4\text{-bit nf4} } while: \boxed{ \text{computation}\approx16\text{-bit} } and: \boxed{ \text{lora parameters}\approx16\text{-bit} } the qlora paper specifically describes the 4-bit storage datatype being dequantized into bf16 for computation, with lora weights operating in higher precision. so never say: “qlora trains the whole model in 4-bit.” that is misleading. a better statement is: qlora stores the frozen base model in a 4-bit representation and performs computation through dequantization while training only the higher-precision lora adapters. 33. quantization vs qat the quantization slides also distinguish: \boxed{\text{ptq = post-training quantization}} from: \boxed{\text{qat = quantization-aware training}}. ptq train first: w_{\text{trained}} then quantize: w_{\text{trained}} \rightarrow w_q. the model never trained while seeing the quantization error. qat the training process includes quantization-like behavior. the supplied slides describe a “fake” quantization step where values are quantized and immediately dequantized, allowing the forward pass to experience the rounding effects while gradients still flow through the higher-precision computation. (source: quantization-slides) this encourages solutions that are more tolerant of the quantization grid. (source: quantization-slides) 34. do not confuse qat with qlora very important: \boxed{\text{qat}\neq\text{qlora}} qat is a broad training strategy where the model is trained with quantization effects in the loop. qlora is: \boxed{ \text{4-bit quantized frozen base} + \text{lora adapters} } plus the specific memory-saving techniques of nf4, double quantization, and paged optimizers. 35. one complete mathematical picture for one linear layer, think of qlora approximately as: \boxed{ y = x\,\operatorname{dequant}(w_q) + xab } where: w_q=\text{frozen 4-bit base weights}. more specifically, with the qlora formulation: \boxed{ y^{bf16} = x^{bf16} \operatorname{doubledequant} (c_1,c_2,w^{nf4}) + x^{bf16}l_1^{bf16}l_2^{bf16} } as given in the qlora paper. and the optimization is conceptually: \boxed{ \min_{a,b} l\left( x\operatorname{dequant}(w_q)+xab \right) } subject to: \boxed{w_q\text{ fixed}}. that is the clean mathematical definition to keep in your head. 36. exam traps you should know trap 1 “4-bit means exactly 4 bits per parameter.” not necessarily. scales and metadata add overhead. the quantization slides explicitly show that practical formats can cost more than the nominal weight bit-width. (source: quantization-slides) trap 2 “lora and qlora both reduce the base model's parameter count.” no. they reduce trainable parameters in lora and storage precision of the frozen base in qlora. trap 3 “qlora updates the 4-bit weights.” no. the base is frozen; gradients are used to update lora adapters. trap 4 “nf4 is simply int4.” no. nf4 is a non-uniform 4-bit representation designed around normally distributed weights. trap 5 “dequantization means the base model becomes permanently fp16.” no. the idea is to keep the compact low-bit representation for storage and reconstruct higher-precision values when needed for computation. 37. exam numerical bank — quantization + qlora q1. number of representable 4-bit codes 2^4=\boxed{16}. q2. raw storage of a 10b-parameter model at 4 bits 10^{10}\times4 = 4\times10^{10}\text{ bits}. convert to bytes: \frac{4\times10^{10}}8 = 5\times10^9 so approximately: \boxed{5\text{ gb}}. ignoring scale/metadata overhead. q3. int8 symmetric scale given: \max|x|=20 and int8: q_{\max}=127. then: s=\frac{127}{20} = \boxed{6.35}. q4. quantize a value given: x=3.14,\qquad s=6.35. then: sx=19.939. therefore: x_q=\boxed{20}. dequantize: x_{\text{deq}} = \frac{20}{6.35} \approx \boxed{3.15}. approximate error: |3.14-3.15| \approx \boxed{0.01}. q5. double-quantization saving given the qlora block-size-64 calculation: 0.5-0.127 = \boxed{0.373\text{ bits/parameter}}. q6. lora + quantization a 7b model is stored in 4-bit. raw weight memory: 7\times10^9\times0.5 = \boxed{3.5\text{ gb}} before scale/metadata/runtime overhead. if rank: r=8 and a square projection has: d=4096, lora parameters are: r(d+d) = 8(8192) = \boxed{65,536}. the two mechanisms address completely different memory terms. 38. the deepest conceptual connection you can now see the progression of the entire chapter: full fine-tuning w_0 \rightarrow w_0+\delta w everything changes. lora w_0+\delta w becomes: \boxed{ w_0+\alpha ab } only the low-rank update learns. qlora now also compress: w_0 \rightarrow w_0^{nf4}. so: \boxed{ \text{frozen nf4 base} + \text{trainable lora} } with: \boxed{\text{double quantization}} and: \boxed{\text{paged optimizer support}}. that is the complete progression: \boxed{ \text{full ft} \rightarrow \text{lora} \rightarrow \text{qlora} } correction: apply the corrected asymmetric multiplier in the master formula. symmetric [-127,127] has 255 codes; signed int8 [-128,127] has 256; nf4 uses 16. complete grounded review 39. master formula sheet for this step symmetric quantization \boxed{ \alpha=\max|x| } \boxed{ s=\frac{2^{b-1}-1}{\alpha} } \boxed{ x_q=\operatorname{round}(sx) } \boxed{ x_{\text{deq}}=\frac{x_q}{s} } asymmetric quantization \boxed{ s=\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2^b-1} } \boxed{ x_q=\operatorname{round}(sx+z) } \boxed{ x_{\text{deq}}=\frac{x_q-z}{s} } lora \boxed{ w'=w_0+\alpha ab } or under the peft convention: \boxed{ w'=w_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}ba } qlora \boxed{ y = x\operatorname{dequant}(w^{4bit}) + xab } with: \boxed{ w^{4bit}\text{ frozen} } and: \boxed{ a,b\text{ trainable} } plus: \boxed{ \text{nf4 + double quantization + paged optimizers} } 40. what you should now be able to explain without memorizing a good exam/interview explanation is: quantization reduces the number of bits used to represent model values, reducing memory at the cost of some numerical precision. in symmetric quantization, the tensor is scaled according to its maximum absolute value, rounded to an integer grid, and later dequantized. block-wise quantization gives different blocks different scales to reduce outlier effects. qlora combines this idea with lora: the pretrained base model is kept frozen in a 4-bit representation, typically nf4, dequantized for higher-precision computation, while only the lora adapters are trained. double quantization further compresses the quantization constants, and paged optimizers help manage training-time memory spikes. (source: quantization-slides) one source note the supplied peft slides only announce qlora as the next lecture , rather than developing nf4/double quantization in detail. #31 we now move from the basic idea of quantization to the question that actually matters in practice: how do we choose the quantization range and the quantized values so that model output changes as little as possible? the supplied quantization deck develops this progression: \boxed{ \text{basic quantization} \rightarrow \text{outliers} \rightarrow \text{clipping} \rightarrow \text{calibration} \rightarrow \text{dynamic/static quantization} \rightarrow \text{gptq} } i’ll take it in exactly that order. 1. the fundamental problem with a quantization grid recall symmetric quantization: s=\frac{127}{\alpha} for int8, where \alpha=\max |x|. then: x_q=\operatorname{round}(sx). this looks perfect until an outlier appears. suppose: x=[-1.0,-0.8,-0.6,-0.4,0,0.5,0.7,256]. then: \alpha=256. therefore: s=\frac{127}{256} \approx0.496. now look at x=1.0 : 1(0.496)=0.496. so: x_q=\operatorname{round}(0.496)=0. and for: x=0.5: 0.5(0.496)=0.248 so again: x_q=0. thus: 0.5\rightarrow0 even though 0.5 is a perfectly meaningful value. the supplied deck explicitly demonstrates this “one outlier ruins the whole grid” problem. (source: quantization-slides) 2. why does one outlier cause such a big problem? because a single global scale must represent the entire interval. with: \alpha=256, the integer interval [-127,127] must represent: [-256,256]. therefore, one integer step corresponds to approximately: \frac{256}{127} \approx2.016. so the grid is extremely coarse. that means: real values: -3 -2 -1 0 1 2 3 | | | | | | | quantized grid: ... 0 ... several distinct small values can collapse to the same integer. 3. first solution: clipping instead of allowing the outlier to determine the range, we deliberately clip the tensor. suppose: x=[-1,-0.8,-0.5,0,0.4,0.9,256]. instead of: [-256,256], we choose: \boxed{[-5,5]}. any value outside this range is clipped. so: 256\rightarrow5. yes, we intentionally destroy the outlier. why? because we may gain much better precision for the huge number of ordinary values. the supplied deck explicitly presents clipping as trading accuracy on extreme values for better precision on the rest of the distribution. (source: quantization-slides) 4. numerical comparison suppose: x=1. without clipping \alpha=256. thus: s=\frac{127}{256} \approx0.496. then: x_q=\operatorname{round}(1\times0.496) = 0. dequantize: x_{\text{deq}}=\frac0{0.496}=0. error: |1-0|=\boxed1. very bad. with clipping to 5 now: \alpha=5. scale: s=\frac{127}{5} = 25.4. then: 1(25.4)=25.4 so: x_q=25. dequantize: x_{\text{deq}} = \frac{25}{25.4} \approx0.984. error: |1-0.984| \approx \boxed{0.016}. huge improvement for the normal value. but the outlier: 256\rightarrow5 has enormous error. this is the central quantization tradeoff: \boxed{ \text{protect the tails} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{protect the bulk} } 5. so how do we choose the clipping threshold? this is the calibration problem . we need to find a good range: [\beta,\alpha] or, for symmetric quantization, [-\alpha,\alpha]. the supplied slides explain that calibration determines the quantization range before computing the scale. (source: quantization-slides) there are several possibilities. 6. calibration method 1 — literal min/max simplest: \alpha=\max|x|. no calibration dataset is needed. but a single extreme outlier can make the grid terrible. so: \boxed{\text{simple but potentially wasteful}} 7. calibration method 2 — percentile clipping instead of using the absolute maximum, choose a high percentile. for example: p_{99.9}. then values above that threshold are clipped. conceptually: \boxed{ 99.9\%\text{ of values are preserved normally} } while the extreme 0.1\% can be clipped. the supplied deck uses percentile-based range selection as one calibration strategy. (source: quantization-slides) 8. why might percentile be better? imagine: 9999 values lie between: [-1,1] but one value is: 100. using max: \alpha=100. using approximately the 99th percentile: \alpha\approx1. then the quantization grid becomes much finer around the region where almost all data lies. so the objective is not necessarily: \boxed{\text{minimize every individual weight error}} but often: \boxed{\text{minimize the useful error over the distribution}} 9. calibration method 3 — choose the clip by minimizing mse this is more principled. for every candidate clipping value c : clip values to [-c,c] . quantize. dequantize. compare reconstructed values with the originals. compute mse. the mean squared error is: \boxed{ \operatorname{mse} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\hat{x}_i)^2 } where: x_i=\text{original} and \hat{x}_i=\text{quantized/dequantized}. then choose the c producing the smallest mse. the supplied deck gives an explicit int4 calibration experiment with candidate clip values of 30%, 40%, 50%, 60%, and 100% of the true maximum. (source: quantization-slides) 10. the slide's numerical example the deck reports: candidate clipping mse 30% 0.127 40% 0.068 50% 0.055 60% 0.063 100% 0.156 therefore: \boxed{50\%\text{ is optimal in this example}} because: 0.055 is the smallest mse. the deck reports that this mse-selected clipping produced about 65% lower mse than naive full-range clipping for that int4 heavy-tailed example. (source: quantization-slides) 11. why doesn't the best clipping always equal 100%? because the objective has two competing errors. error a — quantization resolution larger range: c\uparrow means the quantization interval becomes larger. therefore ordinary values are represented less precisely. error b — clipping distortion smaller range: c\downarrow means more values are clipped. therefore tails are distorted more heavily. so mse is approximately balancing: \boxed{ \text{rounding error} + \text{clipping error} } the optimal c sits somewhere between the extremes. 12. why is this more important for int4 than int8? int8 has: 256 possible codes. int4 has: 2^4=16 codes. so int4 has vastly fewer available quantization levels. therefore every level matters more. the supplied calibration experiment reports that clipping selection mattered strongly for int4 but had much less benefit for int8 in the same setup. (source: quantization-slides) this gives an important general principle: \boxed{ \text{lower bit-width} \rightarrow \text{greater need for careful calibration} } 13. calibration method 4 — kl divergence mse isn't the only objective. suppose the original activation/weight distribution is: p. after quantization, we obtain: q. we can choose the clipping range that minimizes: \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q) } where: d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}. the supplied deck describes kl-divergence calibration as another search-based calibration method, using histograms of original and quantized distributions. (source: quantization-slides) the distinction is: \boxed{ \text{mse compares numerical values} } whereas: \boxed{ \text{kl compares distributions} } 14. very important: weights vs activations now we encounter another practical distinction. weights after training, weights are fixed. therefore their range can be measured ahead of time: w\rightarrow\text{measure range once}. activations activations depend on the input. for one input: x_1\rightarrow a_1 and for another: x_2\rightarrow a_2. usually: a_1\neq a_2. therefore activation ranges can change from one inference to another. the supplied slides explicitly distinguish fixed weight ranges from input-dependent activation ranges. (source: quantization-slides) 15. dynamic quantization dynamic quantization handles changing activation ranges by measuring them during inference . for each new input: \boxed{ \text{measure activation range} \rightarrow \text{compute scale/zero-point} \rightarrow \text{quantize} } the range is freshly computed for the current activation values. the supplied slides describe exactly this behavior. (source: quantization-slides) 16. dynamic quantization flow suppose layer 1 produces: a_1=[-2,3,5]. find: \alpha=5. build quantization parameters. then a different input produces: a_2=[-0.2,0.4,0.7]. now: \alpha=0.7. the scale is recomputed. thus: \boxed{ \text{same layer} \neq \text{same activation scale for every input} } under dynamic quantization. 17. advantage of dynamic quantization no large calibration dataset is required beforehand for the activation range. because: \boxed{ \text{the current input provides the range} } the supplied deck states that dynamic quantization needs no calibration data ahead of time. (source: quantization-slides) 18. disadvantage of dynamic quantization the price is runtime work. for every inference: \text{measure} \rightarrow \text{calculate scale} \rightarrow \text{quantize}. therefore: \boxed{ \text{less offline preparation} \quad\text{but more runtime overhead} } 19. static quantization static quantization does the opposite. we run representative calibration data before deployment . suppose: d_{\text{calibration}} = \{x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n\}. run the model on these. observe the activation ranges. choose fixed: s,z. then deployment uses those fixed parameters. the supplied deck describes exactly this: a small calibration dataset is run offline, activation distributions are recorded, and the resulting s,z are fixed before real inference. (source: quantization-slides) 20. dynamic vs static property dynamic static activation range computed at runtime determined offline calibration dataset not required required runtime overhead higher lower sensitivity to calibration data low important the static method is only as good as the representativeness of its calibration dataset. (source: quantization-slides) 21. numerical static-vs-dynamic example suppose calibration data gives: a\in[-4,4]. static quantization chooses: \alpha=4. for int8: s=\frac{127}{4}=31.75. now suppose an actual deployment input produces: a=[-8,1,2]. the fixed scale was designed for: [-4,4]. the new value: 8 is outside the calibrated range. so it must be clipped. dynamic quantization instead sees: \max|a|=8 and computes: s=\frac{127}{8}=15.875. thus dynamic adapts to the new input. this illustrates the fundamental tradeoff. 22. now the question becomes more interesting so far our objective was: \text{minimize weight/activation reconstruction error}. but is that actually what we care about? suppose: w=0.42 becomes: \hat{w}=0.4286. that's a weight error of: 0.0086. but does that necessarily mean the model output is badly affected? no. a small change in one weight might barely affect the final output. conversely, a tiny change in a highly sensitive weight could matter enormously. this leads to: \boxed{\text{gptq}} 23. gptq — the key idea gptq is post-training quantization designed specifically to minimize the damage quantization does to a layer's outputs. the quantization deck describes gptq as processing a pretrained model one layer at a time , asking: which quantized weights best reconstruct the original layer outputs on calibration data? (source: quantization-slides) this is a much more intelligent objective than: \min\|w-\hat w\|^2. instead, conceptually: \boxed{ \min_{\hat w} \|wx-\hat wx\|^2 } where: w = original layer weights, \hat w = quantized weights, x = calibration activations. the slides explicitly formulate this output-reconstruction objective. (source: quantization-slides) 24. why does gptq use calibration activations? suppose a layer computes: y=wx. a particular weight matters according to the input dimensions that actually pass through that layer. if calibration activations tell us that feature 7 varies strongly and feature 12 barely varies, then perturbing a weight connected to feature 7 may have a much larger effect. therefore: \boxed{ \text{importance depends on the data flowing through the layer} } not simply on the numerical size of the weight itself. 25. deriving the quadratic objective for one output row w : y=wx. after quantization: \hat y=\hat wx. the output error is: \|wx-\hat wx\|^2. define: \delta=w-\hat w. then: wx-\hat wx = (w-\hat w)x = \delta x. therefore: \|\delta x\|^2. using matrix algebra: \boxed{ \|\delta x\|^2 = \delta xx^t\delta^t } so define: \boxed{ h=xx^t } or with regularization: \boxed{ h=xx^t+\lambda i. } the supplied slides identify this h as the hessian-like matrix arising from calibration activations. (source: quantization-slides) correction: for l=δxxᵀδᵀ, the exact hessian is 2xxᵀ. xxᵀ is hessian-like when the factor is declared; normalized inverse-hessian compensation is unchanged by a common factor. complete grounded review 26. why call h a hessian? consider the quadratic objective: l(\delta) = \delta h\delta^t. the curvature of this quadratic depends on: h. so h tells us how sensitive output reconstruction is to movement in different directions of weight space. this is why gptq can make data-aware corrections . 27. the most important gptq insight suppose one weight is quantized. the quantization error is: e=w_q-w. naive quantization says: “too bad. that error is fixed.” gptq says: “can i redistribute the damage across weights that are less sensitive?” the supplied slides explicitly describe this compensation idea. (source: quantization-slides) therefore: \boxed{ \text{one weight's quantization error} \rightarrow \text{compensating changes elsewhere} } while respecting the quantization constraint. 28. worked gptq example from the slides consider: w= [0.42,\ 0.30,\ 0.50]. suppose int4 quantization uses a grid such that: \hat w = \frac{\operatorname{round}(14w)}{14}. for the first element: 0.42\times14=5.88. round: 6. thus: \hat w_1=\frac6{14} = 0.4286. error: e=w_1-\hat w_1 =0.42-0.4286 = \boxed{-0.0086}. these are the values shown in the supplied gptq slides. (source: quantization-slides) 29. naive quantization vs gptq naive: [0.42,0.30,0.50] might become: [0.4286,0.2857,0.5000]. gptq instead first quantizes the first weight and then modifies other still-unquantized weights to compensate for the induced output error. the slides give the sequence: [0.4200,0.3000,0.5000] ↓ [0.4286,0.2966,0.4999] ↓ [0.4286,0.2857,0.5010] ↓ [0.4286,0.2857,0.5000]. (source: quantization-slides) notice something fascinating: the intermediate weights are deliberately moved away from their original values. that sounds wrong until we remember the objective. 30. gptq does not minimize raw weight error this is an extremely important exam/interview point. a student might assume: \boxed{ \text{best quantization} = \min\|w-\hat w\|^2 } gptq says: \boxed{ \text{best quantization} = \text{minimize output damage} } the supplied deck gives a striking result: naive independent rounding has larger output error; gptq produces 52.6% lower output error in its reported experiment; yet gptq can have higher raw weight error . (source: quantization-slides) that sounds paradoxical only until you realize the objective is different. 31. intuition using a road analogy imagine two roads. direction a changing the road by 1 cm causes almost no traffic problem. direction b changing the road by 1 cm causes traffic to collapse. if you only minimize physical distance moved, you treat both directions equally. gptq instead asks: \boxed{\text{“which direction can absorb the quantization error with least output damage?”}} so it may deliberately move some weights more if those dimensions are less sensitive. 32. gptq's compensation equation the slides give the compensation update in terms of the inverse hessian. for the weight being quantized, the quantization error is incorporated into a correction: \boxed{ \delta_q = \frac{e} {[h^{-1}]_{qq}} } and the remaining weights are adjusted using the corresponding column of h^{-1} . the exact form shown in the deck is: \boxed{ w_j \leftarrow w_j-\delta_q \,[h^{-1}]_{j,q} } with normalization by the corresponding diagonal term in the definition of \delta_q . (source: quantization-slides) the important conceptual meaning is more important than memorizing every subscript: \boxed{ h^{-1} = \text{how quantization error should be redistributed} } correction: complete the arithmetic: .30-(-.0086/.1268)(-.0504)=.29658170347≈.2966, with e=w-w_hat. declare the error sign. complete grounded review 33. numerical gptq compensation from the slide the slide gives: e=-0.0086 and: [h^{-1}]_{qq}=0.1268 with another relevant element: [h^{-1}]_{2,1}=-0.0504. the correction produces: w_2 \leftarrow 0.30 - \frac{0.126?}{?} and the supplied result is: \boxed{w_2=0.2966}. the exact displayed algebra is less important for the intuition than the conclusion: 0.30\rightarrow0.2966 before w_2 itself is quantized. that means gptq prepares future weights for the error created by earlier quantization. (source: quantization-slides) correction: the inverse of a remaining hessian block generally differs from a slice of the old inverse. a schur update or equivalent cholesky construction preserves the free-variable problem. complete grounded review 34. why does gptq process weights sequentially? suppose we have: w_1,w_2,w_3,\ldots,w_d. gptq: quantizes one coordinate/column; measures its error; compensates remaining coordinates; moves to the next coordinate; repeats. therefore: \boxed{ \text{quantize} \rightarrow \text{compensate} \rightarrow \text{quantize} \rightarrow \text{compensate} \rightarrow\cdots } the supplied deck explicitly describes this sequential process. (source: quantization-slides) 35. why “one column across all rows”? an important implementation detail. suppose a weight matrix: w\in\mathbb{r}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}. the calibration hessian: h=xx^t depends only on the input activations x . every output row sees the same input features. therefore every row can reuse: h,\quad h^{-1}. the slides say gptq processes one column across all rows simultaneously and reuses the same decomposition, rather than solving a completely independent problem for every row. (source: quantization-slides) this is an important computational optimization. 36. why is gptq computationally practical? if we solved a separate optimization problem independently for every row, that would be expensive. instead: h=xx^t is computed once for the layer. its factorization is then reused. the slide describes a cholesky decomposition being computed once and reused column-by-column across the weight matrix. (source: quantization-slides) the dominant matrix factorization is approximately: \boxed{o(d^3)} for the relevant input dimension, which the deck highlights. (source: quantization-slides) 37. the complete advanced quantization picture we can now see why all these techniques exist: \boxed{ \text{global min/max} } is simple but vulnerable to outliers. therefore: \boxed{ \text{clipping} } can trade tail accuracy for better bulk precision. but how should clipping be selected? \boxed{ \text{calibration} } using: \text{percentiles} or: \text{mse} or: \text{kl divergence}. then activations introduce another issue: \boxed{ \text{dynamic vs static quantization} } because activation ranges depend on the input. finally, instead of minimizing raw tensor reconstruction: \boxed{ \text{gptq minimizes layer-output damage} } using calibration activations and curvature information. 38. exam numerical set — clipping question int8 symmetric quantization. an outlier makes: \alpha=256. calculate the scale. s=\frac{127}{256} \boxed{s\approx0.4961} question what happens to: x=1? x_q=\operatorname{round}(1\times0.4961) \boxed{x_q=0}. question now clip to: [-5,5]. then: s=\frac{127}{5} = \boxed{25.4}. for x=1 : x_q=\operatorname{round}(25.4) = \boxed{25}. dequantize: \frac{25}{25.4} \approx \boxed{0.9843}. 39. exam numerical — mse calibration suppose candidate clipping thresholds yield: \{0.12,\ 0.08,\ 0.05,\ 0.07,\ 0.15\} for mse. minimum is: \boxed{0.05}. therefore choose the corresponding clipping threshold. very simple exam question, but conceptually important: \boxed{ \text{choose the range producing minimum calibration loss} } 40. exam numerical — quantization resolution int8 symmetric range: [-127,127]. total number of usable positive/negative code steps is roughly 254 apart from the centered zero convention. if: [-5,5] is mapped to this grid, approximate step size is: \frac{10}{254} \approx \boxed{0.0394}. if instead: [-256,256], step size becomes: \frac{512}{254} \approx \boxed{2.016}. this immediately shows why clipping can dramatically improve precision for ordinary values. 41. exam numerical — dynamic quantization an activation tensor is: x=[-2,1,4]. int8 symmetric. \alpha=4. therefore: s=\frac{127}{4} = \boxed{31.75}. now another inference produces: x'=[-1,2,8]. dynamic quantization recalculates: \alpha'=8. thus: s'=\frac{127}{8} = \boxed{15.875}. the scale changes. static quantization would retain the previously calibrated scale. 42. exam numerical — gptq conceptual question suppose two quantization methods produce: method weight mse output mse naive 0.010 0.020 gptq 0.015 0.009 which method is better according to gptq's objective ? answer: \boxed{\text{gptq}} because: 0.009<0.020. even though: 0.015>0.010 for raw weight mse. this is one of the most important conceptual exam questions in this section. 43. do not confuse these objectives ordinary quantization often focuses on: \boxed{ \|w-\hat w\| } gptq focuses on: \boxed{ \|wx-\hat wx\| } that one change in objective is the conceptual leap. 44. current roadmap position we have now completed the first major advanced-quantization block: \boxed{ \text{step 3.6a} } covered \boxed{ \text{outliers} \rightarrow \text{clipping} \rightarrow \text{calibration} \rightarrow \text{mse/kl} \rightarrow \text{dynamic/static} \rightarrow \text{gptq} } the quantization deck then continues into: \boxed{ \text{gguf / k-quants} \rightarrow \text{qat} \rightarrow \text{bitnet} \rightarrow \text{1.58-bit / ternary weights} } those are not the same thing as gptq or qlora , and the distinction is important. the deck specifically describes gguf's nested super-block/sub-block scales, qat's “fake quantization” training, and bitnet's replacement of linear with bitlinear. claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 3.6b — gguf, k-quants, qat, bitnet, and 1.58-bit llms plan node: i4 · chat order #32 we now finish the major quantization section. so far we established: \text{fp32/fp16} \rightarrow \text{int8/int4} \rightarrow \text{calibration} \rightarrow \text{gptq} now the supplied quantization deck moves into four related but distinct ideas: \boxed{ \text{gguf/k-quants} \rightarrow \text{qat} \rightarrow \text{bitnet 1-bit} \rightarrow \text{bitnet b1.58} } the crucial thing is that these are not interchangeable . 1. first: what problem is gguf trying to solve? we already learned block-wise quantization. suppose: w= [b_1,b_2,b_3,\ldots] and each block gets its own scale: s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots this is better than giving the entire tensor one scale. but now imagine a large model. every block has: \boxed{\text{quantized weights}+\text{scale}} so we have introduced metadata overhead. gguf's k-quants organize this information more efficiently using two nested levels . (source: quantization-slides) 2. gguf is a format, not simply “another 4-bit algorithm” this distinction is important. think of: \boxed{\text{gguf}} as a model-file/storage format used by the llama.cpp ecosystem. inside that format, you can have different quantization schemes such as: \boxed{\text{q2\_k},\text{ q4\_k},\text{ q6\_k},\ldots} the supplied deck specifically discusses the k-quant family within gguf. (source: quantization-slides) so: gguf is the container/format; q4_k, q6_k, etc. are quantization levels/schemes within it. 3. why two levels of blocks? ordinary block quantization: large tensor | +--- block 1 -> scale s1 | +--- block 2 -> scale s2 | +--- block 3 -> scale s3 gguf k-quants: large super-block | +--- sub-block 1 -> scale s1 | +--- sub-block 2 -> scale s2 | +--- sub-block 3 -> scale s3 | +--- ... the supplied deck describes a super-block containing several sub-blocks , with each sub-block receiving its own scale. (source: quantization-slides) why? because we want: \boxed{\text{fine-grained scaling}} without the overhead of having completely independent full-precision scale information for every tiny piece. 4. then gguf does something clever with the scales suppose: s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots are the sub-block scales. why store every s_i as a full-precision number? gguf can quantize the sub-block scales themselves. so: s_i \rightarrow s_i^{q}. but to reconstruct them, we need another scale: s_{\text{super}}. thus: \boxed{ \text{weights} \rightarrow \text{sub-block scales} \rightarrow \text{super-block scale} } the deck explicitly describes this as a second level of quantization and compares the idea to qlora's double quantization. (source: quantization-slides) 5. visualize the nesting think: super-block ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ sub-block 1 │ │ weights + q(scale) │ │ │ │ sub-block 2 │ │ weights + q(scale) │ │ │ │ sub-block 3 │ │ weights + q(scale) │ │ │ │ super-block scale │ └──────────────────────────┘ this provides two levels of granularity: \boxed{\text{local scale}} and: \boxed{\text{global/super-block scale}}. 6. why not use one scale for every weight? because that would require: n_{\text{weights}} scales. if we have: 7\times10^9 weights, that would be ridiculous metadata overhead. one scale per huge block is too coarse. therefore: \boxed{ \text{nested blocks} } provide a compromise between: \text{precision} and: \text{metadata overhead}. 7. q4_k does not mean exactly 4 bits per parameter this is an excellent exam trap. the nominal weight code is: 4\text{ bits}. but we must also count: sub-block scale information, super-block scale information, other format overhead. therefore the effective cost can be larger. the supplied deck specifically reports: \boxed{\text{q4\_k}\approx4.5\text{ bits/weight}} once scale overhead is included. (source: quantization-slides) so: \boxed{4\text{-bit weight code}\neq4.000\text{ bits/weight overall}} 8. numerical example: effective bits/weight suppose we have: 1000 weights and the total encoded file information works out to: 4500 bits. then: \frac{4500}{1000} = \boxed{4.5\text{ bits/weight}}. that is the correct way to think about practical quantization cost. 9. compare q4_k and q2_k conceptually nominally: q2_k\rightarrow2\text{ bits} q4_k\rightarrow4\text{ bits} q6_k\rightarrow6\text{ bits}. but the actual effective cost includes scale/metadata overhead. therefore lower nominal bit-width does not automatically imply a simple exact: 2,\ 4,\ 6 bits/weight in the stored file. the supplied deck explicitly frames k-quants as trading weight bit-width against how finely scales are represented. (source: quantization-slides) 10. gguf vs qlora double quantization this is another easy place to get confused. both use: \boxed{\text{quantize the quantization constants}} but they are not the same implementation. qlora uses double quantization for its quantization constants in its 4-bit training approach. gguf k-quants use nested sub-block/super-block scale quantization for efficient model storage. the supplied deck explicitly says the idea is analogous, but applied in a different integer-format context. (source: quantization-slides) so: \boxed{\text{same high-level idea, different systems}} 11. now move to qat so far, our quantization discussion has mostly been: \boxed{\text{train first}\rightarrow\text{quantize afterward}} this is: \boxed{\text{ptq = post-training quantization}} the supplied deck now introduces: \boxed{\text{qat = quantization-aware training}} the difference is fundamental. 12. ptq suppose training produces: w^*. then we quantize: w^* \rightarrow q(w^*). the model never experienced that quantization during training. so: train ↓ fp model ↓ finished ↓ quantize ↓ int8 / int4 model 13. qat qat says: let training know that quantization is coming. conceptually: training | +--> quantization simulation | +--> model learns | +--> quantization-aware weights | ↓ deployable low-bit model the deck says qat trains the network while accounting for the quantization grid rather than imposing the grid only after training. (source: quantization-slides) 14. what is “fake quantization”? this is the key mechanism. suppose: x is fp32. we calculate: x_q=\operatorname{round}(sx) and then immediately reconstruct: \hat x=\frac{x_q}{s}. so the training graph sees: x \rightarrow q(x) \rightarrow d(q(x)). the result is not kept compressed permanently. it's a simulation of what low-bit inference will do . the supplied slides call this a “fake” quantization step. (source: quantization-slides) 15. why do this? suppose normal training finds: w^*. imagine w^* lies in a very narrow low-loss region. after quantization: w^*\rightarrow q(w^*) the small rounding perturbation may push the parameters outside that good region. so: \boxed{\text{low training loss before quantization}} does not guarantee: \boxed{\text{low loss after quantization}}. 16. wide minima vs narrow minima imagine the loss landscape: loss ^ | narrow minimum | \/ | / \ | wide / \ | minimum / \ | \______/ \ +----------------------------> weights a narrow minimum is sensitive to small changes. a wide minimum is more tolerant. quantization introduces a perturbation: w\rightarrow w+\epsilon. a wide minimum can remain low-loss: l(w+\epsilon)\approx l(w). a narrow minimum may become: l(w+\epsilon)\gg l(w). the supplied deck uses exactly this wide-vs-narrow-minimum intuition. (source: quantization-slides) 17. why qat can produce more robust weights because during training the model repeatedly sees the quantization effect. therefore optimization is encouraged toward parameter regions where: \boxed{\text{quantization perturbations hurt less}} the supplied slides state that qat can steer training toward wider minima that tolerate quantization. (source: quantization-slides) so: \boxed{ \text{qat learns weights that are friendly to the quantization grid} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{learn first and hope quantization doesn't break them} } 18. but how can gradients pass through rounding? this is where implementation becomes subtle. the exact rounding function: \operatorname{round}(x) has zero derivative almost everywhere and is therefore not directly useful for ordinary gradient descent. the deck does not develop the detailed derivative approximation, but it explains the practical mechanism: forward computation experiences quantization/dequantization while gradients continue in higher precision. (source: quantization-slides) the common implementation concept is a straight-through estimator (ste) . for studying the supplied deck, remember: \boxed{ \text{forward sees rounding} \quad+\quad \text{backward still permits gradient flow} } rather than trying to differentiate the literal integer rounding operation normally. 19. numerical qat example suppose: x=0.83 and: s=10. quantize: x_q=\operatorname{round}(8.3)=8. dequantize: \hat x=\frac8{10}=0.8. so the forward pass effectively uses: \boxed{0.8} instead of: 0.83. the training process therefore experiences the same type of perturbation that deployment will encounter. 20. ptq vs qat property ptq qat quantization introduced after training during training training sees quantization effects no yes calibration/training overhead lower higher can adapt weights to quantization no yes goal compress a finished model train a model robust to low-bit representation the supplied deck explicitly contrasts the two in terms of whether the model “knew” the quantization was coming. (source: quantization-slides) 21. now: bitnet we have: \text{qat} but bitnet takes the idea much further. the deck describes bitnet as: qat taken to its extreme instead of taking an ordinary fp16 linear layer and later quantizing it, bitnet replaces the linear layer with a bitlinear layer whose weights are trained to live in extremely low precision from the beginning. (source: quantization-slides) so: \boxed{ \text{linear} \rightarrow \text{bitlinear} } 22. bitnet 1-bit weights the first bitnet idea is: \boxed{ w_q\in\{-1,+1\} } instead of ordinary floating-point weights. so every weight is represented by one of just two values: -1 or: +1. the supplied deck calls this 1-bit weight quantization. (source: quantization-slides) correction: subtracting the mean centers values but does not guarantee half positive and half negative. a highly skewed weight distribution can violate that intuition. complete grounded review 23. how are the 1-bit weights produced? the deck uses: \boxed{ w_q=\operatorname{sign}(w-\alpha) } where: \alpha=\operatorname{mean}(w). so we first center weights around their mean. then: w-\alpha is positive or negative. the sign function gives: \operatorname{sign}(x)= \begin{cases} +1,&x\ge0\\ -1,&x<0 \end{cases} according to the stated convention. the supplied slides explain that subtracting the mean centers the weights so that approximately half lie on either side before collapsing them to -1/+1 . (source: quantization-slides) 24. numerical bitnet example suppose: w= [0.8,\ 0.2,\ -0.1,\ 0.5,\ -0.4]. mean: \alpha= \frac{0.8+0.2-0.1+0.5-0.4}{5} = \frac{1.0}{5} = 0.2. center: w-\alpha = [0.6,\ 0,\ -0.3,\ 0.3,\ -0.6]. sign: w_q= [+1,+1,-1,+1,-1]. thus: \boxed{ [0.8,0.2,-0.1,0.5,-0.4] \rightarrow [1,1,-1,1,-1] } 25. but 1-bit weights alone aren't enough the deck doesn't simply say: “everything becomes 1 bit.” instead, it uses different precisions for different pieces. the supplied bitlinear pipeline is: \boxed{ \text{fp16 input} \rightarrow \text{layernorm} \rightarrow \text{int8 activations} \rightarrow \text{1-bit weights} } then: \boxed{ \text{matmul} \rightarrow \text{dequantize} \rightarrow \text{fp16 output} } the deck explicitly gives this pipeline. (source: quantization-slides) 26. why int8 activations instead of 1-bit? because activations change with every input. the deck gives the intuition that activations carry more information and therefore are retained at a finer precision than the weights. (source: quantization-slides) so: \boxed{ w:\text{1-bit} } while: \boxed{ x:\text{int8} } this is asymmetric precision by design. 27. bitlinear pipeline mathematically conceptually: x \rightarrow x_q and: w \rightarrow w_q. then: y_q=x_qw_q. finally recover a higher-precision result: y_{\text{deq}} using the relevant scales. the deck states that the product is dequantized back to fp16 before leaving the bitlinear layer. (source: quantization-slides) 28. why is this computationally interesting? now suppose: w_q\in\{-1,+1\}. consider a dot product: y=\sum_i w_i x_i. since: w_i\in\{-1,+1\}, every term becomes: w_ix_i= \begin{cases} +x_i,&w_i=+1\\ -x_i,&w_i=-1. \end{cases} so we no longer need a conventional multiplication for the weight. instead: \boxed{ +x_i\quad\text{or}\quad-x_i } followed by accumulation. this is the key intuition behind low-bit/bitwise computation. 29. numerical 1-bit dot product suppose: x=[3,5,2,7] and: w=[+1,-1,+1,-1]. ordinary multiplication: (+1)(3)+(-1)(5)+(1)(2)+(-1)(7) =3-5+2-7 =\boxed{-7}. notice: +1\times3=3 -1\times5=-5 +1\times2=2 -1\times7=-7 the multiplication by the binary weight itself is trivial. thus: \boxed{\text{multiply-by-weight becomes sign selection}} 30. now bitnet b1.58 the next step is even more interesting. instead of: \{-1,+1\}, bitnet b1.58 uses: \boxed{ \{-1,0,+1\} } for the quantized weights. the supplied deck explains that this adds the zero value, creating three possible states. (source: quantization-slides) 31. why is it called 1.58 bits? three possible states require: \log_2(3) bits to represent information theoretically. compute: \log_2(3)\approx1.58496. therefore: \boxed{ \log_2 3\approx1.58 } hence the name: \boxed{\text{bitnet b1.58}}. the supplied deck explicitly gives this reasoning. (source: quantization-slides) 32. why does zero matter? suppose: w_i=0. then: w_ix_i=0. the input contributes nothing to the dot product. therefore: \boxed{0} acts like a natural “skip this contribution” state. this creates a potentially sparse computation. the deck explicitly connects the ternary weight representation to additions, subtractions, and dropped terms. (source: quantization-slides) 33. ternary dot-product example suppose: x=[4,7,3,9,2] and: w=[+1,0,-1,+1,0]. then: y = (+1)(4) +(0)(7) +(-1)(3) +(+1)(9) +(0)(2) = 4+0-3+9+0 =\boxed{10}. no meaningful multiplication remains: \boxed{4-3+9} with the zero-weight positions dropped. 34. this is why the computation can become addition/subtraction for: w_i\in\{-1,0,+1\}, we have: w_ix_i \in \{-x_i,0,+x_i\}. so: \boxed{ w_ix_i= +x_i,\ -x_i,\ \text{or nothing} } therefore: \boxed{ \text{dot product}\rightarrow \text{additions + subtractions + skips} } the deck explicitly describes this as the multiplication disappearing. (source: quantization-slides) correction: use roundclip(w/(gamma+epsilon),-1,1) for clipping and all-zero protection. absmean quantization does not guarantee most weights are zero. complete grounded review 35. how are b1.58 weights quantized? the deck changes the normalization strategy here. earlier bitnet uses a mean-centering approach. for b1.58, the supplied deck gives absmean quantization . define: \boxed{ \alpha= \operatorname{mean}(|w|) } then: \boxed{ w_q= \operatorname{round} \left( \frac{w}{\alpha} \right) } and because the result is restricted to the ternary set: \boxed{ w_q\in\{-1,0,+1\} } the supplied slide specifically states that dividing by the mean absolute weight causes most values to round to 0 , while larger values round to \pm1 . (source: quantization-slides) correction: declare rounding ties. numpy/pytorch ties-to-even maps .5→0 and 2.5→2, yielding [0,0,-1,1,-1]. the inherited [0,1,-1,1,-1] uses half-away-from-zero. complete grounded review 36. numerical b1.58 example take: w=[0.1,\ 0.2,\ -0.3,\ 1.0,\ -0.4]. calculate mean absolute value: \alpha = \frac{ |0.1|+|0.2|+|{-0.3}|+|1.0|+|{-0.4}| }{5} = \frac{0.1+0.2+0.3+1.0+0.4}{5} = \frac{2.0}{5} = 0.4. now divide: w/\alpha = [0.25,\ 0.5,\ -0.75,\ 2.5,\ -1]. round: [0,\ 1,\ -1,\ 3,\ -1]. but b1.58 restricts the values to: \{-1,0,+1\}. so values beyond +1 are clipped to +1 : \boxed{ w_q=[0,1,-1,1,-1] } under the simple clipped-ternary interpretation. 37. why does zero create sparsity? suppose: w/\alpha contains many values such as: 0.1,\ 0.2,\ -0.3,\ 0.4. these are near zero. rounding them to the ternary grid gives: 0. so many weights become: \boxed{0}. the deck explicitly notes this as a sparsifying side effect of absmean ternary quantization. (source: quantization-slides) thus b1.58 offers: \boxed{ \text{low precision} + \text{potential sparsity} + \text{simple arithmetic} } 38. numerical storage comparison suppose we have: 1,000,000,000 weights. fp16 16\text{ bits/weight} so: 16\times10^9\text{ bits} or: \boxed{2\text{ gb}} ignoring metadata. 1-bit 1\times10^9\text{ bits} or: \boxed{125\text{ mb}}. information-theoretic ternary 1.585\text{ bits/weight} so: 1.585\times10^9\text{ bits} approximately: \boxed{198\text{ mb}}. actual implementation storage is affected by packing and additional scaling information. 39. important conceptual distinction: qlora vs bitnet they look similar because both involve low-bit weights. but they solve different problems. qlora \boxed{ \text{existing pretrained model} + \text{4-bit frozen storage} + \text{lora training} } bitnet \boxed{ \text{architecture/training designed around ultra-low-bit weights} } the supplied deck explicitly describes bitnet as replacing ordinary linear layers with bitlinear layers and training them in the low-bit regime from the outset.
