(source: retool-slides) 5.21.1 start from ordinary language-model rl an llm can be viewed as a policy: \boxed{\pi_\theta} where: \theta = model parameters s_t = state/context at step t o_t = token/action generated at step t the model gives: \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t) which means: probability that the current policy assigns to token o_t , given the current context s_t . for a language model, the state is essentially the current context. so: s_t= (q,o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_{t-1}) where q is the original question. 5.21.2 what does the state look like in retool? this is where retool differs. the context can contain: \boxed{ \text{question} + \text{reasoning} + \text{code} + \text{interpreter output} } for example: question: solve the problem. reasoning: i should search candidate values. code: ... interpreter: 699 reasoning: the candidate appears to be 699... therefore: \boxed{ s_t=(q,o_{}\mid s_t)=0.25 p(\texttt{answer}\mid s_t)=0.05. the model samples one action/token. the important point is: \boxed{ \text{tool invocation itself is generated through the policy} } the model decides to emit code. 5.21.4 then the environment may intervene suppose the model emits: x = 17 * 41 print(x) the sandbox executes it. the result: 697 gets inserted into the context. so the next state becomes: \boxed{ s_{t+1} = \text{previous state} + \text{interpreter feedback} } this is why retool's trajectory is different from ordinary text-only rl. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.5 now ask: how do we update the policy? suppose a rollout eventually gets: r=+1. we want the model to become more likely to repeat useful behavior that led to that successful trajectory. but we do not want: \text{one successful rollout} \rightarrow \text{massive policy change}. this is exactly the problem ppo addresses. 5.21.6 why ppo uses the old policy during rollout collection, we have: \pi_{\text{old}}. after collecting the rollout, we construct a new policy: \pi_\theta. for a sampled token o_t , compare: \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t) against: \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t\mid s_t). define the ratio: \boxed{ r_t(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t) }{ \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t\mid s_t) } } this is the central quantity in ppo. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.7 intuition behind the ratio suppose old policy: p_{\text{old}}(o_t)=0.10 and new policy: p_{\text{new}}(o_t)=0.12. then: r_t = \frac{0.12}{0.10} = \boxed{1.2}. so the new policy increased the probability by: 20\%. if: r_t=1, nothing changed. if: r_t<1, the new policy decreased the probability. 5.21.8 but probability ratio alone isn't enough we also need to know: was this action good or bad? that information is represented by the advantage : \boxed{\hat a_t} this is the crucial quantity in ppo. 5.21.9 what does advantage mean? conceptually: \boxed{ a(s_t,o_t) = \text{how good this action was} - \text{how good we expected the state to be} } for a positive advantage: \hat a_t>0 the action was better than expected. for a negative advantage: \hat a_t<0 the action was worse than expected. therefore: \boxed{ \text{positive advantage} \rightarrow \text{increase probability} } and: \boxed{ \text{negative advantage} \rightarrow \text{decrease probability}. } 5.21.10 where does ppo get advantage from? this is the exact difference from grpo. ppo uses a learned value function: \boxed{ v_\phi(s_t) } where \phi are the parameters of the value model/value head. the supplied reasoning source explicitly explains: ppo's value function estimates expected future outcome quality, while grpo removes this learned value model and gets its relative signal from a sampled group. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.21.11 return vs value suppose the eventual rollout produces reward: r=+1. the value model might predict: v_\phi(s_t)=0.4. then a simple advantage estimate is: \hat a_t = r-v_\phi(s_t). so: \hat a_t = 1-0.4 = \boxed{0.6}. interpretation: the outcome was considerably better than the value model expected. 5.21.12 negative example suppose: r=-1 and: v_\phi(s_t)=-0.2. then: \hat a_t = -1-(-0.2) = \boxed{-0.8}. so: \boxed{ \text{strongly negative advantage} } and ppo pushes the probability of the sampled action downward. 5.21.13 why not simply use reward? this question is extremely important. suppose every token in a 1,000-token trajectory gets the same reward: r=+1. that doesn't tell us what the model expected from each state. the value function provides a baseline: v_\phi(s_t). thus: \boxed{ a_t = \text{actual outcome} - \text{expected outcome} } gives a more informative learning signal. this is the role of the value model in ppo. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.21.14 ppo objective before clipping ignoring clipping for a moment: \boxed{ j(\theta) = \mathbb e \left[ r_t(\theta)\hat a_t \right] } where: r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(o_t|s_t)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_t|s_t)}. so: \boxed{ \text{policy change} \times \text{quality of action} } determines the learning signal. 5.21.15 example with positive advantage suppose: r_t=1.15 and: \hat a_t=0.8. then: r_t\hat a_t = 1.15\times0.8 = \boxed{0.92}. the action was good, and the new policy increased its probability. that is desirable. 5.21.16 example with negative advantage suppose: r_t=0.85 and: \hat a_t=-0.8. then: r_ta_t = 0.85(-0.8) = \boxed{-0.68}. the action was bad and the new policy reduced its probability. that is also desirable. 5.21.17 why clipping is necessary imagine the model suddenly changes: 0.10\rightarrow0.50. then: r_t= \frac{0.50}{0.10} = 5. a fivefold increase is enormous. a single rollout could therefore cause an unstable update. ppo prevents excessive policy movement through clipping. 5.21.18 ppo clipping define: \boxed{ \operatorname{clip}(r_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) } suppose: \epsilon=0.2. then: 1-\epsilon=0.8 and: 1+\epsilon=1.2. therefore: r_t is restricted to: \boxed{[0.8,1.2]}. 5.21.19 full clipped ppo objective the retool slide gives the standard ppo form: \boxed{ j_{\text{ppo}}(\theta) = \mathbb e_t \left[ \min \left( r_t(\theta)\hat a_t,\, \operatorname{clip} (r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat a_t \right) \right] } this is the core retool training objective. (source: retool-slides) now we will understand exactly why the min is there. 5.21.20 case a: positive advantage suppose: a_t=+2 and: r_t=1.5. raw objective: r_ta_t = 1.5\times2 = 3. clipped ratio: \operatorname{clip}(1.5,0.8,1.2) = 1.2. therefore: 1.2\times2 = 2.4. take minimum: \boxed{ \min(3,2.4)=2.4 } so ppo refuses to give the full benefit of the 50% probability increase. 5.21.21 case b: negative advantage now: a_t=-2 and: r_t=0.5. raw: 0.5(-2) = -1. clipped: \operatorname{clip}(0.5,0.8,1.2) = 0.8. then: 0.8(-2) = -1.6. take minimum: \boxed{ \min(-1,-1.6)=-1.6 } this makes excessive policy movement toward a bad action unattractive. 5.21.22 the geometric intuition think of ppo as saying: \boxed{ \text{"improve the policy, but don't move too far in one update."} } so: \text{good action} \rightarrow \text{increase probability} but only moderately. and: \text{bad action} \rightarrow \text{decrease probability} but again with controlled updates. 5.21.23 now bring retool back into the equation here is where everything becomes interesting. the action might be a normal reasoning token: i should search... or: or: for x in range(...) the model may therefore receive credit for a sequence like: \boxed{ \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{call tool} \rightarrow \text{observe} \rightarrow \text{correct} \rightarrow \text{answer} } the probability ratio is calculated for model-generated tokens within that hybrid trajectory. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.24 important subtlety: interpreter output isn't the policy action suppose: print(5*9) produces: 45 the model generated: \boxed{\texttt{print(5*9)}} but the environment generated: \boxed{\texttt{45}} therefore the policy ratio is conceptually associated with model-generated decisions, not with the external environment's generated text. this connects directly to the earlier engineering rule: \boxed{ \text{mask interpreter tokens} } from the retool deck. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.25 full miniature trajectory consider: question: find the valid value of x. model: i should search the candidate space. model: for x in range(1,1000): ... environment: 699 model: the interpreter found 699. model: \boxed{699} policy-generated sequence: \boxed{ \text{reasoning} + \text{code} + \text{final answer} } environment-generated sequence: \boxed{ \text{699} } final reward: r=+1. now ppo computes advantages over the relevant model-generated positions and updates the policy so useful behavior becomes more likely. 5.21.26 full mathematical pipeline here is the entire calculation: step 1 — sample trajectory \tau\sim\pi_{\text{old}} step 2 — execute tool calls \text{code} \rightarrow \text{sandbox} \rightarrow \text{feedback} step 3 — obtain final reward r(\tau)\in\{-1,+1\} step 4 — value prediction v_\phi(s_t) step 5 — advantage conceptually: \hat a_t \approx \text{return}-v_\phi(s_t) step 6 — policy ratio r_t= \frac{\pi_\theta(o_t|s_t)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_t|s_t)} step 7 — clipping \tilde r_t = \operatorname{clip} (r_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) step 8 — ppo objective \boxed{ \min(r_ta_t,\tilde r_ta_t) } step 9 — gradient update \theta \leftarrow \theta+\eta\nabla_\theta j_{\text{ppo}} that is the complete policy-update pipeline at the conceptual level. (source: retool-slides; build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.21.27 why retool does not use grpo here now compare the advantage calculation. ppo \boxed{ \hat a_t \approx r_t-v_\phi(s_t) } requires: \boxed{ \text{learned value function} } grpo uses a group of responses: r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_g and constructs group-relative advantages. for example: a_i= \frac{r_i-\mu_r}{\sigma_r}. no value model is required. the supplied sources make exactly this distinction: grpo replaces the learned value-model path with group-relative normalization. 5.21.28 why this distinction matters computationally ppo: \boxed{ \text{policy model} + \text{value model} } grpo: \boxed{ \text{policy model} + \text{multiple sampled responses} } the value model can be expensive for large llm systems. grpo was attractive in deepseekmath and deepseek-r1 partly because it eliminates that separate learned value model. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) retool nevertheless uses ppo according to the supplied deck. 5.21.29 full numerical ppo example now let's perform one complete calculation. suppose at one model-generated token: \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t|s_t)=0.20 and after the update candidate: \pi_{\theta}(o_t|s_t)=0.24. then: r_t= \frac{0.24}{0.20} = \boxed{1.2}. suppose: v_\phi(s_t)=0.3 and final reward: r=1. then simple advantage estimate: a_t=1-0.3 = \boxed{0.7}. set: \epsilon=0.2. then: \operatorname{clip}(1.2,0.8,1.2)=1.2. raw: 1.2(0.7)=0.84. clipped: 1.2(0.7)=0.84. therefore: \boxed{ j_t=0.84 } no clipping penalty occurs because the ratio is exactly at the upper boundary. 5.21.30 now push beyond the boundary suppose instead: \pi_\theta=0.30. then: r_t=\frac{0.30}{0.20}=1.5. advantage: a_t=0.7. raw: 1.5(0.7)=1.05. clipped: 1.2(0.7)=0.84. ppo chooses: \boxed{ \min(1.05,0.84)=0.84 } so increasing the probability from 0.20 all the way to 0.30 does not receive unlimited optimization credit. 5.21.31 one very important interpretation ppo clipping does not literally force: r_t\in[0.8,1.2]. the new policy can have a ratio outside the interval. instead, the objective stops rewarding the excessive movement in the favorable direction . this is a subtle but highly important exam/interview point. 5.21.32 why this is valuable for retool imagine that one successful trajectory contained: call code → get result → use result → answer correctly without clipping, ppo might aggressively increase the probability of all those actions. with clipping: \boxed{ \text{successful strategy} \rightarrow \text{reinforced gradually} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{successful rollout} \rightarrow \text{huge policy jump} }. 5.21.33 the complete retool learning loop now put all previous steps together: question │ ▼ old policy πold │ ▼ generate reasoning/code │ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ │ normal text │ ▼ sandbox │ ▼ interpreter result │ └──────► context │ ▼ continue generation │ ▼ final answer │ ▼ correctness checker │ ▼ r = ±1 │ ▼ value function vφ │ ▼ advantage ât │ ▼ ppo ratio rt(θ) │ ▼ clipping │ ▼ policy gradient │ ▼ new policy this is the architecture you should have in your head before moving to implementation. the retool deck's central ppo and hybrid-trajectory description supports this structure. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.34 numerical bank — level 5 exam question consider: \pi_{\text{old}}=0.08 \pi_\theta=0.16 v_\phi(s_t)=0.25 r=1 \epsilon=0.2. calculate the clipped ppo term. step 1 r_t=\frac{0.16}{0.08}=2. step 2 a_t=1-0.25=0.75. step 3 clip: \operatorname{clip}(2,0.8,1.2)=1.2. step 4 raw: 2(0.75)=1.5. clipped: 1.2(0.75)=0.9. step 5 \boxed{ \min(1.5,0.9)=0.9 } so the ppo objective contribution is: \boxed{0.9}. 5.21.35 one more exam question: negative advantage suppose: \pi_{\text{old}}=0.20, \pi_\theta=0.10, a_t=-1. then: r_t=0.5. for: \epsilon=0.2, we get: \operatorname{clip}(0.5,0.8,1.2)=0.8. raw: 0.5(-1)=-0.5. clipped: 0.8(-1)=-0.8. therefore: \boxed{ \min(-0.5,-0.8)=-0.8 } this demonstrates how ppo treats large probability movement associated with a negative advantage. 5.21.36 the five things you must remember \boxed{1.\quad r_t= \frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{old}}}} measures how much the new policy changed the probability of the sampled action. \boxed{2.\quad a_t} measures whether the action/outcome was better or worse than expected. \boxed{3.\quad v_\phi(s_t)} provides ppo's learned baseline for estimating advantage. \boxed{4.\quad \operatorname{clip}} prevents one update from receiving excessive incentive for moving too far. \boxed{5.\quad \text{retool's special part}} the state/trajectory contains: \boxed{ \text{reasoning + code + real interpreter feedback} } rather than text alone. (source: retool-slides) the conceptual bridge you should now see the complete progression: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} \rightarrow \text{grpo} \rightarrow \text{deepseek-r1} \rightarrow \text{long reasoning} \rightarrow \text{retool} \rightarrow \text{tool-interacting reasoning} } and mathematically: \boxed{ \text{reward} \rightarrow \text{advantage} \rightarrow \text{probability ratio} \rightarrow \text{clipping} \rightarrow \text{policy update} }

claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.22 — retool cold-start sft plan node: i9 · chat order #63 we now focus on one specific question: \boxed{ \text{how does retool teach a normal llm the basic ability to use the code-interpreter protocol before rl begins?} } this is the cold-start sft stage . the central distinction is: \boxed{ \text{sft teaches the protocol} } while: \boxed{ \text{rl learns the strategy} } the retool slides make this distinction explicitly. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.1 why can't we start ppo immediately? imagine taking an ordinary pretrained/instruction-tuned llm and telling it: you can use python whenever useful. then give it ppo. what should it generate? it may produce: let me calculate this manually... or malformed output such as: print(17 * 41) 697 then check the next candidate... the answer is 699. the important transformation is: \boxed{ \text{manual calculation} \rightarrow \text{code} + \text{real execution result} } the slide explicitly describes automatically rewriting each trace this way. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.6 why must the execution result be real? suppose we merely replaced: 17 × 41 = 697 with: print(17 * 41) but never actually ran the code. then the model would only see: \text{code syntax}. it would not learn what the tool actually returns. retool therefore executes the generated code in a real sandbox and inserts the actual output. thus: \boxed{ \text{code} \rightarrow \text{real execution} \rightarrow \text{real feedback} } this is exactly what later makes the rollout a true model-environment interaction. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.7 why does the sandbox matter during dataset creation? because the cold-start example must teach the model the relationship: \boxed{ \text{my code} \rightarrow \text{environment response} } for example: print(20 + 22) followed by: 42 the model can therefore learn the protocol: \boxed{ \text{code block} \rightarrow \text{pause} \rightarrow \text{feedback} \rightarrow \text{continue} } 5.22.8 what remains unchanged? an important detail from the slide: the surrounding reasoning remains, including failed attempts. so transformation is not : \text{replace the entire reasoning with code}. instead: \boxed{ \text{preserve reasoning} + \text{insert computational tool use} } this gives the model examples of a reasoning process in which code is only one component. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.9 example with a failed attempt suppose original reasoning: i will first try candidate x=500. that doesn't work. maybe we should search the entire range. the augmented trace may retain: i will first try candidate x=500. ... ... that doesn't work. maybe we should search the entire range. the important idea is: \boxed{ \text{failure is not necessarily removed} } because the resulting data can expose the model to realistic interaction patterns. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.10 step 3 — filter the transformed examples the slide says only examples that pass both: \boxed{ \text{format check} } and: \boxed{ \text{answer-correctness check} } are retained. (source: retool-slides) so: d_{\text{init}} \rightarrow \text{rewrite} \rightarrow \text{execute} \rightarrow \text{verify} \rightarrow d_{\text{ci}} where: \boxed{d_{\text{ci}}} is the code-augmented dataset. 5.22.11 why do we need a format check? suppose a generated training example looks like: x = 10 with no closing tag. the protocol is malformed. or: 42 appears before any code call. such an example teaches the wrong interaction structure. therefore: \boxed{ \text{correctness of answer} \neq \text{correctness of protocol} } we need both. 5.22.12 why do we also need an answer-correctness check? a beautifully formatted example can still contain a wrong answer. for example: print(17 * 41) 697 \boxed{699} the protocol is valid, but the final answer is inconsistent. that example should not become supervised training data. therefore: \boxed{ \text{valid format} \land \text{correct answer} } is the filtering condition. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.13 numerical example — filtering suppose we start with: n=1000 candidate traces. after format checking: 850 remain. of those, answer verification retains: 700. therefore: \boxed{|d_{\text{ci}}|=700} the retention rate is: \frac{700}{1000}\times100 = \boxed{70\%}. this is an illustrative numerical example; the slide does not provide these particular counts. 5.22.14 step 4 — sft on the code-augmented data now we have: d_{\text{ci}}. the base model is supervised-fine-tuned on these examples. (source: retool-slides) at this point, training is ordinary autoregressive sft conceptually: \boxed{ \mathcal l_{\text{sft}} = -\sum_t \log p_\theta(y_t\mid y_{ ... ... continue reasoning \boxed{answer} then the model learns statistical patterns such as: \boxed{ \text{when code is written, an interpreter result follows} } and: \boxed{ \text{after interpreter feedback, continue reasoning} } and: \boxed{ \text{eventually produce a final answer} }. this is protocol learning. 5.22.16 what sft does not solve this is perhaps the most important sentence in the retool deck: \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft is not where good tool-use strategy is learned.} } the strategy is learned during rl. (source: retool-slides) why? because the sft examples themselves already demonstrate the behavior. the model is essentially asked: given this context, reproduce this successful example. it is not being explicitly optimized to discover: was using code actually necessary here? or: would another tool call have been better? or: should i use the tool earlier? those decisions are what ppo can discover from reward. 5.22.17 protocol learning vs strategy learning this distinction deserves a clean table. cold-start sft ppo learn syntax learn decisions learn format learn whether to call code learn structure learn when to call code learn how feedback appears learn how useful tool calls are imitate examples explore alternatives supervised signal reward signal the first column is directly supported by the retool deck; the second follows its explicit statement that strategy is what rl discovers. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.18 this is exactly why the word “cold-start” is appropriate the model is not learning the entire task from scratch. it already has: \boxed{ \text{language ability} + \text{reasoning ability} } and the sft stage adds: \boxed{ \text{tool-interaction format} }. then rl adds: \boxed{ \text{strategic tool use} }. so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{base capabilities} + \text{protocol sft} + \text{rl exploration} } 5.22.19 let's walk through one complete example suppose the task is: find the value of x satisfying a complicated constraint. original verified reasoning we need to examine candidate values. trying to calculate everything manually would be tedious. after checking the relevant condition, the answer is 699. now retool augments the computation: we need to examine candidate values. trying to calculate everything manually would be tedious. for x in range(1, 1000): ... 699 the search gives the valid candidate. \boxed{699} now this becomes a supervised example. the model learns: \boxed{ \text{problem} \rightarrow \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{feedback} \rightarrow \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{answer} } 5.22.20 but this still doesn't mean the model has learned optimal tool timing suppose a problem is: what is 2+2 ? a cold-start example might use: print(2+2) the model could therefore learn: \text{math problem} \rightarrow \text{use code}. but that's not necessarily optimal. for a simple task, direct reasoning may be perfectly adequate. retool's rl stage needs to discover: \boxed{ \text{tool use has a cost} } and should therefore be used strategically. the slide explicitly says that nothing tells the model when to use the tool; timing is exactly what rl must teach . (source: retool-slides) 5.22.21 why this is an exploration problem suppose the model has two possible policies: policy a always use code. policy b use code only when computation is difficult. the cold-start sft dataset may contain successful examples of both kinds, depending on the source transformations. sft mainly learns: p(\text{successful-looking sequence}). rl instead evaluates: \boxed{ \text{did this strategy actually produce the correct answer?} } that is much closer to discovering an optimal policy. 5.22.22 the data flow memorize this diagram: verified reasoning traces │ ▼ d_init │ ▼ replace manual computation with executable code │ ▼ execute in sandbox │ ▼ insert real interpreter feedback │ ▼ format check + correctness check │ ▼ d_ci │ ▼ sft model │ ▼ ppo / retool rl │ ▼ strategic tool-using model this is the complete cold-start-to-rl transition described by the supplied retool material. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.23 why the distinction is important for interviews suppose an interviewer asks: why not simply fine-tune the model on tool-use examples and stop there? a strong answer is: \boxed{ \text{sft gives imitation, while retool's rl stage optimizes the actual task outcome.} } sft can teach: “here is how a successful tool-use trajectory looks.” rl can discover: “given this particular problem, using the tool here improves the probability of success.” that is a more powerful learning signal for strategic behavior. 5.22.24 numerical exam question suppose: |d_{\text{init}}|=5000. after automatic rewriting: 4700 examples have valid syntax. after answer checking: 4200 remain. then: \text{final retention} = \frac{4200}{5000}\times100 = \boxed{84\%}. the number rejected after rewriting: 5000-4700 = \boxed{300}. the number rejected by answer verification: 4700-4200 = \boxed{500}. total rejected: 300+500 = \boxed{800}. correction: the supplied source explicitly masks interpreter output during rl. the850position calculation is valid only under an explicitly chosen identical mask; it is not proof of original cold-start sft loss implementation. complete grounded review 5.22.25 numerical exam question — sft token prediction suppose one cold-start example has: \boxed{1000} target tokens. the sequence contains: 780 reasoning/code tokens generated by the model, 150 interpreter-feedback tokens, 70 final-answer/reasoning tokens. if interpreter tokens are excluded from a policy-style loss: 1000-150 = \boxed{850} tokens remain eligible for the model's token-level learning signal. this is an illustrative calculation. the supplied retool deck explicitly says interpreter tokens are masked during rl; it does not give this particular numerical example. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.26 a subtle point: sft and rl have different data roles cold-start sft uses: \boxed{ \text{curated demonstrations} } rl uses: \boxed{ \text{new rollouts generated by the current policy} } so: \boxed{ \text{sft = learn from examples} } while: \boxed{ \text{rl = generate, evaluate, update, repeat} } that difference explains why rl can discover behavior that wasn't explicitly demonstrated in the sft set. the slides' later example of self-correcting after a nameerror is presented as such an emergent behavior. (source: retool-slides) 5.22.27 the three-stage logic of retool you can compress the entire mechanism into: \boxed{ d_{\text{init}} \overset{\text{rewrite + execute}}{\longrightarrow} d_{\text{ci}} \overset{\text{sft}}{\longrightarrow} \pi_{\text{cold}} \overset{\text{ppo + reward}}{\longrightarrow} \pi_{\text{retool}} } where: d_{\text{init}} verified reasoning examples. d_{\text{ci}} code/interpreter-augmented examples. \pi_{\text{cold}} model capable of following the protocol. \pi_{\text{retool}} model that learns strategically when/how to use the tool. 5.22.28 the deepest conceptual lesson there are actually two different learning problems : problem 1 — representation/protocol learning \boxed{ \text{what does a tool interaction look like?} } sft is well suited to this. problem 2 — decision/policy learning \boxed{ \text{when should i invoke the tool to maximize final success?} } rl is well suited to this. therefore: \boxed{ \text{sft teaches the language of tool use} } while: \boxed{ \text{rl teaches the economics of tool use} } that is the central idea of retool's cold-start stage. 5.22.29 final exam-ready picture remember the entire chain: \boxed{ \text{verified text reasoning} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{replace manual computation with executable code} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{run code in real sandbox} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{insert actual output} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{filter: format + correctness} } \downarrow \boxed{ d_{\text{ci}} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{learn protocol} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{ppo with correctness reward} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{learn strategic tool use} } (source: retool-slides) step 5.22 checkpoint before proceeding, the following distinctions should be completely clear: \boxed{ d_{\text{init}}\neq d_{\text{ci}} } because d_{\text{ci}} contains actual tool interactions. \boxed{ \text{sft}\neq\text{rl} } because sft imitates curated demonstrations while rl optimizes reward through exploration. \boxed{ \text{protocol}\neq\text{strategy} } because knowing how to invoke a tool does not imply knowing when invocation is useful. and finally: \boxed{ \text{retool's central learning target} = \text{strategic tool use} }

claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.23 — retool full rollout engine plan node: i9 · chat order #64 now we move from “how the cold-start model is trained” to the most important operational part: \boxed{ \text{how does one complete retool rollout actually execute from start to finish?} } this is where all the pieces we have studied come together: \boxed{ \text{llm} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{sandbox} \rightarrow \text{feedback} \rightarrow \text{llm} \rightarrow \text{answer} \rightarrow \text{reward} \rightarrow \text{ppo} } the retool slides describe the rollout as a single hybrid token sequence containing model reasoning, model-generated code, real interpreter feedback, and the final answer. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.1 start with one question suppose the training question is: \boxed{q=\text{“solve this computationally difficult problem.”}} and the ground-truth answer is: \boxed{a=699}. the model starts generating from q . at this moment, the policy is: \boxed{\pi_{\text{old}}} because this is the policy used to collect the rl rollout. 5.23.2 token 1 onward: ordinary generation the model begins: i need to find the valid candidate. then perhaps: a direct manual search would be tedious. these are ordinary policy-generated tokens. formally: o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_t \sim \pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid s_t). nothing special has happened yet. 5.23.3 the model reaches a tool decision eventually it generates: this is a critical event. the model has effectively taken the action: \boxed{ a_t=\text{invoke computational tool} } the retool prompt gives the model the ability to use executable python, but does not hard-code when to use it. that timing is meant to be learned through rl. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.4 the model now generates code for example: for x in range(1, 1000): ... the model continues until it reaches: at that moment: \boxed{ \text{generation pauses} } the slide explicitly states that code is sent to the real sandbox when is detected. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.5 important: the model does not generate the next observation the model generated: \boxed{\text{code}} but the next result comes from: \boxed{\text{environment}}. so the system executes: \text{code} \longrightarrow \text{sandbox} \longrightarrow \text{output / error}. this is the point where the llm temporarily gives control to an external environment. 5.23.6 the sandbox returns real feedback suppose the code returns: 699 the system inserts something conceptually like: 699 into the rollout. the model now sees: \boxed{ \text{its previous reasoning} + \text{its code} + \text{actual computation result} } and generation resumes. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.7 the rollout is still one trajectory this point is easy to misunderstand. we do not create separate trajectories: \tau_1=\text{reasoning} \tau_2=\text{code} \tau_3=\text{interpreter} instead, retool treats everything as one trajectory: \boxed{ \tau= t_1 \oplus c_1 \oplus f_1 \oplus t_2 \oplus c_2 \oplus f_2 \oplus o } the slide explicitly describes this concatenation into a single token sequence. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.8 why this matters because the eventual reward belongs to the whole strategy . suppose: \tau= \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{feedback} \rightarrow \text{correction} \rightarrow \text{final answer}. the reward doesn't separately say: r_{\text{reason}}=... r_{\text{code}}=... r_{\text{feedback}}=... instead: \boxed{ r(\tau)=+1 } if the final answer is correct. thus ppo must determine how to assign learning signal across the model's own decisions throughout the trajectory. 5.23.9 second tool call now imagine the first result is not enough. the model reasons: the candidate is 699, but i should verify the condition. then it generates another: ... the sandbox executes again. suppose it returns: valid now the trajectory is: \boxed{ t_1 \oplus c_1 \oplus f_1 \oplus t_2 \oplus c_2 \oplus f_2 } and generation resumes again. this can repeat until the model chooses to produce its final answer. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.10 the final answer eventually: \boxed{699} is produced. the system extracts the answer from the \boxed{} expression. so: \hat a=699. ground truth: a=699. 5.23.11 the verifier computes the reward retool uses a rule-based correctness checker. therefore: r(a,\hat a)= \begin{cases} +1,&\text{equivalent}\\ -1,&\text{otherwise} \end{cases} so here: \boxed{ r=+1 } the retool deck explicitly says this is the entire reward and deliberately does not add a separate reward merely for successfully executing code. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.12 why does the reward arrive only at the end? consider two trajectories. trajectory a reason → code → useful result → correct answer reward: +1. trajectory b reason → useless code → useless result → wrong answer reward: -1. the model therefore has to discover that tool use is valuable when it improves eventual task success. that is why the deck says that correctness-only reward forces each code call to “earn its keep” through its contribution to the final result. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.13 now the ppo stage begins the rollout is now complete. we have: \boxed{\tau} and: \boxed{r(\tau)}. we now need to turn that into learning signals. for each policy-generated token o_t , ppo evaluates: \boxed{ r_t(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t;ci) }{ \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t\mid s_t;ci) } } as given in the retool objective. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.14 what exactly is s_t here? this is extremely important. in ordinary text-only rl: s_t= [q,\text{previous generated tokens}]. in retool: \boxed{ s_t= [q,\text{reasoning},\text{code},\text{interpreter feedback},\ldots] } so after the sandbox says: 699 the next policy decision is conditioned on that new observation. this is where the environment actually changes the model's future behavior. 5.23.15 example: before and after tool feedback before execution: p(\text{“699”}\mid s_t) = \text{some probability}. after the interpreter returns: 699, the context changes: s_t\rightarrow s_{t+1}. the model may now assign: p(\text{“the answer is”}\mid s_{t+1}) a much larger probability. therefore the external tool isn't merely attached to the end of the system. it changes the future token distribution of the policy. 5.23.16 now the most important engineering detail: interpreter masking suppose the trajectory is: token 1: i token 2: will token 3: calculate token 4: token 5: print ... token 20: token 21: token 22: 699 token 23: token 24: therefore token 25: ... tokens 21–23 came from the environment. so: \boxed{ \text{do not train the policy to predict them} } the retool slide explicitly says interpreter-generated tokens are excluded from the loss. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.17 why exactly? suppose the sandbox returns: 17\times41=697. the model did not choose: 697. the environment did. therefore giving the policy a token-level prediction loss for 697 would amount to saying: “model, you should have predicted this environment output.” but the model had no control over that output. so: \boxed{ \text{credit only decisions made by the policy} } is the correct learning principle. 5.23.18 visualize the loss mask imagine: tokens: [ reasoning reasoning code code code int int int reasoning reasoning final ] mask: [ 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 1 1 1 ] where: 1=\text{policy token} 0=\text{interpreter token}. thus the policy loss only sees: \boxed{ \text{model-generated tokens} } and ignores: \boxed{ \text{environment-generated tokens} }. 5.23.19 another important point: the feedback is still in the context masking does not mean removing interpreter output. this distinction is critical. the interpreter output is: \boxed{ \text{visible to the model} } but: \boxed{ \text{not treated as a policy prediction target} }. so the model can read: 699 and use 699 in later reasoning. but the loss does not ask the model to generate 699 . 5.23.20 second engineering optimization: kv-cache reuse now suppose the model has already generated: n=5000 tokens before making its code call. all of those tokens already have cached keys and values. when the interpreter returns: m=50 new tokens, retool does not need to recompute the entire previous prefix. instead: \boxed{ k,v_{\text{old prefix}} \text{ are reused} } and only the new feedback is appended. the slide explicitly identifies this as one of the engineering details making multi-turn tool use affordable at rl scale. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.21 why this is such a big deal without cache reuse: \text{tool call} \rightarrow \text{reprocess entire prefix}. with reuse: \text{tool call} \rightarrow \text{reuse prefix cache} + \text{process new observation}. so repeated tool calls become much more manageable. 5.23.22 numerical kv-cache question suppose: l_{\text{old}}=8000 cached tokens. interpreter adds: l_{\text{new}}=100. with kv reuse, the new feedback extends the cache by: \boxed{100\text{ tokens}} rather than requiring the whole 8100-token history to be treated as new input for cache construction. again, this is the conceptual cache-efficiency calculation; the deck's claim is specifically that the old prefix can be reused and only new interpreter-feedback tokens need cache computation/appending. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.23 why asynchronous execution is needed now imagine a batch of 1000 rollouts. one rollout's code: 20\text{ ms} another: 100\text{ ms} another: 2\text{ s} another: 8\text{ s}. if all code execution were strictly synchronous, slow executions could cause the entire generation pipeline to wait. retool therefore uses an asynchronous sandbox pool so slow executions do not stall the rest of rl training. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.24 distributed-systems interpretation you can view the system as: \boxed{ \text{inference workers} } communicating with: \boxed{ \text{sandbox worker pool} } through asynchronous requests/results. conceptually: llm worker │ │ code request ▼ queue │ ├──► sandbox 1 ├──► sandbox 2 ├──► sandbox 3 └──► sandbox n │ ▼ execution result │ ▼ llm worker that architecture follows the slide's description of an asynchronous sandbox pool; details such as the exact queue technology are not specified by the supplied slides. 5.23.25 what happens if the code crashes? this is one of retool's most interesting properties. suppose the model produces: greedy() but greedy is undefined. the environment returns: \boxed{\text{nameerror}} the model sees that real feedback. it can then reason: the function has not been defined. and produce corrected code. the supplied slide presents this as an emergent self-correction behavior that appeared through rl rather than being explicitly demonstrated in a training example. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.26 this is the birth of tool-mediated self-correction text-only self-correction: \text{model} \rightarrow \text{its own critique} \rightarrow \text{its own revision} retool can do: \boxed{ \text{model} \rightarrow \text{real execution} \rightarrow \text{real error} \rightarrow \text{revision} } that is much more grounded because the correction is based on an externally generated observation. 5.23.27 why is an error useful for rl? suppose: \text{code}_1 \rightarrow \text{nameerror} \rightarrow \text{code}_2 \rightarrow \text{correct answer}. the overall trajectory receives: r=+1. thus the successful trajectory contains: \boxed{ \text{failure} + \text{recovery} } the rl optimizer can reinforce the policy behavior surrounding that successful recovery. this is why useful behavior can emerge even without an sft example showing exactly that same error correction. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.28 important distinction: the environment isn't being trained the policy is trained. the sandbox is an environment that provides feedback. so: \boxed{ \theta_{\text{llm}} \rightarrow \text{updated} } while the code interpreter remains the external execution mechanism. this is conceptually the standard agent-environment separation. 5.23.29 full rollout in mathematical notation let's define: \tau= (o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_t) with some positions corresponding to interpreter outputs. the model generates certain positions according to: o_t\sim\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid s_t). when a code boundary is reached: c_i \rightarrow e(c_i) = f_i where e is the sandbox execution function. then: s_{t+1} = s_t\oplus c_i\oplus f_i. eventually: \hat a=\operatorname{extract}(\tau). then: r(\tau) = \begin{cases} +1,&\operatorname{equivalent}(a,\hat a)\\ -1,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} that scalar reward then drives ppo. 5.23.30 the complete lifecycle now the entire retool rollout can be written as: \boxed{ q } \downarrow \boxed{ \pi_{\text{old}}\text{ generates reasoning} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{model chooses code} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{sandbox execution} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{real output/error} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{output inserted into context} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{model resumes} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{repeat if necessary} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{final }\boxed{a} } \downarrow \boxed{ r\in\{-1,+1\} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{ppo advantage + ratio + clipping} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{update policy} } 5.23.31 full numerical example let's make one trajectory. model-generated tokens: t_m=900. interpreter tokens: t_i=100. total trajectory: t=1000. the model makes two tool calls. first call code tokens: 150. interpreter: 30. second call code tokens: 200. interpreter: 70. the remaining model-generated tokens are: 900-(150+200)=550 which can include reasoning and final answer. check: 550+150+200+30+70 = \boxed{1000}. thus the interpreter contributes: \frac{100}{1000} = \boxed{10\%} of trajectory tokens. but those 100 tokens are masked from the policy loss while remaining visible in the context. 5.23.32 ppo numerical example on one generated token suppose a model-generated token has: \pi_{\text{old}}=0.10 and candidate new policy: \pi_\theta=0.13. so: r_t=1.3. suppose: \hat a_t=0.6 and: \epsilon=0.2. then: \operatorname{clip}(1.3,0.8,1.2)=1.2. raw: 1.3(0.6)=0.78. clipped: 1.2(0.6)=0.72. therefore: \boxed{ j_t=\min(0.78,0.72)=0.72. } the model still benefits from making that useful action more likely, but ppo limits the optimization incentive for a movement beyond the clipping region. 5.23.33 what exactly is being learned? not simply: \boxed{\text{“use python.”}} the model is learning something much richer: \boxed{ \text{given the current state, what action sequence maximizes eventual correctness?} } the action sequence can contain: \text{text} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{interpretation} \rightarrow \text{text} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{final answer}. that is why retool is better understood as strategic tool-use learning , not merely tool calling. 5.23.34 why the result is interesting the supplied results show a dramatic difference between: \text{sft only} \text{text-only rl} and: \boxed{\text{rl + real code interpreter}} on aime2024 for the specified qwen2.5-32b-instruct setup: 26.7\% \rightarrow 40.9\% \rightarrow 40.0\% \rightarrow 67.0\%. the supplied slide attributes the large jump specifically to combining rl with the ability to call a real code interpreter, rather than to sft or text-only rl alone. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.35 training efficiency result the supplied deck also reports that retool's accuracy curve rises much faster and reaches its plateau around step 400, while the text-only baseline continues improving beyond step 1000. it reports retool reaching its higher accuracy using approximately: \boxed{37\%} of the training steps used by that text-only rl baseline. (source: retool-slides) this supports a deeper interpretation: \boxed{ \text{tools don't merely increase capability; they can simplify exploration} } because certain computations no longer have to be discovered entirely through token-level reasoning. 5.23.36 one subtle but powerful conclusion earlier we said: \text{rl} = \text{discover/strengthen behavior}. retool reveals what kind of behavior can be discovered: \boxed{ \text{interaction strategy} } not just verbal reasoning. the model can discover: \text{“i should calculate now.”} \text{“that output looks suspicious.”} \text{“the interpreter gave me an error.”} \text{“i should fix the code.”} \text{“now i have enough evidence to answer.”} that is a qualitatively richer policy than: \boxed{ \text{keep generating text until answer} }. 5.23.37 exam checkpoint you should now be able to explain all six of these without memorizing the deck: 1. what is the retool rollout? \boxed{ \text{single hybrid trajectory of reasoning + code + interpreter feedback + answer} } 2. who generates interpreter tokens? \boxed{\text{the external sandbox}} 3. are interpreter tokens trained with the policy loss? \boxed{\text{no, they are masked.}} 4. why reuse kv cache? \boxed{ \text{to avoid recomputing the entire prefix after tool execution} } 5. why asynchronous sandbox execution? \boxed{ \text{to prevent slow code executions from stalling rl generation} } 6. what does ppo actually learn? \boxed{ \text{which model-generated actions, including tool-use decisions, lead to successful outcomes} } these points are directly grounded in the retool rollout and engineering slides. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.38 master picture for steps 5.20–5.23 we can now compress everything into one equation chain: \boxed{ \underbrace{ d_{\text{init}} \rightarrow d_{\text{ci}} \rightarrow \text{sft} }_{\text{learn protocol}} } then: \boxed{ \underbrace{ \text{policy rollout} \rightarrow \text{code execution} \rightarrow \text{environment feedback} \rightarrow \text{final answer} }_{\text{generate hybrid trajectory}} } then: \boxed{ \underbrace{ r=\pm1 \rightarrow \hat a_t \rightarrow r_t \rightarrow \operatorname{clip} \rightarrow \nabla_\theta }_{\text{ppo learns strategy}} } so the overall retool idea is: \boxed{ \textbf{sft teaches the model how to talk to the tool;} \quad \textbf{rl teaches the model when and why to use it.} }

(source: retool-slides) 5.24.1 first understand what is being measured at every saved rl checkpoint, retool evaluates the model's own generated responses. the six metrics are: \boxed{ \text{response length} } \boxed{ \text{code ratio} } \boxed{ \text{code lines} } \boxed{ \text{correct code count} } \boxed{ \text{code pass rate} } \boxed{ \text{code invocation timing} } the important point is: \boxed{ \text{none of these were separately optimized as explicit rewards} } according to the slide. the only reward was: \boxed{ r= \begin{cases} +1 & \text{correct}\\ -1 & \text{incorrect} \end{cases} } yet the six behaviors changed systematically. (source: retool-slides) that is the first major lesson. 5.24.2 signal 1 — response length before rl, the model's responses were approximately: \boxed{10,000\text{ tokens}} on the reported measurement. after rl, they ended around: \boxed{6,000\text{ tokens}} which is roughly a: \frac{10000-6000}{10000}\times100 = \boxed{40\%} reduction. (source: retool-slides) but something more interesting happens during training. the curve does not simply decrease monotonically. the slide says response length: falls sharply at first, then rises again, and ultimately ends substantially shorter than before rl. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.3 why does response length initially fall? before rl, the model may perform computation manually in text: first calculate this... then calculate that... let's check another possibility... now substitute... let's recompute... after discovering useful code-based strategies, it can replace many textual arithmetic steps with: ... followed by: <interpreter> ... </interpreter> so: \boxed{ \text{manual textual computation} \rightarrow \text{compact executable computation} } this compresses the reasoning trajectory. the slide explicitly attributes the initial length reduction to code replacing laborious manual calculation. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.4 why does response length rise again? this is the subtle part. after learning basic code usage, the model starts discovering more elaborate computational strategies . so the trajectory becomes: \text{simple reasoning} \rightarrow \text{compact code} \rightarrow \text{more sophisticated code strategies}. the code itself can become larger and more powerful. therefore: \boxed{ \text{better tool use does not necessarily mean fewer tokens at every stage} } the final result is still about 40% shorter, but the path there involves more sophisticated behavior. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.5 signal 2 — code ratio now define the intuition behind code ratio . conceptually: \boxed{ \text{code ratio} = \frac{\text{responses containing code}} {\text{total responses}} } the reported trend is striking. initially: \boxed{\text{under }20\%} of responses used code. by the end: \boxed{\text{nearly }98\%} of responses used code. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.6 what does that mean? before rl: \text{most responses} \rightarrow \text{text-only}. after rl: \text{almost all responses} \rightarrow \text{tool-augmented}. so the policy has discovered: \boxed{ \text{code is broadly useful for this task distribution} } under the learned reward. this is extremely important because nobody directly said: “use python in 98% of your answers.” instead: \boxed{ \text{correctness reward} \rightarrow \text{policy discovers high-value code use} } according to the reported analysis. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.7 but doesn't this look like overuse? yes—and this is an important nuance. a code ratio of nearly 98% means the model learned to use code very frequently on the evaluated task distribution. that does not imply: \boxed{ \text{98\% is universally optimal} } the deck only reports the behavior that emerged in this training/evaluation setup. you should not generalize that number to arbitrary tasks. this is a source-derived observation, not a universal law. 5.24.8 signal 3 — number of code lines now we go deeper. the model isn't merely calling code more often. the code itself becomes more substantial. the slide reports that the number of code lines rises throughout training and becomes nearly: \boxed{5\times} longer by the end. (source: retool-slides) so we have: \boxed{ \text{code frequency}\uparrow } and simultaneously: \boxed{ \text{code complexity/size}\uparrow } at least as measured by line count. 5.24.9 why is that important? suppose early behavior is: print(a * b) that is raw arithmetic. later behavior might look more like: for candidate in candidates: if condition_1(candidate): if condition_2(candidate): ... now the model is using the tool not merely as a calculator. it's delegating a larger computational subproblem. therefore: \boxed{ \text{tool role expands} } from: \text{calculator} toward: \boxed{ \text{computational reasoning module} }. 5.24.10 signal 4 — correct code counts the slide reports that the number of correct code executions on the test set rises approximately: \boxed{5\times}. so we now have three simultaneous trends: \text{more responses use code} \text{code blocks become longer} \text{more of those code executions are correct}. this is evidence that the model is not merely generating random or increasingly verbose code. the useful computational behavior itself is improving. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.11 signal 5 — code pass rate this is arguably the most informative metric. the reported pattern is: \boxed{ \text{correct final-answer responses} \rightarrow \text{code pass rate near 100\%} } while: \boxed{ \text{incorrect final-answer responses} \rightarrow \text{lower code pass rate}. } the deck calls buggy code a leading indicator of a wrong final answer . (source: retool-slides) 5.24.12 why is this important? consider: successful trajectory \text{correct code} \rightarrow \text{useful result} \rightarrow \text{correct answer}. failed trajectory \text{buggy code} \rightarrow \text{bad/no result} \rightarrow \text{wrong answer}. so code correctness is strongly associated with final reasoning success in the reported experiment. this suggests that the external tool doesn't merely act as a computational accelerator: \boxed{ \text{the quality of the interaction itself becomes diagnostic} } for the final answer. 5.24.13 signal 6 — tool invocation timing this is especially important for understanding strategy . early in training, the model tends to: \boxed{ \text{reason in text first} \rightarrow \text{use code later} } the slide reports that tool invocation gradually shifts earlier in the response. (source: retool-slides) so the model learns: \boxed{ \text{reach for the tool sooner} } when it recognizes that computation will be useful. 5.24.14 why does earlier tool use help? imagine a problem that requires a long search. text-first strategy: 500\text{ reasoning tokens} \rightarrow \text{finally invoke code}. tool-early strategy: 50\text{ reasoning tokens} \rightarrow \text{invoke code}. the second strategy can obtain an objective computational result earlier, which can then influence all subsequent reasoning. so: \boxed{ \text{earlier external feedback} \rightarrow \text{earlier correction/grounding} } this is one reason tool integration can simplify the exploration problem. the source explicitly reports the timing shift but does not give a universal mathematical rule saying “earlier is always better.” that broader claim would be an inference. 5.24.15 put all six signals together now the six signals tell a coherent story. 1. response length \boxed{\downarrow} overall. 2. code ratio \boxed{\uparrow} from under 20% to nearly 98%. 3. code line count \boxed{\uparrow} nearly 5×. 4. correct code count \boxed{\uparrow} approximately 5×. 5. code pass rate \boxed{ \text{high for correct responses} } and lower for incorrect ones. 6. invocation timing \boxed{ \text{moves earlier} } the interesting combination is: \boxed{ \text{less textual labor} + \text{more sophisticated computation} } 5.24.16 this is a genuine strategy shift the phrase to remember is: \boxed{ \textbf{rl is changing how the model solves the problem} } rather than merely: \boxed{ \textbf{rl is changing demonstrated this exact “fix after error” behavior, yet it emerged through optimizing correctness reward. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.18 why is this an “aha moment”? because the model has effectively learned: \boxed{ \text{tool failure} \rightarrow \text{inspect feedback} \rightarrow \text{diagnose} \rightarrow \text{repair} \rightarrow \text{continue} } this is much more sophisticated than: \text{generate code} \rightarrow \text{hope it works}. it has acquired an interaction strategy. 5.24.19 where did the learning signal come from? the model did not receive a reward saying: +0.3 for fixing errors. it only received the final correctness reward: r= \begin{cases} +1\\ -1 \end{cases} therefore, the reasoning is: \boxed{ \text{successful recovery} \rightarrow \text{higher chance of final correctness} } and ppo reinforces trajectories containing such useful behavior. this is precisely why the deck calls it emergent. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.20 numerical reward illustration imagine two policies encountering the same code bug. policy a \text{error} \rightarrow \text{give up} \rightarrow r=-1. policy b \text{error} \rightarrow \text{inspect traceback} \rightarrow \text{fix} \rightarrow \text{correct answer} \rightarrow r=+1. then trajectories resembling policy b receive the better learning signal. over repeated rl updates: p(\text{error recovery behavior}) can increase. this is the mechanism by which a self-correction strategy can emerge without a dedicated error-repair reward. 5.24.21 another major discovery: code's role changes before rl, the slide says code is used predominantly for: \boxed{ 79.1\% } of code snippets for raw calculation . after rl: \boxed{ 51.4\% } of code snippets are for calculation. (source: retool-slides) that means: 79.1\%-51.4\% = \boxed{27.7\text{ percentage points}} of the distribution shifts away from raw calculation. 5.24.22 where does that usage go? the slide identifies new roles including: \boxed{\text{optimization}} \boxed{\text{geometric calculation}} \boxed{\text{solution search}} so code evolves from: \boxed{ \text{calculator} } toward: \boxed{ \text{general computational reasoning tool} }. this is an especially important result because it demonstrates that the model learned new uses for the tool , not merely more frequent use of the same calculator behavior. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.23 let's quantify that shift suppose, purely illustratively, there are: 1000 code snippets before rl. at 79.1% calculation: 791 are calculation-oriented. after rl, at 51.4%: 514 are calculation-oriented. thus: 791-514 = \boxed{277} fewer snippets fall into that category. the remaining: 486 snippets belong to other categories. these numbers are a direct arithmetic illustration of the percentages reported in the slide, not additional source statistics. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.24 why is this result so important? because it demonstrates: \boxed{ \text{tool use} \neq \text{calculator use} } a sufficiently capable model can learn to use code for: \text{search} \text{optimization} \text{geometry} and other computational subroutines. thus: \boxed{ \text{external computation becomes part of the reasoning strategy} } 5.24.25 same question, two reasoning styles the slide provides a particularly useful comparison. for the same four-digit-integer problem: text-only reasoning the model performs a long manual modular-arithmetic derivation and reaches: \boxed{629} which is wrong. a single arithmetic mistake propagates through later steps. code-interpreter reasoning the model delegates the arithmetic to two short code blocks and reaches: \boxed{699} which is confirmed by the interpreter. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.26 this illustrates the core advantage text-only: \boxed{ \text{many dependent manual operations} } a single error: \boxed{ e_1 \rightarrow e_2 \rightarrow e_3 \rightarrow \cdots } can corrupt the entire chain. tool-assisted: \boxed{ \text{delegate exact computation} } and receive: \boxed{ \text{externally verified intermediate result} }. the model can then reason from a more reliable computational observation. 5.24.27 tool use therefore changes the location of computation this is an excellent mental model. before: \boxed{ \text{llm} \rightarrow \text{does everything itself} } after retool: \boxed{ \text{llm} \leftrightarrow \text{external computation} } the intelligence is no longer just: \text{generate tokens}. it becomes: \boxed{ \text{decide what to compute internally} + \text{decide what to delegate externally} } 5.24.28 why this is “agentic rl” now the final slide's conclusion makes sense. the course's progression is: \boxed{ \text{single answer trajectory} } then: \boxed{ \text{long reasoning trajectory} } then: \boxed{ \text{reasoning + external actions + feedback} } that corresponds to: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} \rightarrow \text{deepseek-r1} \rightarrow \text{retool} } the supplied deck calls this progression toward a richer notion of trajectory and identifies it as the essence of agentic rl . (source: retool-slides) 5.24.33 the most important takeaway retool does not simply teach: \boxed{ \text{“llm + calculator”} } it teaches a policy of: \boxed{ \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{decide whether computation helps} \rightarrow \text{invoke tool} \rightarrow \text{read feedback} \rightarrow \text{adapt} \rightarrow \text{verify} \rightarrow \text{answer} } and the remarkable part is that the rl objective does not explicitly specify all those intermediate behaviors. instead: \boxed{ \text{correctness reward} \rightarrow \text{emergent strategy} } this is the central lesson of step 5.24. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.4 what does this comparison prove? it shows that: \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft is useful} } for this setup. more specifically, the sft stage provides a substantial gain before rl begins. this is consistent with what we learned earlier: \boxed{ \text{sft teaches the model the code/interpreter protocol} } so the model can participate in the later rl environment. 5.25.5 what does it not prove? it does not prove: \boxed{ \text{sft is better than rl generally} } because that isn't the experiment being performed. it also does not prove that: \boxed{ \text{sft alone is sufficient} } because the full retool system later improves substantially beyond 40.9%. so our scientifically correct statement is: in this reported setup, cold-start sft produces a 14.2-point improvement over the untrained base model on aime2024. not: sft solves tool-use reasoning. 5.25.6 comparison 2 — cold-start sft vs text-only rl now compare: 40.9\% versus: 40.0\%. difference: 40.0-40.9 = \boxed{-0.9\text{ percentage points}}. so text-only rl is actually 0.9 points lower than cold-start sft in this reported comparison. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.7 this is the surprising result you might have expected: \text{sft}+rl > \text{sft}. but in the reported comparison, the text-only rl configuration reaches: 40.0\% while sft alone reaches: 40.9\%. so: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl adds almost nothing beyond sft here} } the slide explicitly emphasizes this interpretation. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.8 why is this important? because it isolates something very specific. it tells us that: \boxed{ \text{rl by itself is not the source of the giant improvement} } at least in this particular comparison. the big gain comes when rl has access to: \boxed{ \text{real code execution} } 5.25.9 comparison 3 — base → text-only rl the slide also shows: 26.7\%\rightarrow40.0\%. so the absolute improvement is: 40.0-26.7 = \boxed{13.3\text{ points}}. this is the slide's reported \delta . (source: retool-slides) so text-only rl does improve over the raw base model . but compare: 13.3 to sft's: 14.2. they are very similar. thus the important conclusion isn't: text-only rl does nothing. instead: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl helps relative to the raw base, but provides little additional gain over the cold-start sft baseline in this experiment} } that is a much more precise interpretation. 5.25.10 comparison 4 — text-only rl → retool now comes the major jump. text-only rl: 40.0\%. retool: 67.0\%. improvement: 67.0-40.0 = \boxed{27.0\text{ percentage points}}. this is the critical comparison. 5.25.11 comparison 5 — sft → retool cold-start sft: 40.9\%. retool: 67.0\%. improvement: 67.0-40.9 = \boxed{26.1\text{ percentage points}}. so almost the entire extraordinary jump occurs when the system moves from: \boxed{ \text{sft/text reasoning} } to: \boxed{ \text{rl + actual code execution} }. 5.25.12 comparison 6 — base → retool from: 26.7\% to: 67.0\%. absolute improvement: 67.0-26.7 = \boxed{40.3\text{ percentage points}}. that is the slide's reported overall gain. (source: retool-slides) so relative to the original base performance: \frac{67.0-26.7}{26.7}\times100 \approx \boxed{151.3\%} relative improvement. be careful: \boxed{40.3\text{ points}} and: \boxed{151.3\%\text{ relative improvement}} are different quantities. the slide reports the former; the latter is our arithmetic calculation. 5.25.13 now identify the actual experimental variable let's construct the progression: 26.7 \downarrow +14.2 40.9 \downarrow -0.9 40.0 \downarrow +27.0 67.0. what changes most dramatically in the last transition? \boxed{ \text{real code-interpreter interaction} } that is why the slide concludes that the gain is specifically associated with learning when and how to use the tool , rather than with rl or tools alone. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.14 why can't we just say “the tool caused everything”? because that would be too strong. retool contains multiple ingredients: \text{cold-start sft} + \text{rl} + \text{code interpreter}. the 67.0% result belongs to the combination . the ablation demonstrates that the combination performs dramatically better than the text-only variants. but a single ablation table cannot establish every possible causal decomposition under every alternative training setup. so the careful statement is: \boxed{ \text{in the reported experiment, the large additional gain appears when rl is combined with real tool interaction.} } that is exactly the interpretation supported by the deck. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.15 why is the “rl without tool” baseline necessary? this is a very important experimental-design principle. suppose the authors only reported: 40.9\%\rightarrow67.0\%. someone could argue: maybe rl itself creates the 26-point improvement. to test that hypothesis, they include: \boxed{ \text{rl without code interpreter} } and obtain: 40.0\%. that comparison weakens the explanation: \text{“rl alone caused the 27-point jump.”} because under this setup: \boxed{ 40.0\% \not\approx 67.0\% } 5.25.16 this is how you should read ablations when you see: a=40.9 b=40.0 c=67.0 ask: what changed between a and c? and: what changed between b and c? here: a vs c \text{sft} \rightarrow \text{sft + rl + tool interaction} b vs c \text{text-only rl} \rightarrow \text{tool-integrated rl}. the second comparison is especially informative because both involve rl, so it more directly isolates the contribution of adding the tool interaction to the rl setup described in the slide. 5.25.17 a simple causal diagram conceptually: base model │ ┌───────┴────────┐ │ │ sft text rl │ │ 40.9 40.0 │ │ └──────┬─────────┘ │ + real tool │ 67.0 the exact experimental paths are those shown in the deck; this diagram is just a visualization of the ablation logic. 5.25.18 retool versus external baselines the headline slide reports that on the specified setup: retool aime2024: \boxed{67.0\%} aime2025: \boxed{49.3\%}. it says this exceeds every listed baseline, including: openai o1-preview 44.6\% / 37.9\% and: qwen2.5-math-instruct-tir 72b 40.0\% on aime2024. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.19 but there is another important result the slide says replacing the backbone with: \boxed{\text{deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b}} raises performance further to: \boxed{ 72.5\%\text{ aime2024} } and: \boxed{ 54.3\%\text{ aime2025}. } (source: retool-slides) 5.25.20 what does this teach us? it reinforces an idea we already encountered during distillation: \boxed{ \text{base-model quality matters} } retool isn't independent of the backbone. same broad tool/rl idea: \text{different backbone} \rightarrow \text{different ceiling}. so: \boxed{ \text{tool use is an additional capability, not a replacement for model capability} } that broader wording is an inference from the reported comparison; the deck itself simply reports the stronger-backbone result. 5.25.21 let's compare the two backbones numerically qwen2.5-32b-instruct retool: 67.0\%. deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b backbone: 72.5\%. difference: 72.5-67.0 = \boxed{5.5\text{ points}}. for aime2025: 54.3-49.3 = \boxed{5.0\text{ points}}. these are arithmetic calculations from the slide's reported numbers. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.22 training efficiency: why fewer steps matter now consider the learning curves. the slide reports: \boxed{ \text{retool plateau }\approx\text{ step }400 } while: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl continues past step }1000 } and retool reaches its higher accuracy using approximately: \boxed{37\%} of the training steps of the text-only rl baseline. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.23 numerical interpretation suppose the text-only baseline requires: 1000 steps. then: 0.37\times1000 = \boxed{370} steps. the reported plateau around 400 steps is therefore broadly consistent with the approximate 37% statement. but notice the wording: \boxed{\text{about }37\%} and: \boxed{\text{around step }400}. these are approximate empirical observations, not an exact algebraic identity. 5.25.24 why could tool use make exploration easier? this is the deeper interpretation proposed by the slide. consider text-only rl. the model must discover: \text{how to reason} + \text{how to calculate} + \text{how to search} + \text{how to verify}. all inside generated text. with a computational tool: \boxed{ \text{computation is delegated to an external mechanism} } so the model can explore higher-level strategies such as: \text{what to calculate} rather than having to manually simulate every arithmetic step in language. thus the slide's interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{tools do not merely increase the final ceiling;} \text{they make the exploration problem easier.} } (source: retool-slides) 5.25.25 be careful about the word “easier” the slide says: tool use doesn't just raise the ceiling; it makes the exploration problem itself easier to solve. (source: retool-slides) this is an interpretation of the observed learning curve. it does not give a formal theorem that external tools mathematically reduce rl sample complexity in every setting. so in an exam: good: \boxed{ \text{the reported learning curve suggests improved exploration efficiency.} } too strong: \boxed{ \text{tools always reduce sample complexity.} } 5.25.26 another important numerical comparison compare: 67.0 with: 40.0. relative improvement from text-only rl: \frac{67.0-40.0}{40.0}\times100 = \boxed{67.5\%}. so retool's aime2024 accuracy is about 67.5% higher relative to the text-only rl baseline in this particular reported comparison. again: 27\text{ points} is the source-friendly quantity; 67.5\% is our derived relative-improvement calculation. 5.25.27 what exactly do the ablations support? let's formalize the conclusions. conclusion a \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft is useful.} } evidence: 26.7\rightarrow40.9. conclusion b \boxed{ \text{text-only rl does not provide a large additional gain over sft in this setup.} } evidence: 40.9\rightarrow40.0. conclusion c \boxed{ \text{adding real code interaction to rl produces the major gain.} } evidence: 40.0\rightarrow67.0. conclusion d \boxed{ \text{a stronger reasoning backbone can raise the retool result further.} } evidence: 67.0\rightarrow72.5. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.28 what the ablation does not prove this is equally important. the table does not establish that: \boxed{\text{retool is universally better than every rl method}} or: \boxed{\text{code interpreters are universally better than other tools}} or: \boxed{\text{67\% is a universal upper bound}} or: \boxed{\text{sft is unnecessary}} or: \boxed{\text{text-only rl never works}} those claims go beyond the supplied evidence. the experiment is about the reported setup and comparisons. 5.25.29 why this matters for research-paper reading a common mistake is: \boxed{ \text{correlation} \rightarrow \text{absolute causal claim} } the correct research mindset is: identify the controlled comparison. identify what changed. identify what stayed approximately constant. attribute the result only to what the experiment actually isolates. for retool, the most informative isolation is: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{rl + real code interpreter} } because both are rl variants in the reported ablation.
