(source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.1 first: what is indiccorp v2? indiccorp v2 is the pretraining corpus component of the overall indic work. the deck describes it as: \boxed{20.9\text{b tokens}} across: \boxed{24\text{ languages}} and: \boxed{4\text{ language families}}. its purpose is to provide substantially better indic-language monolingual pretraining data. (source: indicxtreme-slides) remember the separation: \boxed{ \text{indiccorp}=\text{training data} } \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme}=\text{evaluation benchmark} } \boxed{ \text{indicbert v2}=\text{model trained on indiccorp and evaluated on indicxtreme} } 5.27.2 step 1 — find good source websites the first question is: where should the text come from? the deck says the corpus prioritizes clean, diverse text , and therefore chooses news articles as the primary source . this is a deliberate departure from generic web corpora such as: \boxed{\text{cc-100}} and: \boxed{\text{mc4}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.3 why news? think about the alternatives. a generic commoncrawl-style dump may contain: \text{forums} + \text{blogs} + \text{spam} + \text{machine-generated pages} + \text{duplicated pages} + \text{navigation text} + \text{advertising} + \text{clean articles}. a news source is much more likely to provide structured natural-language prose. so the corpus construction process deliberately prioritizes: \boxed{ \text{high-quality source domains} } rather than simply maximizing raw token count. this is source-derived from the deck; the expanded list of typical web-noise categories is explanatory context. 5.27.4 step 2 — discover new sources the researchers did not rely only on existing indiccorp v1 sources. the deck says new sources were found using: \boxed{\text{news repositories}} and: \boxed{\text{automatic web search}}. the search queries are generated from frequent words in the target language . retrieved pages are then inspected to identify candidate source urls. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.5 why use frequent words as search queries? suppose the target language is hindi. a corpus builder can obtain frequent hindi words and use them as search queries. conceptually: w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_k are frequent words. then: w_i \rightarrow \text{search engine} \rightarrow \text{candidate pages} \rightarrow \text{candidate source domains}. this increases the chance of discovering websites that actually publish text in the target language. the deck emphasizes that this discovery stage is noisy. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.6 why is source discovery noisy? because a page retrieved using a language-specific word does not guarantee: \boxed{ \text{clean indic-language text} }. a retrieved url might contain: \text{offensive content} or: \text{machine-generated content}. so the researchers need another stage: \boxed{ \text{human verification} }. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.7 step 3 — human verification before crawling this is one of the most important design decisions. before crawling a candidate site: \boxed{ \text{a human checks the url} } the annotator visits the candidate url and verifies that it is: a genuine website, containing clean data, in the language of interest. only verified urls are then passed to the web-crawling system. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.8 why verify the url before crawling? because crawling is expensive. imagine discovering: 100,000 candidate websites. suppose many are: \text{spam} or: \text{wrong language} or: \text{machine-generated}. if you crawl everything first and clean it later, you waste: \boxed{\text{crawl bandwidth + storage + processing}} on obviously bad sources. so indiccorp inserts a quality gate early: \boxed{ \text{candidate url} \rightarrow \text{human verification} \rightarrow \text{crawl} } rather than: \text{candidate url} \rightarrow \text{crawl everything} \rightarrow \text{huge cleanup}. the deck explicitly identifies this as the distinction in the “verified source urls” row compared with cc-100 and mc4. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.9 how aggressive is this gate? across languages: \boxed{1\%-33\%} of candidate urls are discarded as noisy. so different languages have different source quality. that itself is informative. a language with: 1\% rejection is very different from one with: 33\% rejection. the exact language-by-language values are not given on this slide, only the overall range. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.10 numerical example — url verification suppose: 10,000 candidate urls are collected. if: 20\% are rejected, then: 10,000\times0.20 = \boxed{2,000} urls are rejected. accepted: 10,000-2,000 = \boxed{8,000}. this is an illustrative calculation; the actual slide gives a rejection range of 1–33%, not this specific 20% example. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.11 step 4 — crawl the verified sources once urls pass human review, they are handed to the: \boxed{\text{open-source webcorpus toolkit}} for crawling. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so the sequence is: \boxed{ \text{search} \rightarrow \text{candidate url} \rightarrow \text{human verification} \rightarrow \text{web crawl} } this separation is very important. 5.27.12 why not make the entire pipeline human? because the corpus is: \boxed{20.9\text{ billion tokens}} which is far too large for full manual inspection. so the design is hybrid: \boxed{ \text{human supervision at strategic quality gates} } plus: \boxed{ \text{automatic large-scale filtering} }. this pattern appears repeatedly throughout the indic work. 5.27.13 step 5 — language identification (lid) after crawling, the raw text needs to be checked for language. the deck says paragraph-level language filtering is performed using: \boxed{\text{cld3}} and: \boxed{\text{langdetect}} in parallel. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so conceptually: \text{paragraph} \rightarrow \begin{cases} \text{cld3}\\ \text{langdetect} \end{cases} \rightarrow \text{language decision}. 5.27.14 why use two language-id tools? the deck's reason is practical rather than theoretical: \boxed{ \text{one tool has language-specific limitations} } it notes that cld3 misses: \boxed{\text{assamese and oriya}} and that neither of the two tools supports: \boxed{\text{bodo and dogri}}. therefore lid filtering is skipped for bodo and dogri. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a very useful data-engineering lesson: \boxed{ \text{automation is only as good as its coverage on the target population} } 5.27.15 why is skipping lid for bodo and dogri not necessarily a contradiction? because a filter that cannot correctly recognize the language could be worse than not applying it. suppose the true language is: l. if the detector doesn't support l , then applying its output may cause systematic false rejection. so: \boxed{ \text{unsupported detector} \rightarrow \text{do not blindly trust detector output} } the deck specifically says lid filtering is skipped for bodo and dogri. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.16 step 6 — script-based cleaning language identification alone isn't enough. a page can still contain: \text{indic text} + \text{english phrases} + \text{latin transliteration}. therefore the next filter checks the proportion of characters written in the language's native script. the deck uses a threshold: \boxed{0.75}. a sentence is dropped if: \boxed{ \frac{\text{native-script characters}} {\text{total characters}} <0.75 } (source: indicxtreme-slides) this formula is a direct expression of the threshold described by the slide. 5.27.17 numerical example — script threshold suppose a sentence contains: 200 characters. of these: 150 are in the native script. then: \frac{150}{200} = 0.75. so it is: \boxed{\text{not dropped under the stated }<0.75\text{ rule}} because the fraction is exactly 0.75, not below 0.75. 5.27.18 another example suppose: 200 characters total and: 140 native-script characters. then: \frac{140}{200} = 0.70. because: 0.70<0.75, the sentence is: \boxed{\text{dropped}}. excellent exam-style threshold question. 5.27.19 why use a script threshold? because a sentence can technically pass language identification while still being dominated by another script. for example: indic-language words + english terminology + transliteration could produce a misleadingly mixed corpus. the script threshold therefore improves: \boxed{ \text{language-pure text quality} }. that is the purpose described by the slide. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.20 step 7 — punctuation-based cleaning now punctuation is stripped from each sentence. then the system asks: \boxed{ \text{how many words remain?} } if the resulting content is shorter than: \boxed{10\text{ words}} the document is discarded entirely. (source: indicxtreme-slides) notice the granularity: sentence-level punctuation stripping, document-level discard condition. that's easy to miss. 5.27.21 why strip punctuation? because punctuation and formatting can contribute noise to corpus statistics. the deck's pipeline uses this cleaning stage before deciding whether the remaining textual content is substantial enough. the specific 10-word threshold is source-derived. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.22 numerical example — 10-word threshold suppose after punctuation stripping a document contains: 8 remaining words. since: 8<10, it is: \boxed{\text{discarded}}. if it contains: 10 words: 10<10 is false. therefore: \boxed{\text{it survives this particular threshold}} assuming it passes the other filters. 5.27.23 why is this not just sentence filtering? because the slide explicitly says: if what remains is shorter than 10 words, the document is discarded entirely. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a useful exam trap. do not accidentally write: \text{discard sentence if <10 words}. the stated operation is: \boxed{ \text{discard document if remaining content <10 words} }. 5.27.24 step 8 — offensive-content filtering now comes another important cleaning stage. web-crawled indic text can contain offensive material. the deck uses two blacklists . blacklist a — in-house list native annotators create an in-house list covering: \boxed{17\text{ languages}} with about: \boxed{90\text{ words/phrases per language}} and including some borderline expressions identified as contextually offensive by native speakers. (source: indicxtreme-slides) blacklist b — nllb list a second independently released blacklist covers: \boxed{209\text{ languages}}. this is merged with the in-house list to widen coverage. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.25 why use two lists? because one list has: \boxed{\text{deep native/context coverage}} for the 17 languages, while the other provides: \boxed{\text{much wider language coverage}}. thus: \boxed{ \text{local expertise} + \text{broad external coverage} } produces a stronger filtering mechanism. that interpretation follows the stated purposes of the two lists. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.26 how is the offensive filter applied? the deck says: for a blacklisted word remove the sentence if the word occurs. for a blacklisted phrase remove the sentence if the whole phrase appears verbatim . so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{blacklisted word} \rightarrow \text{remove sentence} } and: \boxed{ \text{blacklisted phrase appears verbatim} \rightarrow \text{remove sentence} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.27 the surprising scale effect before this offensive-content filter: \boxed{23.1\text{b tokens}} after: \boxed{20.9\text{b tokens}}. reduction: 23.1-20.9 = \boxed{2.2\text{b tokens}}. percentage reduction: \frac{2.2}{23.1}\times100 \approx \boxed{9.52\%} which the deck reports as: \boxed{9.5\%}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.28 exam question — filtering percentage question: a corpus contains 23.1b tokens before filtering and 20.9b after filtering. what percentage was removed? \frac{23.1-20.9}{23.1}\times100 = \frac{2.2}{23.1}\times100 \approx \boxed{9.52\%} so the reported: \boxed{9.5\%} is mathematically consistent. 5.27.29 step 9 — deduplication after the cleaning pipeline, the resulting corpus is deduplicated . this matters because web crawling often finds the same material multiple times. for example: d_1=d_2 could happen because: multiple urls mirror the same article, syndication duplicates content, crawlers encounter repeated copies. if duplicated text remains, a language model effectively sees: \boxed{ \text{same evidence repeatedly} } which inflates the apparent dataset size. the deck reports the final corpus as de-duplicated . (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.30 final corpus after these steps: \boxed{ 20.9\text{b tokens} } remain across: \boxed{ 24\text{ languages} }. this is indiccorp v2. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.31 compare with indiccorp v1 indiccorp v1: \boxed{ 8.79\text{b tokens} } across: \boxed{ 12\text{ languages} }. indiccorp v2: \boxed{ 20.9\text{b tokens} } across: \boxed{ 24\text{ languages} }. so the token-scale ratio is: \frac{20.9}{8.79} \approx \boxed{2.38\times}. the deck states that the paper rounds this to approximately: \boxed{2.3\times}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.32 and language coverage doubled v1: 12 languages. v2: 24. so: \frac{24}{12} = \boxed{2\times}. this is a simple but useful observation from the reported figures. so the improvement is not merely: \boxed{\text{more text}} but also: \boxed{\text{broader language coverage}}. 5.27.33 hindi growth the deck reports that hindi alone grew: \boxed{3.28\times} from v1 to v2, with the paper rounding it to: \boxed{3.3\times}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this shows why simply saying “the corpus grew 2.38×” is incomplete. different languages experienced different growth. 5.27.34 low-resource tail this is an extremely important observation. the bottom: \boxed{11} lowest-resource languages together contribute only: \boxed{1.08\text{b tokens}}. the deck explicitly contrasts this with hindi alone. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so even within a corpus described as “indic”: \boxed{ \text{data distribution remains highly unequal} } 5.27.35 numerical interpretation of the low-resource tail the 11-language tail contributes: 1.08\text{b} out of: 20.9\text{b}. fraction: \frac{1.08}{20.9} \approx 0.0517. therefore: \boxed{\approx5.17\%} of the total corpus is contributed by those bottom 11 languages. this is our derived calculation from the deck's reported numbers. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.36 why this is important for the later benchmark results this connects directly to what we'll eventually see. even after creating a massive indic corpus: 20.9\text{b tokens} the data is still not evenly distributed. therefore we should expect: \boxed{ \text{resource-rich languages} > \text{resource-poor languages} } in many downstream tasks. and indeed, later in the deck, the lowest-resource languages show sharp performance drops. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so the data-construction section isn't isolated. it explains the benchmark results we will study later. 5.27.37 complete indiccorp pipeline now memorize the architecture: frequent-language words │ ▼ news repositories / web search │ ▼ candidate urls │ ▼ human url verification │ ▼ verified sources │ ▼ web crawling │ ▼ raw crawled text │ ├──► language id │ cld3 + langdetect │ ├──► native-script threshold │ >= 0.75 │ ├──► punctuation stripping │ document must retain >= 10 words │ ├──► offensive-content filtering │ in-house + nllb lists │ ▼ deduplication │ ▼ 20.9b-token indiccorp v2 the major stages and thresholds are directly from the supplied deck. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.38 what is human and what is automatic? this is another exam-important classification. human \boxed{ \text{source url verification} } and: \boxed{ \text{creation of the in-house offensive blacklist} } automatic \boxed{ \text{web crawling} } \boxed{ \text{lid} } \boxed{ \text{script filtering} } \boxed{ \text{punctuation/length filtering} } \boxed{ \text{blacklist filtering} } \boxed{ \text{deduplication} } the in-house blacklist itself comes from human annotators, while its application to text is automatic. 5.27.39 the underlying engineering philosophy indiccorp v2 follows a pattern: \boxed{ \text{human judgment where semantic quality is difficult} } and: \boxed{ \text{automation where scale is essential} }. humans are good at answering: “is this website actually a trustworthy source in the language?” machines are good at applying: \text{millions/billions of repetitive filtering operations}. that hybrid architecture is one of the most important lessons from the corpus-construction section. 5.27.40 exam-style level 5 problem suppose a hypothetical crawl produces: 10\text{b tokens}. after: lid filtering: 85% remain script filtering: 80% of the previous stage remains punctuation/length filtering: 90% remain offensive filtering: 90% remain deduplication: 95% remain then final size is: 10 \times0.85 \times0.80 \times0.90 \times0.90 \times0.95 = \boxed{5.2334\text{b tokens approximately}}. this is an illustrative multi-stage filtering problem, not an indiccorp reported statistic. the exam lesson is: \boxed{ \text{successive percentages multiply; they do not simply add} } 5.27.41 another exam trap suppose: 23.1\text{b} becomes: 20.9\text{b}. do not say: “the corpus lost 2.2%.” it lost: 2.2\text{b tokens} and the percentage loss is: \boxed{9.5\%}. always distinguish: \boxed{\text{absolute reduction}} from: \boxed{\text{relative percentage reduction}}. 5.27.42 another exam trap: 0.75 threshold the rule is: \text{drop if native-script fraction}<0.75. so: 0.749 \rightarrow \boxed{\text{drop}} but: 0.750 \rightarrow \boxed{\text{keep under this particular rule}}. because the inequality is strictly less than . 5.27.43 final mental model you should now visualize indiccorp v2 as: \boxed{ \text{discovery} } find candidate sources. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{human quality gate} } verify sources before crawling. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{web crawl} } collect massive raw text. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{automatic linguistic cleaning} } lid + script + length. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{safety/quality filtering} } offensive-content filtering. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{deduplication} } remove repeated material. \downarrow \boxed{ 20.9\text{b tokens / 24 languages} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.44 the deepest lesson the most important thing about indiccorp is not: \boxed{20.9\text{b}} it is the pipeline philosophy : \boxed{ \text{more data is not automatically better data} } a useful pretraining corpus must optimize: \boxed{ \text{coverage} + \text{quality} + \text{language correctness} + \text{script purity} + \text{safety} + \text{deduplication} } while still operating at billion-token scale. and there is a fundamental tension: \boxed{ \text{corpus-wide scale} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{low-resource language balance} } the final 20.9b-token corpus is much larger than v1, but the deck makes clear that its language distribution is still highly uneven. (source: indicxtreme-slides) step 5.27 checkpoint for an exam, you should be able to reproduce this without the slides: \boxed{ \text{search} \rightarrow \text{human url verification} \rightarrow \text{crawl} \rightarrow \text{lid} \rightarrow \text{script }(0.75) \rightarrow \text{length }(10\text{ words}) \rightarrow \text{offensive filter} \rightarrow \text{deduplicate} } and remember: \boxed{ 23.1b\rightarrow20.9b = 2.2b\text{ removed} = 9.5\%\text{ reduction} } \boxed{ 20.9/8.79\approx2.38\times } \boxed{ 24\text{ languages in indiccorp v2} } \boxed{ \text{bottom 11 languages}=1.08b\text{ tokens} } (source: indicxtreme-slides)

claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.28 — indicxtreme benchmark architecture plan node: i10 · chat order #69 we now move from “how was indiccorp built?” to: \boxed{ \text{how do we actually measure an indic-language model?} } this is the purpose of indicxtreme . the benchmark is designed around: \boxed{ 9\text{ tasks} \quad+\quad 4\text{ task categories} } the four categories are: \boxed{ \text{classification} } \boxed{ \text{structure prediction} } \boxed{ \text{question answering} } \boxed{ \text{retrieval} } the supplied task-suite slide lists 5 classification tasks, 2 structure-prediction tasks, 1 qa task, and 1 retrieval task , for 105 evaluation sets across languages/tasks , with 52 being new contributions. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.1 first understand why there are multiple tasks suppose a model gets: 90\% on sentiment. does that mean the model understands an indic language? not necessarily. it could be good at: \text{classification} but weak at: \text{ner} or: \text{question answering} or: \text{retrieval} or: \text{causal reasoning}. so indicxtreme intentionally evaluates multiple capabilities. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{language ability} \approx \text{many different downstream capabilities} } this is why the benchmark is a task suite , not one single test. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.2 the 9 tasks the benchmark table gives: classification — 5 \boxed{\text{indicsentiment}} \boxed{\text{indicxnli}} \boxed{\text{indiccopa}} \boxed{\text{indicpara}} \boxed{\text{m-intent}} structure prediction — 2 \boxed{\text{naamapadam}} \boxed{\text{m-slotfill}} qa — 1 \boxed{\text{indicqa}} retrieval — 1 \boxed{\text{flores}} (source: indicxtreme-slides) let's understand them sequentially. step 5.28.3 task 1 — indicsentiment the first task is: \boxed{\text{indicsentiment}} its purpose is sentiment classification. the model receives a review and predicts its sentiment category. for example: "the product looks excellent and works perfectly." the model might predict: \boxed{\text{positive}} while: "the material is poor and the product broke quickly." might be: \boxed{\text{negative}}. the benchmark table lists: 13 languages, 1,000 test examples, accuracy as the metric, product reviews as the domain. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.4 why is sentiment useful? sentiment appears simple, but multilingual sentiment is not merely: \text{translate english words} \rightarrow \text{predict polarity}. a model has to understand the actual indic-language input. the deck's later creation slide also deliberately makes indicsentiment harder than ordinary polarized review datasets by constructing reviews around specific product aspects rather than using only strongly positive/negative generic reviews. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.5 important creation detail the supplied deck says indicsentiment was built by: curating products from 15 popular categories on amazon, flipkart, and myntra; identifying product aspects; asking annotators to write positive/negative reviews around particular aspects; translating the english reviews into 13 indic languages manually. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is important because it attempts to create a more nuanced sentiment task. 5.28.6 metric: accuracy for classification: \boxed{ \text{accuracy} = \frac{\text{correct predictions}} {\text{total predictions}} } suppose: n=1000 test examples. if the model gets: 850 correct: \text{accuracy} = \frac{850}{1000} = \boxed{85\%}. 5.28.7 exam numerical a model gets 920 correct out of 1,000 indicsentiment examples. \frac{920}{1000}\times100 = \boxed{92\%}. very straightforward, but this type of calculation should be automatic for you. step 5.28.8 task 2 — indicxnli next: \boxed{\text{indicxnli}} this is the natural language inference (nli) task. the input is typically: \boxed{ \text{premise} + \text{hypothesis} } and the model determines their relationship. conceptually, the classes are: \boxed{ \text{entailment} } \boxed{ \text{contradiction} } \boxed{ \text{neutral} } the benchmark table lists: \boxed{12\text{ languages}} and: \boxed{5010\text{ test examples}}. the table marks its construction as machine-translated (mt), while the later deck explains that the resulting test set is being manually re-verified and corrected. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.9 example of nli premise: “rahul went to the market and bought vegetables.” hypothesis: “rahul bought vegetables.” then: \boxed{\text{entailment}} because the premise supports the hypothesis. hypothesis: “rahul did not buy anything.” then: \boxed{\text{contradiction}}. hypothesis: “rahul went to the market on sunday.” then: \boxed{\text{neutral}} unless the premise supplies that information. 5.28.10 why is indicxnli interesting for multilingual evaluation? because the original xnli-style setup is based on cross-lingual transfer. the important benchmark question becomes: \boxed{ \text{can a model learn the inference task from english and transfer it to an indic language?} } that question becomes central to the zero-shot evaluation protocol we'll study later. 5.28.11 metric again: \boxed{\text{accuracy}} suppose 5,010 test cases exist and the model gets 3,758 correct. then: \frac{3758}{5010}\times100 \approx \boxed{74. \! \ \text{?}} let's calculate carefully: 3758/5010\approx0.7501. so: \boxed{\approx75.0\%}. 5.28.12 task 3 — indiccopa now we get to a much more reasoning-oriented task: \boxed{\text{indiccopa}} copa stands for: \boxed{\text{choice of plausible alternatives}} it tests causal commonsense reasoning . the model receives: \boxed{\text{premise}} and two possible alternatives. it must choose which alternative is the more plausible: \boxed{\text{cause}} or: \boxed{\text{effect}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.13 example premise: “the road became extremely slippery.” question: what was the likely cause? options: a. it had rained heavily. b. the shop opened late. correct: \boxed{a} the model needs causal commonsense rather than simple keyword matching. 5.28.14 how indiccopa was constructed the deck gives a very interesting anti-bias procedure. the english copa test set is manually translated into: \boxed{18\text{ indic languages}}. but before translation: \boxed{ \text{premise + option 1 + option 2} } are randomized and reassigned across translators. that means one translator does not see the entire original item. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.15 why randomize the pieces? suppose a translator sees the whole item. they might unconsciously preserve: \text{sentence length} or: \text{word choice} or: \text{stylistic cues} that reveal the answer. then the benchmark could contain a translation artifact. the bias-guard procedure attempts to prevent this. so: \boxed{ \text{randomization} \rightarrow \text{reduced translation leakage} } this is directly from the dataset-construction description. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.16 important training detail copa itself has no training split. therefore fine-tuning uses: \boxed{\text{english social iqa}} according to the slide. this is another example of the benchmark's cross-lingual transfer idea. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.17 task 4 — indicpara next: \boxed{\text{indicpara}} this is a paraphrase/equivalence classification task. the question is: \boxed{ \text{do two sentences express essentially the same meaning?} } the benchmark table lists: \boxed{10\text{ languages}} and: \boxed{2002\text{ test instances}}. metric: \boxed{\text{accuracy}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.18 example sentence a: “the boy fell and injured himself.” sentence b: “the boy was hurt when he fell.” these can be: \boxed{\text{paraphrase}} because the meaning is substantially equivalent. but: “the girl pushed the boy and he fell.” is not equivalent. 5.28.19 how indicxparaphrase was created the deck says: \boxed{1001} english sentences of at least 10 words were machine-translated into: \boxed{10\text{ languages}}. annotators then: verified/corrected translations, wrote one paraphrase, wrote one non-paraphrase. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.20 the important anti-shortcut rule for paraphrases, annotators were instructed to minimize word overlap. they could use: \text{synonyms} \text{active/passive changes} \text{temporal phrase restructuring}. for non-paraphrases, they could change things like: \text{named entities} \text{pronouns} \text{adjectives} \text{adverbs}. the goal is: \boxed{ \text{meaning} > \text{surface word overlap} } the deck explicitly contrasts this construction with paws-x and says it did not use back-translation or noisy alignment to manufacture non-paraphrases. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.21 task 5 — m-intent the fifth classification task is: \boxed{\text{m-intent}} this is intent classification over spoken/user-query data. the benchmark table lists: \boxed{7\text{ languages}} with: \boxed{2974\text{ test examples}} and: \boxed{\text{accuracy}} as the metric. its domain is: \boxed{\text{spoken queries}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.22 example of intent classification suppose the user says: “set an alarm for seven tomorrow morning.” possible intents: \text{weather} \text{alarm} \text{music} \text{navigation}. correct: \boxed{\text{alarm}} this tests whether the model can map multilingual natural-language input to the correct user intent. 5.28.23 why does this task matter? because intent recognition tests a practical capability: \boxed{ \text{understand what the user wants} } rather than just: \boxed{ \text{understand what the sentence literally says} }. it is particularly relevant to spoken-agent systems. the dataset comes from the massive resource, whose 7-language indic subset is taken as-is according to the deck. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.24 now classification is complete we have: \boxed{ \text{indicsentiment} } sentiment. \boxed{ \text{indicxnli} } inference. \boxed{ \text{indiccopa} } causal commonsense reasoning. \boxed{ \text{indicpara} } semantic equivalence. \boxed{ \text{m-intent} } intent recognition. so the five tasks probe very different abilities. 5.28.25 numerical classification-bank suppose we get: task correct total sentiment 920 1000 nli 3758 5010 copa 410 500 paraphrase 1750 2002 intent 2600 2974 their individual accuracies are: sentiment 92.0\%. nli 75.01\%\approx75.0\%. copa 82.0\%. paraphrase \frac{1750}{2002}\times100 \approx \boxed{87.4\%}. intent \frac{2600}{2974}\times100 \approx \boxed{87.4\%}. these numbers are illustrative calculations, not reported model results. step 5.28.26 category 2 — structure prediction now classification ends. we move to: \boxed{\text{structure prediction}} there are: \boxed{2\text{ tasks}} in this category: \boxed{\text{naamapadam}} and: \boxed{\text{m-slotfill}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) the fundamental difference is: classification one label for the whole example. x\rightarrow y structure prediction labels are assigned to parts of the input. x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n \rightarrow y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n. this is a major conceptual shift. 5.28.27 task 6 — naamapadam naamapadam is the: \boxed{\text{named entity recognition (ner)}} task. suppose: aniket studies at bits pilani. the model should identify entities such as: \boxed{\text{aniket}} and: \boxed{\text{bits pilani}}. this is not one label for the sentence. instead, we assign a label to each relevant token/span. 5.28.28 iob2 representation the deck says naamapadam uses: \boxed{\text{iob2 format}} after projecting tags and then having annotators verify/correct them. (source: indicxtreme-slides) iob2 means: b=\text{beginning of entity} i=\text{inside entity} o=\text{outside entity}. example: aniket b-per studies o at o bits b-org pilani i-org so: \boxed{ \text{token sequence} \rightarrow \text{structured label sequence} } 5.28.29 how naamapadam is constructed the deck describes this pipeline: \boxed{ \text{english sentence} \rightarrow \text{off-the-shelf ner} } then: \boxed{ \text{project tags onto indic sentence using word alignment} } then: \boxed{ \text{human verification + correction} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a classic example of: \boxed{ \text{automatic generation} + \text{human quality control} } rather than blindly trusting projection. 5.28.30 metric: f1 because ner is structured prediction, the benchmark uses: \boxed{f1} rather than simple accuracy. recall: precision= \frac{tp}{tp+fp} recall= \frac{tp}{tp+fn} and: \boxed{ f1= \frac{2pr}{p+r} } where p is precision and r is recall. 5.28.31 numerical ner example suppose: tp=80,\quad fp=20,\quad fn=10. then: p=\frac{80}{80+20}=0.8. r=\frac{80}{80+10} = 0.8889. therefore: f1= \frac{2(0.8)(0.8889)} {0.8+0.8889} \approx \boxed{0.8421} or: \boxed{84.21\%}. this is an exam-style f1 calculation. 5.28.32 task 7 — m-slotfill the second structure-prediction task is: \boxed{\text{m-slotfill}} it comes from the massive family and evaluates slot filling. think: \boxed{ \text{intent} + \text{slot values} } for example: “play arijit singh songs tomorrow evening.” potential structure: \text{intent}=\text{play music} \text{artist}=\text{arijit singh} \text{time}=\text{tomorrow evening}. the model must identify spans and assign slot types. the benchmark table lists: \boxed{7\text{ languages}} and evaluates it with: \boxed{f1}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.33 why f1 again? because a slot-filling system can: miss an entity, produce an incorrect span, assign the wrong slot. accuracy would be a poor fit because the output is structured. so: \boxed{ \text{precision + recall} \rightarrow f1 } is more appropriate. step 5.28.34 category 3 — question answering now: \boxed{\text{qa}} has one task: \boxed{\text{indicqa}}. its task type is: \boxed{\text{span extraction}} and its metric is: \boxed{f1}. the table lists: \boxed{11\text{ languages}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.35 what is span extraction? suppose context says: “rabindranath tagore was born in kolkata.” question: where was rabindranath tagore born? the answer is a span from the context: \boxed{\text{kolkata}}. so the model must identify: \boxed{ [start,end] } of the answer span. this is fundamentally different from classification. correction: indicqa has indic-source contexts rather than translated english contexts. english translations are nevertheless used as an annotation aid (deckp14), so “no english-source translation anywhere” should not be read literally. complete grounded review 5.28.36 indicqa was built differently this is a particularly important dataset-construction idea. the deck says indicqa was created from scratch , without an english-source translation pipeline. (source: indicxtreme-slides) the researchers first identify topics connected to indic: \text{history} \text{monuments} \text{authors} \text{politicians} \text{festivals} etc. they then rank topics according to the number of indic-language wikipedia articles available and remove topics whose articles average fewer than 10 sentences. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.37 why is this important? because the benchmark is trying to test: \boxed{ \text{actual indic-language reading comprehension} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{translation of an english qa task} }. that is a crucial benchmark-design distinction. 5.28.38 the clever anti-leakage trick indicqa has a two-phase process. phase 1 — write question the context is split into: \boxed{\text{larger first part}} and: \boxed{\text{smaller second part}} of 2–3 sentences. these are machine-translated into english, and the annotator writes indic-language questions from the english translation. phase 2 — mark answer a different annotator sees only the original indic first part and marks the answer span. questions based on the withheld second part become naturally: \boxed{\text{unanswerable}} for the visible context. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a very clever way of generating both: \boxed{\text{answerable}} and: \boxed{\text{unanswerable}} questions. correction: qa totals require explicit discrepancy note:18,579−(13,283+5,292)=4. preserve the source figures; do not force them to sum by inventing a value. complete grounded review 5.28.39 indicqa annotation rules the deck specifies: \boxed{\ge 2\text{ questions per paragraph}} answer span: \boxed{\le5\text{ continuous words}} and: answer must be in one sentence; never use an entire sentence as an answer; never use a pronoun; minimize phrase overlap; choose the relevant occurrence if the answer string appears more than once. (source: indicxtreme-slides) these constraints are designed to make the 11 independently annotated languages comparable. 5.28.40 numerical qa example suppose the gold answer span is: [\text{kolkata}] and the model outputs: [\text{kolkata city}]. token overlap: 1 of: 1 gold token. precision: p=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 recall: r=\frac{1}{1}=1. therefore: f1= \frac{2(0.5)(1)}{0.5+1} = \boxed{0.667}. so: \boxed{66.7\%}. the benchmark's reported metric is f1, though the exact implementation details of tokenization/normalization are not specified on this slide. step 5.28.41 category 4 — retrieval the final category is: \boxed{\text{retrieval}} with: \boxed{\text{flores}}. the task is: \boxed{\text{sentence retrieval}} with: \boxed{1012} test sentences and: \boxed{18\text{ indic languages}}. the table lists: \boxed{\text{accuracy}} as the metric. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.42 what does sentence retrieval mean? conceptually, suppose we have: q a query sentence. and a collection: d=\{d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_n\}. the model must find the correct corresponding sentence: \boxed{ d^* } for the query. a retrieval system therefore computes some notion of: \text{similarity}(q,d_i) and selects the best candidate. the exact retrieval model architecture is not specified by this slide; this is the general retrieval formulation. 5.28.43 why flores is useful the deck says flores is already an: \boxed{n\text{-way parallel, human-translated dataset}} and the benchmark directly incorporates it for sentence-retrieval evaluation. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so unlike some newly constructed datasets: \boxed{ \text{no new translation creation pipeline is required here} } because the resource already exists. 5.28.44 complete task-suite map now we can finally see the whole benchmark: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} } classification \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\text{indicsentiment}\\ &\text{indicxnli}\\ &\text{indiccopa}\\ &\text{indicpara}\\ &\text{m-intent} \end{aligned} } structure prediction \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\text{naamapadam}\\ &\text{m-slotfill} \end{aligned} } qa \boxed{ \text{indicqa} } retrieval \boxed{ \text{flores} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.45 why the metrics differ this is very important for the exam. classification \boxed{\text{accuracy}} because the output is a class. ner / slot filling / qa \boxed{f1} because outputs involve structured spans/tags. retrieval \boxed{\text{accuracy}} in the benchmark table because the correct retrieval target is evaluated as a discrete outcome. thus: \boxed{ \text{metric depends on output structure} } not simply on whether the task is “hard” or “easy.” 5.28.46 human annotation vs machine translation another key table dimension is: \boxed{ha=\text{human annotated}} and: \boxed{mt=\text{machine translated}}. the benchmark table marks, for example: \text{indicsentiment}\rightarrow ha \text{indicxnli}\rightarrow mt \text{indiccopa}\rightarrow ha and other tasks accordingly. (source: indicxtreme-slides) but don't misinterpret mt . it does not mean: \boxed{ \text{“no humans involved.”} } the later slide explicitly emphasizes: \boxed{ \text{every indicxtreme evaluation set contains a human-supervision step} } through translation, post-editing, creation, verification, or correction. (source: indicxtreme-slides) correction: keep annotation pathways distinct: paraphrase translates english seeds and ner projects english tags. “entirely no english translation at any stage” is not supported by the documented pipelines. complete grounded review 5.28.47 the four construction pathways the deck summarizes four broad paths: \boxed{\text{translated from scratch}} \boxed{\text{built without any english source}} \boxed{\text{machine-translated then verified}} \boxed{\text{tag-projected then corrected}} yet all retain human supervision. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a fundamental benchmark-quality principle. 5.28.48 why benchmark construction itself matters suppose benchmark translations contain systematic artifacts. then a model can exploit: \boxed{\text{translation artifacts}} instead of: \boxed{\text{actual language understanding}}. therefore benchmark design is itself part of model evaluation. this is why indicxtreme spends so much attention on: \text{human verification} \text{bias guards} \text{anti-overlap rules} \text{natural indic-language content}. the individual examples of these mechanisms are documented across the dataset-construction slides. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.50 another exam numerical there are: 105 evaluation sets in total. of these: 52 are brand-new contributions. then reused/adapted evaluation sets: 105-52 = \boxed{53}. so approximately: \frac{52}{105}\times100 = \boxed{49.5\%} of the evaluation sets are new. the 105 and 52 figures are source-derived; the percentage is our calculation. claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.29 — indicxtreme zero-shot fine-tuning protocol plan node: i10 · chat order #70 now we reach one of the most important experimental-design concepts in the indicxtreme material. we already know: \boxed{\text{indicxtreme has many indic-language test sets}} but that alone does not tell us whether the benchmark is measuring: \boxed{\text{cross-lingual transfer}} or simply: \boxed{\text{ordinary supervised learning in each indic language}}. the solution is the benchmark's zero-shot fine-tuning protocol . (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.1 first understand the problem imagine a model is trained directly on hindi data. then we test it on hindi. suppose it gets: 90\%. what have we learned? the model is good at hindi. but we have not learned whether it can transfer knowledge from another language into hindi. now consider: \boxed{ \text{english training} \rightarrow \text{hindi testing} } if the model succeeds, that is evidence of: \boxed{ \text{cross-lingual transfer} }. that is what indicxtreme is designed to evaluate. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.2 what does “zero-shot” mean here? it means the model receives no indic-language training examples for the target benchmark task . the supplied slide is very explicit: \boxed{ \text{indic-language training data = none} } instead: \boxed{ \text{training data = english} } and the target evaluation is performed directly on indic-language test data. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.3 the exact pipeline the deck gives three steps. step 1 — fine-tune on english for each task: \boxed{ \text{pretrained lm} \rightarrow \text{english task training data} } this is done independently for the task. for example: \text{english sentiment training} for indicsentiment. or: \text{english nli training} for indicxnli. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.4 step 2 — select hyperparameters using english development data suppose we test: \text{learning rate}\in \{10^{-5},2\times10^{-5},5\times10^{-5}\} and: \text{weight decay}\in \{0,0.01\}. we evaluate candidate configurations on the: \boxed{\text{english development set}} and choose the best one. crucially: \boxed{ \text{indic test data is not used for model selection} } according to the protocol. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.5 step 3 — evaluate directly on indic test sets after selecting the model/configuration: \boxed{ \text{english-trained model} \rightarrow \text{indic-language test set} } no indic-language examples were used during the task training or model-selection process. so if we write: \theta^* = \arg\max_\theta \text{score}_{en-dev}(\theta), then evaluation is: \boxed{ \text{score}_{indic-test}(\theta^*) } this equation is a conceptual formalization of the protocol; the source states the three-stage procedure rather than presenting this exact notation. 5.29.6 why is this powerful? suppose: \text{english training accuracy}=95\% and: \text{hindi test accuracy}=85\%. the model has transferred: \boxed{ \text{task knowledge from english to hindi} }. the benchmark is therefore asking: does the multilingual pretrained representation allow knowledge learned in english to transfer into an indic language? that is the fundamental scientific question. 5.29.7 why not train on hindi too? because then we would be measuring something different. consider: setup a \text{english + hindi training} \rightarrow \text{hindi test}. setup b \text{english training} \rightarrow \text{hindi test}. setup a measures: \boxed{ \text{in-language supervised performance} } while setup b measures: \boxed{ \text{zero-shot cross-lingual transfer} }. indicxtreme is specifically interested in setup b. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.8 the most important anti-leakage condition the deck states: \boxed{ \text{no indic data is seen during training or model selection} } this prevents a hidden source of information. suppose the model is allowed to see 1000 hindi development examples. then choosing hyperparameters based on them could indirectly adapt the model to hindi. the resulting performance would no longer represent a clean zero-shot evaluation. so the protocol creates: \boxed{ \text{training language} \neq \text{evaluation language} } 5.29.9 numerical example: why leakage matters imagine two configurations. model a english dev: 82\% hindi dev: 77\%. model b english dev: 80\% hindi dev: 85\%. if we select using english dev: \boxed{\text{model a wins}} because: 82>80. if we select using hindi dev: \boxed{\text{model b wins}} because: 85>77. thus using hindi development data changes model selection. that would introduce target-language information into the process. the actual deck uses english development selection specifically to avoid that issue. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.10 a subtle point: zero-shot does not mean zero training this is a common exam trap. zero-shot here does not mean: \boxed{\text{the model receives no fine-tuning}} instead: \boxed{ \text{the model is fine-tuned} } but: \boxed{ \text{not on the target indic language} }. so: \boxed{ \text{zero-shot target-language transfer} } is more precise. 5.29.11 example: indicsentiment suppose the english training set contains: 100,000 english reviews. we fine-tune the multilingual model using those reviews. then: \boxed{\text{no hindi reviews}} are used for training. finally: \boxed{\text{hindi reviews}} are used only for evaluation. if the model gets: 88\% on hindi, that result is evidence of transfer. 5.29.12 example: indicxnli english training: \text{premise + hypothesis} \rightarrow \text{english nli labels} then hindi test: \text{hindi premise + hypothesis} \rightarrow \text{prediction}. the model has to carry the nli capability across languages. 5.29.13 why task-specific hyperparameter tuning matters the deck makes another methodological point. many earlier approaches reused one fixed hyperparameter configuration across tasks. indicxtreme instead performs a: \boxed{ \text{task-specific grid search} } for: \boxed{ \text{learning rate} } and: \boxed{ \text{weight decay} }. this is done for every model and task. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.14 why is this fairer? suppose: task a works best with: lr=10^{-5}. task b works best with: lr=5\times10^{-5}. if we force both to use: lr=10^{-5}, task b may be artificially weakened. then we'd be measuring: \boxed{ \text{quality under a poor hyperparameter choice} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{quality of the underlying model} }. so task-specific tuning makes the comparison more informative. the source explicitly motivates this as part of fair comparison. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.15 but doesn't hyperparameter tuning introduce target information? the benchmark avoids that by selecting configurations on: \boxed{\text{english development data}} rather than the target indic test data. so the target language remains hidden from model selection. this is a crucial experimental-design principle. 5.29.16 full experimental pipeline keep this picture in your head: multilingual pretrained lm │ ▼ english task training │ ▼ english development │ hyperparameter selection │ ▼ final model θ* │ ▼ ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ hindi test tamil test bengali test │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ zero-shot zero-shot zero-shot transfer transfer transfer no indic-language training data enters before evaluation. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.17 now comes the interesting extension the researchers ask: does using an in-language development set help model selection? at first, the benchmark says: \boxed{\text{english dev}} is used. but they investigate alternatives. this produces an important distinction: \boxed{ \text{in-language} } versus: \boxed{ \text{in-family} } versus: \boxed{ \text{english} }. 5.29.18 what is an in-language dev set? suppose we're evaluating: \boxed{\text{bengali}}. an in-language dev set is: \boxed{\text{bengali development data}}. this gives direct feedback about the target language. but using it changes the strict zero-shot protocol because the target language now influences model selection. 5.29.19 what is an in-family dev set? this is a very interesting intermediate idea. the deck uses: \boxed{\text{hindi}} as a representative language for: \boxed{\text{indo-european}} and: \boxed{\text{tamil}} as a representative language for: \boxed{\text{dravidian}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so instead of having bengali-specific dev data, one can potentially select using a related language. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{hindi dev} \rightarrow \text{select for other indo-european languages} } and: \boxed{ \text{tamil dev} \rightarrow \text{select for other dravidian languages} }. 5.29.20 why might that work? suppose two languages share some useful linguistic structure. then a model configuration that works well on: l_1 may also work reasonably well on: l_2 within the same family. this can provide a compromise: \boxed{ \text{better than english-only selection} } without needing a separate development set for every target language. the source reports that these in-family dev sets perform on par with true in-language dev sets and clearly ahead of english-only selection. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.21 let's inspect the reported table the slide compares: english development selection, in-language development selection, in-family development selection. the table shows that for the reported tasks, in-family selection tends to be close to actual in-language selection and better than english-only selection. (source: indicxtreme-slides) for example, on indicsentiment , the table reports approximately: \text{mbert: }72.9 for in-language and: 72.9 for in-family, compared with a smaller english-dev-selected result. for indicbert, the reported numbers similarly show in-family selection tracking in-language performance closely. (source: indicxtreme-slides) we should interpret the pattern rather than memorize every table cell. 5.29.22 what does this tell us? there appears to be a useful hierarchy: \boxed{ \text{english dev} < \text{related-language dev} \approx \text{target-language dev} } for the reported experiments. the key lesson is: \boxed{ \text{language-aware model selection can matter} } even when actual target-language training remains absent. the precise numerical gains are task/model dependent; the deck's broad conclusion is the important point. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.23 why is hindi particularly interesting? now the deck goes one step further. it asks: what happens if hindi itself becomes the transfer language? the slide reports: \boxed{\text{hindi is a better transfer language than english}} for the evaluated tasks. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a major observation. 5.29.24 “gold zero-shot” the deck defines: \boxed{\text{gold zero-shot}} as using real hindi training data for the tasks. so instead of: \text{english training} \rightarrow \text{indic test}, we have: \boxed{ \text{hindi training} \rightarrow \text{other indic-language test} }. this is not strict zero-shot with respect to hindi, because the model sees hindi training data. it is better understood as cross-indic transfer from hindi . the slide explicitly uses the term “gold zero-shot” for this setup. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.25 “silver zero-shot” the deck also constructs: \boxed{\text{silver zero-shot}} by machine-translating the english training set into hindi. so: \text{english training} becomes: \boxed{ \text{machine-translated hindi training} } and then the model transfers from hindi to the other indic languages. this provides: \boxed{ \text{hindi-language supervision without manually creating hindi data} } although translation errors can be introduced. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.26 reported hindi transfer gains the deck reports that switching the transfer language from english to hindi in the evaluated setup lifts: \boxed{\text{ner by }+3.5} \boxed{\text{intent by }+3.1} \boxed{\text{slot-filling by }+10.6} percentage points. (source: indicxtreme-slides) these are source-derived results. 5.29.27 why might hindi help? the deck's result supports the idea that: \boxed{ \text{english is not necessarily the optimal transfer language for indic targets} } because hindi may share more useful linguistic properties with other indic languages than english does. we should be careful, though: \boxed{ \text{hindi} \neq \text{equally close to every indic language} } and the source does not establish a universal rule that hindi must always be the best transfer language. the conclusion is specific to the experiments reported. 5.29.28 gold vs silver transfer here is the distinction: gold zero-shot \boxed{ \text{real hindi task training data} } silver zero-shot \boxed{ \text{machine-translated hindi task training data} } the silver approach is cheaper/easier to construct, but introduces translation errors. the deck reports that silver transfer helps: \boxed{ \text{sentiment} } \boxed{ \text{xnli} } \boxed{ \text{paraphrase} } similarly, but hurts: \boxed{ \text{indiccopa} } and: \boxed{ \text{indicqa} }. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.29 why would translation hurt copa and qa? the source explicitly attributes this to the sensitivity of these tasks to small translation errors. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this makes intuitive sense. for causal reasoning: \boxed{ \text{one subtle wording change} } can alter which cause is plausible. for qa: \boxed{ \text{small translation error} } can change: \text{answer span} or: \text{question/context relationship}. so: \boxed{ \text{translation noise} \rightarrow \text{task-dependent degradation} } is the important lesson. 5.29.30 numerical example — transfer improvement suppose a baseline ner score is: 70.0. the reported hindi-transfer improvement is: +3.5. then: 70.0+3.5 = \boxed{73.5}. for slot filling, suppose: 60.0 baseline. then: 60.0+10.6 = \boxed{70.6}. these are illustrative starting scores; the actual source provides the gains, not these hypothetical baselines. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.31 a very important conceptual distinction don't confuse these three experiments. strict indicxtreme zero-shot \boxed{ \text{english train} \rightarrow \text{indic test} } gold hindi transfer \boxed{ \text{hindi train} \rightarrow \text{other indic test} } silver hindi transfer \boxed{ \text{machine-translated hindi train} \rightarrow \text{other indic test} } all are evaluating transfer, but they answer different scientific questions. 5.29.32 why the benchmark starts with english because english is the conventional high-resource transfer language. so the baseline question is: \boxed{ \text{can multilingual pretraining transfer task knowledge from english into indic languages?} } then the hindi experiments ask a deeper question: \boxed{ \text{would a linguistically closer indic transfer language work better?} } that is a much more sophisticated benchmark study. 5.29.33 exam-style numerical question suppose: \text{english transfer score}=65.0 and hindi transfer gives: +10.6. then: 65.0+10.6 = \boxed{75.6}. relative improvement: \frac{10.6}{65.0}\times100 \approx \boxed{16.31\%}. again, the +10.6 is source-derived for slot filling; 65.0 is hypothetical. 5.29.34 another exam question: strict zero-shot a student says: “the model was fine-tuned on english and hindi before being evaluated on bengali, so this is zero-shot bengali.” under the deck's strict protocol, that statement is: \boxed{\text{incorrect}} because hindi-language training data was used. strict zero-shot requires: \boxed{ \text{no target indic-language training data} } and the benchmark's main protocol uses english training only. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.35 another exam question: model selection suppose there are three learning rates: 10^{-5},\;2\times10^{-5},\;5\times10^{-5}. their english-dev accuracies are: 80,\;84,\;82. choose: \boxed{2\times10^{-5}}. then test this configuration on hindi. suppose hindi accuracy is: 78. you must not go back and select the learning rate because another learning rate gave: 82 on hindi test. that would contaminate the evaluation. this is exactly why model selection is restricted to english development data. 5.29.36 why this protocol is experimentally clean the sequence: \boxed{ \text{train on english} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{choose using english dev} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{freeze the choice} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{test on indic} } means the target-language test set is truly an unseen evaluation environment. this reduces the chance that the benchmark score is inflated by target-language adaptation. 5.29.37 but there is still a deeper question suppose english is a very different language from hindi. then perhaps: \boxed{ \text{english transfer} } is simply a poor experimental baseline for indic languages. the hindi experiments investigate exactly that. if hindi is a better transfer language, then the problem isn't necessarily: \text{multilingual model failure}. it may partially be: \boxed{ \text{choice of source/transfer language} }. this is one of the most interesting implications of the deck's later analysis. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.38 complete conceptual picture we started with: \boxed{ \text{english} \rightarrow \text{indic} } and discovered that transfer is imperfect. then we tested: \boxed{ \text{in-language dev} } and: \boxed{ \text{in-family dev} } and found that in-family selection can approach in-language selection in the reported experiments. (source: indicxtreme-slides) then we tested: \boxed{ \text{hindi} \rightarrow \text{other indic} } and found substantial gains on some tasks. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so the experiment evolves from: \boxed{ \text{can english transfer?} } to: \boxed{ \text{does language-aware model selection help?} } to: \boxed{ \text{is a related indic language a better transfer source?} } that is the logic of the entire section. 5.29.39 exam-ready summary strict indicxtreme protocol \boxed{ \text{english train} \rightarrow \text{english dev for model selection} \rightarrow \text{indic test} } why? to measure: \boxed{ \text{zero-shot cross-lingual transfer} } without indic-language training or model selection contamination. (source: indicxtreme-slides) hyperparameters task-specific search over at least: \boxed{ \text{learning rate + weight decay} } using english development data. (source: indicxtreme-slides) in-family selection \boxed{ \text{hindi for indo-european} } \boxed{ \text{tamil for dravidian} } performed close to in-language selection and ahead of english-only selection in the reported study. (source: indicxtreme-slides) hindi transfer reported gains: \boxed{ ner:+3.5 } \boxed{ intent:+3.1 } \boxed{ slotfill:+10.6 } percentage points. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.40 final mental model the most important equation from this whole section is: \boxed{ \underbrace{ \text{english supervision} }_{\text{task learning}} \rightarrow \underbrace{ \text{indic evaluation} }_{\text{language transfer}} } that lets us separate: \boxed{ \text{“does the model know the task?”} } from: \boxed{ \text{“can the model transfer that knowledge across languages?”} } and the later hindi experiment adds a third question: \boxed{ \text{“which language is the best source for cross-lingual transfer?”} } that is the central experimental logic of indicxtreme's zero-shot section. (source: indicxtreme-slides)

(source: indicxtreme-slides) the word family matters. it does not mean that the plain indicbert v2 row itself beats the best multilingual baseline on all seven. the strongest variants are considered as part of the family. 5.30.8 let's verify the “7 of 9” claim ourselves take the strongest multilingual baseline per task: task best of mbert/xlm-r/muril indicsentiment 85.1 indicxnli 72.4 indiccopa 60.1 indicxpara 60.8 massive intent 77.2 naamapadam 74.3 slotfill 57.0 indicqa 48.8 flores 52.3 now use the strongest result within the indicbert v2 family, represented by the indicbert-ss row: 88.1,\ 73.9,\ 64.2,\ 56.4,\ 80.7,\ 66.6,\ 57.3,\ 49.7,\ 71.2. (source: indicxtreme-slides) compare. 5.30.9 task-by-task comparison indicsentiment 88.1>85.1 gain: \boxed{+3.0} indicxnli 73.9>72.4 gain: \boxed{+1.5} indiccopa 64.2>60.1 gain: \boxed{+4.1} indicxpara 56.4<60.8. so the multilingual baseline remains higher. massive intent 80.7>77.2 gain: \boxed{+3.5} naamapadam 66.6<74.3. multilingual baseline remains higher. massive slotfill 57.3>57.0 gain: \boxed{+0.3}. indicqa 49.7>48.8 gain: \boxed{+0.9}. flores 71.2>52.3 gain: \boxed{+18.9}. therefore: \boxed{ 7\text{ wins out of }9 } and the two losses are: \boxed{\text{indicxpara}} and: \boxed{\text{naamapadam}}. this directly reproduces the deck's “7 of 9” statement. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.10 this is a much stronger way to read the table instead of memorizing: “indicbert wins 7 of 9.” understand: \boxed{ \text{indic-focused pretraining produces an advantage on most benchmark capabilities} } but: \boxed{ \text{not every task} } and: \boxed{ \text{not by the same margin} }. that is a scientifically more useful interpretation. 5.30.11 biggest gain: retrieval on flores: strongest multilingual baseline: 52.3. indicbert-ss: 71.2. gain: 71.2-52.3 = \boxed{18.9\text{ points}}. relative improvement: \frac{18.9}{52.3}\times100 \approx \boxed{36.1\%}. the 18.9-point gap is our calculation from the reported table. 5.30.12 another strong gain: intent best multilingual: 77.2. indicbert-ss: 80.7. gain: \boxed{3.5\text{ points}}. the improvement is much smaller than flores. this teaches us: \boxed{ \text{“wins the task” does not mean “wins by a huge margin.”} } 5.30.13 another important result: indicbert-only ablation the deck says that the pattern persists even for the ablation trained purely on: \boxed{\text{indiccorp v2}} using: \boxed{\text{mlm}} with: \boxed{\text{no parallel data}}. the slide's explanation is that models that do not need to share capacity with unrelated high-resource languages perform better on indic tasks. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a very important experiment. 5.30.14 why is the ablation important? suppose the improvement came only because the model received a lot of parallel multilingual data. then we might conclude: \boxed{ \text{parallel translation data caused the gain} } but the indiccorp-only mlm ablation still performs strongly. that suggests: \boxed{ \text{indic-focused monolingual pretraining itself is valuable} } in the reported benchmark. the source explicitly highlights this observation. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.15 why does “no parallel data” matter? parallel data looks like: \boxed{ \text{sentence in language a} \leftrightarrow \text{corresponding sentence in language b} } for example: \text{hindi sentence} \leftrightarrow \text{english sentence}. the ablation instead relies purely on: \boxed{ \text{indiccorp v2 + mlm} } so the model can learn indic-language structure directly from monolingual text. this makes the experiment stronger evidence for the usefulness of indic-focused pretraining. 5.30.16 think about capacity sharing a general multilingual model has to represent: \text{english} + \text{chinese} + \text{arabic} + \text{hindi} + \text{tamil} +\cdots inside one model. indicbert focuses heavily on indic languages. so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{shared model capacity} } versus: \boxed{ \text{indic-focused capacity} }. the deck interprets the ablation result as evidence that avoiding capacity sharing with unrelated high-resource languages can benefit indic tasks. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.17 important caution do not turn that into: “multilingual models are bad.” the table shows: \boxed{ \text{mbert/xlm-r/muril can be very strong} } on particular tasks. for example: \text{muril naamapadam}=74.3 beats the strongest listed indicbert-family result: 66.6. and: \text{xlm-r indicxpara}=56.7 is above the strongest indicbert-family result: 56.4. so specialization improves many tasks, but not every one. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.18 now we move to the bigger issue: language-level performance a model can have: \boxed{\text{excellent average performance}} while still failing badly on particular languages. therefore the researchers break performance down by language. this produces the next major result: \boxed{ \text{winners vs left-behinds} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.19 what are winners and left-behinds? the taxonomy used earlier assigns languages a resource class. at one extreme: \boxed{ 5=\text{winner} } meaning resource-rich. at the other: \boxed{ 1=\text{left-behind} } meaning extremely under-resourced. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so the benchmark can ask: \boxed{ \text{does performance track resource availability?} } 5.30.20 the answer is yes the deck says extremely low-resource languages—those below the 10th percentile of the corpus-resource distribution—show a sharp and consistent performance drop. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is one of the most important findings of the entire indicxtreme material. 5.30.21 the concrete copa example on indiccopa: \boxed{\text{santhali}} scores: \boxed{25.9\%} lower than hindi. and: \boxed{\text{sindhi}} scores: \boxed{17.7\%} lower than hindi. (source: indicxtreme-slides) these are percentage-point gaps , not relative percentage reductions. that distinction matters. 5.30.22 percentage points vs percentage reduction suppose hindi gets: 60\% and santhali is: 25.9\text{ points lower}. then santhali would be: 60-25.9 = \boxed{34.1\%}. but saying “santhali is 25.9% worse” would normally suggest a relative reduction: 60(1-0.259) = 44.46\%. that is not what the deck's wording means. so: \boxed{ 25.9\text{ points lower} \neq 25.9\%\text{ relative lower} } very important exam distinction. 5.30.23 why are left-behinds performing worse? the slide identifies three related causes. first: \boxed{\text{lack of pretraining data}} second: \boxed{\text{no shared script}} third: \boxed{ \text{no linguistic “cousin” in the corpus to bridge transfer} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) let's unpack them. 5.30.24 cause 1 — lack of pretraining data suppose hindi has a huge amount of training text but a low-resource language has very little. then the model receives much more statistical evidence for hindi. conceptually: n_{\text{hindi}}\gg n_{\text{low-resource}}. the model can therefore learn: p(\text{patterns}\mid\text{hindi}) much more reliably than: p(\text{patterns}\mid\text{very-low-resource language}). this follows directly from the resource-imbalance problem established earlier in the deck. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.25 cause 2 — no shared script this is particularly interesting. suppose a low-resource language uses a script that is also well represented in the training corpus. then there may be useful shared orthographic patterns. but if its script is poorly represented: \boxed{ \text{less direct script-level transfer} } is available. the deck explicitly identifies the lack of a shared script as one of the compounding reasons for the performance drop. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.26 cause 3 — no linguistic “cousin” suppose a low-resource language has related languages that are well represented. then the model may potentially exploit transfer through shared linguistic structure. conceptually: l_{\text{low}} \leftrightarrow l_{\text{related}} and: l_{\text{related}} \rightarrow \text{learned representations}. but if there is no well-represented linguistic cousin in the corpus: \boxed{ \text{less indirect transfer support} } is available. again, the “linguistic cousin” explanation is explicitly given by the slide. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.27 this gives us a three-factor failure model for an extremely low-resource language: \boxed{ \text{small data} } + \boxed{ \text{weak script sharing} } + \boxed{ \text{weak linguistic-transfer support} } can compound. so the problem is not merely: \boxed{ \text{“not enough text.”} } it can be: \boxed{ \text{not enough text + poor representational bridges}. } that is the more complete lesson. 5.30.28 the benchmark itself still has a limitation here is an extremely important detail. indiccorp v2 contains: \boxed{24\text{ languages}}. but indicxtreme can evaluate only: \boxed{19} of them. therefore: 24-19 = \boxed{5} languages still have no evaluation set . the deck calls these remaining languages “left-behind” in the context of benchmark coverage. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.29 why is this ironic? the benchmark was created to address: \boxed{ \text{poor benchmark coverage} } but it still cannot evaluate: \boxed{5/24} of the corpus languages. the fraction is: \frac{5}{24} \approx 0.2083. so approximately: \boxed{20.8\%} of the indiccorp v2 language set lacks indicxtreme evaluation according to this slide. this is our calculation from the source's explicit 24 and 19 figures. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.30 this is a major research lesson a benchmark itself can have a coverage frontier . even if we improve: \text{model} and: \text{training corpus}, we still cannot measure performance on a language for which: \boxed{ \text{no reliable evaluation dataset exists}. } so: \boxed{ \text{data problem} \rightarrow \text{model problem} \rightarrow \text{evaluation problem} } are interconnected. 5.30.31 let's connect corpus size to benchmark behavior earlier we learned: 20.9\text{b tokens} total. but the bottom 11 lowest-resource languages contribute only: 1.08\text{b}. therefore: \frac{1.08}{20.9}\times100 \approx \boxed{5.17\%}. so nearly all of the corpus is concentrated outside that bottom group. this explains why simply saying: “the model has 20.9b indic tokens” can hide the real distribution problem. 5.30.32 important numerical inference suppose two models both see: 20.9\text{b total tokens}. model a has balanced distribution. model b has highly concentrated distribution. they have the same total: \boxed{20.9\text{b}} but potentially very different low-resource performance. therefore: \boxed{ \text{total corpus size} \neq \text{resource balance} } this is a conceptual inference from the corpus and benchmark results. 5.30.33 why does the benchmark distinguish good models? we can now answer the original question at three levels. level 1 — task level models differ significantly across the 9 tasks. level 2 — model level indicbert v2 family outperforms major multilingual baselines on 7/9 tasks. level 3 — language level performance changes sharply according to language resource level, especially for left-behinds. so: \boxed{ \text{benchmark discriminates both models and languages} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.34 the strongest conceptual conclusion the results suggest: \boxed{ \text{indic-specific pretraining helps} } but also: \boxed{ \text{indic-specific pretraining does not eliminate the low-resource gap} } that is extremely important. we improve the overall model: \text{indicbert v2 family} yet still see: \text{winner} > \text{left-behind}. so better indic resources reduce some problems without magically solving resource inequality. 5.30.35 full causal chain now connect the entire indicxtreme lecture: \boxed{ \text{some indic languages have little/no data} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{generic multilingual models allocate uneven capacity} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{existing benchmarks omit many indic languages} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indiccorp + indicxtreme} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indic-focused pretraining improves many tasks} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{but extreme low-resource languages remain substantially weaker} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{future work must improve both data and evaluation coverage} } this is the central story of the indicxtreme material. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.36 exam numerical bank numerical 1 — v1 → v2 indicsentiment 88.3-61.8 = \boxed{26.5\text{ points}} numerical 2 — v1 → v2 indicxnli 73.0-42.8 = \boxed{30.2\text{ points}} numerical 3 — v1 → v2 flores 69.4-1.1 = \boxed{68.3\text{ points}} numerical 4 — best multilingual → indicbert-ss flores 71.2-52.3 = \boxed{18.9\text{ points}} numerical 5 — relative flores improvement \frac{18.9}{52.3}\times100 \approx \boxed{36.1\%}. numerical 6 — languages without benchmark 24-19 = \boxed{5}. fraction: 5/24 \approx \boxed{20.8\%}. numerical 7 — low-resource corpus share 1.08/20.9\times100 \approx \boxed{5.17\%}. all source figures used here come from the supplied indicxtreme slides. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.37 exam-style conceptual question question: why is the 7/9 result more informative than saying “indicbert v2 has a higher average score”? because a single average can hide task-specific failures. the 7/9 comparison shows that the indicbert v2 family beats the strongest massively multilingual baseline on most individual benchmark tasks while still losing on two, namely indicxpara and naamapadam in the strongest-family comparison. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.38 another exam question question: why is the indiccorp-only mlm ablation important? because it shows that the reported indic gains are not dependent entirely on parallel multilingual data. the supplied slide says the advantage persists for a model trained purely on indiccorp v2 with mlm and no parallel data, supporting the value of indic-focused pretraining. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.39 another exam question question: why do left-behind languages perform worse? the source identifies: \boxed{ \text{insufficient pretraining data} + \text{lack of shared script} + \text{lack of a linguistic cousin represented in the corpus} } as compounding factors. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.30.40 final mental model the entire results section can be reduced to: \boxed{ \text{indic specialization} \rightarrow \text{better performance on most tasks} } but: \boxed{ \text{resource inequality} \rightarrow \text{persistent language inequality} } therefore: \boxed{ \text{better model} \neq \text{problem solved for every language} } and there is one final warning: \boxed{ \text{24 corpus languages} \quad\neq\quad \text{24 evaluated languages} } because the deck says only 19 can currently be evaluated, leaving 5 without an evaluation set. (source: indicxtreme-slides) where we are in the indic section we have now completed the logical chain: \boxed{ \text{why indic benchmark?} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indiccorp v2 construction} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme task suite} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{zero-shot fine-tuning protocol} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{model comparison} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{winners vs left-behinds} } ➜ extra / deeper material in the appendix: g.7 — indicxtreme slides not covered by the lessons — indicqa statistics, ethics and annotator practices
