claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.31 — indicgenbench: why a second indic benchmark is needed plan node: i11 · chat order #72 we now enter the indicgenbench material. this is the natural continuation after indicxtreme. the key distinction is: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme asks: “can the model understand/classify indic text?”} } while: \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench asks: “can the model actually generate useful indic text?”} } the supplied deck explicitly frames indicgenbench as a benchmark for generation capabilities such as summarization, translation, and question answering, in contrast to indicxtreme's classification/nlu emphasis. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.1 start with the problem suppose an llm performs well on an indic classification task: \text{hindi sentence}\rightarrow\text{positive}. that tells us something about: \boxed{\text{understanding}} but a real user often wants the model to produce language . for example: \text{english article} \rightarrow \text{hindi summary} or: \text{english sentence} \rightarrow \text{tamil translation} or: \text{hindi question} \rightarrow \text{hindi answer}. these are generation problems. so the benchmark needs to test: \boxed{ \text{can the model produce correct, faithful, fluent indic-language output?} } 5.31.2 the motivation slide gives a striking result the deck says that singh et al. built indicgenbench to expose a large generation gap: on every one of five generation tasks , even the best model scores far below its own english performance. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{english capability} > \text{indic generation capability} } across all five reported generation tasks. this is important because a multilingual model can appear strong globally while still having a substantial target-language generation deficit. 5.31.3 why is generation harder to evaluate than classification? consider classification: x\rightarrow y where y might be: \{\text{positive, negative}\}. evaluation is easy: \boxed{ \hat y=y? } generation is different. suppose the gold summary is: “the mission launched successfully after several delays.” the model writes: “after multiple delays, the mission was finally launched successfully.” are these equivalent? yes, semantically. but exact string matching would say: \boxed{\text{different}} even though the generation is good. therefore generation benchmarks need metrics capable of handling: \boxed{ \text{multiple valid ways of expressing the same meaning} }. that is why indicgenbench's metric design becomes important. 5.31.4 scope of indicgenbench the deck defines: \boxed{29\text{ indic languages}} across: \boxed{13\text{ scripts}} and: \boxed{4\text{ language families}}. the 29 languages are divided into three resource tiers: \boxed{9\text{ higher}} \boxed{7\text{ medium}} \boxed{13\text{ low}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is already a major difference from our previous benchmark discussion. indicgenbench explicitly makes resource level a central experimental variable. 5.31.5 “higher-resource” does not mean high-resource globally this is an important source-specific warning. the deck gives hindi as an example: \boxed{\sim160,000\text{ wikipedia articles}} versus: \boxed{6.6\text{m+ for english}}. so “higher” means: \boxed{ \text{higher relative to other indic languages} } not: \boxed{ \text{high-resource by global standards} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this prevents a very common misinterpretation. 5.31.6 why classify languages into resource tiers? because we want to ask: \boxed{ \text{does generation quality decline as language resources decline?} } so instead of reporting only one average: \text{average performance}=x, we can investigate: \boxed{ \text{higher} \rightarrow \text{medium} \rightarrow \text{low} } and observe whether performance follows the same direction. the later results slide says it does: performance drops from high to medium to low across every task. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.7 the five generation tasks indicgenbench contains five generation tasks. the deck describes them as: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} cross-lingual summarization, \boxed{\text{flores-in}} machine translation, \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} multilingual qa, and two versions of: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in}} cross-lingual qa. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so: \boxed{ 1+1+1+2=5 } generation tasks. 5.31.8 why does the benchmark mostly translate existing datasets? this is one of the most important design decisions in the deck. instead of creating every benchmark entirely from scratch, the researchers start with existing english-source benchmarks: \boxed{\text{crosssum}} \boxed{\text{flores-200}} \boxed{\text{xquad}} \boxed{\text{xor-tydi}}. then they add professional human translations into indic languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) at first this may seem like a weakness: why not create everything directly in indic languages? the deck gives three explicit reasons . 5.31.9 reason 1 — multi-way parallel data suppose we start from the same source example: x and create: y_{\text{hindi}}, y_{\text{tamil}}, y_{\text{bengali}}, \ldots all corresponding to the same source. now comparisons become much cleaner. we can ask whether a model's performance difference comes from: \boxed{\text{language}} rather than: \boxed{\text{different underlying task content}}. this is exactly why the deck values multi-way parallel data . (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.10 example suppose the source is one english sentence: x=\text{“the satellite launched successfully.”} create translations into: \text{hindi} \text{tamil} \text{bengali} and so on. because every language began with the same x , comparisons become: \boxed{ \text{same task} + \text{same underlying content} + \text{different target language} } which is very useful for studying cross-lingual generalization. 5.31.11 reason 2 — clean source text may not exist in low-resource languages suppose researchers want to build a fresh qa dataset in a very low-resource language. they need: \text{clean documents} + \text{questions} + \text{answers} + \text{quality control}. but high-quality source material may not exist at sufficient scale. the deck specifically points out that some low-resource languages do not have clean knowledge corpora such as wikipedia at the level needed for fresh dataset construction. (source: indicgenbench-slides) translation provides a way around that. instead of: \boxed{ \text{find huge clean indic source corpus} } we can: \boxed{ \text{start from already-developed english benchmark} } and translate it. 5.31.12 reason 3 — reuse existing quality control existing datasets have already gone through substantial: \text{design} \text{validation} \text{quality control}. so indicgenbench can inherit that work and focus additional effort on: \boxed{ \text{high-quality human indic translation} }. the deck explicitly lists this as its third motivation. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.13 this is an important benchmark-design tradeoff translation-based construction gives: \boxed{ \text{comparability} + \text{scalability} + \text{reusable task design} } but introduces another possible problem: \boxed{ \text{translation artifacts/errors} }. and the deck later demonstrates exactly that translation quality matters, especially for some tasks. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the design tradeoff is: \boxed{ \text{clean common source} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{native-language authenticity} } and the benchmark tries to balance the two through professional human translation. 5.31.14 human translators the deck says the translators were: \boxed{\text{professional data labelers}} working through the authors' organization and an external vendor. they were paid competitively according to the labor laws and prevailing market rates of each region. (source: indicgenbench-slides) one reported detail is particularly interesting: \boxed{2.80\text{ usd/hour}} for pashto versus: \boxed{15.90\text{ usd/hour}} for tibetan. that is a: \frac{15.90}{2.80} \approx \boxed{5.68\times} difference, which the slide summarizes as a: \boxed{5.7\times} pay range across languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.15 why is this mentioned in a technical lecture? because dataset construction is not just: \boxed{\text{nlp algorithm}} it is also: \boxed{ \text{human annotation process} + \text{labor practices} + \text{quality control} }. the quality of a benchmark depends on the people producing and validating its data. 5.31.16 first major task: crosssum-in now we begin the individual task architecture. \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} is cross-lingual summarization . the source benchmark is: \boxed{\text{crosssum}} which itself comes from: \boxed{\text{xl-sum}} and is based on bbc news articles and summaries across languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the generation task is: \boxed{ \text{article} \rightarrow \text{summary in target language} } 5.31.17 why is this “cross-lingual” summarization? the source article and target summary can involve different languages. in the benchmark's construction, the deck starts from english article-summary pairs and creates target-language summaries. the key requirement is that the model should generate the summary: \boxed{ \text{directly in the target language} } rather than: \text{source} \rightarrow \text{english intermediate} \rightarrow \text{target}. the example slide explicitly emphasizes faithful compressed generation directly in the target language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.18 crosssum-in construction for each language, the dataset uses: \boxed{ 100\text{ train} + 100\text{ dev} + 500\text{ test} } examples. thus: 100+100+500 = \boxed{700} examples per language. there are: \boxed{29\text{ languages}}. therefore: 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300} examples total. the deck explicitly reports this number and confirms it by direct arithmetic. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.19 numerical exam question given: 29\text{ languages} and: 700\text{ examples/language}, compute total examples: 29\times700 = \boxed{20,300}. then: training examples: 29\times100 = \boxed{2,900}. development: 29\times100 = \boxed{2,900}. test: 29\times500 = \boxed{14,500}. check: 2900+2900+14500 = \boxed{20,300}. 5.31.20 second major task: flores-in the next task is: \boxed{\text{flores-in}} for machine translation. the source dataset is: \boxed{\text{flores-200}}. unlike crosssum, flores already contains high-quality human-annotated multilingual parallel data. so indicgenbench reuses as much as possible and translates into languages not already covered. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.21 flores split structure the source flores-200 split has: \boxed{997\text{ dev}} \boxed{1012\text{ devtest}} \boxed{992\text{ test}} but the deck says the non-public test is not used for this construction. therefore: 997+1012 = \boxed{2009} sentences per language. for: 29 languages: 2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261} examples. the slide reports approximately: \boxed{58.2k}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.22 important exception the deck says flores-in is: \boxed{\text{the only task with no training split}} in indicgenbench. why? because this is fundamentally a benchmark of translation over an established parallel evaluation set, and the source flores structure is reused directly rather than creating a new task-specific training split for the benchmark. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.23 what does flores-in actually ask the model to do? very simply: \boxed{ \text{source sentence} \rightarrow \text{target-language sentence} } no question. no long context. no multiple-choice alternatives. just translation. the deck emphasizes that the same source sentence is represented across all target languages, making the dataset n-way parallel . (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.24 why is n-way parallelity valuable? suppose: x_{\text{english}} has translations: y_{\text{hindi}}, y_{\text{tamil}}, y_{\text{punjabi}}, y_{\text{bengali}}, \ldots then each language is being tested against the same semantic source. thus: \boxed{ \text{language comparison becomes cleaner} } because the underlying content is held constant. 5.31.25 third task: xquad-in the next task is: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} for multilingual reading comprehension / qa. the source is: \boxed{\text{xquad}} which itself derives from: \boxed{\text{squad}} and contains english wikipedia passages and short-span questions/answers. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the generation problem is: \boxed{ \text{context + question} \rightarrow \text{answer} } in the target language. 5.31.26 fourth and fifth tasks: xorqa-in this is particularly interesting because one underlying translation effort produces two tasks . the source is: \boxed{\text{xor-tydi}}. the original data has: \boxed{\text{non-english question}} paired with: \boxed{\text{english evidence passage}} and an answer. (source: indicgenbench-slides) indicgenbench expands this into: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-en}} and: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-xx}}. we will study the exact distinction in the next step. 5.31.27 why two variants? because the model can be asked to: variant 1 read a target-language question, retrieve evidence from english, and answer in: \boxed{\text{english}}. variant 2 read the same kind of cross-lingual setup but generate the answer in: \boxed{\text{the target language}}. so these test different abilities. 5.31.28 first major metric: chrf for: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} and: \boxed{\text{flores-in}}, the benchmark uses: \boxed{\text{chrf}} or character-level f-score . the deck specifically chooses character-level scoring because token-based metrics such as: \boxed{\text{rouge}} and: \boxed{\text{bleu}} can be unreliable for low-resource languages, where tokenization itself may be problematic. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.29 why character-level evaluation? suppose a tokenizer splits one word into: 5 subword pieces in one language but only: 1 piece in another. then a token-level metric can become sensitive to tokenizer behavior. character-level comparison is less dependent on the model's subword segmentation. so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{tokenization artifact} \downarrow } when moving from token-level to character-level evaluation. the source specifically motivates chrf on this basis. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.30 second metric family: token f1 for: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} and both: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in}} variants, the benchmark uses: \boxed{\text{token-overlap f1}}. this is inherited from the squad-style qa literature. (source: indicgenbench-slides) recall: precision=\frac{tp}{tp+fp} recall=\frac{tp}{tp+fn} and: \boxed{ f1= \frac{2pr}{p+r} }. 5.31.31 so the benchmark has two metric families \boxed{ \text{generation of free text} \rightarrow \text{chrf} } for: \text{summary} and: \text{translation}. while: \boxed{ \text{short-span qa} \rightarrow \text{token f1} } because the answer is expected to overlap a gold answer span. this is an important exam distinction. 5.31.32 numerical chrf intuition the source does not give the underlying chrf formula on this slide, so we should not invent a full implementation equation and pretend it comes from the deck. the safe understanding is: \boxed{ \text{chrf compares character-level n-gram overlap using an f-score formulation} } which reduces sensitivity to subword/tokenization differences. that is the benchmark-design lesson supported by the source. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.33 indicgenbench vs indicxtreme now the distinction should be crystal clear. indicxtreme indicgenbench primarily nlu primarily generation classification-heavy summarization/translation/qa accuracy/f1 chrf/token f1 9 tasks 5 generation tasks tests understanding/transfer tests output generation 20-language contribution scope stated in deck 29-language scope the first five columns are conceptual descriptions grounded in the supplied decks. the language counts come directly from their respective slides. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.34 the important conceptual relationship we should not think: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme vs indicgenbench} = \text{same benchmark twice} } instead: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} = \text{can the model understand?} } and: \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench} = \text{can the model generate?} } a model can be strong at one and weak at the other. 5.31.35 why is that scientifically important? imagine a model with: 90\% classification performance. but when asked to generate an indic summary, its chrf is poor. then: \boxed{ \text{understanding capability} \not\rightarrow \text{generation capability} } this is one of the central gaps that indicgenbench is designed to expose. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.36 numerical exam bank question 1 crosssum-in: 100+100+500=700 per language. for 29 languages: 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300}. question 2 flores-in: 997+1012 = \boxed{2009}. for 29 languages: 2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) question 3 translator wage ratio: 15.90/2.80 \approx \boxed{5.68\times}. rounded: \boxed{5.7\times}. question 4 five generation tasks: \boxed{ 1\text{ crosssum} + 1\text{ flores} + 1\text{ xquad} + 2\text{ xorqa} = 5 } 5.31.37 exam-style conceptual question question: why does indicgenbench translate established benchmarks instead of constructing every dataset from scratch? the deck gives three reasons: \boxed{ \text{multi-way parallel data} } for separating task knowledge from language effects and measuring cross-lingual generalization, \boxed{ \text{lack of clean source data for many low-resource languages} } and: \boxed{ \text{reuse of existing benchmark quality control} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.38 exam-style conceptual question question: why does indicgenbench use chrf for summarization and translation rather than simply bleu/rouge? because the deck argues that token-level metrics can be unreliable for low-resource languages where tokenization itself is a weak link. character-level f-score reduces this dependence. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.39 the deeper lesson indicgenbench is not merely “another multilingual benchmark.” it addresses a different failure mode: \boxed{ \text{a model can understand an indic language without being able to generate it well.} } therefore the evaluation chain becomes: \boxed{ \text{indiccorp} \rightarrow \text{pretraining resources} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} \rightarrow \text{understanding/nlu evaluation} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench} \rightarrow \text{generation evaluation} } together they give a much more complete view of multilingual indic capability. 5.31.40 final mental model remember: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} = \text{understand} } \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench} = \text{generate} } indicgenbench covers: \boxed{29\text{ languages}} \boxed{13\text{ scripts}} \boxed{4\text{ families}} \boxed{3\text{ resource tiers}} and: \boxed{5\text{ generation tasks}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) its construction philosophy is: \boxed{ \text{existing high-quality benchmark} \rightarrow \text{professional human translation} \rightarrow \text{parallel indic evaluation} } rather than rebuilding the entire task ecosystem from scratch. and the first major warning is already visible: \boxed{ \text{even the best models perform substantially worse in indic generation than in english} } across all five generation tasks in the benchmark's reported analysis. (source: indicgenbench-slides)

claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.32 — indicgenbench: task-by-task dataset construction plan node: i11 · chat order #73 now we go through how each indicgenbench task is actually constructed . the four construction ideas we just established are now going to become concrete: \boxed{ \text{reuse} + \text{translate} + \text{preserve parallel structure} + \text{human quality control} } we will go in the exact task order of the supplied deck: \boxed{ \text{crosssum-in} \rightarrow \text{flores-in} \rightarrow \text{xquad-in} \rightarrow \text{xorqa-in} } with xorqa then splitting into two evaluation tasks. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.1 task 1 — crosssum-in start with: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} this is the cross-lingual summarization task. its source is: \boxed{\text{crosssum}} which itself derives from: \boxed{\text{xl-sum}} and contains bbc news articles paired with summaries in another language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the model's task is ultimately: \boxed{ \text{article} \rightarrow \text{compressed summary in target language} } 5.32.2 step 1 — start from english article-summary pairs the benchmark first samples: \boxed{700} english article-summary pairs. the split is: 100\text{ train} 100\text{ dev} 500\text{ test}. therefore: 100+100+500 = \boxed{700}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.3 step 2 — what about languages already covered by crosssum? crosssum already has: \boxed{9} of the target languages. for those 9 languages, the benchmark does not simply translate another 700 english pairs. instead, it resamples: \boxed{100/100/500} from the existing crosssum data. the reason is straightforward: \boxed{ \text{keep every language at the same dataset size} } so one language does not receive many more evaluation examples merely because an existing resource happened to be larger. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.4 step 3 — what about the remaining 20 languages? there are: 29-9 = \boxed{20} remaining target languages. for these, professional human translators translate the english summaries into the target language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the construction is: \boxed{ 9\text{ languages} \rightarrow \text{reuse existing crosssum examples} } while: \boxed{ 20\text{ languages} \rightarrow \text{new human translation} } 5.32.5 total size every language receives: 700 examples. there are: 29 languages. therefore: 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300} total examples. this is explicitly confirmed in the supplied slide. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.6 exam numerical training: 100\times29 = \boxed{2,900}. development: 100\times29 = \boxed{2,900}. test: 500\times29 = \boxed{14,500}. total: 2900+2900+14500 = \boxed{20,300}. 5.32.7 what does a crosssum-in example look like? conceptually: input: long news article output: short summary in hindi the target is not another full article. it is: \boxed{ \text{compressed preservation of the important information} } the deck's example highlights alignment between article information such as “nasa,” “problem,” “launch,” “spacecraft,” and “scheduled” and corresponding content in a hindi summary. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.8 why does the deck emphasize “never via an intermediate english summary”? because a poor multilingual system might conceptually do: \text{article} \rightarrow \text{english summary} \rightarrow \text{target language}. but the benchmark is testing whether the model can directly produce: \boxed{ \text{article} \rightarrow \text{target-language summary} } this matters because an intermediate-language step can hide weaknesses in direct target-language generation. the supplied example specifically emphasizes direct target-language generation rather than an english intermediary. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.9 crosssum-in metric crosssum-in uses: \boxed{\text{chrf}} because it is a free-form generation task and the benchmark wants a character-level metric less dependent on tokenization. (source: indicgenbench-slides) we will later derive why chrf is particularly useful for low-resource languages. 5.32.10 task 2 — flores-in now: \boxed{\text{flores-in}} is the machine-translation task. its source is: \boxed{\text{flores-200}} from the nllb work. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the important feature here is that flores-200 already contains: \boxed{ \text{human-annotated multi-way parallel translation data} } for many languages. therefore indicgenbench follows: \boxed{ \text{reuse where possible} } and: \boxed{ \text{translate where necessary}. } 5.32.11 what does “multi-way parallel” mean? suppose one english sentence is: x. it has translations: y_{\text{hindi}}, y_{\text{tamil}}, y_{\text{punjabi}}, y_{\text{bengali}}, \ldots all corresponding to the same x . so: \boxed{ x \rightarrow \{y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_k\} } where each y_i belongs to a different language. this gives direct comparability across languages. 5.32.12 flores-in source coverage the source slide says flores-200 already covers: \boxed{22\text{ of the 29 target languages}}. therefore: 29-22 = \boxed{7} languages still need new human translations. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.13 flores splits the source dataset has: \boxed{997\text{ dev}} \boxed{1012\text{ devtest}} and: \boxed{992\text{ non-public test}}. the benchmark uses: 997+1012 = \boxed{2009} sentences per language. it does not use the non-public test set in this construction. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.14 total flores-in size there are: 2009 sentences per language and: 29 languages. therefore: 2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261}. the deck reports this as approximately: \boxed{58.2k}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.15 exam calculation check: 2009\times30 = 60,270. subtract one language: 60,270-2,009 = \boxed{58,261}. useful mental-math approach. 5.32.16 important special case: no training split the supplied deck explicitly says: \boxed{ \text{flores-in is the only task with no training split}. } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is important to memorize because the other generation tasks have training/dev/test structures in the benchmark. 5.32.17 what does a flores-in example look like? it is extremely simple: \boxed{ \text{source sentence} \rightarrow \text{target-language sentence} } there is: \text{no question} and: \text{no context passage}. it is sentence-level translation. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.18 why is flores-in especially useful experimentally? suppose english sentence x is translated independently into: 29 target languages. because all outputs correspond to the same source sentence: \boxed{ \text{content is controlled} } while: \boxed{ \text{language changes}. } this makes flores-in particularly useful for comparing generation quality across languages. 5.32.19 task 3 — xquad-in now we move to: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}}. this tests multilingual reading comprehension. its source is: \boxed{\text{xquad}} which itself derives from: \boxed{\text{squad}}. the original structure is: \boxed{ \text{passage} + \text{question} \rightarrow \text{short answer span} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.20 step 1 — reuse existing xquad data the benchmark starts from: \boxed{240\text{ passages}} containing: \boxed{1190\text{ qa pairs}}. these are already human-translated into: \boxed{10\text{ higher-resource languages}} and hindi is the only indic language among them. these are reused as the test component. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.21 step 2 — create train/dev data the benchmark additionally selects: \boxed{20\text{ passages}/100\text{ qa pairs}} from squad's training set, and: \boxed{20\text{ passages}/100\text{ qa pairs}} from squad's development set. thus: 20+20 = \boxed{40\text{ new passages}} and: 100+100 = \boxed{200\text{ new qa pairs}} for the train/dev construction. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.22 total xquad-in source material so overall: 240+20+20 = \boxed{280\text{ passages}} and: 1190+100+100 = \boxed{1390\text{ qa pairs}}. this is exactly what the slide reports. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.23 step 3 — human translation into indic languages all: 280 passages and: 1390 qa pairs are professionally translated into: \boxed{12\text{ indic languages}}. therefore: 280\times12 = \boxed{3360} passage-language instances. and: 1390\times12 = \boxed{16,680} qa-language instances. the deck reports these as approximately: \boxed{3.3k\text{ passages}} and: \boxed{16.6k\text{ qa pairs}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.24 important distinction: passage count vs qa count do not confuse: \boxed{3360} with: \boxed{16,680}. the first counts: \text{passage × language} while the second counts: \text{qa pair × language}. there can be multiple questions per passage. this is a classic exam-data-counting trap. 5.32.25 what makes xquad-in “multilingual”? suppose: \text{passage}=\text{punjabi} \text{question}=\text{punjabi} \text{answer}=\text{punjabi}. then: \boxed{ \text{everything matches in one language} } for that example. the deck emphasizes that this is what “multilingual” means here: the model handles one language at a time, repeated across 12 languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is important because the next xorqa task is deliberately different. 5.32.26 xquad-in versus xorqa-in xquad-in \boxed{ \text{question: target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage: target language} } \boxed{ \text{answer: target language} } everything is within one language. xorqa-in \boxed{ \text{question: target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage: english} } \boxed{ \text{answer: english or target language} } that distinction is crucial. 5.32.27 task 4/5 — xorqa-in now we reach the most conceptually interesting construction. \boxed{\text{xorqa-in}} comes from: \boxed{\text{xor-tydi}}. the original source contains: \boxed{\text{non-english question}} paired with: \boxed{\text{english evidence passage}} and an answer. its purpose already involves cross-lingual retrieval. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.28 initial indic coverage the original xor-tydi source covers two indic languages: \boxed{\text{bengali}} with: 302 examples, and: \boxed{\text{telugu}} with: 237 examples. so total original indic examples: 302+237 = \boxed{539}. this is a useful source-derived numerical calculation. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.29 the problem with pairwise translation suppose there are: 29 target languages. if you independently translated every language pair, you'd face roughly: 29\times28 = 812 directed language pairs. or: \frac{29\times28}{2} = 406 undirected pairs. that becomes a huge translation-routing problem. the source therefore uses a clever pivot. 5.32.30 stage 1 — normalize through english first: \boxed{ \text{bengali/telugu question} \rightarrow \text{english} } professional translators translate the original question into english. now every source question has a common english representation. 5.32.31 stage 2 — fan out from english then: \boxed{ \text{english question} \rightarrow \text{all target languages} } and independently: \boxed{ \text{english answer} \rightarrow \text{all target languages} }. this is far more scalable than pairwise translation among every language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.32 the pivot architecture think of english as a hub: english / / | \ / / | \ hindi tamil telugu bengali ... instead of: hindi ↔ tamil ↔ telugu ↔ bengali ↔ ... the hub-and-spoke architecture dramatically simplifies the translation workflow. 5.32.33 why is this called normalization? because all original questions are first mapped into the same intermediate representation: \boxed{\text{english}} before being expanded outward. so: q_{\text{bengali}} \rightarrow q_{\text{english}} \rightarrow q_{\text{hindi}},q_{\text{tamil}},\ldots and: q_{\text{telugu}} \rightarrow q_{\text{english}} \rightarrow q_{\text{hindi}},q_{\text{tamil}},\ldots this creates a consistent multilingual source for the later benchmark variants. 5.32.34 now the clever part: one dataset becomes two tasks the same stage-2 translations provide: \boxed{\text{question in every target language}} and: \boxed{\text{answer in every target language}}. these are recombined into two different evaluation tasks. 5.32.35 xorqa-in-en in: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-en}} we have: \boxed{ \text{question = target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage = english} } \boxed{ \text{answer = english} } so the model must understand a target-language question and find/produce the relevant answer using english evidence. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.36 xorqa-in-xx in: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-xx}} we have: \boxed{ \text{question = target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage = english} } but: \boxed{ \text{answer = target language} }. so now the model must perform both: \boxed{ \text{cross-lingual comprehension} } and: \boxed{ \text{target-language generation} }. this makes xorqa-in-xx harder in a different way than xorqa-in-en. 5.32.37 why is xorqa-in-xx particularly interesting? consider: \text{telugu question} \rightarrow \text{english evidence} \rightarrow \text{telugu answer}. the model must: interpret telugu; retrieve relevant information from english; map the information back into telugu; generate the answer correctly. so it combines: \boxed{ \text{cross-lingual understanding} + \text{cross-lingual retrieval} + \text{target-language generation} }. the deck explicitly contrasts this with xorqa-in-en, where the answer is generated in english. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.38 compare all three qa designs xquad-in \boxed{ l_q=l_c=l_a } where all three are the same target language. xorqa-in-en \boxed{ l_q\neq l_c,\quad l_a=l_c=\text{english} } xorqa-in-xx \boxed{ l_q=l_a\neq l_c } where l_c is english. this is a very useful symbolic way to memorize the difference. correction: use12xquad-in languages: official repository dataset sizes and a c l2024paperphysicalp4 confirm12. the supplieddeckp16 says11; it conflicts withdeckp11 construction. complete grounded review 5.32.39 coverage across languages the deck says: crosssum-in \boxed{29\text{ languages}} flores-in \boxed{29\text{ languages}} xquad-in \boxed{11\text{ languages}} xorqa-in \boxed{28\text{ languages}} with: \boxed{\text{nepali excluded}} from the latter due to not being translated. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is another example of why benchmark coverage depends partly on the availability of usable source resources. correction: recomputexquad coverage as12/29=41.3793%, not11/29=37.9310%. keep28/29=96.5517%for xorqa. complete grounded review 5.32.41 numerical coverage comparison crosssum/flores: 29/29 = \boxed{100\%} of the target language set in this benchmark. xquad: 11/29 \approx \boxed{37.9\%}. xorqa: 28/29 \approx \boxed{96.6\%}. these percentages are our calculations from the deck's reported language counts. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.42 why are the benchmark tasks not equally broad? because the source datasets are different. crosssum has a route to 29 languages. flores already has broad multilingual coverage. xquad has more constrained existing translation coverage. xor-tydi starts from only certain source-language questions and then expands them. therefore: \boxed{ \text{benchmark coverage is constrained by source-resource structure} } not just by the researchers' desired language count. 5.32.43 complete dataset-construction table task source what is generated languages crosssum-in crosssum / xl-sum target-language summaries 29 flores-in flores-200 target-language translations 29 xquad-in xquad / squad target-language qa 11 xorqa-in-en xor-tydi target-language question + english answer 28 xorqa-in-xx xor-tydi target-language question + target-language answer 28 (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.44 exact numerical bank crosssum-in 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300}. flores-in (997+1012)\times29 =2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261}. xquad-in (240+20+20)\times12 = 280\times12 = \boxed{3,360\text{ passages}}. qa pairs: (1190+100+100)\times12 = 1390\times12 = \boxed{16,680}. original indic xor-tydi 302+237 = \boxed{539} examples. all of these are directly derived from the deck's reported figures. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.45 the deepest construction idea the most interesting thing about indicgenbench is that the researchers are not merely increasing: \boxed{\text{number of languages}} they are trying to control the experimental variables . for example: crosssum same underlying article/task structure, different output languages. flores same source sentence, many target languages. xquad same passage/question structure, translated consistently into target language. xorqa same evidence language, different question/output-language configurations. therefore: \boxed{ \text{language} } can be varied while holding much of the underlying task constant. that is exactly what makes these datasets scientifically useful for cross-lingual comparison. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.46 one final conceptual comparison imagine these two systems. system a \text{english question} \rightarrow \text{english answer}. system b \text{telugu question} \rightarrow \text{english evidence} \rightarrow \text{telugu answer}. system b requires much more than ordinary generation. it requires: \boxed{ \text{language understanding} + \text{cross-lingual information retrieval} + \text{target-language generation} }. this is why xorqa-in-xx is an especially valuable task conceptually. 5.32.47 exam-ready master structure memorize this: \boxed{ \text{crosssum-in} = \text{summarization} } \boxed{ \text{flores-in} = \text{translation} } \boxed{ \text{xquad-in} = \text{same-language qa} } \boxed{ \text{xorqa-in-en} = \text{target-question + english-evidence + english-answer} } \boxed{ \text{xorqa-in-xx} = \text{target-question + english-evidence + target-answer} } and the key language counts are: \boxed{ 29,\ 29,\ 11,\ 28,\ 28 } respectively. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.48 final mental model the construction can be summarized as: \boxed{ \text{existing benchmark} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{reuse existing multilingual data where possible} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{professionally translate missing indic languages} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{preserve parallel correspondence} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{evaluate generation across resource levels} } this is the core engineering philosophy of indicgenbench. and the most important distinction between the tasks is: \boxed{ \text{xquad-in keeps question, context, and answer in the same language} } while: \boxed{ \text{xorqa-in deliberately separates the question language from the evidence language} } and then tests both english and target-language answer generation. claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.33 — indicgenbench: metrics, resource gaps, directionality, and in-context learning plan node: i11 · chat order #74 we now move from how indicgenbench was constructed to: \boxed{ \text{how do we score generation quality, and what do the results reveal?} } this step contains some of the most important insights in the indic material because the benchmark does more than rank models. it exposes why generation quality breaks down for lower-resource indic languages . the major chain is: \boxed{ \text{metric choice} \rightarrow \text{model comparison} \rightarrow \text{resource-tier gap} \rightarrow \text{translation asymmetry} \rightarrow \text{few-shot behavior} \rightarrow \text{tokenizer bottleneck} } 5.33.1 first: why ordinary accuracy is not enough for classification we had: x\rightarrow y so accuracy was natural. but generation looks like: x\rightarrow \hat y where many different outputs can be valid. suppose gold: the mission launched after several delays. model: after being delayed several times, the mission finally launched. the strings are different, but the meaning is very similar. therefore: \boxed{ \text{exact string equality is too strict} } for most generation tasks. indicgenbench therefore uses two major metric families: \boxed{\text{chrf}} for summarization/translation, and: \boxed{\text{token-level f1}} for qa. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.2 chrf — character-level f-score the deck uses: \boxed{\text{chrf}} for: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} and: \boxed{\text{flores-in}}. the important idea is: \boxed{ \text{compare character-level n-gram overlap rather than token overlap} } the deck specifically motivates this because token-level metrics such as bleu and rouge can be unreliable for low-resource languages when tokenization itself is problematic. (source: indicgenbench-slides) correction: word-level bleu/rouge tokenization is not automatically the llm bpetokenizer. the character-metric motivation addresses segmentation reliability; keep inference-tokencost separate. complete grounded review 5.33.3 why character-level evaluation helps suppose the same word is tokenized differently. language a: w\rightarrow[t_1] language b: w\rightarrow[t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4]. a token-level metric now depends partly on the tokenizer. at the character level, we instead compare something closer to: \text{c-a-t} against another string's character sequence. thus: \boxed{ \text{evaluation becomes less tied to subword segmentation} } the deck calls this important because tokenization is itself a weakness for some low-resource languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.4 why not say chrf is “perfect”? we should be careful. the deck says character-level scoring sidesteps the tokenization problem. it does not claim that chrf perfectly captures semantics. two sentences can have high character overlap but different meanings, or low overlap while expressing the same meaning. so the correct lesson is: \boxed{ \text{chrf reduces one important low-resource evaluation problem} } not: \boxed{ \text{chrf completely solves generation evaluation} }. that stronger statement is not supported by the slide. 5.33.5 token-f1 for qa for: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} and: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-en}} \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-xx}}, the benchmark uses squad-style: \boxed{\text{token-overlap f1}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) recall: p=\frac{tp}{tp+fp} r=\frac{tp}{tp+fn} and: \boxed{ f1=\frac{2pr}{p+r} }. 5.33.6 numerical qa example suppose: p=0.8 and: r=0.6. then: f1= \frac{2(0.8)(0.6)}{0.8+0.6} = \frac{0.96}{1.4} = \boxed{0.6857}. so: \boxed{68.57\%}. 5.33.7 why f1 is appropriate for short answers suppose gold answer: [\text{new delhi}] and prediction: [\text{delhi}] the model is partially correct. accuracy would force a binary: 0\text{ or }1. f1 can reflect partial overlap. that makes it much more useful for span-based qa. the exact normalization/tokenization details are not specified on this deck page, so we shouldn't invent them. 5.33.8 now: do bigger models actually do better? the benchmark asks: \boxed{ \text{does indicgenbench distinguish model quality?} } the answer from the deck is: \boxed{\text{yes}} and several patterns emerge. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.9 pattern 1 — larger models within a family generally perform better the deck states: \boxed{ \text{larger models within a family consistently do better} } the reported comparison includes models such as: \text{palm-2-xxs} \text{palm-2-xs} \text{palm-2-s} \text{palm-2-l} and llama variants. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is a classic scaling observation. 5.33.10 why is the family comparison useful? suppose: m_1<m_2<m_3 in model size. if performance consistently follows: p(m_1)<p(m_2)<p(m_3), then the benchmark has some sensitivity to model capability. that doesn't prove size is the only factor, because architecture, training data, and training procedure can also differ. but within one model family, size comparisons become more informative. 5.33.11 palm-2-l the deck reports that: \boxed{\text{palm-2-l wins on 4 of the 5 tasks}} among the listed comparisons. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the largest model in that family is very strong, but notably: \boxed{ \text{not necessarily the winner on all five} }. again: \text{larger} \not\rightarrow \text{automatic universal dominance}. 5.33.12 llama result the slide reports that open-source llama models lag substantially in this benchmark setup. it even notes that: \boxed{ \text{llama-65b underperforms the smallest palm-2-xxs} } in the reported comparisons. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is extremely important. it tells us: \boxed{ \text{parameter count alone does not determine multilingual generation quality} } because a much larger model can still underperform a smaller model from another training family. correction: bloomzwins3/5 among the open source comparisons in table2, not overall against palm. thedeck omits this comparison-group qualification. complete grounded review 5.33.13 bloomz the deck reports: \boxed{\text{bloomz wins 3 of 5 tasks}} among the listed models. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the deck describes bloomz as: \boxed{ \text{instruction-tuned + broad multilingual pretraining} }. so multilingual training and instruction tuning can be particularly valuable for this benchmark. again, this doesn't establish a universal ranking outside the reported benchmark. correction: do not assert everymodel has a measured20+englishgap: the paper table2 supplies english baselines for gpt-4 and palm-2-l, not everyrow. complete grounded review 5.33.14 the biggest result: indic performance trails english the most important sentence on that results slide is: \boxed{ \text{every model, even the best, trails its own english performance by 20+ points.} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is a very strong diagnosis. the benchmark isn't merely showing: \text{different models behave differently}. it is showing: \boxed{ \text{the same model is substantially weaker when generating indic languages than when generating english} }. 5.33.15 numerical illustration suppose a model scores: 85\% on english. if it trails english by 22 points on an indic task: 85-22 = \boxed{63\%}. the source says the gap is 20+ points across the reported models; 22 is just an illustrative example. (source: indicgenbench-slides) correction: resource-tier degradation is a broadtrend, not universal strict h>m>l. paper table3 includes palm-2-l xorqa-in-en57.3high,57.9medium,53.9low andllama-65bcrosssum4.4,4.6,4.7. complete grounded review 5.33.16 now the resource-tier analysis the next question is: is this degradation uniform across all indic languages? no. the deck reports a clear ordering: \boxed{ \text{high resource} > \text{medium resource} > \text{low resource} } across every task . (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is one of the central findings. 5.33.17 what is being measured? for every task, the benchmark groups languages into: \boxed{h=\text{higher}} \boxed{m=\text{medium}} \boxed{l=\text{low}}. then it computes performance by tier. so rather than one number: p_{\text{all}} we look at: \boxed{ p_h,\quad p_m,\quad p_l }. the reported pattern is: p_h>p_m>p_l. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.18 why is this stronger than one overall average? suppose: p_h=70 p_m=60 p_l=40. overall average could still look respectable: \frac{70+60+40}{3} = \boxed{56.7}. but that average hides the fact that the lowest-resource languages are far weaker. this is why resource-tier breakdown is much more revealing. 5.33.19 translation direction changes the story now comes one of the strongest findings in the entire deck. consider: \boxed{\text{flores-in}}. the benchmark evaluates translation in both directions. for palm-2-l: english → target language high: 56.9 low: 41.9. so the drop is: 56.9-41.9 = \boxed{15.0\text{ points}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.20 now reverse the direction target language → english high: 68.2 low: 62.6. drop: 68.2-62.6 = \boxed{5.6\text{ points}}. so: \boxed{ 15.0\text{ points} } vs: \boxed{ 5.6\text{ points} }. that is a huge difference. 5.33.21 calculate the ratio \frac{15.0}{5.6} \approx \boxed{2.68}. so the resource-tier degradation reported for palm-2-l is roughly 2.7 times larger in the: \boxed{ \text{english}\rightarrow\text{target} } direction than in: \boxed{ \text{target}\rightarrow\text{english} }. this ratio is our calculation from the source numbers. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.22 this reveals a major asymmetry the deck's interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{current llms are better at understanding low-resource languages than generating them} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) think about the direction: understanding low-resource language \text{low-resource language} \rightarrow \text{english} the model receives the difficult language and produces english. generating low-resource language \text{english} \rightarrow \text{low-resource language} now the model has to produce target-language text. the second is much more fragile. 5.33.23 why is generation harder? the source reports the empirical asymmetry, but does not give a single definitive mathematical cause. a reasonable interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{understanding requires recognizing patterns} } whereas generation requires: \boxed{ \text{reliably producing those patterns} }. the model may have enough representation to understand some low-resource input but insufficient learned generation statistics to produce fluent target-language output. this explanatory distinction is model reasoning/inference, not a direct formula from the slide. 5.33.24 exam question: directionality suppose: p_{h}^{en\rightarrow indic}=60 p_{l}^{en\rightarrow indic}=40. drop: 20. for reverse direction: p_h^{indic\rightarrow en}=70 p_l^{indic\rightarrow en}=65. drop: 5. then: \boxed{ \text{generation-side resource sensitivity is }4\times\text{ larger} } because: 20/5=4. this is an illustrative exam problem modeled on the directionality finding. correction: shot performance is not universally monotonic: paper table4 givesllama-7bflores11.5one-shot versus11.4five-shot. preserve it as an empirical trend, not a theorem. complete grounded review 5.33.25 now the few-shot question suppose the model receives: 0 examples. that is: \boxed{\text{zero-shot}}. what happens if we give: 1 worked example? the deck reports that: \boxed{ \text{every model family improves monotonically as in-context examples increase} } and the biggest jump is often: \boxed{0\rightarrow1\text{ shot}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.26 the striking example for palm-2-xxs on flores-in: \boxed{0\text{-shot}=0.8} and: \boxed{1\text{-shot}=24.0}. improvement: 24.0-0.8 = \boxed{23.2\text{ points}}. relative increase: \frac{23.2}{0.8}\times100 = \boxed{2900\%}. this enormous percentage is mathematically correct, but because the original score is tiny, the more meaningful source-friendly statement is: \boxed{+23.2\text{ points}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.27 why does one example help so much? the source reports the phenomenon but does not claim a single mechanism. a reasonable interpretation is that one example gives the model: \boxed{ \text{task format} + \text{translation style} + \text{expected output structure} }. so the model does not need to infer the entire task from instructions alone. this is an inference from general in-context learning, not a statement explicitly established as a theorem by the slide. 5.33.28 but “more examples” has a limit the slide title is: \boxed{ \text{more in-context examples help — up to a point} } why does the improvement stop being straightforward? because every example consumes context. and for indic languages: \boxed{ \text{tokenization itself can become the bottleneck} }. that takes us to the tokenizer section. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.29 language-specific exemplars now the benchmark asks: which language should the in-context examples be written in? the reported ordering is: \boxed{ \text{test language} > \text{hindi} > \text{english} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is a very elegant result. 5.33.30 why is the ordering interesting? suppose the test language is punjabi. then the model benefits most from: \boxed{\text{punjabi examples}} then: \boxed{\text{hindi examples}} then: \boxed{\text{english examples}}. the deck says this matches the order of linguistic relatedness to the test language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so: \boxed{ \text{similar-language demonstration} > \text{distant-language demonstration} } in the reported experiments. 5.33.31 especially important for smaller models the deck says: \boxed{ \text{for smaller models, hindi exemplars can come extremely close to, and sometimes beat, test-language exemplars} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this suggests that hindi can function as a useful bridge language in prompting. again, that is a reported empirical finding, not a universal guarantee for every indic language. 5.33.32 numerical example suppose a model scores: 50 with english exemplars, 56 with hindi exemplars, and: 60 with test-language exemplars. then: \boxed{ 60>56>50 } matching the reported ordering. 5.33.33 now the biggest hidden bottleneck: tokenizer fertility this is one of the most important technical concepts in the entire indicgenbench deck. the slide defines: \boxed{ \text{fertility} = \text{average number of subword tokens per word} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this connects directly to everything we learned earlier about tokenization. 5.33.34 example of fertility suppose a language has 100 words. after tokenization, those words become: 500 subword tokens. then: \text{fertility} = \frac{500}{100} = \boxed{5}. so on average: \boxed{5\text{ tokens per word}}. 5.33.35 reported fertility values the deck says: \boxed{\text{english}\approx1} and among indic languages: \boxed{\text{pashto}=4.1} while: \boxed{\text{tibetan}=19.9}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the important consequence is: one tibetan word can consume roughly 20 tokens under the evaluated tokenizer. 5.33.36 why is this not a statement about the language itself? the slide makes this explicit. high fertility is: \boxed{ \text{a tokenizer artifact} } and is not a measure of intrinsic language complexity. so: \boxed{ \text{language is not “hard” because fertility is high} } rather: \boxed{ \text{the chosen tokenizer represents the language inefficiently} }. this distinction is extremely important. 5.33.37 context-window mathematics suppose the model has a context budget: b=1920 tokens. for english: f_e\approx1. suppose an example requires: 100 words. approximate token cost: 100\times1 = 100. now suppose a target language has: f=10. the same 100 words consume approximately: 100\times10 = \boxed{1000} tokens. so the same semantic amount of text consumes: \boxed{10\times} more context. this is a conceptual calculation directly based on the fertility definition. 5.33.38 why does this hurt few-shot prompting? suppose each demonstration has: 200 words. for a language with fertility: f=1, rough estimate: 200\text{ tokens}. five examples: 5\times200 = 1000. easy to fit in: 1920. now fertility: f=8. each example costs: 200\times8 = 1600. even one demonstration consumes most of the budget. so: \boxed{ \text{high fertility} \rightarrow \text{fewer demonstrations fit} }. that is the central mechanism highlighted by the deck. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.39 the actual 1920-token result at: \boxed{1920\text{ tokens}} of context budget: english the deck reports that english still fits: \boxed{5\text{ in-context examples}} for more than: \boxed{80\%} of its test set. oriya and punjabi the deck reports that these high-fertility languages fall to nearly: \boxed{0\%} of test cases being able to fit the required examples by only: \boxed{2-3\text{ examples}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.40 this creates a hidden disadvantage suppose two languages have identical model reasoning capability. language a can fit: 5 examples. language b can fit: 1 example. then even if the model would benefit equally from demonstrations, language b receives less usable prompting support. so: \boxed{ \text{measured performance} = \text{model capability} + \text{context/tokenizer effects} } conceptually. the second equation is a general inference; the source's direct point is that fertility causes some languages to fit fewer worked examples. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.41 why this changes how we interpret low-resource performance earlier we might conclude: low-resource language models perform poorly because they understand the language poorly. the tokenizer analysis adds another layer: \boxed{ \text{they may also receive fewer effective in-context examples} } because their text consumes more tokens. so the gap may contain both: \boxed{\text{representation/understanding difficulty}} and: \boxed{\text{context-budget inefficiency}}. the deck explicitly connects the high-fertility result to the low-resource in-context performance gap. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.42 numerical exam question — fertility a language has: f=4.1. a document contains: 500 words. approximate token cost: 500\times4.1 = \boxed{2050\text{ tokens}}. if the context budget is: 1920, the document alone exceeds the budget under this simplified calculation. this is an illustrative estimate using the source's fertility concept and pashto value; real token counts vary from word to word. 5.33.43 numerical exam question — tibetan suppose: f=19.9 and: 200 words need to be included. approximate token count: 200\times19.9 = \boxed{3980}. so a 1920-token context cannot even hold that 200-word text under this average-based approximation. this illustrates why fertility can become a severe practical bottleneck. 5.33.44 the full causal chain now becomes visible we began with: \boxed{ \text{low-resource language} } then: \downarrow \boxed{ \text{less training data} } then: \boxed{ \text{weaker learned generation} } but there is another path: \boxed{ \text{high tokenizer fertility} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{same content consumes more tokens} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{fewer in-context examples fit} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{less prompting support} } thus the low-resource challenge isn't only a data quantity problem. 5.33.45 another surprising result: fine-tuning vs few-shot the deck compares: \boxed{\text{mt5}} and: \boxed{\text{palm-2}} under fine-tuning and few-shot prompting. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the reported pattern is: qa mt5 performs very strongly because it is purpose-built for short-span generation. crosssum palm-2 performs better on the longer-form generation task. and: \boxed{ \text{palm-2-xs few-shot} \approx \text{or exceeds its fine-tuned performance on qa} } while: \boxed{ \text{fine-tuning remains clearly better for long-form generation} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.46 why is this distinction useful? it tells us: \boxed{ \text{there is no universally best adaptation method} } the task structure matters. for short-span qa: \boxed{\text{few-shot prompting can be surprisingly competitive}} for long-form summarization: \boxed{\text{additional training data is more valuable}} in the reported experiments. 5.33.47 exam-style conceptual question question: why can few-shot prompting beat fine-tuning on some qa tasks but not on long-form summarization? the reported benchmark suggests that short-span qa can be performed very effectively through in-context examples, while long-form generation benefits more strongly from task-specific fine-tuning. the result is task-dependent rather than a universal rule. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.48 master comparison of the major findings phenomenon reported finding larger model within family generally better palm-2-l wins 4/5 listed tasks bloomz wins 3/5 llama-65b can underperform smaller palm-2 model indic vs english every model trails english by 20+ points resource tiers high > medium > low across every task en → low-resource large drop low-resource → en much smaller drop in-context examples more helps, especially 0→1 example language test language > hindi > english tokenizer fertility can strongly restrict context usage qa adaptation few-shot can match/beat fine-tuning long-form generation fine-tuning remains stronger all of these are directly grounded in the supplied indicgenbench results slides. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.49 the deepest takeaway the benchmark reveals that poor indic generation is not one single problem . there are multiple interacting factors: \boxed{ \text{resource availability} } + \boxed{ \text{model/training quality} } + \boxed{ \text{generation direction} } + \boxed{ \text{tokenizer fertility} } + \boxed{ \text{available in-context demonstrations} } all affect observed performance. that is why a simple statement such as: “the model is bad at low-resource languages” is too coarse. the deck gives us a more detailed diagnosis. 5.33.50 the most important chain for the exam remember this sequence: \boxed{ \text{low-resource language} \rightarrow \text{high fertility} \rightarrow \text{more tokens per word} \rightarrow \text{context budget fills faster} \rightarrow \text{fewer demonstrations fit} \rightarrow \text{lower few-shot support} } and independently: \boxed{ \text{low-resource training} \rightarrow \text{weaker generation} } together: \boxed{ \text{data scarcity + generation difficulty + tokenizer inefficiency} } help explain the benchmark's observed low-resource gap. 5.33.51 final numerical bank 1. crosssum size 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300}. 2. flores size 2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261}. 3. palm-2-l en→target low-resource drop 56.9-41.9 = \boxed{15.0}. 4. palm-2-l target→english low-resource drop 68.2-62.6 = \boxed{5.6}. 5. difference between the drops 15.0-5.6 = \boxed{9.4\text{ points}}. 6. 0→1 shot flores improvement 24.0-0.8 = \boxed{23.2\text{ points}}. 7. pashto fertility \boxed{4.1\text{ tokens/word}} so 500 words approximately: 500(4.1) = \boxed{2050\text{ tokens}}. 8. tibetan fertility 200(19.9) = \boxed{3980\text{ tokens}}. all source values used in these calculations are from the indicgenbench deck; the word-count examples are illustrative. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.52 final mental model the complete indicgenbench evaluation story is now: \boxed{ \text{generation quality} } is measured with metrics adapted to low-resource conditions: \boxed{ \text{chrf for translation/summarization} } and: \boxed{ \text{token-f1 for qa} }. then the benchmark reveals: \boxed{ \text{larger models usually improve} } but: \boxed{ \text{every model still has a large indic-vs-english gap} }. then: \boxed{ \text{high resource}>\text{medium}>\text{low} } and: \boxed{ \text{understanding low-resource language} > \text{generating low-resource language} } in the reported flores direction comparison. (source: indicgenbench-slides) finally: \boxed{ \text{few-shot examples help} } but: \boxed{ \text{tokenizer fertility controls how many examples can physically fit} }. that last connection is particularly important because it links tokenization , which we studied at the beginning of the course, directly to multilingual benchmark performance .

(source: indicgenbench-slides) so if punjabi is the target: \boxed{ \text{punjabi demonstrations} > \text{hindi demonstrations} > \text{english demonstrations} } in the reported setup. 5.34.4 why would hindi beat english? the benchmark's empirical interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{closer linguistic relationship} \rightarrow \text{more useful demonstrations} } hindi is itself an indic language and can therefore provide a more relevant demonstration distribution than english for many indic targets. this is a source-supported interpretation of the reported ordering. (source: indicgenbench-slides) we should not turn it into: hindi is equally close to every indic language. that is not what the source establishes. 5.34.5 why is this surprising? you might initially assume: \boxed{ \text{english is best} } because english is the dominant training/evaluation language for many multilingual benchmarks. but the experiment suggests: \boxed{ \text{related-language examples can be more useful than english examples} } for indic generation. this is an important shift in how we think about multilingual prompting. 5.34.6 small-model effect the deck gives an especially interesting observation: \boxed{ \text{for smaller models, hindi exemplars can come very close to, and sometimes exceed, target-language exemplars} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) that suggests that a strong bridge language can be particularly valuable when the model has less capacity. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{small model} + \text{related-language demonstrations} \rightarrow \text{stronger task induction} } in the reported experiments. 5.34.7 think of the exemplar as a compressed task description an exemplar communicates several things at once: \boxed{ \text{input structure} + \text{output structure} + \text{expected linguistic style} + \text{task mapping} } suppose the task is qa. a hindi example can simultaneously teach: \text{how the question is phrased in an indic language} and: \text{what the answer format looks like}. an english example may communicate the task just fine, but it may be less useful for target-language generation. this latter explanation is a model-level interpretation rather than a separately quantified claim in the source. 5.34.8 numerical example suppose a model obtains: \boxed{45} with english exemplars, \boxed{55} with hindi exemplars, and: \boxed{60} with target-language exemplars. then the ordering is: 60>55>45. english → hindi improvement: 55-45 = \boxed{10\text{ points}}. hindi → target-language improvement: 60-55 = \boxed{5\text{ points}}. these numbers are illustrative; the source provides the qualitative ordering rather than these hypothetical values. 5.34.9 now ask: is prompting always better than fine-tuning? no. the deck directly compares: \boxed{\text{fine-tuning}} with: \boxed{\text{few-shot prompting}}. the interesting result is task dependent . (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.10 qa behaves differently from long-form generation the deck says: \boxed{ \text{mt5 beats palm-2 on qa tasks even when fine-tuned} } while: \boxed{ \text{palm-2 wins on longer-form crosssum-in} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so model architecture and task type matter. 5.34.11 few-shot vs fine-tuning on qa for qa, the deck reports that: \boxed{ \text{few-shot prompting on palm-2-xs can match or beat fine-tuning it} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is an important result. it means: \boxed{ \text{training the model further is not always necessary for strong task performance} } at least for the reported qa settings. 5.34.12 but long-form generation is different for: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} the deck says: \boxed{ \text{fine-tuning still wins outright} } and calls long-form generation the setting where extra training data clearly pays off. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so we now have: \boxed{ \text{short-span qa} \rightarrow \text{few-shot can be highly competitive} } versus: \boxed{ \text{long-form generation} \rightarrow \text{fine-tuning remains very valuable} }. 5.34.13 why is this plausible? qa usually requires a relatively short output: \boxed{ \text{one span / short answer} } while summarization requires: \boxed{ \text{long, coherent generation} }. a few examples can strongly specify a short-answer format. long-form generation requires learning more extensive target-language generation behavior. this is a natural explanation, but the source itself reports the empirical distinction rather than proving this causal mechanism. 5.34.14 numerical example suppose: qa fine-tuned model: 70 few-shot model: 72. then few-shot wins by: \boxed{2\text{ points}}. summarization fine-tuned: 60 few-shot: 48. then: \boxed{12\text{-point advantage for fine-tuning}}. these are illustrative examples capturing the source's reported pattern, not its exact table values. 5.34.15 now we reach the biggest specialization experiment the next question is: what if we simply train a model mostly on hindi? maybe hindi is a useful bridge language, so perhaps a hindi-specialized model will generalize extremely well across indic languages. to test this, the deck examines: \boxed{\text{airavata}}. 5.34.16 what is airavata in this experiment? the deck says airavata is fine-tuned almost exclusively on: \boxed{\text{hindi + english}} (source: indicgenbench-slides) so its training emphasis is highly concentrated compared with broad multilingual systems such as bloomz. 5.34.17 first result: hindi improves the deck says airavata: \boxed{ \text{clearly beats llama on hindi} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is exactly what we might expect. if we specialize the model toward hindi: \text{hindi performance} \uparrow. so specialization can work very well for the language it was trained on . 5.34.18 the surprising part: other indic languages now test airavata on: \boxed{\text{bengali}} \boxed{\text{punjabi}} \boxed{\text{assamese}} \boxed{\text{manipuri}} \boxed{\text{santali}}. the deck says airavata performs much worse than bloomz on these other indic languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) therefore: \boxed{ \text{hindi specialization} \not\rightarrow \text{broad indic transfer} } 5.34.19 this is an extremely important distinction earlier we learned: \boxed{ \text{hindi exemplars can be useful} } now we learn: \boxed{ \text{hindi-only specialization can fail to transfer broadly} } these are not contradictory . why? because prompting and training are fundamentally different interventions. 5.34.20 prompting with hindi the model remains broadly multilingual. you are adding: \boxed{ \text{hindi examples at inference time} } to help guide behavior. so the underlying model may retain broad language representations. 5.34.21 fine-tuning heavily on hindi now the model parameters are changed toward: \boxed{ p_\theta(\text{hindi behavior}) } and the training distribution is concentrated. this can improve hindi while failing to preserve or develop equally strong behavior for other languages. the source's airavata result demonstrates this experimentally. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.22 think of the difference as “bridge” vs “destination” hindi prompting can function as a: \boxed{\text{bridge}} between a general model and another indic language. but hindi-only model training can create: \boxed{\text{specialization}} rather than universal indic competence. so: \boxed{ \text{bridge language} \neq \text{universal replacement language} } this is an important conceptual lesson. 5.34.23 numerical specialization example suppose: airavata hindi: 85 bengali: 50 punjabi: 48 bloomz hindi: 80 bengali: 65 punjabi: 63. airavata wins hindi: 85>80 but loses bengali: 50<65 and punjabi: 48<63. this is an illustrative representation of the qualitative pattern in the deck, not the source's exact numbers. 5.34.24 why does broad multilingual training help here? the deck's comparison suggests that: \boxed{ \text{broad language coverage} } can be more useful for cross-indic transfer than: \boxed{ \text{extreme specialization in one indic language} }. the model still needs some specialization to perform well, but narrowing the training distribution too aggressively can hurt transfer. this conclusion is an interpretation grounded in the airavata/bloomz comparison. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.25 connect this to the earlier “hindi exemplar” result now we can build a very useful framework. strategy a — english exemplars \text{general multilingual model} + \text{english examples} strategy b — hindi exemplars \text{general multilingual model} + \text{hindi examples} strategy c — hindi-specialized model \text{hindi-heavy fine-tuning} the source results indicate: \boxed{ b>a } for the reported few-shot prompting comparison, but: \boxed{ c\text{ does not generalize broadly to other indic languages} }. that is an extremely useful conceptual distinction. 5.34.26 the mathematical intuition prompting modifies the conditioning context : p_\theta(y\mid x) becomes: \boxed{ p_\theta(y\mid x,e) } where e is the set of exemplars. the model parameters: \theta stay fixed. fine-tuning instead changes: \boxed{ \theta \rightarrow \theta' } by optimizing a training objective over a particular distribution. so: \boxed{ \text{prompting changes context} } while: \boxed{ \text{fine-tuning changes parameters} }. this is standard ml notation used here to clarify the source's experimental distinction. 5.34.27 why specialization can hurt transfer imagine a model has learned representations shared across: l_1,l_2,l_3,\ldots,l_{29}. now training overwhelmingly on l_1 changes the optimization pressure. the model is pushed toward: \boxed{ \text{perform extremely well on }l_1 } rather than: \boxed{ \text{maintain broad multilingual generalization} }. this can lead to specialization without broad transfer. the source gives empirical evidence of exactly this pattern with airavata. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.28 an important connection to catastrophic forgetting we should be careful here. the supplied deck does not explicitly analyze airavata in terms of catastrophic forgetting , so we should not claim that this experiment proves catastrophic forgetting. a reasonable interpretation is that highly concentrated fine-tuning can reduce transfer to other languages, but the source's supported conclusion is simply: \boxed{ \text{single-language specialization does not transfer effectively to the rest} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.29 resource-tier connection now connect this to everything from steps 5.29 and 5.33. we already found: \boxed{ \text{high resource} > \text{medium} > \text{low} } in generation performance. (source: indicgenbench-slides) and now: \boxed{ \text{hindi specialization} \not\rightarrow \text{all indic languages} }. therefore, solving the low-resource problem is not as simple as: “choose one major indic language and train heavily on it.” we need: \boxed{ \text{broad language coverage} } and: \boxed{ \text{transfer mechanisms} } that preserve performance across many languages. 5.34.30 the role of hindi is therefore nuanced hindi appears in two different ways. as an inference-time exemplar \boxed{ \text{useful bridge} } because hindi demonstrations are often better than english demonstrations. as a dominant training language \boxed{ \text{insufficient as a universal substitute} } because a hindi-heavy model does not generalize well to every other indic language. these two findings together are more informative than either one alone. 5.34.31 exam-style question question: does the result “hindi exemplars outperform english exemplars” imply that a hindi-specialized llm should outperform a broad multilingual llm on all indic languages? \boxed{\text{no.}} the first result concerns in-context prompting , while the second experiment concerns parameter specialization through hindi/english fine-tuning . the deck reports that airavata performs better on hindi but substantially worse than bloomz on several other indic languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) scenario 2 — short qa task few-shot prompting may be highly competitive with fine-tuning. (source: indicgenbench-slides) scenario 3 — long-form summarization fine-tuning is more valuable in the reported experiments. (source: indicgenbench-slides) scenario 4 — build a model for all indic languages do not simply specialize on hindi. the airavata result shows that broad indic transfer can suffer. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.35 connect to tokenizer fertility there is one more important interaction. suppose target-language demonstrations are best. but the target language has very high fertility. then: \boxed{ \text{best exemplar language} } may still be constrained by: \boxed{ \text{how many examples fit in the context window} }. so the practical hierarchy becomes: \boxed{ \text{choose useful language for exemplars} } then: \boxed{ \text{fit as many useful examples as the tokenizer allows} }. that connects step 5.34 directly to step 5.33. 5.34.36 full conceptual chain we can now put everything together: \boxed{ \text{target-language exemplars} > \text{hindi exemplars} > \text{english exemplars} } but: \boxed{ \text{hindi-heavy specialization} \not\rightarrow \text{strong all-indic transfer} } and: \boxed{ \text{few-shot} \approx/\!> \text{fine-tuning for some qa settings} } but: \boxed{ \text{fine-tuning} > \text{few-shot for long-form generation} } in the reported experiments. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.37 the deeper lesson there are three different notions of “transfer”: in-context transfer \boxed{ \text{examples in another language help the model perform the task} } cross-lingual model transfer \boxed{ \text{multilingual pretraining enables one language's knowledge to support another} } parameter specialization \boxed{ \text{fine-tuning one language changes the model itself} } these should not be conflated. hindi can be an excellent: \boxed{\text{prompting bridge}} without being an adequate: \boxed{\text{universal training substitute}} for the entire indic language family. that distinction is one of the most useful conceptual conclusions from this section. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.38 exam master sheet \boxed{ \text{prompting order} = \text{test language} > \text{hindi} > \text{english} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) \boxed{ \text{qa} \rightarrow \text{few-shot can match/beat fine-tuning} } \boxed{ \text{crosssum long-form} \rightarrow \text{fine-tuning wins} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) \boxed{ \text{airavata} = \text{hindi/english specialization} } and: \boxed{ \text{airavata strong on hindi} } but: \boxed{ \text{poor transfer to other indic languages relative to bloomz} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.34.39 final mental model think of the three strategies as: \boxed{ \text{prompt with hindi} } = borrow a bridge at inference time versus: \boxed{ \text{train mostly on hindi} } = specialize the parameters the first can improve cross-lingual prompting performance. the second can improve the target training language but does not guarantee broad transfer. therefore: \boxed{ \text{related-language prompting} \neq \text{single-language specialization} } and that distinction is crucial for understanding multilingual llm behavior.
