claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.35 — indicgenbench: qualitative failure analysis plan node: i11 · chat order #76 we now move from: \boxed{\text{“how badly does the model perform?”}} to the more important diagnostic question: \boxed{\text{“what exactly goes wrong?”}} the indicgenbench authors manually inspected model outputs to understand the failure modes behind the quantitative gaps. the supplied deck focuses on three major failure patterns: \boxed{\text{hallucination}} \boxed{\text{language bleeding}} \boxed{\text{polysemy / meaning-selection errors + missing information}} (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.1 why qualitative analysis is necessary suppose a model gets: \text{chrf}=40. that tells us the output is imperfect. but it does not tell us why . the model could be failing because of: \text{wrong facts} or: \text{wrong language} or: \text{wrong word meaning} or: \text{missing information}. so: \boxed{ \text{quantitative score} + \text{qualitative inspection} } gives a more useful diagnosis. 5.35.2 how did the authors perform the qualitative analysis? the deck says the authors manually reviewed: \boxed{20} predictions from: \boxed{\text{palm-2-l}} for each of: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} and: \boxed{\text{flores-in}} across: \boxed{5\text{ languages}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the analysis examines actual outputs rather than only aggregate benchmark scores. 5.35.3 numerical interpretation of the sample size for one task: 20\text{ predictions/language} \times 5\text{ languages} = \boxed{100} manually reviewed predictions. for both tasks: 100\times2 = \boxed{200}. so the qualitative inspection covers: \boxed{200\text{ predictions}} under this reading of the deck's sampling description. this is a derived calculation; the slide states the per-task/per-language counts rather than explicitly writing “200.” 5.35.4 failure mode 1 — hallucination the first major failure is: \boxed{\text{hallucination}} the deck says that in cross-lingual summarization, the model regularly invents details that are absent from the source article . (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is particularly serious for summarization. 5.35.5 what should a summary do? suppose source document d contains facts: f(d)=\{f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_n\}. a faithful summary should primarily compress information already supported by d : \boxed{ s\approx \text{compressed representation of }d } it should not introduce an unsupported: f_{n+1}\notin d. the source doesn't provide this mathematical formulation; it is a conceptual way to describe the failure. 5.35.6 example of hallucination imagine the source article says: “the spacecraft was scheduled to launch next month.” a bad summary might say: “the spacecraft successfully launched last week.” the second statement introduces at least two unsupported changes: \text{scheduled} \rightarrow \text{successful} and: \text{next month} \rightarrow \text{last week}. the model has generated a plausible sentence that is not faithful to the source. that is exactly the kind of issue the qualitative analysis is intended to uncover. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.7 why is hallucination especially problematic in low-resource generation? the benchmark already showed: \boxed{ \text{indic generation} < \text{english generation} } and: \boxed{ \text{low-resource} < \text{medium} < \text{high} }. hallucination gives us a concrete mechanism behind part of that poor generation quality. a score decrease is now connected to: \boxed{ \text{failure to preserve source-grounded facts} }. 5.35.8 hallucination vs ordinary wording difference do not confuse: \boxed{\text{paraphrasing}} with: \boxed{\text{hallucination}}. suppose source: “the mission was delayed twice.” valid paraphrase: “the launch was postponed on two occasions.” same factual content. but: “the mission was delayed five times.” changes the factual content. so: \boxed{ \text{surface change} \neq \text{factual error} } and qualitative analysis is needed to distinguish them. 5.35.9 exam question question: why can a generation metric alone fail to fully diagnose hallucination? because a numerical similarity score tells us how similar the generated output is to the reference under that metric, but qualitative inspection is needed to determine whether the model introduced unsupported facts that were not in the source. the indicgenbench authors explicitly use manual analysis to expose such errors. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.10 failure mode 2 — language bleeding now comes a very interesting multilingual failure: \boxed{\text{language bleeding}} the deck focuses on: \boxed{\text{awadhi}} \boxed{\text{haryanvi}} \boxed{\text{chhattisgarhi}} which are related to hindi and share its: \boxed{\text{devanagari script}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) when translating into these languages, the model frequently: \boxed{\text{mixes in hindi words}} and produces: \boxed{\text{incorrectly inflected verb forms}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.11 what does language bleeding mean? suppose the requested output language is: l_t=\text{awadhi}. but the model generates: \text{awadhi} + \text{hindi} instead of pure awadhi. so: \boxed{ p(\text{target-language token}) } is being contaminated by a closely related language's patterns. this is a conceptual interpretation of the observed behavior. 5.35.12 why are related languages especially vulnerable? because they may share: \boxed{\text{script}} and: \boxed{\text{linguistic structure}} but still have different: \boxed{\text{vocabulary}} and: \boxed{\text{morphology}} and: \boxed{\text{inflection}} rules. so the model may learn: “this input belongs to a hindi-like region of representation space.” but fail to maintain the precise target-language boundary. the source explicitly identifies the shared-devanagari/related-language setting and the resulting hindi mixing. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.13 important distinction: related language ≠ same language consider: \boxed{ \text{hindi} \neq \text{awadhi} } even if: \text{related} and: \text{same script}. thus: \boxed{ \text{shared script can help transfer} } but can also create: \boxed{ \text{cross-language contamination} }. this is a very useful multilingual-model insight. 5.35.14 language bleeding and tokenizer effects are different problems do not mix these up. tokenizer problem \text{language} \rightarrow \text{too many subword tokens} this affects: \boxed{\text{context efficiency}}. language bleeding \text{target language} \rightarrow \text{wrong related-language words/forms} this affects: \boxed{\text{generation correctness}}. they can coexist, but they are different failure mechanisms. 5.35.15 example of incorrect morphology suppose the target language requires: \text{verb form }v_t. the model instead generates: v_h following hindi morphology. then even if: \text{semantic meaning} is roughly correct, the generated language is still wrong. so: \boxed{ \text{semantic adequacy} \neq \text{language correctness} }. this is particularly important when evaluating generation in closely related languages. 5.35.16 failure mode 3 — polysemy the third failure is: \boxed{\text{polysemy / word-sense selection}} a single source word can have multiple meanings depending on context. the deck gives a concrete example involving: \boxed{\text{“hearing”}} which can refer to a: \text{court hearing} or: \text{listening}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.17 what went wrong? in the konkani example, the same english word appears in two different senses. the model chooses the: \boxed{\text{“listening”}} sense both times. but the first occurrence refers to: \boxed{\text{a court hearing}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the model failed to use context to disambiguate the word. 5.35.18 why is this important for machine translation? machine translation is not: \boxed{ \text{word} \rightarrow \text{fixed dictionary translation} } it should be: \boxed{ \text{word + context} \rightarrow \text{appropriate target meaning} }. this is the essence of polysemy. the same source word: w can represent: m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_k. the model must estimate: \boxed{ p(m_i\mid w,\text{context}) } rather than always choosing the same m_i . that equation is general nlp reasoning, not a source-provided formula. 5.35.19 numerical polysemy example suppose a word has two possible senses: p(m_1\mid context)=0.8 p(m_2\mid context)=0.2. correct interpretation: \boxed{m_1}. but if the model uses a context-insensitive prior: p(m_1)=0.4, p(m_2)=0.6, it may choose: \boxed{m_2} incorrectly. again, this is an illustrative mathematical explanation, not a reported model probability. 5.35.20 failure mode 4 — missing information the same qualitative-analysis slide identifies another issue: \boxed{ \text{information omission} } the deck gives an assamese example where: \boxed{\text{“to shop”}} is simply absent from the generated translation. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.21 what does omission mean mathematically? suppose source information contains: f=\{f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4\}. a complete translation should preserve all relevant information. if the model produces: \hat f=\{f_1,f_2,f_4\}, then: \boxed{f_3} has disappeared. this is different from hallucination. hallucination \boxed{ \hat f=f+\{f_{\text{false}}\} } omission \boxed{ \hat f\subset f } this distinction is extremely useful. 5.35.22 four-way failure taxonomy we can now organize the qualitative results: hallucination \boxed{ \text{adds unsupported information} } language bleeding \boxed{ \text{mixes target language with a related language} } polysemy error \boxed{ \text{chooses the wrong sense of an ambiguous word} } omission \boxed{ \text{drops information from the source} } all four are explicitly represented in the final qualitative-analysis slides. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.23 why these four failures are connected notice that these are not random errors. they correspond to different requirements of generation: \boxed{ \text{faithfulness} } requires avoiding hallucination. \boxed{ \text{target-language control} } requires avoiding language bleeding. \boxed{ \text{contextual semantic understanding} } requires correct polysemy resolution. \boxed{ \text{information preservation} } requires avoiding omission. so a good translation requires all four simultaneously. 5.35.24 connect to the quantitative results earlier we observed: \boxed{ \text{high resource} > \text{medium} > \text{low} } and: \boxed{ \text{english generation} > \text{indic generation} }. qualitative analysis now tells us what some of those failures look like in practice: \boxed{ \text{wrong facts} + \text{wrong language} + \text{wrong sense} + \text{missing content} }. so: \boxed{ \text{aggregate score} \rightarrow \text{diagnostic failure modes} } is the important methodological connection. 5.35.25 why related-language transfer is a double-edged sword earlier: \boxed{ \text{hindi exemplars} > \text{english exemplars} } for many target languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) but now: \boxed{ \text{hindi} \rightarrow \text{awadhi/haryanvi/chhattisgarhi} } can cause hindi to bleed into the target output. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so linguistic similarity has two sides: \boxed{ \text{similarity} \rightarrow \text{better transfer} } but also: \boxed{ \text{similarity} \rightarrow \text{greater risk of confusion} }. that is a very important research insight. 5.35.26 numerical conceptual model of this tradeoff suppose linguistic relatedness gives: +10 points of transfer benefit. but language confusion causes: -4 points of bleeding-related degradation. then net: 10-4 = \boxed{+6}. this is purely an illustrative decomposition. the source does not provide separate numeric contributions for language bleeding. the key idea is that relatedness can be both: \boxed{\text{an advantage}} and: \boxed{\text{a source of interference}}. 5.35.27 connect hallucination with summarization crosssum-in is: \boxed{ \text{long source} \rightarrow \text{short target output} }. that compression creates a difficult requirement: \boxed{ \text{remove redundancy without inventing facts} }. the qualitative result shows that the model can fail specifically on the second requirement. so summarization quality is not just: \text{shorter text}. it is: \boxed{ \text{compression} + \text{faithfulness} }. 5.35.28 connect polysemy to cross-lingual translation in machine translation: \text{source word} \rightarrow \text{target word} is insufficient. the actual process is closer to: \boxed{ \text{source word} + \text{sentence context} + \text{discourse context} \rightarrow \text{target meaning} }. the konkani “hearing” example demonstrates a failure when context isn't used correctly to choose between senses. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.29 connect omission to information preservation for translation, a good system should preserve: \boxed{ \text{who} + \text{what} + \text{when} + \text{where} + \text{relevant action} }. if an important action such as: \boxed{\text{“to shop”}} disappears, the output may sound fluent while still being incomplete. that's an especially important lesson: \boxed{ \text{fluency} \neq \text{faithfulness}. } the assamese example in the deck demonstrates exactly this point. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.30 the qualitative-analysis matrix you can organize the failures like this: failure what model does what should happen hallucination adds unsupported fact preserve source facts language bleeding uses hindi in another target language stay in requested language polysemy picks wrong word sense use contextual sense omission drops source information preserve relevant content (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.31 exam-style scenario suppose the source says: “the court scheduled a hearing for monday.” model translation interprets “hearing” as “listening.” classification: \boxed{\text{polysemy error}} not hallucination. suppose instead the model writes: “the court scheduled a hearing for monday and the judge ordered five arrests.” when the source says nothing about arrests. classification: \boxed{\text{hallucination}}. suppose: “the boy went to the shop and bought food.” becomes: “the boy went to the shop.” classification: \boxed{\text{omission}}. suppose the target is awadhi but half the generated words are hindi. classification: \boxed{\text{language bleeding}}. these distinctions are directly grounded in the failure categories shown by the deck. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.32 why this matters for model improvement different errors require different interventions. hallucination potential direction: \boxed{ \text{better source grounding / factuality control} } language bleeding potential direction: \boxed{ \text{better target-language conditioning / language-specific training} } polysemy potential direction: \boxed{ \text{better contextual semantic modeling} } omission potential direction: \boxed{ \text{better coverage/content preservation} } these are general remediation ideas. the supplied deck identifies the failure modes but does not prescribe a complete solution for each, so these improvement directions should be treated as model-level inference rather than source claims. 5.35.33 final section: licensing the deck closes with a practical but important issue: \boxed{ \text{dataset licensing} }. because indicgenbench builds on existing datasets, it inherits their licensing constraints. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the reported licenses are: \boxed{ \text{xquad-in, flores-in} \rightarrow \text{cc by-sa 4.0} } \boxed{ \text{crosssum-in} \rightarrow \text{cc by-nc-sa 4.0} } \boxed{ \text{xorqa-in} \rightarrow \text{mit} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.34 why does source lineage affect licensing? because: \boxed{ \text{new benchmark} } doesn't necessarily mean: \boxed{ \text{new legal status}. } if a benchmark extends: \text{dataset a}, its derived data may inherit constraints from dataset a. so: \boxed{ \text{technical lineage} \rightarrow \text{licensing lineage} }. the deck explicitly calls this another consequence of the translation-based approach. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.35 why should engineers care? suppose you build: \text{new multilingual dataset} from: \text{existing benchmark}. even if: \text{your annotations are new}, you still need to check: \boxed{ \text{license of original data} }. a dataset being publicly available does not automatically mean unrestricted commercial or derivative use. the exact legal obligations depend on the license. the deck's point is specifically that benchmark lineage determines these constraints. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.36 complete indicgenbench story we can now connect the whole benchmark from beginning to end. step 1 why build it? \boxed{ \text{indic generation quality was insufficiently measured} } step 2 how? \boxed{ 29\text{ languages} + 5\text{ generation tasks} } step 3 how construct data? \boxed{ \text{existing benchmarks} + \text{professional translation} } step 4 how score? \boxed{ \text{chrf} + \text{token-f1} } step 5 what happens quantitatively? \boxed{ \text{high}> \text{medium}> \text{low} } and: \boxed{ \text{indic generation}<\text{english generation} } step 6 what actually goes wrong? \boxed{ \text{hallucination} + \text{language bleeding} + \text{polysemy errors} + \text{omissions} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.37 the deepest takeaway the most important lesson from the qualitative analysis is: \boxed{ \text{a multilingual model can produce fluent-looking text and still fail in several fundamentally different ways.} } it can: \boxed{ \text{invent facts} } while sounding fluent. it can: \boxed{ \text{mix languages} } while remaining understandable. it can: \boxed{ \text{choose the wrong meaning} } while producing grammatical text. and it can: \boxed{ \text{omit important source information} } while generating a concise output. therefore: \boxed{ \text{good generation} \neq \text{fluency alone} } a robust multilingual generator needs: \boxed{ \text{faithfulness} + \text{language fidelity} + \text{semantic correctness} + \text{information preservation} }. that is the most important conclusion from the final indicgenbench slides. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.38 final exam bank q1 a model inserts facts absent from the source. \boxed{\text{hallucination}} q2 a model translates into awadhi but repeatedly inserts hindi words. \boxed{\text{language bleeding}} q3 “hearing” is translated as “listening” even when the context indicates a court proceeding. \boxed{\text{polysemy / sense-selection error}} q4 the source says “to shop,” but the translation omits that action. \boxed{\text{information omission}} q5 why inspect outputs manually? \boxed{ \text{aggregate metrics tell you that performance is poor; qualitative analysis tells you what kind of errors produced the poor performance.} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.35.39 course-level conclusion of the indic benchmark section we have now completed the major indic benchmark story: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} } measures multilingual understanding/nlu . \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench} } measures multilingual generation . together: \boxed{ \text{understand} + \text{generate} } give a much broader picture of indic-language llm capability. and both reveal the same fundamental reality: \boxed{ \text{language-resource imbalance remains a major obstacle} } even when multilingual or indic-focused models become substantially stronger. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.3 the key observation for causal decoding: \boxed{ k_i,v_i } for an old token do not change merely because a new token arrived. so why recompute them? we can calculate: k_i=x_iw_k and: v_i=x_iw_v once. then store them. that is the: \boxed{\text{kv cache}}. 5.36.4 kv cache idea at generation step t : \boxed{ k_{\le t},v_{\le t} } are stored. when token t+1 arrives, we calculate only its new: k_{t+1} and: v_{t+1}, then append them to the cache. so: k_{\text{cache}} \leftarrow [k_{\text{cache}};k_{t+1}] and: v_{\text{cache}} \leftarrow [v_{\text{cache}};v_{t+1}]. the book explicitly describes the cache as being maintained independently at each layer and attention head. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.5 why this speeds up generation without kv caching: \boxed{ \text{recompute old k/v every step} } with caching: \boxed{ \text{compute old k/v once, reuse thereafter} } so the repeated historical projection work disappears. the book gives an actual gpt-2 experiment: \text{100 generated tokens} without cache: \boxed{30.9818\text{ s}} with cache: \boxed{6.1630\text{ s}}. reported speedup: \frac{30.9818}{6.1630} \approx \boxed{5.03\times}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.6 exam numerical if an uncached implementation requires: 25\text{ s} and cached inference requires: 5\text{ s}, then: \text{speedup} = \frac{25}{5} = \boxed{5\times}. percentage time reduction: \frac{25-5}{25}\times100 = \boxed{80\%}. 5.36.7 but there is a catch caching saves: \boxed{\text{computation}} but consumes: \boxed{\text{memory}}. the book explicitly calls this the: \boxed{\text{“dark side” of the kv cache}}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.8 where does the memory come from? for each past token we store: \boxed{k} and: \boxed{v}. if the model has: l layers, batch size b , sequence length s , n heads, head dimension h , then for standard mha the source gives the scaling: \boxed{ \text{kv memory} \propto l\times b\times s\times n\times h\times2\times\text{bytes/value} } where the first factor 2 corresponds to: \boxed{k+v}. the book's formula uses another factor of 2 because its example assumes 16-bit values: \boxed{2\text{ bytes/value}}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) thus the source's mha form can be written as: \boxed{ m_{\text{mha}} = l\,b\,s\,n\,h\,(2)(2) } bytes, under the source's fp16/bfloat16-style 2-byte assumption. 5.36.9 understand every symbol l = number of transformer layers. b = batch size. s = context/sequence length. n = number of attention heads. h = dimension per head. first: 2 = two things stored: k,v. second: 2 = two bytes per 16-bit value. this distinction is very important. 5.36.10 numerical kv-memory example suppose: l=32 b=1 s=4096 n=32 h=128. then: n h = 32\times128 = 4096. so: m = 32\times1\times4096\times4096\times2\times2. compute: 32\times4096\times4096 = 536,870,912. then: 536,870,912\times4 = 2,147,483,648\text{ bytes}. approximately: \boxed{2.00\text{ gib}}. that is for only: \boxed{1\text{ sequence}} under this illustrative architecture. this demonstrates why long-context inference can become memory-heavy. 5.36.11 why sequence length hurts so much in practice the cache size scales linearly with: s. so if: s\rightarrow2s, then: m\rightarrow2m. if: s\rightarrow4s, then: m\rightarrow4m. this is cache memory , not the quadratic self-attention compute formula we studied earlier. don't mix those two. 5.36.12 deepseek-scale example the book gives a deepseek-v3-scale architecture: 61\text{ layers} 128\text{ heads} h=128 and: s=100,000. it reports approximately: \boxed{400\text{ gb}} of kv cache for one sequence under standard mha assumptions. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this is the motivation for architectural innovation. 5.36.13 first attempted solution: mqa the obvious idea is: why store a separate k,v for every head? multi-query attention answers: \boxed{ \text{all query heads share one k/v pair} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so instead of: k_1,k_2,\ldots,k_n we have: \boxed{k_{\text{shared}}} and similarly: \boxed{v_{\text{shared}}}. 5.36.14 mqa memory reduction standard mha scales with: n. mqa scales with: 1. so the theoretical kv-cache reduction is: \boxed{n\times}. for: n=32, mqa can reduce the k/v head-related cache factor by: \boxed{32\times}. that is a huge memory saving. 5.36.15 but why is mqa not the final solution? because mha's strength comes partly from: \boxed{ \text{head specialization} }. head 1 may learn: \text{local syntax}. head 2: \text{long-range relation}. head 3: \text{semantic association}. and so forth. with mqa: k_1=k_2=\cdots=k_n and: v_1=v_2=\cdots=v_n. so different query heads no longer have completely independent k/v representations. the book identifies the resulting loss of expressive power/head specialization as mqa's fundamental drawback. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.16 so mqa creates a trade-off \boxed{ \text{memory efficiency}\uparrow } but: \boxed{ \text{expressive diversity}\downarrow } conceptually: \text{mha} \rightarrow \text{maximum head diversity} \text{mqa} \rightarrow \text{maximum k/v sharing}. 5.36.17 second solution: gqa grouped-query attention introduces: \boxed{g} groups. instead of: n different k/v pairs: \boxed{ g } unique k/v pairs are stored. so: 1\le g\le n. the source gives: \boxed{ m_{\text{gqa}} = l\,b\,g\,h\,s\,2\,2 } under its 16-bit assumption. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.18 mqa and mha become special cases of gqa set: \boxed{g=1} then: \boxed{\text{gqa}=\text{mqa}}. set: \boxed{g=n} then: \boxed{\text{gqa}=\text{mha}}. so g becomes a: \boxed{\text{tunable knob}} between memory and expressivity. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.19 numerical gqa example suppose: n=32 and: g=8. then: \frac{32}{8} = \boxed{4} query heads share each k/v group. so: 4\text{ query heads} \rightarrow 1\text{ k/v group}. the cache reduction relative to mha is: \frac{32}{8} = \boxed{4\times}. the book gives llama 3 8b's 32-head/8-group example exactly in this form. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.20 visualize the three architectures mha q1 ── k1 v1 q2 ── k2 v2 q3 ── k3 v3 q4 ── k4 v4 all heads have unique k/v. mqa q1 ─┐ q2 ─┤ q3 ─┤── k v q4 ─┘ all heads share one k/v. gqa q1 ─┐ q2 ─┘── k1 v1 q3 ─┐ q4 ─┘── k2 v2 two groups for four query heads. 5.36.21 the unresolved problem now we have: \boxed{\text{mha}} excellent expressive power but large cache. \boxed{\text{mqa}} excellent cache efficiency but reduced k/v diversity. \boxed{\text{gqa}} a compromise. the deepseek book explicitly describes gqa as choosing a better point on the performance-memory curve, but not eliminating the underlying trade-off . so the question becomes: \boxed{ \text{can we reduce the amount of information stored without reducing the number of heads?} } that is the conceptual leap to mla. 5.36.22 deepseek's different question mqa/gqa ask: how many k/v heads should we store? mla asks: can we compress the information inside k/v ? this is a completely different design direction. so: \boxed{ \text{mqa/gqa}= \text{reduce number of k/v representations} } while: \boxed{ \text{mla}= \text{compress k/v information} }. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.23 core mla idea instead of caching: k and: v, mla first computes a smaller latent representation: \boxed{c_{kv}} and caches that. the book describes it as: \boxed{ \text{compress for storage} \rightarrow \text{decompress for calculation} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.24 down-projection the input: x is projected into a smaller latent space: \boxed{ c_{kv}=xw_{d-kv} } where w_{d-kv} is the down-projection. conceptually: d_{\text{model}} \rightarrow d_{\text{latent}} with: d_{\text{latent}}\ll d_{\text{model-related k/v dimension}}. 5.36.25 what actually gets cached? only: \boxed{c_{kv}}. not: k and: v separately. so the cache becomes: \boxed{ c_{kv}= [c_{kv}^{(1)},c_{kv}^{(2)},\ldots,c_{kv}^{(t)}] }. the book's toy example shows a latent cache with shape: \boxed{(4,4)} and later: (5,4) after one new token is appended. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.26 up-projection reconstructs k and v when attention needs k and v, mla reconstructs them. conceptually: \boxed{ k=c_{kv}w_{uk} } and: \boxed{ v=c_{kv}w_{uv} } where w_{uk} and w_{uv} are up-projection matrices. the book's toy example describes both k and v as being reconstructed from the latent matrix. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.27 wait — didn't we just add more computation? yes. mla introduces: \boxed{\text{down-projection}} and: \boxed{\text{up-projection}}. at first glance: \boxed{ \text{more matrix multiplications} } sounds worse. but inference has a very important asymmetry: \boxed{ \text{memory traffic for long history} } can be more expensive than a modest amount of additional computation. mla trades: \boxed{ \text{some compute} } for: \boxed{ \text{massive cache/memory savings} }. the source explicitly describes the method as exchanging additional projection/reconstruction work for a much smaller cached representation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.28 the key engineering trick: head diversity returns remember mqa's problem: k_1=k_2=\cdots because all heads share k. mla doesn't have to do that. after reconstruction: \boxed{ k_1\neq k_2\neq\cdots } and: \boxed{ v_1\neq v_2\neq\cdots } can still be maintained because the up-projection matrices are head-specific. the book explicitly emphasizes that each head can reconstruct its own unique k and v from the shared latent cache. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this is the crucial difference from gqa. 5.36.29 so what did mla actually compress? it did not say: “all heads should share the same information.” instead: \boxed{ \text{all heads share a compressed storage representation} } while: \boxed{ \text{each head can reconstruct its own representation} }. this is a subtle but extremely important distinction. 5.36.30 toy numerical example suppose mha has: n=8 heads and: h=64. then total k dimension is: 8\times64 = \boxed{512}. and because we store both k and v: 2\times512 = \boxed{1024} cached values per token, ignoring batch/layers and bytes. suppose mla instead uses: d_{\text{latent}}=64. then we cache: \boxed{64} values per token. the compression factor is: \frac{1024}{64} = \boxed{16\times}. this is an illustrative mla calculation. 5.36.31 the actual deepseek-scale comparison in the book for its deepseek-scale example: n=128 h=128. thus: n h = 128\times128 = \boxed{16,384}. mha's k+v cache dimension factor: 2(nh) = 2(16,384) = \boxed{32,768}. the book's simplified mla latent dimension is approximately: \boxed{512}. therefore: \frac{32,768}{512} = \boxed{64\times}. the book reports this as a 64× reduction in its simplified mla cache calculation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.32 why is this such a big deal? compare: \boxed{ 32,768 } cached dimensions per token under the mha k/v factor, with: \boxed{ 512 } for mla's latent representation in that example. that's: \boxed{ 64\times } less cached information. and yet the attention computation can still reconstruct full, head-specific k/v representations. that is the core engineering idea of mla. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.33 another reported empirical result the book also trains small models using: \text{mha} \text{mqa} \text{gqa} \text{mla} with otherwise controlled model settings. it reports: attention validation loss kv cache mha 2.3721 48 mb mqa 2.4080 6 mb gqa 2.3776 24 mb mla 2.3089 12 mb and corresponding perplexities: 10.72,\ 11.11,\ 10.78,\ 10.06. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.34 what does that experiment show? the source's controlled experiment suggests: mha large cache: 48\text{ mb}. mqa smallest cache: 6\text{ mb} but somewhat worse validation performance. gqa middle cache: 24\text{ mb}. mla only: 12\text{ mb} while achieving the lowest reported validation loss: \boxed{2.3089}. this supports the book's claim that mla can achieve strong learning performance while dramatically reducing cache memory. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.35 numerical comparison of cache sizes mla vs mha: \frac{48}{12} = \boxed{4\times}. so mla uses one-quarter of the cache memory in this experiment. mha vs mqa: \frac{48}{6} = \boxed{8\times}. so mqa gives even more cache reduction in the experiment, but with the reported higher loss. this makes the trade-off visible. 5.36.36 important distinction: toy experiment vs deepseek-scale theory don't mix: \boxed{4\times} with: \boxed{64\times}. the: 4\times figure is the source's small controlled experiment . the: 64\times figure is from the source's deepseek-scale cache-dimension calculation . they answer different questions. 5.36.37 the next problem: position we have solved: \boxed{ k/v\text{ memory} } but attention also needs positional information. modern transformers often use: \boxed{\text{rope}} rotary positional encoding. this creates a complication because the compressed latent cache is designed around a representation that can be reused, while rope introduces position-dependent transformations. the deepseek book therefore develops a decoupled rope architecture after introducing mla. we will treat that as the next substep rather than mixing it into the current derivation. 5.36.38 what you should remember from today's step the entire architecture problem is: \boxed{ \text{mha} \rightarrow \text{excellent expressivity, huge kv cache} } \boxed{ \text{mqa} \rightarrow \text{tiny cache, reduced head diversity} } \boxed{ \text{gqa} \rightarrow \text{middle ground} } then: \boxed{ \text{mla} \rightarrow \text{compress information instead of simply reducing heads} } the deepseek idea is: \boxed{ \text{cache a compact latent representation} } and: \boxed{ \text{reconstruct expressive k/v representations when needed} }. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.39 exam master formulas standard mha kv cache \boxed{ m_{\text{mha}} = l\,b\,s\,n\,h\,2\,2 } under the source's two-byte-per-value assumption. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) gqa \boxed{ m_{\text{gqa}} = l\,b\,s\,g\,h\,2\,2 } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) mqa set: g=1. mha set: g=n. mla concept \boxed{ c_{kv}=xw_{d-kv} } then reconstruct: \boxed{ k=c_{kv}w_{uk} } \boxed{ v=c_{kv}w_{uv} } these equations summarize the compression/decompression mechanism described in the book. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.40 numerical bank level 1 for: n=32,\quad g=8, cache reduction: \boxed{4\times}. level 2 for: n=128,\quad h=128, mha k+v dimension: 2(128)(128) = \boxed{32,768}. level 3 mla latent dimension: 512. reduction: 32768/512 = \boxed{64\times}. level 4 mha cache: 48\text{ mb} mla: 12\text{ mb}. reduction: \boxed{4\times}. level 5 deepseek-style model: 61\text{ layers},\quad128\text{ heads},\quad h=128,\quad s=100000. the supplied book reports roughly: \boxed{400\text{ gb}} for the standard mha kv cache for one sequence under its stated assumptions. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.41 final conceptual picture the engineering progression is: \boxed{ \text{naive decoding} } recomputes history. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{kv cache} } stores history and speeds inference. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{kv memory becomes the bottleneck} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{mqa} } reduces k/v heads aggressively. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{gqa} } provides a tunable compromise. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{mla} } changes the problem itself: \boxed{ \text{compress the information, not simply the number of heads}. } that is the architectural insight we carry into the next step.

(source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.37.41 why not cache q ? during autoregressive decoding, the query belongs to the current token . we only need the current query to compare against historical keys. historical queries are not needed in the same way. therefore the cache focuses on historical information needed for attention: \boxed{ k/v\text{-side state} } or, in mla: \boxed{ c_{kv}+k_r. } this follows the standard causal-decoding structure and the source's cache descriptions. 5.37.42 full inference loop with decoupled mla at a new token x_t : content path compute its latent: c_{kv,t}=x_tw_{d-kv}. append: c_{kv,t} to the latent cache. compute absorbed content query. then: s_c = q_{c,\text{abs}}c_{kv}^{\top}. position path compute: q_{r,t} and: k_{r,t}. apply rope. append: k_{r,t} to the positional cache. then: s_r=q_{r,t}k_r^\top. combine \boxed{ s=s_c+s_r } then: a=\operatorname{softmax} \left( \frac{s}{\sqrt{d_h}} \right) and finally use the content value path to produce the context. this is the complete high-level flow described by the source's decoupled implementation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.37.43 why the position path does not destroy mla efficiency because the position path is deliberately small . the source example uses: d_{\text{rope}}=64 instead of: nh=16,384. so we retain only a compact positional representation. thus: \boxed{ \text{small content cache} + \text{small positional cache} } replaces: \boxed{ \text{full k cache} + \text{full v cache}. } that is the architectural trick. 5.37.44 one complete conceptual diagram input x │ ┌──────────┴──────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ content path position path mla rope │ │ x → ckv x → qr, kr │ │ ┌───────┴───────┐ │ │ │ │ qc kc,vc │ │ │ │ └── absorption ─┘ │ │ │ sc = qckcᵀ sr = qrkrᵀ │ │ └────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ s = sc + sr │ ▼ softmax │ ▼ content value path │ ▼ context vector the two-cache idea is: \boxed{ c_{kv}\quad+\quad k_r } rather than: \boxed{ k\quad+\quad v. } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.37.45 the most important mathematical insight the absorption trick is fundamentally: \boxed{ (xw_q) (c_{kv}w_{uk})^\top } = \boxed{ xw_qw_{uk}^{\top}c_{kv}^{\top} } because: \boxed{ (ab)^\top=b^\top a^\top } and: \boxed{ abc=(ab)c. } then: \boxed{ w_qw_{uk}^{\top} } is fixed during inference. therefore: \boxed{ \text{historical state needed} = c_{kv}, } not the full historical k . that's the whole trick. 5.37.46 the most important architectural insight rope then says: \boxed{ \text{position must modify q/k} } and that breaks the fixed-factor assumption. deepseek therefore says: \boxed{ \text{don't put position inside the compressed content path.} } instead: \boxed{ \text{content path}+\text{position path}. } then: \boxed{ s=s_c+s_r. } that is decoupled rope . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.37.47 exam-style numerical: cache reduction given: n=128,\quad h=128,\quad d_{\text{latent}}=512,\quad d_{\text{rope}}=64. mha factor: 2nh=32768. mla+rope: 512+64=576. reduction: 32768/576 = \boxed{56.89\times}. rounded: \boxed{57\times}. 5.37.48 exam-style numerical: pure mla same model but ignoring the positional path: 32768/512 = \boxed{64\times}. so: \boxed{ \text{rope adds only }64 } to the cached dimension in this source example, but reduces the theoretical compression ratio from: 64\times to: 57\times. 5.37.49 exam-style matrix-shape question given: x\in\mathbb r^{8\times512} and: w_{d-kv}\in\mathbb r^{512\times64}, then: c_{kv}=xw_{d-kv} has shape: \boxed{8\times64}. if: w_{uk}\in\mathbb r^{64\times512}, then: k=c_{kv}w_{uk} has: (8\times64)(64\times512) = \boxed{8\times512}. the compression is therefore: 512\rightarrow64 for the cached latent representation before reconstruction. 5.37.50 final checkpoint at this point, you should be able to answer four questions. why does mla save memory? \boxed{ \text{because historical k/v information is stored in a much smaller latent cache} } rather than full k and v matrices. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) why doesn't mqa solve the problem completely? \boxed{ \text{it saves memory by sharing k/v, reducing head specialization} } while mla instead compresses the information and can reconstruct head-specific k/v. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) why is decoupled rope needed? because: \boxed{ \text{position-dependent rotations break the fixed matrix factorization needed for absorption} } so position is moved to a separate path. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.2 standard dense ffn mathematically let: x\in\mathbb r^{d_{\text{model}}}. choose hidden dimension: d_{\text{hidden}}. then: h=xw_1 where: w_1\in \mathbb r^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{hidden}}}. apply activation: z=\operatorname{gelu}(h). then: y=zw_2 with: w_2\in \mathbb r^{d_{\text{hidden}}\times d_{\text{model}}}. therefore: \boxed{ y= \operatorname{gelu}(xw_1)w_2 } in the simplified source-style representation. 5.38.3 why does a dense ffn become expensive? suppose: d_{\text{model}}=4096 and: d_{\text{hidden}}=16384. then w_1 alone contains: 4096\times16384 = \boxed{67,108,864} parameters. w_2 contains the same number. total: 2(67,108,864) = \boxed{134,217,728} parameters. and every token activates all of them. the source identifies exactly this issue: dense ffns activate all of their parameters for every token and therefore become a major computational bottleneck. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.4 the natural idea instead of one giant ffn: \boxed{ ffn } create many smaller ffns: \boxed{ e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_n } where each: e_i is called an: \boxed{\text{expert}}. the source explicitly defines each expert as essentially a standard two-layer ffn/mlp. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.5 why call them “experts”? the intuition is: \boxed{ \text{different experts can specialize} } during training. for example, the source gives conceptual examples such as: \text{punctuation expert} \text{verb expert} \text{python/code expert}. these examples are illustrative descriptions of specialization, not a claim that every trained moe literally develops exactly those named experts. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.6 the apparent problem suppose we replace one ffn with: 8 experts. it may seem that computation becomes: 8\times more expensive. but this ignores the key idea: \boxed{\text{sparsity}}. we don't execute every expert for every token. 5.38.7 sparse activation for each token, only: \boxed{k} experts are activated. usually: k\ll n. for example: n=8,\qquad k=2. then each token sees: \boxed{2} experts instead of: 8. the source's basic example uses: \boxed{k=2} out of three available experts. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.8 computational intuition dense model: \boxed{ 1\text{ token} \rightarrow 8\text{ experts} } sparse moe: \boxed{ 1\text{ token} \rightarrow 2\text{ experts} } so approximately: \frac{2}{8} = \boxed{25\%} of the expert computations are activated per token, ignoring router/dispatch overhead and shared components. this is why we can have: \boxed{ \text{large total parameter capacity} } without paying the full dense computation for every token. 5.38.9 total parameters vs active parameters this distinction is fundamental. suppose: n=16 experts, each with: 100\text{m} parameters. then total expert parameters: 16\times100m = \boxed{1.6b}. but suppose: k=2. then a token activates: 2\times100m = \boxed{200m} expert parameters. so: \boxed{ 1.6b\text{ total} \quad\text{but}\quad 200m\text{ expert parameters active for a token} } under this simplified model. this is one of the most important moe ideas. 5.38.10 important caveat “active parameters” does not mean: \boxed{\text{the rest of the model doesn't exist}} the inactive experts still have parameters stored somewhere. they simply are not involved in that token's expert computation. so: \boxed{ \text{total model memory} \neq \text{per-token active compute} } this distinction will become extremely important when we later connect moe to deepseek-r1's: 671b total parameters but approximately: 37b active parameters per token. 5.38.11 now we need a router we have many experts. but who decides which experts receive a token? answer: \boxed{\text{router}} the source calls the router a small learnable linear mechanism that generates scores for the experts. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.12 router input and output suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{d_{\text{model}}} and there are: n experts. the router has parameters: w_r\in \mathbb r^{d_{\text{model}}\times n}. then: \boxed{ r=xw_r } where: r\in\mathbb r^n. so for each token, the router produces one score per expert. 5.38.13 example suppose: n=4. the router outputs: \boxed{ r=[1.2,\;0.3,\;2.1,\;1.4] } for a token. interpretation: e_1:1.2 e_2:0.3 e_3:2.1 e_4:1.4. these are raw router scores/logits. they are not yet expert weights . 5.38.14 why aren't they weights yet? because they can be: \text{negative} or: >1. for example: [1.2,0.3,2.1,1.4] does not sum to: 1. we need normalized gating weights. the basic source pipeline is: \boxed{ \text{router logits} \rightarrow \text{top-k} \rightarrow \text{softmax} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.15 step 1 — router logits formally: \boxed{ l=xw_r } for an entire batch: x\in\mathbb r^{t\times d_{\text{model}}} gives: \boxed{ l\in\mathbb r^{t\times n} } where t is the number of tokens being routed. this tensor-shape question is extremely exam-important. 5.38.16 numerical shape question suppose: b=4 sequences, s=128 tokens each. then: t=b\times s = 4\times128 = \boxed{512}. suppose: d_{\text{model}}=4096 and: n=64 experts. then: x\in\mathbb r^{512\times4096}. router matrix: w_r\in\mathbb r^{4096\times64}. therefore: l=xw_r has shape: \boxed{ 512\times64 }. so we have: \boxed{ 512\text{ tokens}\times64\text{ expert scores}. } 5.38.17 step 2 — top-k expert selection now suppose: k=2. our logits: [1.2,0.3,2.1,1.4]. the two largest values are: 2.1 and: 1.4. therefore selected experts are: \boxed{e_3,e_4}. the others: e_1,e_2 are dormant for this token. this is the source's core sparse-routing operation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.18 important: top-k happens before softmax this ordering matters. we do: \boxed{ \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{top-k} \rightarrow \text{softmax on selected logits} } not: \text{softmax all experts} \rightarrow \text{top-k}. the source implementation explicitly does: topk_logits, topk_idx = torch.topk(...) gate = softmax(topk_logits) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.19 step 3 — softmax the selected logits our selected logits are: [2.1,1.4]. compute: e^{2.1}\approx8.166 and: e^{1.4}\approx4.055. sum: 8.166+4.055 = 12.221. therefore: w_3= \frac{8.166}{12.221} \approx \boxed{0.668}. and: w_4= \frac{4.055}{12.221} \approx \boxed{0.332}. check: 0.668+0.332=1. so: \boxed{ e_3:66.8\% } and: \boxed{ e_4:33.2\% }. 5.38.20 why softmax after top-k? the model is not saying: “use two experts equally.” instead: \boxed{ \text{which experts} } and: \boxed{ \text{how much each selected expert contributes} } are two separate decisions. top-k answers: \boxed{\text{who?}} softmax answers: \boxed{\text{how much?}} this is a very useful mental model. 5.38.21 step 4 — send the token to selected experts suppose the token representation is: x. it is sent only to: e_3 and: e_4. so: y_3=e_3(x) and: y_4=e_4(x). the other outputs: e_1(x),e_2(x) are never computed. that is the actual source of sparse computation. 5.38.22 step 5 — weighted aggregation now compute: \boxed{ y= w_3y_3+w_4y_4 } with: w_3=0.668 and: w_4=0.332. the source gives exactly this concept: selected expert outputs are multiplied by their gate weights and summed. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.23 complete vector example suppose: y_3= \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 4 \end{bmatrix} and: y_4= \begin{bmatrix} 6\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. then: y = 0.668 \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 4 \end{bmatrix} + 0.332 \begin{bmatrix} 6\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. first component: 0.668(2)+0.332(6) = 1.336+1.992 = \boxed{3.328}. second: 0.668(4)+0.332(1) = 2.672+0.332 = \boxed{3.004}. so: \boxed{ y= \begin{bmatrix} 3.328\\ 3.004 \end{bmatrix}. } 5.38.24 why is the output shape unchanged? suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{d}. each expert maps: \mathbb r^d\rightarrow\mathbb r^d. therefore: y_i\in\mathbb r^d. the weighted sum: \sum_{i\in topk}w_i y_i also belongs to: \boxed{\mathbb r^d}. thus the moe layer preserves the transformer residual-stream dimension. the source demonstrates this with a toy input/output matrix of shape: \boxed{4\times8}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.25 batch-level shape suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{b\times s\times d}. flatten: x_{\text{flat}} \in \mathbb r^{(bs)\times d}. router: l= x_{\text{flat}}w_r gives: \boxed{ (bs)\times n. } after selecting k experts: \boxed{ (bs)\times k } expert indices and gating weights are retained. after dispatch and aggregation: \boxed{ (bs)\times d } is restored. then reshape: \boxed{ b\times s\times d. } this is exactly the structure visible in the source implementation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.26 now we can write the complete basic moe equation for token x : l=wx+b router logits. then: i(x)=topk(l,k) selected experts. then: w_i= \frac{e^{l_i}} {\sum_{j\in i(x)}e^{l_j}}, \qquad i\in i(x). then: \boxed{ moe(x)= \sum_{i\in i(x)} w_ie_i(x) } this compactly captures the entire basic sparse-routing mechanism. the exact source implementation additionally contains deepseek's dynamic bias; we will add that in the load-balancing step. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.27 compare dense ffn and sparse moe dense ffn \boxed{ y=ffn(x) } every token executes the entire ffn. moe \boxed{ y=\sum_{i\in topk(x)}w_ie_i(x) } only selected experts execute. so: \boxed{ \text{dense} = \text{all parameters active} } while: \boxed{ \text{moe} = \text{large total capacity + sparse activation} }. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.28 parameter-count numerical suppose a dense ffn has: 100m parameters. now create: 16 experts, each with: 25m parameters. total expert parameters: 16\times25m = \boxed{400m}. if: k=2, then each token activates: 2\times25m = \boxed{50m} expert parameters. so compared with the dense model: \boxed{4\times} the total expert parameter capacity exists: 400/100=4. yet only half the dense ffn's parameters are activated per token: 50/100=0.5. this illustrates the core moe scaling idea. these numbers are illustrative. 5.38.29 compute intuition ignoring routing overhead, suppose one expert costs: c. dense equivalent with one ffn: c. an moe with n=16 experts and k=2 : \boxed{ 2c } expert compute per token. but the model stores: 16\times the number of expert networks. thus: \boxed{ \text{total capacity}\uparrow } much faster than: \boxed{ \text{per-token expert computation}\uparrow }. that is the fundamental sparsity advantage. 5.38.30 but there is a hidden danger suppose the router always chooses: e_1,e_2. then: e_1,e_2 receive enormous amounts of training. the other experts receive almost nothing. this creates: \boxed{\text{imbalanced routing}}. the source describes exactly this failure mode. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.31 why does imbalance create a feedback loop? suppose early in training: e_1 happens to perform slightly better. then the router favors: e_1. so: e_1 \rightarrow \text{more tokens} \rightarrow \text{more training} \rightarrow \text{becomes even better} \rightarrow \text{router favors }e_1\text{ even more}. this is: \boxed{ \text{positive feedback} } the source explicitly describes this self-reinforcing behavior. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.32 why are unused experts a problem? an expert that is rarely selected receives few updates. so: \boxed{ \text{expert utilization}\downarrow } leads to: \boxed{ \text{expert learning}\downarrow. } eventually it can become effectively: \boxed{\text{dead weight}}. the source uses exactly this idea. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.33 why are overloaded experts a problem? suppose: e_1 receives almost all tokens. then even though the other experts are idle: e_1 becomes a computational bottleneck. so: \boxed{ \text{some hardware/expert capacity overloaded} } while: \boxed{ \text{other capacity wasted} }. this is both a utilization and systems problem. 5.38.34 numerical routing example suppose: t=12 tokens, n=4 experts, and: k=2. total routed assignments: t\times k = 12\times2 = \boxed{24}. perfectly balanced load would be: \frac{24}{4} = \boxed{6} assignments per expert. suppose actual counts are: [10,8,4,2]. total: 10+8+4+2 = 24. so expert 1 is heavily overloaded, while expert 4 is underused. 5.38.35 this is why “tokens per expert” matters the raw token count is not enough. for top- k routing, each token can contribute: k assignments. so if: t=1000 and: k=2, then total expert assignments are: \boxed{2000}. with: n=8, ideal average: 2000/8 = \boxed{250} assignments per expert. that is the baseline against which imbalance can be judged. 5.38.36 the source's simple example the book gives a three-expert example where: expert 1 receives 2 tokens, expert 2 receives 2, expert 3 receives 4. thus: 2+2+4 = \boxed{8} total routed assignments. average: 8/3 = \boxed{2.67}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so relative to the average: e_1:2-2.67=-0.67 e_2:2-2.67=-0.67 e_3:4-2.67=+1.33. this tells us: \boxed{ e_1,e_2\text{ underloaded} } and: \boxed{ e_3\text{ overloaded}. } 5.38.37 another key concept: expert capacity before we discuss deepseek's balancing method, understand the older hard constraint. each expert can be given a maximum number of tokens it is allowed to process in a batch. the source calls this: \boxed{\text{expert capacity}}. if more tokens are routed to an expert than its capacity: \boxed{\text{excess tokens are dropped for that forward pass}} in the traditional scheme. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.38 capacity formula the source describes capacity conceptually as: \boxed{ \text{capacity} = \text{fair-share tokens} \times \text{capacity factor} } where fair share is: \frac{\text{tokens per batch}\times k} {\text{number of experts}}. so: \boxed{ c = \frac{t\,k}{n} \times cf } where cf is the capacity factor. the exact details can vary by implementation; this is the formula structure given in the source discussion. 5.38.39 numerical capacity example suppose: t=1000 k=2 n=8 and: cf=1.25. fair share: \frac{1000\times2}{8} = 250. capacity: 250\times1.25 = \boxed{312.5}. in an implementation requiring integer capacity, this would need an appropriate rounding convention. the important idea is: \boxed{ \text{capacity factor gives a buffer above ideal balance} }. the source specifically emphasizes that cf>1 gives flexibility for moderate imbalance. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.40 why is capacity only a partial solution? because it says: “don't process more than this many tokens.” it does not directly teach the router: “please distribute tokens more evenly.” so capacity is: \boxed{\text{hard guardrail}} whereas load-balancing losses/biases are: \boxed{\text{routing-control mechanisms}}. the source explicitly distinguishes these. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.38.41 complete basic moe forward pass now we can finally write it as one sequence. given: x\in\mathbb r^{b\times s\times d} step 1 — flatten x_f\in \mathbb r^{bs\times d}. step 2 — router l=x_fw_r giving: bs\times n. step 3 — select i=topk(l,k). step 4 — normalize g=\operatorname{softmax}(l_i). step 5 — dispatch send each token only to its selected experts. step 6 — expert computation y_i=e_i(x_i). step 7 — weighted combine y_t= \sum_{i\in i_t} g_{t,i}y_{t,i}. step 8 — reshape y\in \mathbb r^{b\times s\times d}. this is the complete basic sparse moe mechanism described in the source. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.1 first, remember what ordinary moe gave us suppose we start with a conventional moe: \boxed{16\text{ experts}} and each expert has hidden dimension: \boxed{4096}. conceptually: e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_{16} are sixteen relatively large ffns. a router chooses, say: k=2 for each token. so: \boxed{ 16\text{ available experts} \rightarrow 2\text{ active experts/token} } this is efficient. but the source asks: are 16 large experts really the best way to divide knowledge? the answer is no. 5.40.2 problem #1 — knowledge hybridity imagine the training data contains: \text{python} + \text{mathematics} + \text{law} + \text{history} + \text{conversational text}. with only a few large experts, an individual expert may receive tokens belonging to several unrelated domains. so instead of becoming: \boxed{\text{python specialist}} it becomes something like: \boxed{ \text{python} + \text{law} + \text{grammar} + \text{history} +\cdots } that is what the source calls: \boxed{\text{knowledge hybridity}}. the source's intuition is that with too few experts, each expert becomes a “jack-of-all-trades,” preventing deep specialization. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.3 the obvious idea instead of: 16 large experts, create many smaller experts. for example: \boxed{64\text{ experts}} with a smaller hidden dimension: \boxed{1024}. so: conventional 16\times4096 fine-grained 64\times1024 the source deliberately gives this exact example. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.4 first numerical observation conventional expert capacity: 16\times4096 = \boxed{65,536}. fine-grained expert capacity: 64\times1024 = \boxed{65,536}. therefore: \boxed{ 16\times4096 = 64\times1024 } the total hidden-dimension capacity is unchanged. this is the key trick. 5.40.5 what actually changed? we did not necessarily make the model larger. we changed: \boxed{\text{number of containers}} and: \boxed{\text{size of each container}}. before: 16\text{ large containers} after: 64\text{ smaller containers}. so the same overall capacity is divided more finely. the source explicitly says the total number of expert parameters and activated parameters can remain the same while the knowledge is divided into a larger number of more specialized containers. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.6 why does this improve specialization? suppose the model has only 4 broad experts: e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4. a single expert may have to represent: \text{code + legal + mathematics}. but with 64 experts, the routing space is much finer. the source's conceptual examples include possibilities such as a specialist for: \text{python syntax} another for: \text{legal terminology} another for: \text{poetic language}. these are illustrative descriptions of possible specialization, not a guarantee that the learned experts acquire exactly those labels. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.7 why “fine-grained”? because the routing granularity changes. think of conventional moe as having broad bins: \boxed{ \text{bin a} \quad \text{bin b} \quad \text{bin c} \quad \text{bin d} } while fine-grained moe has: \boxed{ 64\text{ narrower bins} } the router gets more choices. therefore the token-to-expert mapping can become more precise. 5.40.8 the subtle point about top-k suppose conventional moe uses: n=16,\quad k=2. then a token gets: 2/16 of the expert choices activated. now fine-grained moe uses: n=64. if we still use: k=2, then the token sees two of sixty-four experts. this creates a much narrower routing decision. but there is another important design possibility: increase n while also changing expert size and k so that total activated parameters remain approximately comparable. the source explicitly notes that the total expert parameters and activated parameters can remain the same under the fine-grained construction. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so don't memorize: “fine-grained always means more experts and the exact same k .” the deeper principle is: \boxed{ \text{more experts} + \text{smaller experts} } with capacity controlled appropriately. 5.40.9 parameter-count derivation let an expert ffn have: d_{\text{model}}=d and hidden dimension: h. ignoring biases, a two-layer ffn has approximately: dh+hd parameters: \boxed{ 2dh }. for n experts: \boxed{ p_{\text{experts}} \approx 2ndh }. now suppose we increase experts from: n to: an and reduce hidden dimension from: h to: \frac{h}{a}. then: p'_{\text{experts}} = 2(an)d\left(\frac ha\right). cancel a : \boxed{ p'_{\text{experts}} = 2ndh }. so total expert parameters remain approximately unchanged. this is the mathematical reason the source's example works. 5.40.10 exam numerical suppose: d=2048. conventional moe: n=8,\quad h=4096. expert parameters: 2(8)(2048)(4096) = \boxed{134,217,728}. now create: n'=32 experts and: h'=1024. then: 2(32)(2048)(1024) = \boxed{134,217,728}. same total expert parameter count. but instead of 8 broad experts: \boxed{32\text{ narrower experts}}. that is fine-grained segmentation. 5.40.11 activated-parameter numerical suppose the original model has: n=16,\qquad h=4096 and activates: k=2. activated expert parameters per token are approximately: 2\times2d(4096) = 4d(4096). now split into: n=64,\qquad h=1024 and suppose the architecture chooses: k'=8 to preserve the same activated capacity. then: 8\times2d(1024) = 16d(1024) = 4d(4096). thus: \boxed{ k'h'=kh } is the key relation for preserving approximately the same activated ffn capacity. this is an exam-style inference from the parameter formulas; the source's exact discussion states that activated parameters can remain the same, but does not prescribe this exact symbolic derivation. 5.40.12 this solves one problem—but not the other fine-grained experts address: \boxed{\text{knowledge hybridity}} because experts can become narrower specialists. but now consider this: every specialized expert still needs foundational knowledge. for example: python expert needs: \text{basic grammar}. medical expert needs: \text{basic grammar}. legal expert needs: \text{basic grammar}. mathematics expert needs: \text{basic language understanding}. so common information gets duplicated across experts. that is: \boxed{\text{knowledge redundancy}}. the source explicitly uses this reasoning to motivate the second innovation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.13 why redundancy is expensive suppose each specialized expert has: 100m parameters. if every expert spends: 20m parameters learning shared/common information, then with: 64 experts: 64\times20m = \boxed{1.28b} parameters are being used for repeated common knowledge. that capacity could instead be devoted to specialized knowledge. this numerical example is illustrative; the source's point is qualitative: duplicated foundational knowledge consumes expert capacity and hinders specialization. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.14 deepseek's second idea instead of asking every routed expert to relearn common knowledge: \boxed{\text{create dedicated shared experts}} these are a small set of dense experts. so now we divide the moe layer into: \boxed{ \text{shared experts} + \text{routed experts} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.15 routed experts these are our fine-grained specialists. each token is sent only to: k of them. thus: \boxed{ \text{routed experts} = \text{sparse} } for a token: x_t, the router determines: topk(x_t) and only those experts execute. 5.40.16 shared experts the shared experts are completely different. every token passes through: \boxed{\text{all shared experts}}. so: \boxed{ \text{shared experts} = \text{dense} } this is explicitly stated in the source. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.17 why should every token see shared experts? because they store common knowledge. think of the division as: \boxed{ \text{shared path} = \text{general knowledge} } and: \boxed{ \text{routed path} = \text{specialized knowledge} }. therefore the routed experts don't have to waste as much capacity learning the same fundamentals. the source describes the shared experts as the central repository for common foundational knowledge, while routed experts are freed to focus on narrower domains. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.18 simple analogy imagine a hospital. every patient first receives care from: \boxed{\text{general physician}} for common medical needs. then the patient is routed to: \boxed{\text{cardiologist}} or: \boxed{\text{neurologist}} or: \boxed{\text{orthopedic specialist}}. the general physician handles: \text{common knowledge}. the specialist handles: \text{specific knowledge}. that is a useful conceptual analogy for: \boxed{ \text{shared experts + routed experts} }. 5.40.19 mathematical architecture let: x be a token representation. shared expert outputs: s_j(x),\qquad j=1,\ldots,n_s. the dense shared output is: \boxed{ s(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{n_s}s_j(x) } for the source-style simplified implementation. now the routed path: r(x) = \sum_{i\in topk(x)} g_ie_i(x). so the moe result becomes: \boxed{ y= x+s(x)+r(x) } in the source's complete implementation, where the direct x term is the residual path. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) correction: standalone book moe includes residual; the full transformer moe should return transformation only if outer block adds it. assign residual ownership once. complete grounded review 5.40.20 why is the residual x included? the source's complete architecture has three parallel paths: \boxed{ \text{residual} } \boxed{ \text{shared experts} } \boxed{ \text{routed experts} } and sums: \boxed{ x+shared\_out+routed\_out }. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the residual path preserves the original representation and maintains the transformer residual-stream structure. 5.40.21 full data flow now the architecture looks like this: \boxed{x} splits into two computational branches. branch a x \rightarrow \boxed{\text{shared expert 1}} x \rightarrow \boxed{\text{shared expert 2}} \cdots all tokens pass through them. branch b x \rightarrow \boxed{\text{router}} \rightarrow \boxed{\text{top-k}} \rightarrow \boxed{\text{selected routed experts only}} then: \boxed{ y=x+shared+routed } this is the architectural picture you should have in your mind. 5.40.22 the three responsibilities this gives us a beautiful division: component main responsibility shared experts common/foundational knowledge routed experts specialized knowledge router select which specialists to activate so: \boxed{ \text{shared = generalist} } \boxed{ \text{routed = specialist} } \boxed{ \text{router = dispatcher} } 5.40.23 why shared experts do not destroy sparsity a common confusion is: “if shared experts process every token, haven't we lost moe sparsity?” no. only the shared path is dense. the large pool of routed experts remains sparse. suppose: n_r=64 routed experts and: k=8. every token executes: 8 routed experts, not 64. then suppose: n_s=2 shared experts. every token executes those 2 shared experts as well. so total expert executions per token: \boxed{2+8=10} rather than: 66. this is the key architectural balance. 5.40.24 parameter numerical: shared + routed suppose: d=2048. each routed expert has: h_r=1024. there are: 64 routed experts. total routed parameters: 2(64)(2048)(1024) = \boxed{268,435,456}. now create: 2 shared experts of hidden dimension: 1024. their total parameters: 2(2)(2048)(1024) = \boxed{8,388,608}. total expert parameters: 268,435,456+8,388,608 = \boxed{276,824,064}. but per token, only: 8 routed experts are active plus the: 2 shared experts. so: \boxed{10\text{ expert computations/token}} instead of: 66. again, these numbers are illustrative. 5.40.25 why this creates better specialization before: e_i = \boxed{\text{specialized knowledge + common knowledge}} after shared isolation: \boxed{ e_i \approx \text{specialized knowledge} } while: \boxed{ s_j \approx \text{common knowledge} }. therefore: \boxed{ \text{routed experts can spend more capacity on specialization} }. this is exactly the conceptual benefit the source attributes to shared expert isolation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.26 connecting both innovations now notice how the two ideas solve two different problems. innovation 1 fine-grained segmentation: \boxed{ \text{many small experts} } solves: \boxed{ \text{knowledge hybridity} } because each expert has a narrower role. innovation 2 shared expert isolation: \boxed{ \text{small dense generalist path} } solves: \boxed{ \text{knowledge redundancy} } because common knowledge is centralized. together: \boxed{ \text{fine-grained specialists} + \text{shared generalists} } produce the deepseek specialization strategy. 5.40.27 a compact comparison conventional moe \boxed{ \text{few large routed experts} } potential issue: \text{knowledge hybridity} and: \text{redundancy}. deepseek-style \boxed{ \text{many small routed experts} + \text{few shared dense experts} } this gives: \boxed{ \text{narrow specialists} + \text{common foundation} }. 5.40.28 now combine it with step 5.39 remember our loss-free balancing: l'=l+b. now the routed path becomes: l' \rightarrow topk \rightarrow softmax \rightarrow specialized experts. thus all three deepseek innovations now fit together: \boxed{ \text{fine-grained experts} } give specialization. \boxed{ \text{shared experts} } give common knowledge. \boxed{ \text{dynamic bias} } keeps routing balanced. this is why these innovations are much more meaningful together than individually. 5.40.29 complete deepseek-moe conceptual equation a source-style simplified expression is: \boxed{ y_t = x_t + \sum_{j=1}^{n_s}s_j(x_t) + \sum_{i\in topk_t}g_{t,i}e_i(x_t) } where: x_t : original token representation, s_j : shared expert j , e_i : routed expert i , topk_t : selected routed experts for token t , g_{t,i} : routing weight. and before selecting routed experts: \boxed{ l_t'=l_t+b } where b is the dynamically adjusted expert bias. the source's implementation follows precisely this three-path structure. 5.40.30 tensor shapes suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{b\times s\times d}. flatten: x_f\in\mathbb r^{bs\times d}. suppose: n_r routed experts. router matrix: w_r\in\mathbb r^{d\times n_r}. therefore: l=x_fw_r has: \boxed{ bs\times n_r }. after top-k: \boxed{ bs\times k } indices and gating weights. routed result: \boxed{ bs\times d }. shared path: \boxed{ b\times s\times d }. final: \boxed{ b\times s\times d }. thus the moe layer still fits neatly into the transformer residual stream. 5.40.31 exam numerical — tensor routing suppose: b=8, s=1024, d=4096, n_r=128, k=8. total tokens: 8\times1024 = \boxed{8192}. router logits: \boxed{ 8192\times128 }. top-k indices: \boxed{ 8192\times8 }. total routed expert assignments: 8192\times8 = \boxed{65,536}. ideal average assignments per routed expert: \frac{65,536}{128} = \boxed{512}. excellent exam question because it combines: \text{batch shape} + \text{router} + \text{top-k} + \text{load balancing}. 5.40.32 exam numerical — fine-grained preservation conventional: n=16,\quad h=4096. fine-grained: n'=64,\quad h'=1024. check: 16\times4096 = 65,536 and: 64\times1024 = 65,536. thus: \boxed{ \text{same aggregate expert hidden capacity} }. the expert count increased: 64/16 = \boxed{4\times}. the individual expert size decreased: 1024/4096 = \boxed{1/4}. so: \boxed{ 4\times\text{ more experts} ,\quad 1/4\text{ size per expert} }. 5.40.33 exam numerical — specialization reasoning suppose a conventional moe has: 8 experts. the dataset effectively contains 8 broad domains. in a simplified idealization: 1\text{ expert/domain}. now split into: 64 experts. the router has: 64/8 = \boxed{8\times} more expert choices. the source's argument is not that there will literally be exactly one expert per semantic category. the point is that the larger pool provides finer routing granularity and therefore more opportunity for specialization. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.34 one subtle but important correction to your mental model do not memorize: \boxed{\text{one expert = one topic}} that is too simplistic. a trained expert's function is learned from optimization. it may respond to: \text{linguistic patterns} + \text{domain patterns} + \text{syntactic structures} + \text{other learned features}. the source uses “python specialist,” “legal terminology,” etc. as intuition for specialization, not as a strict partition of the knowledge space. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the correct mental model is: \boxed{ \text{experts tend toward differentiated specialization} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{each expert owns exactly one human-defined subject}. } 5.40.35 put everything we've learned together we started with: \boxed{\text{dense ffn}} ↓ too expensive. then: \boxed{\text{sparse moe}} ↓ only a few experts execute. then: \boxed{\text{load balancing}} ↓ prevent expert collapse. then: \boxed{\text{fine-grained segmentation}} ↓ more, smaller specialists. then: \boxed{\text{shared expert isolation}} ↓ centralize common knowledge. then: \boxed{\text{auxiliary-loss-free bias}} ↓ balance the routed specialists without adding a competing balancing loss. so the conceptual architecture becomes: \boxed{ \text{shared generalists} + \text{balanced fine-grained specialists} + \text{sparse routing} } 5.40.36 final architecture for each token x_t : shared path \boxed{ x_t\rightarrow s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_{n_s} } every token. routed path x_t \rightarrow l_t \rightarrow l_t+b \rightarrow topk \rightarrow \text{selected }e_i only selected specialists. combine \boxed{ y_t= x_t+ \sum_js_j(x_t) + \sum_{i\in topk_t}g_{t,i}e_i(x_t) } this is the most important equation from the entire moe section so far. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.37 the four questions you should be able to answer in an exam q1. why does deepseek increase the number of experts? because few large experts create: \boxed{\text{knowledge hybridity}} and many smaller experts provide finer specialization. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) q2. why reduce expert size when increasing expert count? to preserve approximately the same total expert parameter capacity: \boxed{ n'h'\approx nh } in the source's illustrative construction. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) q3. why add shared experts? to provide common foundational knowledge so routed experts don't redundantly relearn it. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) q4. are shared experts sparse? no. \boxed{ \text{shared experts are dense} } every token uses them. the routed experts are the sparse part. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.40.38 final memory trick remember: \boxed{ \text{more} } m — many many small experts. o — one common path shared experts handle common knowledge. r — route sparsely only a few routed experts per token. e — equalize load dynamic bias keeps expert utilization balanced. so: \boxed{ \text{many specialists + one shared foundation + sparse routing + equalized load} } that is the deepseek-moe story we have built so far.
