(source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.49.5.1 first: recall what a scaling factor is from our earlier quantization foundation: suppose a tensor is: x=[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n]. find its maximum absolute value: \boxed{ \alpha=\max_i|x_i| } then derive a scaling factor from the target representable range. for the simple symmetric int8 example we used: \boxed{ s=\frac{q_{\max}}{\alpha} } where: q_{\max}=127. then: \boxed{ q_i=\operatorname{round}(x_i s). } so everything depends on: \boxed{\alpha}. and that gives us the question behind pillar 5: where does \alpha come from? 5.49.5.2 two possibilities suppose we are currently quantizing: x_t. there are two broad approaches. approach a — use old statistics use something like: \alpha_{t-1} or a running historical estimate. this is what the source calls: \boxed{\text{delayed quantization}}. approach b — inspect the current tensor calculate: \alpha_t=\max|x_t|. this is: \boxed{\text{online quantization}}. the source contrasts exactly these two approaches. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.49.5.3 what does “delayed” mean? suppose the previous batches looked like: x_{t-3},x_{t-2},x_{t-1}. their maximum magnitudes might have been: 10,\quad12,\quad11. a delayed scheme keeps history such as: \alpha_{\text{history}}\approx12. then when the new tensor arrives: x_t, you quantize it using information derived from the past. the important point is: \boxed{ \text{the scale used now is not necessarily determined by the current tensor}. } the source explicitly describes delayed quantization as maintaining a running history of maximum values and using that historical information for the current step. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.49.5.4 why could that be a problem? because the distribution of neural-network tensors can change. the source identifies two opposite cases. case 1 current maximum: \alpha_t \gg \alpha_{\text{history}}. case 2 current maximum: \alpha_t \ll \alpha_{\text{history}}. these create two different numerical failures. 5.49.5.5 case 1 — current values are much larger suppose historical maximum: \alpha_{\text{history}}=10. but the current tensor contains: \alpha_t=100. suppose the target fp8 range has some maximum representable magnitude q_{\max} . the old scale was derived from: 10. therefore the scale is approximately: s_{\text{old}} = \frac{q_{\max}}{10}. but the current value is: 100. so its scaled value becomes: 100 \frac{q_{\max}}{10} = 10q_{\max}. that is far beyond the intended target range. so: \boxed{ \text{old scale + unexpectedly large current tensor} \rightarrow \text{overflow}. } the source explicitly identifies this failure. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.49.5.6 concrete toy numerical for simplicity, use: q_{\max}=127. historical maximum: \alpha_h=10. therefore: s_h=\frac{127}{10}=12.7. now current tensor contains: x=100. quantization tries: 100(12.7)=1270. but the target range is: [-127,127]. so: \boxed{1270>127}. overflow occurs. this example is derived from the source's stated failure mode. 5.49.5.7 case 2 — current values are much smaller now reverse the situation. historical maximum: \alpha_h=100. current maximum: \alpha_t=1. the old scale: s_h=\frac{127}{100}=1.27. take a current value: x=0.1. then: 0.1(1.27)=0.127. after rounding: \boxed{q=0}. so: 0.1 \rightarrow 0 in the quantized representation. the source describes this as underflow / catastrophic precision loss, connected to the same “squashing” problem we encountered earlier. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.49.5.8 why is this the same “squashing” problem? remember our earlier example: [2,3,500]. the 500 forced the global scale to accommodate a huge range. then: 2,3 were mapped into a tiny part of the quantized range. here the problem is temporal rather than spatial. previously: \boxed{ \text{one scale is shared by very different values}. } now: \boxed{ \text{one old scale is reused for a very different current tensor}. } so both create: \boxed{ \text{poor use of the available quantization range}. } 5.49.5.9 the important difference between pillar 2 and pillar 5 this is a very useful distinction. pillar 2 — fine-grained quantization question: \boxed{ \text{how large should the region be?} } answer: \text{small groups/blocks}. pillar 5 — online quantization question: \boxed{ \text{when should the scaling factor be measured?} } answer: \text{from the current tensor}. so: \boxed{ \text{pillar 2 = spatial/local adaptation} } while: \boxed{ \text{pillar 5 = temporal/current-step adaptation}. } this is an important conceptual connection that emerges from the source's two sections. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.49.5.10 online quantization now the deepseek solution. the source says: calculate the scaling factor in real time from the current tensor itself. the source's three-step workflow is: \boxed{ 1.\text{ scan current tensor} } \boxed{ 2.\text{ calculate current maximum} } \boxed{ 3.\text{ derive and apply fresh scale} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.49.5.11 step 1 — current tensor arrives suppose: x_t. we do not first consult: x_{t-1}. instead: \boxed{ \text{inspect }x_t. } 5.49.5.12 step 2 — find current maximum compute: \boxed{ \alpha_t=\max_i|x_i|. } suppose: x_t= [-2.1,\;0.4,\;1.7,\;-3.8,\;2.2]. then: |x_t| = [2.1,0.4,1.7,3.8,2.2]. therefore: \boxed{ \alpha_t=3.8. } 5.49.5.13 step 3 — calculate the fresh scale using our symmetric quantization example: s_t=\frac{127}{3.8}. therefore: \boxed{ s_t\approx33.421. } now the current tensor is calibrated specifically for the current dynamic range. 5.49.5.14 step 4 — quantize for: x=-2.1: q = \operatorname{round} (-2.1\times33.421). approximately: -70.18. so: \boxed{-70}. for: x=0.4: 0.4\times33.421 \approx13.37 so: \boxed{13}. for: x=-3.8: -3.8\times33.421 \approx-127 so: \boxed{-127}. notice that the largest current magnitude maps almost exactly to the maximum available representation. 5.49.5.15 why this is “perfectly calibrated” the source uses the phrase that the fresh scaling factor is tailored to the dynamic range of the tensor being processed at that exact moment. claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.46 — distributed moe: expert parallelism, all-to-all communication, pipeline bubbles, and dualpipe plan node: a5 · chat order #87 we have finished the single-gpu mathematical view of moe. now we have to answer the much harder systems question: what happens when the 64, 128, or hundreds of experts do not live on the same gpu? this is where moe changes from primarily a neural-network idea into a distributed-systems problem . the source explicitly explains that large moe models introduce an expensive all-to-all token exchange , because selected experts are distributed across devices. it then motivates deepseek's dualpipe as a scheduling strategy that overlaps this communication with useful computation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.1 first understand the problem suppose we have four gpus: gpu 0 → experts e1 e2 gpu 1 → experts e3 e4 gpu 2 → experts e5 e6 gpu 3 → experts e7 e8 now suppose a token is currently on: gpu_0 but the router selects: e_7. expert 7 is on: gpu_3. therefore the token representation must move: \boxed{ gpu_0\rightarrow gpu_3 } before expert 7 can process it. after expert 7 computes the result, the result must be associated with the original token again. that is the fundamental communication problem. 5.46.2 why can't every gpu simply contain every expert? it could, conceptually. but then each gpu would store: \boxed{\text{the entire moe expert pool}} which largely defeats the memory advantage of distributing experts. remember the deepseek-r1 example: 671b total parameters. a single gpu cannot simply replicate all of those weights. so we distribute the experts across devices. this is the motivation for: \boxed{\text{expert parallelism}} in large moe systems. the source explicitly identifies the combination of expert parallelism + dualpipe-style scheduling as the approach used to train massive moe systems efficiently. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.3 what is expert parallelism? the basic idea is: \boxed{ \text{different gpus own different experts} } for example: n=64 experts and: p=8 gpus. if distributed evenly: 64/8 = \boxed{8} experts per gpu. so: gpu 0 → e1 ... e8 gpu 1 → e9 ... e16 gpu 2 → e17 ... e24 ... gpu 7 → e57 ... e64 the exact production mapping can be more sophisticated, but this is the core concept. 5.46.4 why expert parallelism is attractive without expert parallelism: \text{every gpu} \rightarrow \text{all experts}. with expert parallelism: \text{gpu} \rightarrow \text{its local subset of experts}. therefore expert weights can be partitioned across gpus. so: \boxed{ \text{model memory per gpu decreases} } for the expert portion. but the price is: \boxed{ \text{communication between gpus}. } this is the recurring pattern of distributed deep learning: \boxed{ \text{split memory} \rightarrow \text{introduce communication}. } the source explicitly describes communication as a primary source of overhead in parallel computing. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.5 let's return to our token routing example suppose the current gpu has four tokens: t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4. router decisions: t_1\rightarrow e_1,e_3 t_2\rightarrow e_5,e_6 t_3\rightarrow e_2,e_8 t_4\rightarrow e_7,e_8. suppose: e1,e2 → gpu 0 e3,e4 → gpu 1 e5,e6 → gpu 2 e7,e8 → gpu 3 then: t_1 local: e_1 remote: e_3 t_2 remote: e_5,e_6 t_3 local: e_2 remote: e_8 t_4 remote: e_7,e_8. so many token activations need to leave the current gpu. 5.46.6 the communication happens because routing is dynamic the router computes: topk(x_t). the selected experts depend on: x_t. therefore the system does not know in advance that every token belongs to gpu 2 or gpu 3. the dispatch pattern changes with the data. so communication is: \boxed{\text{dynamic}} rather than a fixed tensor partition. that makes moe more complicated than ordinary layer-based model parallelism. 5.46.7 what does all-to-all mean? suppose we have: p gpus. each gpu may hold tokens that need experts on multiple other gpus. so one communication phase logically looks like: \boxed{ \text{every gpu sends data to every other relevant gpu} } and each gpu receives token representations destined for its local experts. this is an all-to-all communication pattern . the source identifies moe token shuffling between expert devices as an expensive cross-gpu data exchange and specifically calls out all-to-all communication. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.8 two-stage mental model think of distributed moe as: \boxed{ \text{dispatch all-to-all} } followed by: \boxed{ \text{local expert computation} } followed by: \boxed{ \text{combine / return communication} } so: tokens ↓ router ↓ top-k ↓ dispatch all-to-all ↓ tokens grouped by destination gpu ↓ local expert ffns ↓ combine return results to original token locations this is the distributed extension of the index_add_ logic we learned earlier. 5.46.9 communication is not the same as router computation this is important. router computation: xw_r is arithmetic. communication: gpu_i\leftrightarrow gpu_j is data movement. you can have a very cheap router and still have a very expensive moe system because: \boxed{ \text{communication latency/bandwidth} } can dominate. the source explicitly says the moe all-to-all operation can be more time-consuming than the pipeline bubble itself. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.10 a simple communication-volume derivation suppose: t tokens are processed. each token has hidden dimension: d. each token selects: k experts. so the total number of routed token representations is: tk. each representation contains: d numbers. if each number occupies: s bytes, then the total volume of routed representation data is approximately: \boxed{ tkds } bytes. this is the gross routed-data volume before accounting for whether some expert assignments are local, and before accounting for communication protocol overhead. this formula is derived from the tensor dimensions. 5.46.11 numerical communication example suppose: t=8192 tokens, k=8, d=4096, and fp16: s=2\text{ bytes}. then: t k = 8192\times8 = 65,536 routed representations. each is: 4096\times2 = 8192 bytes. therefore gross data volume: 65,536\times8192 = \boxed{536,870,912\text{ bytes}} approximately: \boxed{512\text{ mib}}. that is a lot of data movement for one routing event in this illustrative example. 5.46.12 important qualification the: 512\text{ mib} is not automatically the exact amount sent across the network. some assignments may remain on the same gpu. so: \boxed{ \text{network volume} \le tkds } in an ideal accounting. actual traffic can also include: \text{metadata} + \text{headers} + \text{padding} + \text{collective-operation overhead} depending on implementation. the source does not provide a single universal communication-volume formula, so this calculation is our systems derivation. 5.46.13 why load balancing suddenly becomes even more important previously, load imbalance meant: \boxed{ e_1\text{ has too many tokens} } while: e_2\text{ has too few}. in distributed moe, it additionally means: \boxed{ \text{gpu containing }e_1\text{ becomes a communication/computation hotspot} }. so bad routing causes: \text{expert imbalance} \downarrow \text{gpu imbalance} \downarrow \text{communication/compute bottleneck}. that's why load balancing is both a machine-learning and systems concern. the source's figures explicitly contrast hotspot experts in standard moe with more balanced deepseek-moe routing. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.14 example suppose four gpus receive routed token assignments: [4000,4000,4000,4000]. perfect. now suppose: [7000,5000,2000,2000]. gpu 0 and gpu 1 carry significantly more expert work. even if total work remains: 16,000, the system's throughput can become limited by the busiest devices. this is why: \boxed{ \text{average load} } is not enough. we also care about: \boxed{ \text{maximum load} }. 5.46.15 now connect to the pipeline suppose the transformer has: 8 pipeline stages. these stages are spread across gpus. the source calls a group of layers on one gpu a stage and describes activations flowing from one stage to the next like an assembly line. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) for example: gpu 0 → layers 1–10 gpu 1 → layers 11–20 gpu 2 → layers 21–30 gpu 3 → layers 31–40 gpu 4 → layers 41–50 gpu 5 → layers 51–60 gpu 6 → layers 61–70 gpu 7 → layers 71–80 that's pipeline parallelism. 5.46.16 what is the pipeline bubble? at the beginning: gpu_0 starts computing. but: gpu_1 cannot compute until gpu 0 sends its activation. then gpu 2 waits for gpu 1. and so on. likewise at the end, gpus may become idle while the remaining gradients drain through the pipeline. that idle region is: \boxed{\text{pipeline bubble}}. the source defines the bubble as gpu idle time while waiting for required data or gradients. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.17 naive gpipe suppose: p=4 pipeline stages and: m=8 micro-batches. gpipe essentially fills the pipeline with forward passes and then drains it with backward passes. the source explains that this creates significant idle time at fill/drain boundaries. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.18 pipeline efficiency formula the source gives the illustrative theoretical efficiency: \boxed{ \eta_{\text{pipeline}} \approx \frac{m}{m+(p-1)} } for the simplified equal-time setting used in its discussion. for: m=8,\quad p=4: \eta= \frac8{8+3} = \frac8{11} \approx \boxed{72.7\%}. the source explicitly gives this example as approximately 73%. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.19 what reduces the bubble? increase: m the number of micro-batches. for example: m=8 gives: 8/11\approx72.7\%. if: m=32, then: \frac{32}{32+3} = \frac{32}{35} \approx \boxed{91.4\%}. so: m\uparrow \rightarrow \text{bubble fraction}\downarrow. the source explicitly explains this relationship. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.20 why not simply increase micro-batches forever? because activations must be stored for backward computation. the source explains: gpipe holds activations for many micro-batches during the forward phase. 1f1b reduces this memory pressure by running backward sooner and freeing activations earlier. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) thus: \boxed{ \text{more micro-batches} } helps efficiency but can increase activation-memory requirements. 5.46.21 1f1b schedule the idea is: don't wait until all forwards finish before starting backwards. instead: \boxed{ 1f1b = \text{one forward, one backward} } in the steady state. the source describes the three phases: \boxed{\text{warm-up}} \boxed{\text{steady state}} \boxed{\text{cool-down}}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.22 why 1f1b is better for memory suppose a micro-batch's forward activation is stored. under naive gpipe: \text{many micro-batches} \rightarrow \text{many stored activations}. under 1f1b: \text{forward}(m_i) \rightarrow \text{soon backward}(m_i) \rightarrow \text{free activation}. so peak activation memory is lower. this is why 1f1b allows more micro-batches in practice even though its theoretical bubble efficiency for a fixed m,p can be similar to gpipe. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.23 but 1f1b meets a new problem with moe here's the critical chain: \boxed{ 1f1b } solves: \text{pipeline bubble}. then we add: \boxed{\text{moe}} which introduces: \boxed{\text{all-to-all communication}}. therefore: \boxed{ \text{gpu can still become idle while waiting for expert communication} }. the source explicitly says the all-to-all communication can be even more time-consuming than the pipeline bubble. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.24 this is the engineering progression think: \boxed{ \text{pipeline parallelism} } solves: \text{model too large}. ↓ \boxed{ \text{gpipe} } but creates: \text{bubble}. ↓ \boxed{ 1f1b } reduces: \text{bubble}. ↓ \boxed{ \text{moe} } introduces: \text{all-to-all communication}. ↓ \boxed{ \text{dualpipe} } tries to hide: \boxed{\text{communication inside computation}}. this is one of the most important engineering stories in the entire deepseek architecture. 5.46.25 now understand dualpipe the key idea is: \boxed{ \text{don't let communication happen while compute waits} } instead: \boxed{ \text{communication for one micro-batch} \parallel \text{computation for another} }. the source explicitly says dualpipe schedules communication-heavy all-to-all operations alongside compute-heavy attention/expert operations. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.26 simple timeline imagine: time → ──────────────────────────────────────────── micro-batch a: all-to-all micro-batch b: expert compute micro-batch c: attention micro-batch d: all-to-all instead of: all-to-all ↓ wait ↓ expert ↓ wait ↓ attention we try to overlap them: all-to-all a + expert b + attention c the gpu's compute resources and communication/network resources can work concurrently. that is the central dualpipe idea in the source. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.27 why this works different operations stress different resources. conceptually: expert/attention computation uses: \boxed{\text{gpu compute}} network communication uses: \boxed{\text{network/interconnect}} if the hardware can progress them concurrently, then: t_{\text{total}} can approach the larger of the two costs rather than their sum. suppose: t_c=8\text{ ms} computation, and: t_{comm}=6\text{ ms} communication. sequential: 8+6 = \boxed{14\text{ ms}}. perfect overlap: \max(8,6) = \boxed{8\text{ ms}}. potential hidden communication: 14-8 = \boxed{6\text{ ms}}. the source uses the qualitative idea of “hiding” communication rather than providing this exact numerical formula. this is our systems derivation. 5.46.28 what does “hide communication” actually mean? it does not mean: \boxed{\text{communication takes zero time}}. it means: \boxed{ \text{communication time overlaps with useful computation} } so less of its latency appears on the critical path. this distinction is extremely important in interviews. 5.46.29 fine-grained scheduling the source says dualpipe doesn't merely interleave whole forward and backward passes. it breaks computation into smaller components such as: \boxed{\text{attention}} \boxed{\text{mlp/expert}} \boxed{\text{all-to-all communication}} and schedules them carefully. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) therefore: \boxed{ \text{fine-grained overlap} } is a major part of the innovation. 5.46.30 why the scheduler is complicated because dependencies must still be respected. for example: \text{routing} \rightarrow \text{dispatch} \rightarrow \text{expert compute} must occur in the correct logical order. you cannot arbitrarily reorder: \text{expert compute} before the token has arrived. so the scheduler has to identify operations that are: \boxed{\text{independent enough to overlap}} while preserving: \boxed{\text{data dependencies}}. 5.46.31 dualpipe and backward computation the source describes blocks such as: \boxed{\text{forward}} and: \boxed{\text{backward for weights}} being overlapped with communication and with computation from another micro-batch. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so a simplified picture is: micro-batch a: communication micro-batch b: forward compute micro-batch c: backward compute micro-batch d: expert compute the scheduler interleaves these at a fine granularity. 5.46.32 pipeline folding dualpipe introduces another idea: \boxed{\text{folding the pipeline}} instead of: gpu 0 → stage 0 gpu 1 → stage 1 gpu 2 → stage 2 gpu 3 → stage 3 gpu 4 → stage 4 gpu 5 → stage 5 gpu 6 → stage 6 gpu 7 → stage 7 the folded arrangement puts two distant stages on each gpu. for eight stages and four gpus, the source gives: gpu_0:\ stage\ 0,\ stage\ 7 gpu_1:\ stage\ 1,\ stage\ 6 gpu_2:\ stage\ 2,\ stage\ 5 gpu_3:\ stage\ 3,\ stage\ 4. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.33 why this creates a v-shape suppose a micro-batch travels: stage\ 0 \rightarrow stage\ 1 \rightarrow stage\ 2 \rightarrow stage\ 3 then turns: stage\ 4 on the same physical gpu that owns stage 3. then: stage\ 4 \rightarrow stage\ 5 \rightarrow stage\ 6 \rightarrow stage\ 7. so physically it travels: \boxed{ down \rightarrow turn \rightarrow up } forming a: \boxed{v}. the source calls this: \boxed{\text{dualpipev / v-shape / cut-in-half}}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.34 why is this useful? the source says the v-shaped variant can run an: n\text{-stage pipeline} using only: \boxed{n/2} physical gpus. so: 8\text{ stages} \rightarrow 4\text{ gpus}. but there is an explicit trade-off: each gpu holds: \boxed{2\times} the parameter memory of a conventional one-stage-per-gpu layout. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.46.35 numerical: folded pipeline suppose: n=16 stages. dualpipev can, in the source's simplified description, use: 16/2 = \boxed{8\text{ physical gpus}}. but each gpu holds two stages. therefore parameter memory per gpu is approximately: \boxed{2\times} the standard one-stage-per-gpu arrangement. so: \boxed{ \text{gpu count}\downarrow \quad\text{but}\quad \text{per-gpu parameter memory}\uparrow }. this is a deliberate trade-off. 5.46.36 why would deepseek accept that trade-off? because the source says other techniques already help reduce per-gpu parameter memory, including: \boxed{\text{fp8}} and: \boxed{\text{expert parallelism}}. so the system can trade additional parameter memory for: \boxed{ \text{better utilization} + \text{better communication hiding} }. the source explicitly frames this as an engineering trade-off. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.1 first: one gpu is not enough our deepseek-style model contains: \boxed{\text{mla}} \boxed{\text{moe}} and potentially hundreds of billions of parameters. the source's deepseek-r1 example has: 671b total parameters and: 37b active per token. yet the entire model weights still need to remain available. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so we need multiple gpus. but there are several ways to distribute the workload. 5.47.2 the first distinction: split data or split model? there are two fundamental approaches in the source: \boxed{\text{data parallelism}} and: \boxed{\text{model parallelism}}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the difference is extremely simple: data parallelism keep copies of the model, split the data. model parallelism split the model itself across gpus. 5.47.3 data parallelism suppose you have: 4 gpus. instead of processing one batch on one gpu: batch ↓ gpu 0 we split the batch: batch / | | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ gpu0 gpu1 gpu2 gpu3 each gpu owns a replica of the model. the source explicitly describes data parallelism this way: replicate the model and give each device a different shard of the batch. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.4 why data parallelism speeds training suppose one gpu takes: 100\text{ ms} to process: 32 examples. four gpus can process: 4\times32=128 examples approximately concurrently, subject to communication and scaling efficiency. so throughput can approach: \boxed{4\times} in the ideal case. but there is a major problem. 5.47.5 the data-parallel memory problem every gpu has a full copy of: \boxed{\text{the model}}. if the model is: 671b parameters, replicating it on every gpu is obviously impossible. the source explicitly says ddp does not solve the model-memory problem because every gpu contains the full model. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) thus: \boxed{ \text{ddp solves throughput} } but not: \boxed{ \text{model-too-large} }. 5.47.6 gradient accumulation before moving into model parallelism, the source introduces gradient accumulation . suppose your desired effective batch is: b_{\text{eff}}=64 but your gpu can only fit: b_{\text{physical}}=16. then: n_{\text{acc}} = \frac{64}{16} = \boxed{4}. the source derives this relationship explicitly. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.7 why gradient accumulation works for a batch of b examples: g_{\text{batch}} = \frac1b \sum_{i=1}^{b}g_i. instead of calculating all gradients at once, divide the batch into chunks. suppose: g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4 are the gradients for four mini-batches. then accumulate: g_{\text{acc}} = g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4 with appropriate normalization. then perform one optimizer update. the source emphasizes that this lets a smaller physical batch simulate a larger effective batch without requiring all examples simultaneously in vram. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.8 numerical physical batch: 16 accumulation steps: 4. effective batch: 16\times4 = \boxed{64}. another example: b_{\text{physical}}=8 and: n_{\text{acc}}=16. then: \boxed{ b_{\text{effective}}=128. } 5.47.9 important distinction gradient accumulation does not mean: \boxed{\text{the gpu suddenly has more vram}}. it means: \boxed{ \text{process smaller pieces sequentially} } instead of: \boxed{ \text{process the entire effective batch simultaneously}. } so: \boxed{ \text{memory}\downarrow } but: \boxed{ \text{number of forward/backward iterations}\uparrow }. 5.47.10 now model parallelism suppose the model itself is too large for one gpu. then: \boxed{ \text{split the model}. } the source describes this as model parallelism . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) two major forms in the source's discussion are: \boxed{\text{pipeline parallelism}} and other forms such as tensor/model splitting. for the deepseek story, pipeline parallelism and expert parallelism are particularly important. 5.47.11 pipeline parallelism suppose there are: 8 transformer stages. split them across: 8 gpus: gpu0 → stage 0 gpu1 → stage 1 gpu2 → stage 2 gpu3 → stage 3 gpu4 → stage 4 gpu5 → stage 5 gpu6 → stage 6 gpu7 → stage 7 a batch enters gpu 0. its activation flows: gpu_0 \rightarrow gpu_1 \rightarrow gpu_2 \rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow gpu_7. the source compares this to an assembly line. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.12 why micro-batches are necessary suppose the whole batch is treated as one unit. then the pipeline becomes: gpu0: █████ gpu1: █████ gpu2: █████ gpu3: █████ ... most gpus spend much of the time waiting. to keep the pipeline active, split the batch into: m micro-batches. example: b=64 could be split into: m=8 micro-batches of: 8 samples each. 5.47.13 the pipeline idea instead of: m_1 moving through all 8 stages before: m_2 starts, we pipeline them: time → gpu0: m1 m2 m3 m4 m5 ... gpu1: m1 m2 m3 m4 ... gpu2: m1 m2 m3 ... gpu3: m1 m2 ... ... this is what makes pipeline parallelism useful. 5.47.14 the problem: pipeline bubble at the beginning: gpu_0 starts first. other gpus must wait. at the end: later gpus finish before earlier gpus have fully drained. this creates: \boxed{\text{pipeline bubble}}. the source defines this as idle time while stages wait for activations or gradients. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.15 bubble formula in the simplified equal-time model used by the source: \boxed{ \eta_{\text{pipeline}} = \frac{m}{m+(p-1)} } where: m = number of micro-batches, p = number of pipeline stages. the source gives the example: m=8,\quad p=4. thus: \eta= \frac8{8+3} = \frac8{11} \approx \boxed{72.7\%}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.16 numerical: increase micro-batches suppose: p=4. m=8 \eta= \frac8{11} = 72.7\%. m=32 \eta= \frac{32}{35} = \boxed{91.4\%}. m=128 \eta= \frac{128}{131} = \boxed{97.7\%}. so: \boxed{ m\uparrow \rightarrow \text{bubble fraction}\downarrow. } 5.47.17 why not just use enormous m ? because each forward pass creates activations needed by backward. the source explains that naive gpipe can require holding activations from many micro-batches, increasing memory usage. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so: m\uparrow helps: \text{pipeline efficiency} but can hurt: \text{activation memory}. 5.47.18 1f1b the source then introduces the 1f1b schedule . the core principle: \boxed{ \text{don't run all forwards first.} } instead: \boxed{ \text{forward one micro-batch, then backward another as soon as dependencies allow.} } the schedule has: \boxed{\text{warm-up}} \boxed{\text{steady state}} \boxed{\text{cool-down}}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.19 why 1f1b matters suppose gpu 2 finishes the forward pass of: m_3. rather than waiting for: m_4,m_5,\ldots to finish their forwards, it can begin useful backward work once the necessary downstream gradients are available. therefore the gpu spends less time holding unused activations. this makes 1f1b much more memory-efficient than naive gpipe. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.20 so far the progression is \boxed{\text{pipeline parallelism}} solves: \text{model too large}. but creates: \boxed{\text{pipeline bubble}}. then: \boxed{\text{1f1b}} reduces the practical impact of that bubble and lowers activation-memory pressure. but then deepseek adds: \boxed{\text{moe}}. and now we discover another bottleneck. 5.47.21 expert parallelism remember our distributed experts: gpu0 → e1,e2 gpu1 → e3,e4 gpu2 → e5,e6 gpu3 → e7,e8 a token may be on gpu 0 but select: e_7. therefore: \boxed{ \text{token must move across gpus} }. that is: \boxed{\text{expert parallelism + all-to-all communication}}. the source explicitly identifies distributed experts and this cross-gpu token exchange as the moe scaling problem. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.22 why 1f1b is no longer enough imagine: t_{\text{compute}}=8\text{ ms} and: t_{\text{all-to-all}}=10\text{ ms}. suppose 1f1b schedules compute normally. a gpu can now spend: 10\text{ ms} waiting for communication. so even though we solved the traditional pipeline bubble, we have reintroduced idle time through communication. the source explicitly states that moe all-to-all communication can become more expensive than the pipeline bubble itself. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.23 this is the central deepseek systems problem we now have: \boxed{ \text{pipeline bubble} } and: \boxed{ \text{moe communication} }. we need a schedule that handles both. this leads to: \boxed{\text{dualpipe}}. 5.47.24 dualpipe's central idea suppose: a = \text{communication}. and: b = \text{computation}. naive: a\rightarrow b. time: t_a+t_b. dualpipe tries to arrange: \boxed{ a\parallel b } for operations belonging to different micro-batches. ideal time: \boxed{ \max(t_a,t_b) } rather than: t_a+t_b. the source describes exactly this fine-grained overlap of communication-heavy and compute-heavy operations. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.47.25 numerical suppose: t_{\text{comm}}=12\text{ ms} and: t_{\text{compute}}=8\text{ ms}. sequential: 12+8 = \boxed{20\text{ ms}}. ideal overlap: \max(12,8) = \boxed{12\text{ ms}}. potential speedup: 20/12 = \boxed{1.67\times}. potentially hidden communication: 20-12 = \boxed{8\text{ ms}}. this is an idealized calculation. 5.47.26 what exactly is overlapped? the source says dualpipe breaks large operations into finer pieces such as: \boxed{\text{attention}} \boxed{\text{mlp / expert}} \boxed{\text{all-to-all}} and schedules them against one another. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so the scheduler may conceptually arrange: micro-batch 1 → all-to-all micro-batch 2 → expert compute micro-batch 3 → attention micro-batch 4 → backward at overlapping times where dependencies permit. 5.47.27 why “fine-grained” matters suppose the scheduler only knows: \text{whole forward pass} and: \text{whole backward pass}. it has relatively few opportunities to overlap communication. instead, break the computation into: \text{attention} \rightarrow \text{dispatch} \rightarrow \text{expert} \rightarrow \text{combine} and backward components. now the scheduler has much finer opportunities to place independent work in communication gaps. this is the source's main scheduling insight. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the important constraint is: \boxed{\text{the whole physical mini-batch must fit in gpu vram}} that becomes a problem for large models or large batches. 2. why do we want large batches? suppose we have 64 training examples. a standard batch computes: g_{\text{batch}} = \frac{1}{64} \left( g_1+g_2+\cdots+g_{64} \right) where: g_i=\nabla_\theta l(x_i). the gradient is therefore an average over many examples. the source explains that using more examples can give a more stable gradient and reduce the noise in individual updates. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) but there is a problem: 64 examples ↓ forward ↓ backward may require more vram than the gpu has. 3. the central insight this is the key idea of gradient accumulation: we don't necessarily need to have all 64 examples in gpu memory at the same time. instead, split them into smaller chunks. for example: 64=4\times16. so: effective batch = 64 ┌────────┐ │ 16 │ ├────────┤ │ 16 │ ├────────┤ │ 16 │ ├────────┤ │ 16 │ └────────┘ each physical batch has only 16 examples. 4. what changes? normally: loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zero_grad() happens every batch. with gradient accumulation: batch 1 → backward batch 2 → backward batch 3 → backward batch 4 → backward ↓ optimizer.step() ↓ zero_grad() the critical change is: \boxed{ \text{do backward multiple times before step()} } and: \boxed{ \text{do not zero the gradients between accumulation steps}. } pytorch naturally adds new gradients to the existing .grad values when zero_grad() has not been called. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5. why divide the loss? the source's implementation uses: loss = loss / accumulation_steps for: accumulation\_steps=4, each loss is divided by 4. why? suppose the four physical batches produce gradients: g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4. we want the effective batch gradient to represent their average: \boxed{ g_{\text{effective}} = \frac{g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4}{4} } dividing each loss by 4 causes its corresponding gradient to also be divided by 4: \frac{g_1}{4} + \frac{g_2}{4} + \frac{g_3}{4} + \frac{g_4}{4} = \frac{g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4}{4}. so the accumulated gradient corresponds to the desired effective batch average. this normalization is explicitly shown in the source's gradient-accumulation code. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 8. iteration 2 second batch gives: \frac{g_2}{4}. pytorch adds this to the existing gradient: \frac{g_1}{4}+\frac{g_2}{4}. therefore: \boxed{ \frac{g_1+g_2}{4} } is now stored. 9. iteration 3 another backward pass adds: \frac{g_3}{4}. stored gradient becomes: \frac{g_1+g_2+g_3}{4}. 10. iteration 4 fourth batch adds: \frac{g_4}{4}. now: \boxed{ \frac{g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4}{4} } is stored. the condition: (i + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0 becomes true because: (3+1)\%4=0. so now: optimizer.step() runs. the source describes this as producing an update equivalent to using the effective batch of 64 while only having 16 examples resident at a time. claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. r101.2 — data parallelism: using multiple gpus to make training faster plan node: a5 · chat order #114 we have just seen gradient accumulation solve one problem: \boxed{\text{gpu memory limitation}} but it creates a new realization: even when we can fit the model and batch, training may still be too slow. the source now introduces data parallelism as the first major multi-gpu strategy. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1. the problem changes suppose one gpu can process: 16\text{ samples} per training operation. with one gpu: gpu 0 ↓ 16 samples ↓ forward ↓ backward then it processes the next batch. so computation happens sequentially. the obvious question is: \boxed{ \text{can several gpus process different data at the same time?} } yes. that is the core idea of data parallelism . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 2. what does "data parallel" actually mean? the key is: \boxed{ \text{same model, different data} } suppose we have four gpus. we create: gpu 0 → model copy 0 gpu 1 → model copy 1 gpu 2 → model copy 2 gpu 3 → model copy 3 each model copy has the same parameters . but each gpu receives a different part of the batch: global batch │ ┌────┼────┬────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ gpu0 gpu1 gpu2 gpu3 16 16 16 16 the source describes exactly this arrangement: split the batch across gpus while each gpu holds an identical copy of the entire model. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 3. what happens on each gpu? each gpu independently performs: \boxed{ \text{forward} \rightarrow \text{loss} \rightarrow \text{backward} } for example: gpu 0: data a → model → gradients a gpu 1: data b → model → gradients b gpu 2: data c → model → gradients c gpu 3: data d → model → gradients d this happens in parallel . so rather than waiting for gpu 0 to finish before beginning gpu 1, all gpus work simultaneously. 4. but now we have a problem each gpu has calculated a different gradient. for example: g_0,\quad g_1,\quad g_2,\quad g_3. if gpu 0 updates using only g_0 , while gpu 1 updates using only g_1 , the models would start moving in different directions. then: gpu 0 model ≠ gpu 1 model which is not what we want. we want every gpu to apply the same global gradient. 5. the solution: synchronize gradients the source explains that after the local backward passes, gradients are: \boxed{\text{gathered, aggregated, and averaged}} across gpus. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) conceptually: g_{\text{global}} = \frac{ g_0+g_1+g_2+g_3 }{4}. then every gpu uses: g_{\text{global}} to update its local model. 6. full data parallel workflow the source's conceptual workflow is: global batch │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ gpu 0 gpu 1 gpu 2 ... gpu n model model model copy 0 copy 1 copy 2 │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ forward forward forward │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ backward backward backward │ │ │ └───────────┼───────────┘ ▼ gradient averaging │ ▼ same update │ ▼ synchronized models (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 7. why does this make training faster? suppose one gpu needs: t seconds to process its mini-batch. with four gpus, four different mini-batches can be processed approximately simultaneously. ideally: \boxed{ \text{throughput}\approx4\times } compared with one gpu. the exact speedup will not be perfectly linear because communication and other overheads exist, but the source presents data parallelism as the direct "more gpus, less time" approach. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 8. very important: data parallelism does not make the model smaller this is one of the most important interview points. suppose the model requires: 20\text{ gb} of memory. in 4-gpu data parallelism: gpu 0 → 20 gb model gpu 1 → 20 gb model gpu 2 → 20 gb model gpu 3 → 20 gb model so the model is replicated . we have not split its parameters. therefore: \boxed{ \text{data parallelism solves throughput, not model-size memory.} } this distinction becomes crucial later when the source introduces model parallelism. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 9. two pytorch approaches in the source the source introduces two implementations: \boxed{\texttt{nn.dataparallel}} and: \boxed{\texttt{nn.distributeddataparallel}} or: \boxed{\text{dp vs ddp}}. it describes dp as the older and simpler approach, while ddp is the modern industry-standard approach for serious large-scale training. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) we need to understand why . 10. nn.dataparallel — the centralized design think of dp as: main gpu gpu 0 │ ┌────────┼────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ gpu 1 gpu 2 gpu 3 gpu 0 acts as the central coordinator. the source gives a five-stage flow. 11. dp step 1 — scatter the full batch is initially loaded on the main gpu. then gpu 0 scatters chunks of the batch to the other gpus. for example: full batch = 64 gpu 0 → 16 gpu 1 → 16 gpu 2 → 16 gpu 3 → 16 (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 12. dp step 2 — parallel forward pass each gpu runs a forward pass using its local data chunk. gpu 0 → forward(batch0) gpu 1 → forward(batch1) gpu 2 → forward(batch2) gpu 3 → forward(batch3) so far this looks good. 13. dp step 3 — gather here is where the centralized design starts hurting. the outputs from the gpus are sent back to gpu 0. conceptually: gpu 1 ──┐ gpu 2 ──┼──→ gpu 0 gpu 3 ──┘ the source says the logits are gathered back to the main gpu. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 14. dp step 4 — centralized computation gpu 0 now performs the centralized loss/backward work described by the source. so gpu 0 is handling much more responsibility: gpu 0: - receives the data - distributes the data - gathers outputs - computes centralized work - updates weights while the other gpus have a much simpler role. this creates the fundamental bottleneck. 15. dp step 5 — replicate the updated model again after gpu 0 updates its model, the newly updated model has to be replicated out to the other gpus for the next forward pass. so the cycle becomes: gpu 0 ↓ scatter ↓ other gpus ↓ forward ↓ gather ↓ gpu 0 ↓ update ↓ copy model again ↓ repeat (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 16. why is dp bad for large-scale llm training? the source identifies two major problems. problem 1 — central bottleneck gpu 0 does substantially more work. problem 2 — communication bottleneck a lot of communication is funneled through one main gpu. therefore: \boxed{ \text{poor load balance} + \text{communication bottleneck} \rightarrow \text{poor scalability} } the source consequently says dp is rarely used for modern large-scale training. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 17. dp vs single gpu let's make the distinction very concrete. single gpu data ↓ gpu ↓ model ↓ gradient ↓ update dataparallel gpu 0 / | \ / | \ ▼ ▼ ▼ gpu1 gpu2 gpu3 │ ▼ gather │ ▼ gpu0 │ update the multiple gpus exist, but gpu 0 remains the boss. 18. why ddp is fundamentally different the source introduces ddp as a decentralized model. instead of: \boxed{\text{one boss gpu}} we have: \boxed{\text{peer gpus}} each gpu has: its own process, its own model copy, its own optimizer, its own data shard. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this is the key conceptual leap. 19. ddp architecture instead of: gpu 0 / \ gpu 1 gpu 2 | gpu 3 think: gpu 0 ↔ gpu 1 ↕ ↕ gpu 2 ↔ gpu 3 there is no central "boss" gpu. the source describes each gpu as an independent peer/process. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 20. ddp step 1 — one process per gpu each gpu gets its own process. so with four gpus: process 0 → gpu 0 process 1 → gpu 1 process 2 → gpu 2 process 3 → gpu 3 each process owns its local copy of the model. 21. ddp step 2 — shard the data each process gets its own unique data slice. so: dataset │ ├── process 0 → shard 0 ├── process 1 → shard 1 ├── process 2 → shard 2 └── process 3 → shard 3 there is no central gpu distributing the batch every iteration. the source uses distributedsampler for this partitioning. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 22. ddp step 3 — local forward + backward each process independently computes: l_0,l_1,l_2,l_3 and: g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3. so: gpu 0 → local forward/backward gpu 1 → local forward/backward gpu 2 → local forward/backward gpu 3 → local forward/backward everything is happening in parallel. 23. ddp step 4 — all-reduce this is the heart of ddp. the source calls out all-reduce as the core communication mechanism. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) conceptually: g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3 are combined into: \boxed{ g_{\text{avg}} = \frac{g_0+g_1+g_2+g_3}{4} } and every process ends up with the same averaged gradient. 24. why is all-reduce better? because we no longer make gpu 0 do all the communication. instead, the gpus participate as peers. the source mentions efficient communication algorithms such as ring-allreduce and explains that communication can be overlapped with backward computation, hiding some communication latency. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this gives: \boxed{ \text{better utilization} + \text{less central bottleneck} } 25. ddp step 5 — every gpu updates locally once every gpu has the same averaged gradient: g_{\text{avg}}, each process can independently execute: optimizer.step() because every gpu started with the same parameters and has the same gradient. therefore: \theta_0' = \theta_1' = \theta_2' = \theta_3'. the replicas remain synchronized. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 26. this gives us the key ddp invariant after synchronization: \boxed{ \text{all model replicas have identical weights} } that invariant must continue after every optimizer update. otherwise the replicas would diverge. 27. dp vs ddp — the interview table property dataparallel (dp) distributeddataparallel (ddp) model copies one per gpu one per gpu architecture centralized decentralized processes central mechanism one process/gpu data distribution main gpu scatters distributed sampler gradient synchronization centralized all-reduce main bottleneck main gpu much better balanced scalability poorer much better source's recommendation older/simple modern/industry-standard (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 28. the most important distinction so far remember these three ideas: \boxed{ \text{gradient accumulation} } means: same gpu(s), process several small batches before one optimizer update. \boxed{ \text{data parallelism} } means: replicate the model and split the data across gpus. \boxed{ \text{model parallelism} } means: split the model itself across gpus. the first two solve different bottlenecks.

claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. r101.3 — model parallelism: when the model itself does not fit plan node: a5 · chat order #115 we now hit the limitation of ddp. ddp solved: \boxed{\text{“training is too slow”}} by using multiple gpus. gradient accumulation solved: \boxed{\text{“my desired batch is too large”}} but ddp makes a complete copy of the model on every gpu . so if the model itself cannot fit on one gpu, ddp cannot solve the problem. the source gives the example of a 671b-parameter deepseek-v3-class model, whose half-precision weights alone require hundreds of gb of memory. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) that leads to: \boxed{\text{model parallelism}} instead of splitting the data , we split the model across gpus. 1. data parallelism vs model parallelism this distinction must be absolutely clear. data parallelism same full model ┌────────┬────────┬────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ gpu 0 gpu 1 gpu 2 gpu 3 data data data data a b c d every gpu stores the whole model. model parallelism one model │ ┌────┼────┬────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ gpu0 gpu1 gpu2 gpu3 part part part part the model itself is divided. the source frames this as the fundamental distinction: data parallelism accelerates by splitting data; model parallelism bypasses hardware memory limits by splitting the model. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 2. why can the model exceed gpu memory? the vram requirement isn't only the model's parameters. during training we may need memory for: \text{weights} + \text{gradients} + \text{optimizer states} + \text{activations}. the source specifically emphasizes that parameters, gradients, and optimizer states can collectively exceed one gpu's vram. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so imagine: \text{required memory}=200\text{ gb} but: \text{one gpu}=80\text{ gb}. then: 200>80. no amount of ordinary ddp replication fixes this. 3. the key idea: split the computation the source next introduces pipeline parallelism , the most intuitive form of model parallelism discussed here. instead of splitting the inside of one layer, we split the model between layers . suppose our transformer has 80 layers: layer 1 layer 2 ... layer 80 we can partition it into stages: gpu 0 → layers 1–20 gpu 1 → layers 21–40 gpu 2 → layers 41–60 gpu 3 → layers 61–80 the source describes these groups as stages , with activations flowing from one stage to the next like an assembly line. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 4. why is it called pipeline parallelism? because data moves through the stages sequentially. for one micro-batch: x \rightarrow stage_0 \rightarrow stage_1 \rightarrow stage_2 \rightarrow stage_3. visually: micro-batch │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ gpu 0 │ stage 0 │ layers │ └────┬────┘ │ activation ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ gpu 1 │ stage 1 └────┬────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ gpu 2 │ stage 2 └────┬────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ gpu 3 │ stage 3 └─────────┘ so the model can be larger than one gpu because no single gpu has to hold all the layers. 5. three terms you must know the source defines several terms before discussing schedules. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) communication whenever gpus exchange tensors. for example: gpu_0\rightarrow gpu_1. the source identifies communication as a major source of overhead. micro-batch a large batch can be divided into smaller chunks. for example: 32 \rightarrow 4+4+4+4+4+4+4+4. those chunks are micro-batches . they become especially important for pipeline parallelism. stage a portion of the model assigned to a gpu. for example: stage_0=\text{layers 1–20}. 6. the most important term: pipeline bubble this is the concept you should remember most strongly. imagine four gpus: gpu 0 → stage 0 gpu 1 → stage 1 gpu 2 → stage 2 gpu 3 → stage 3 a micro-batch starts at gpu 0. gpu 1 cannot work until gpu 0 sends its activation. gpu 2 must wait for gpu 1. gpu 3 must wait for gpu 2. therefore, at the beginning: time → gpu 0 █████ gpu 1 █████ gpu 2 █████ gpu 3 █████ the blank spaces are gpus doing nothing. that idle region is the: \boxed{\text{pipeline bubble}} the source defines the bubble as gpu idle time while waiting for data from a previous stage during forward propagation or for gradients from a later stage during backward propagation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 7. why micro-batches are necessary suppose we have one large batch. we don't want: gpu 0 → entire batch ↓ gpu 1 ↓ gpu 2 ↓ gpu 3 because then downstream gpus sit idle for too long. instead, break the batch into micro-batches: m_1,m_2,m_3,m_4,\ldots then pipeline them: gpu0 gpu1 gpu2 gpu3 m1 f f f f m2 f f f m3 f f m4 f eventually, several gpus are simultaneously processing different micro-batches. that is the point of pipeline parallelism. 8. the naive schedule: gpipe the source next discusses the original gpipe-style schedule. the basic process has a fill phase . all micro-batches are sent forward through the pipeline. for example: time → gpu0 m1f m2f m3f m4f gpu1 m1f m2f m3f m4f gpu2 m1f m2f m3f m4f gpu3 m1f m2f m3f m4f notice what happens. gpu 3 is initially doing nothing. gpu 2 is initially doing nothing. gpu 1 is initially doing nothing. this is the fill bubble . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 9. then comes the backward pass once all forward passes have happened, the pipeline must perform backward propagation. conceptually: forward: gpu0 → gpu1 → gpu2 → gpu3 backward: gpu3 → gpu2 → gpu1 → gpu0 this creates another period where some gpus are idle. the source calls this the drain phase . so gpipe effectively has: \boxed{ \text{fill bubble} + \text{drain bubble} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 10. why is the bubble bad? suppose you have expensive gpus. during the bubble: gpu 0 → work gpu 1 → idle gpu 2 → idle gpu 3 → idle you paid for four gpus, but only one is doing useful computation. the source emphasizes that this makes the naive pipeline inefficient, especially as the number of pipeline stages increases. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 11. a numerical example from the source the source gives: 8\text{ micro-batches} and: 4\text{ stages}. the bubble size is: 4-1=3. the theoretical pipeline efficiency is: \frac{8}{8+3} \approx \boxed{73\%}. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this means, in this simplified analysis, only about 73% of the schedule is useful pipeline computation. the remaining fraction corresponds to pipeline overhead/bubble. 12. a very useful intuition the number of stages hurts us. suppose: s=4. then the bubble component is: s-1=3. if: s=8, the corresponding fill/drain overhead becomes larger. therefore: \boxed{ \text{more stages} \rightarrow \text{larger relative bubble} } unless we use better scheduling and enough micro-batches. the source explicitly states that the naive bubble grows with the number of pipeline stages. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 13. the clever idea: 1f1b now the source asks the natural question: why run all forwards first and only then do backwards? once a micro-batch has completed enough forward computation and its gradient becomes available later in the pipeline, we can start doing its backward work while other micro-batches are still moving forward. that gives: \boxed{ \text{1f1b = one forward, one backward} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 14. the 1f1b intuition instead of: ffff ffff ffff then bbbb bbbb bbbb we do something like: f → b → f → b → f → b during the steady state. the source describes the core intuition exactly this way: why wait to finish all forwards before starting backward? start backward as soon as an appropriate gradient is available. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 15. 1f1b has three phases the source describes three phases. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) phase 1 — warm-up the pipeline is being filled. some gpus still have to wait. gpu0: f gpu1: idle → f gpu2: idle → idle → f ... this is the initial bubble. phase 2 — steady state now things become much denser. a gpu alternates between forward and backward work: \boxed{ f\rightarrow b\rightarrow f\rightarrow b\rightarrow\cdots } this keeps the gpus occupied for much more of the training step. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) phase 3 — cool-down eventually all forward passes are finished, but some backward work remains. so the pipeline drains. there is a smaller ending bubble. 16. gpipe vs 1f1b conceptually: gpipe: f f f f f f f f b b b b b b b b 1f1b: f f f b f b f b b f b f b the exact timeline depends on stage and micro-batch, but the critical difference is: \boxed{ \text{1f1b interleaves forward and backward work} } instead of separating them into long uninterrupted phases. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 17. a subtle but important point the source makes an excellent distinction: for a fixed number of stages and micro-batches , gpipe and 1f1b can have the same theoretical pipeline efficiency. yet 1f1b is practically superior. why? \boxed{\text{memory}} (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 18. why 1f1b uses memory better during forward propagation, intermediate activations must be retained because backward propagation needs them. in gpipe: forward m1 → store activation forward m2 → store activation forward m3 → store activation ... forward mn → store activation so many activations may remain in memory simultaneously. in 1f1b: forward mi ↓ store activation ↓ backward mi ↓ discard activation the source describes this as a first-in, first-out pattern that reduces peak activation memory. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) therefore 1f1b can often fit more micro-batches within the same vram budget . and more micro-batches means: \boxed{ \text{smaller relative bubble} } because the steady-state portion becomes longer. 19. this is the engineering progression look at what has happened. we started with: ddp problem: \text{training too slow} solution: \text{more gpus + replicated model}. but: \text{model must fit on every gpu}. so we move to: pipeline parallelism problem: \text{model too large for one gpu}. solution: \text{split layers across gpus}. but: \text{pipeline bubble}. so we move to: 1f1b problem: \text{pipeline bubble}. solution: \text{interleave forward/backward}. but now the deepseek-specific issue appears: \boxed{\text{moe all-to-all communication}} which becomes the next major bottleneck. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 20. why moe changes everything we already learned that in deepseek-style moe, different tokens can be routed to different experts. when experts are distributed across gpus, tokens may need to move between devices. conceptually: gpu 0 experts a b gpu 1 experts c d gpu 2 experts e f gpu 3 experts g h a token currently on gpu 0 might be routed to an expert on gpu 3. so we need cross-gpu communication: \boxed{\text{all-to-all}} the source explains that this token shuffling can become so expensive for huge moe models that its cost can exceed the pipeline bubble itself. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) and this is precisely where the next innovation enters: \boxed{\textbf{dualpipe}} 21. final mental model keep this hierarchy in your head: scaling training │ ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐ │ │ data parallelism model parallelism split data split model │ │ ddp pipeline parallelism │ gpipe │ pipeline bubble │ 1f1b │ reduces practical waste │ but moe introduces expensive all-to-all │ ▼ dualpipe that is the exact engineering story the source is building toward. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) one-line exam memory \boxed{ ddp:\ \text{replicate model, split data} } \boxed{ pipeline:\ \text{split model by layers} } \boxed{ gpipe:\ \text{simple pipeline, large bubble} } \boxed{ 1f1b:\ \text{interleave forward/backward, better memory utilization} } \boxed{ moe:\ \text{all-to-all becomes the next bottleneck} }

(source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1. why 1f1b is no longer enough recall what 1f1b does: forward → backward → forward → backward this keeps the pipeline busy. but now imagine an moe layer. a token arrives at gpu 0, but its selected expert may live on gpu 3: gpu 0 token │ │ routed to expert 7 ▼ gpu 3 expert 7 the token must physically move. so the system has to perform communication such as: \boxed{\text{all-to-all}} across the gpus. the source describes this as dynamically reorganizing and moving tokens to the devices hosting their selected experts. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 2. the new idle-time problem suppose the computation has finished but the required tokens have not arrived: compute ↓ wait for communication ↓ expert computation the gpu may have powerful compute hardware sitting idle while networking/communication finishes. so now we have: old problem: gpu idle because pipeline isn't filled. new problem: gpu idle because moe communication hasn't finished. thus: \boxed{ \text{1f1b solves pipeline bubble} \neq \text{1f1b solves communication latency} } the source explicitly says vanilla 1f1b cannot hide this moe communication cost. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 3. deepseek's question the source essentially asks: can we schedule computation so that while communication is happening for one piece of work, useful computation happens for another? that is the key idea. instead of: communication ↓ wait ↓ compute we want: communication ─────────────── compute ──────────── at the same time. this is: \boxed{ \text{computation–communication overlap} } and this is the central innovation of dualpipe. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 4. first innovation: pipeline folding the first structural change is called pipeline folding in the source's explanation. a normal pipeline has stages assigned sequentially: gpu 0 → stage 0 gpu 1 → stage 1 gpu 2 → stage 2 gpu 3 → stage 3 gpu 4 → stage 4 gpu 5 → stage 5 gpu 6 → stage 6 gpu 7 → stage 7 every gpu has one contiguous portion. dualpipe rearranges this. one physical gpu holds: \boxed{\text{one early stage + one late stage}} the source gives this example for 8 stages and 4 physical gpus. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5. the folded mapping the source's mapping is: rank 0: stage 0 + stage 7 rank 1: stage 1 + stage 6 rank 2: stage 2 + stage 5 rank 3: stage 3 + stage 4 so instead of: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 being eight separate physical devices, we have: gpu 0: [0 ............... 7] gpu 1: [1 ........... 6] gpu 2: [2 ....... 5] gpu 3: [3 ... 4] this is why the pipeline looks folded . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 6. why is this useful? because now the physical device near one end of the pipeline also owns a stage from the opposite end. this creates much more flexibility in scheduling. the model is no longer simply: gpu0 → gpu1 → gpu2 → gpu3 → gpu4 → ... instead, execution can be arranged around a folded topology. that is the structural foundation for the later v-shape schedule. 7. full dualpipe is more than folding there is an important source distinction here. the source says the deepseek paper's full dualpipe uses a true bidirectional schedule with two data streams . but the book chooses to focus on a more intuitive variant: \boxed{\text{dualpipev}} also called: \boxed{\text{v-shape / cut-in-half}} schedule. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so don't treat the names as completely interchangeable. for our learning sequence: \boxed{ \text{dualpipe idea} \rightarrow \text{dualpipev practical/intuitive variant} } 8. the second innovation: fine-grained scheduling this is perhaps the most important conceptual part. 1f1b essentially thinks in fairly large units: forward backward forward backward dualpipe breaks those operations into smaller pieces. the source explicitly identifies components such as: attention mlp / expert computation all-to-all communication and schedules them more finely. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so rather than treating: \text{forward} as one indivisible block, the scheduler can reason about its internal components. 9. why this matters suppose micro-batch m_1 is waiting on: \text{all-to-all}. instead of leaving the gpu idle, the scheduler can perform: \text{attention computation for }m_2 or another useful computation. so: timeline → m1: all-to-all ─────────── m2: attention ──────── m3: expert ── the communication for one workload is hidden underneath computation from another. the source describes this as the key mechanism for hiding the large moe communication cost. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 10. think of it like cpu + network overlap a useful conceptual analogy is: task a: network transfer ─────────────── task b: computation ───── if the hardware can make progress on both resources simultaneously, total wall-clock time can be much lower than: network ↓ finish ↓ computation ↓ finish dualpipe is applying this idea at extremely fine granularity to distributed llm training. the source's specific emphasis is: \boxed{ \text{keep compute resources and communication resources busy simultaneously} } 11. what does "overlap" actually mean? suppose: t_{\text{communication}}=5 and: t_{\text{computation}}=5. if done sequentially: t_{\text{total}}=5+5=10. if they can be perfectly overlapped: t_{\text{total}}\approx5. this is an idealized illustration of the reason overlap is valuable; it is not a performance number stated by the source. real systems have dependencies and imperfect overlap. but the engineering goal is exactly this: \boxed{ \text{hide communication behind useful computation} } 12. now understand dualpipev the source calls dualpipev the more intuitive "cut-in-half" or v-shape schedule. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) use the earlier example: 8\text{ stages} on: 4\text{ physical gpus}. the stage assignment is: gpu 0 → stage 0 + stage 7 gpu 1 → stage 1 + stage 6 gpu 2 → stage 2 + stage 5 gpu 3 → stage 3 + stage 4 now follow one micro-batch. 13. the downstroke the micro-batch first travels: stage_0 \rightarrow stage_1 \rightarrow stage_2 \rightarrow stage_3. so physically: gpu 0 ↓ gpu 1 ↓ gpu 2 ↓ gpu 3 the source calls this the downstroke . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 14. the turnaround here comes the clever part. gpu 3 contains: stage_3 and stage_4. so after the micro-batch finishes stage 3: stage_3\rightarrow stage_4 does not require another gpu. the pipeline effectively turns around on the same physical device . the source calls this the turnaround . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 15. the upstroke after stage 4, the micro-batch moves: stage_4 \rightarrow stage_5 \rightarrow stage_6 \rightarrow stage_7. physically: gpu 3 ↓ gpu 2 ↓ gpu 1 ↓ gpu 0 so the overall forward path is: gpu0 ↓ gpu1 ↓ gpu2 ↓ gpu3 ↘ stage4 ↗ gpu2 ↑ gpu1 ↑ gpu0 which visually forms: \boxed{v} hence v-shape schedule . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 16. why "cut-in-half"? normally, 8 pipeline stages might imply: 8\text{ physical devices} for one stage per device. dualpipev can place those 8 stages onto: \boxed{4\text{ physical devices}} because each device stores two stages. that is the source's "cut-in-half" idea. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 17. but there is a price nothing is free. each gpu now owns: \boxed{2\text{ stages}} instead of: 1\text{ stage}. so each physical gpu must store more model parameters. the source states the trade-off as approximately: \boxed{ 2\times\text{ parameter memory per gpu} } compared with the corresponding standard 1f1b folded-stage arrangement described there. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so: \boxed{ \text{less hardware / better bubble behavior} \quad\leftrightarrow\quad \text{more parameter memory per gpu} } 18. why this trade-off can be worthwhile for deepseek this is especially relevant to an moe architecture. we already learned that deepseek uses other mechanisms such as: \text{fp8} and: \text{expert parallelism} to reduce or manage per-device memory and communication pressure. the source argues that these techniques make the extra parameter-memory cost of the folded arrangement more favorable.
