(source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 6.1.1.1 what does the model actually need? the language model was trained earlier conceptually with the objective: \boxed{ \text{predict the next token from previous tokens} } so we cannot simply give it: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] and say “learn this.” we need two aligned sequences: \boxed{x} and: \boxed{y}. the first is what the model sees . the second is what the model is supposed to predict . 6.1.1.2 the crucial one-token shift suppose the token stream is: [10,20,30,40,50,60]. choose a sequence length: t=5. then the source constructs: x=[10,20,30,40,50] and: y=[20,30,40,50,60]. so: \boxed{ y_t=x_{t+1} } for every valid position. this is the entire next-token prediction mechanism in its simplest form. 6.1.1.3 why is the shift necessary? consider: input: 10 20 30 40 50 target: 20 30 40 50 60 at position 1, the model receives: 10 and should predict: 20. at position 2: 10,20 and should predict: 30. at position 3: 10,20,30 and should predict: 40. and so on. so the training pair is really: \boxed{ (x_1,\ldots,x_t) \rightarrow (y_1,\ldots,y_t) } where: \boxed{ y_i=x_{i+1}. } this is the same causal language-model objective we established earlier; here chapter 6 finally implements it. 6.1.1.4 the source's exact mechanism the source uses: x = torch.stack([ torch.from_numpy( (data[i:i+block_size]).astype(np.int64) ) for i in ix ]) y = torch.stack([ torch.from_numpy( (data[i+1:i+1+block_size]).astype(np.int64) ) for i in ix ]) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) notice the difference: input data[i : i + block_size] target data[i + 1 : i + 1 + block_size] that single +1 is the heart of next-token training. 6.1.1.5 let's inspect it numerically suppose: data= [100,101,102,103,104,105,106,107]. let: block\_size=4 and: i=2. then: input data[2:6] gives: \boxed{[102,103,104,105]}. target data[3:7] gives: \boxed{[103,104,105,106]}. therefore: x = [102, 103, 104, 105] y = [103, 104, 105, 106] the model is trained to predict: 102 → 103 103 → 104 104 → 105 105 → 106 6.1.1.6 but our dataset is one giant stream recall what we built previously: story 1 tokens eot story 2 tokens eot story 3 tokens eot ... stored as: \boxed{\text{one flat array}}. so get_batch() does not need to know anything about stories at this point. it simply sees: \boxed{ [t_0,t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_{n-1}] } and extracts contiguous windows. the eot tokens remain inside this stream and tell the model where document boundaries were encoded. 6.1.1.7 why use random starting positions? the source uses: ix = torch.randint( len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,) ) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this means: \boxed{ \text{randomly choose }batch\_size\text{ starting locations}. } suppose: batch\_size=4. we might get: i=[1032, 7811, 22501, 46290]. then four different chunks are extracted. 6.1.1.8 why not simply take the first 256 tokens every time? because then every iteration would see almost the same training example. for example: iteration 1: tokens 0–255 iteration 2: tokens 0–255 iteration 3: tokens 0–255 that would be extremely wasteful. random starting offsets let the model see many different portions of the corpus across training steps. the source explicitly says get_batch randomly selects batch_size starting positions. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 6.1.1.9 what is block_size ? this is one of the most important hyperparameters in the data loader. the source configuration uses: \boxed{ block\_size=256. } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) it means each training example contains: \boxed{ 256\text{ input tokens} } and: \boxed{ 256\text{ target tokens}. } so for one sample: x\in\mathbb z^{256} and: y\in\mathbb z^{256}. 6.1.1.10 why block_size matters to the transformer the transformer does not normally process the whole corpus at once. it sees a context window: \boxed{ t=256 } in this source configuration. so the model operates on: x= [x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{256}]. the model produces logits for all positions: z\in\mathbb r^{256\times v}. then the targets are: y= [y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_{256}]. and cross-entropy compares: z_t against: y_t. 6.1.1.11 what is batch_size ? the source configuration uses: \boxed{ batch\_size=24. } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so we don't train on just one sequence. we build: 24 different random sequences. therefore: \boxed{ x\in\mathbb z^{24\times256} } and: \boxed{ y\in\mathbb z^{24\times256}. } this is the first major tensor-shape checkpoint. 6.1.1.12 the complete shape transformation we begin with: \boxed{ \text{1-d token stream} } of shape: [n]. randomly choose: b=24 starting points. extract: t=256 tokens at each point. therefore: \boxed{ [n] \rightarrow [b,t] } which becomes: \boxed{ [n] \rightarrow [24,256]. } and because targets are shifted by one: \boxed{ x:[24,256] } \boxed{ y:[24,256]. } 6.1.1.13 why len(data) - block_size ? look closely at: torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, ...) suppose: len(data)=1000 and: block\_size=256. a starting position needs enough room for: 256 input tokens plus the next-token target . the source's indexing makes the valid-start constraint explicit through the len(data) - block_size bound. the important idea is: \boxed{ \text{don't choose a starting point so close to the end that a full training pair cannot be extracted}. } 6.1.1.14 why convert from uint16 to int64? this line is interesting: .astype(np.int64) the saved dataset is: \boxed{uint16} because that is an efficient storage representation. but before constructing the pytorch training tensor, the source converts those token ids to: \boxed{int64}. why? because token ids are being prepared as integer indices for the model's embedding lookup and later loss computation. so we have an important distinction: \boxed{ \text{storage dtype} \neq \text{training tensor dtype}. } storage: uint16 training token tensor: int64. 6.1.1.15 why not store everything as int64 from the beginning? because that would waste storage. we already established: uint16=2\text{ bytes}. whereas: int64=8\text{ bytes}. so a billion token ids would require approximately: uint16 1b\times2 = 2\text{ gb}. int64 1b\times8 = 8\text{ gb}. thus: \boxed{ \text{compact storage} \rightarrow \text{expand only when needed for computation}. } the source explicitly implements this distinction. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 6.1.1.16 torch.from_numpy the source wraps the numpy slices with: torch.from_numpy(...) this converts the numpy array representation into a pytorch tensor representation. then: torch.stack(...) combines the individual sequences into a batch. conceptually: sequence 1 → [t] sequence 2 → [t] sequence 3 → [t] ... sequence b → [t] ↓ stack [b,t] so: \boxed{ [t]\times b \rightarrow [b,t]. } 6.1.1.17 let's visualize the batch suppose: b=3,\qquad t=5. we might obtain: x: [ 10 20 30 40 50 ] [ 72 91 33 14 18 ] [201 202 203 204 205 ] y: [ 20 30 40 50 60 ] [ 91 33 14 18 19 ] [202 203 204 205 206 ] each row is an independent training example. the model processes all three in parallel. 6.1.1.18 what does the transformer see? the transformer receives: \boxed{ x=[b,t] } of integer token ids. for the source configuration: \boxed{ x=[24,256]. } the embedding layer then converts: [24,256] into: \boxed{ [24,256,d_{\text{model}}]. } for the flagship configuration later in the source: d_{\text{model}}=768. so conceptually: \boxed{ [24,256] \rightarrow [24,256,768]. } that is where the token ids become continuous vectors. 6.1.1.19 then the normal transformer pipeline begins now our previously learned architecture can finally be connected. train.bin │ ▼ memmap │ ▼ random starting positions │ ▼ x, y │ ▼ x: [b,t] │ ▼ token embedding │ ▼ [b,t,d_model] │ ▼ deepseek transformer │ ├── mla ├── rope ├── moe └── repeated blocks │ ▼ mtp during training │ ▼ logits │ ▼ cross-entropy │ ▼ loss the source later confirms that the model's training path receives x and targets y , computes the main loss and mtp losses, and returns the combined loss. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 6.1.1.20 now let's understand the causal relationship suppose: x= [x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]. because of causal masking: position 1 the model can use: x_1 to predict: y_1=x_2. position 2 it can use: x_1,x_2 to predict: y_2=x_3. position 3 it can use: x_1,x_2,x_3 to predict: y_3=x_4. so the batch construction and the causal mask work together. \boxed{ \text{shifted targets} + \text{causal attention} = \text{next-token language modeling}. } this is a key connection. 6.1.1.21 what would happen without the shift? suppose: x=[10,20,30] and incorrectly: y=[10,20,30]. then the model would be rewarded for reproducing the current token rather than predicting the next one. that would no longer implement the intended autoregressive next-token objective. therefore: \boxed{ y=x\text{ shifted left by one}. } 6.1.1.22 what would happen without causal masking? this is equally important. suppose: x = [10, 20, 30, 40] y = [20, 30, 40, 50] at position 1, if attention could see all tokens including: 30,40, then the model could use future information to help predict 20. that creates information leakage. so the two mechanisms have different jobs: \boxed{ \text{batch shift} \rightarrow \text{defines the prediction target} } while: \boxed{ \text{causal mask} \rightarrow \text{prevents seeing future inputs}. } 6.1.1.23 cpu → gpu the source adds: if 'cuda' in device: return ( x.pin_memory().to(device, non_blocking=true), y.pin_memory().to(device, non_blocking=true) ) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this introduces another systems concept. we have: \boxed{ \text{cpu memory} \rightarrow \text{gpu vram}. } 6.1.1.24 what is pinned memory? the source specifically describes pin_memory() as a performance optimization for transferring data from cpu ram to gpu vram. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so conceptually: normal cpu memory │ ▼ gpu transfer │ ▼ gpu pinned cpu memory │ │ optimized transfer path ▼ gpu it doesn't change the model's mathematical computation. it improves the data movement path . 6.1.1.25 what does non_blocking=true mean here? the source uses: .to(device, non_blocking=true) together with pinned memory. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the practical intention is to allow the transfer to be issued without unnecessarily forcing the cpu-side execution to wait synchronously at that point, when the underlying conditions permit asynchronous transfer. so this belongs to: \boxed{ \text{performance engineering} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{language-model mathematics}. } 6.1.1.26 why does this matter at scale? imagine: 1000 training iterations. if each iteration spends excessive time waiting for: \text{cpu}\rightarrow\text{gpu} data transfer, the gpu can sit idle. the goal is therefore: \boxed{ \text{keep gpu computation busy}. } this is another recurring theme in large-scale ml: \boxed{ \text{computation isn't the only bottleneck; data movement matters too}. } 6.1.1.27 the complete get_batch() logic let's now translate the entire source function into plain english. def get_batch(split): means: give me one batch from either the training or validation dataset. then: data = np.memmap( os.path.join(data_dir, f'{split}.bin'), dtype=np.uint16, mode='r' ) means: open the appropriate binary token stream without loading the entire file into ram. then: ix = torch.randint( len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,) ) means: choose batch_size random starting positions. then: x = ... means: extract block_size consecutive tokens from each position. then: y = ... means: extract the immediately shifted sequence so every token becomes the target of the preceding token. then: pin_memory() means: prepare cpu memory for efficient gpu transfer. and: .to(device) means: move the batch to the compute device. all of this is directly represented in the source's listing 6.20 . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1. why do we need mtp? a normal autoregressive transformer primarily learns: t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_i \rightarrow t_{i+1}. so at each position it is trained for immediate next-token prediction. the source's mtp idea asks the model to learn a longer predictive horizon. for prediction depth: d=3 we construct: main trunk │ ▼ h⁰ │ ▼ mtp 1 │ ▼ h¹ │ ▼ mtp 2 │ ▼ h² │ ▼ mtp 3 │ ▼ h³ the source emphasizes that this is a causal chain , not a set of independent heads. the hidden state produced by one mtp module becomes the input hidden state of the next. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 2. the fundamental difference from independent prediction heads imagine we want to predict three future positions. an independent-head design might do: h⁰ ──→ head 1 │ ├──→ head 2 │ └──→ head 3 each head independently sees h^0 . deepseek's causal design instead does: h⁰ ↓ mtp 1 ↓ h¹ ↓ mtp 2 ↓ h² ↓ mtp 3 ↓ h³ so: \boxed{ h^1=f_1(h^0,\text{future information}) } \boxed{ h^2=f_2(h^1,\text{future information}) } \boxed{ h^3=f_3(h^2,\text{future information}) } the source describes this as cascaded latent refinement . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 3. what exactly is inside one mtp module? the mini-deepseek implementation defines: class mtpmodule(nn.module): def __init__(self, args): super().__init__() self.projection = nn.linear( args.d_model * 2, args.d_model, bias=false ) self.block = transformerblock(args) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so there are only two major pieces: \boxed{ \text{projection} } and: \boxed{ \text{dedicated transformerblock}. } 4. why is the projection input 2d ? the module receives two vectors. first the hidden state from the previous mtp stage: h^{k-1}. second the embedding of a future token: e(t_{i+k}). the source explicitly describes these as the two inputs to each mtp stage. during training, that future-token embedding is the ground-truth embedding . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) each has dimensionality: d. so concatenating them gives: \boxed{2d}. 5. concatenation the source does: x = torch.cat( [h_prev, next_token_embeds], dim=-1 ) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) suppose: h_{\text{prev}}\in\mathbb r^{b\times l\times d} and: e_{\text{future}}\in\mathbb r^{b\times l\times d}. concatenating along the final dimension gives: \boxed{ [b,l,d] \rightarrow [b,l,2d]. } so the module has combined: \boxed{ \text{contextual state} + \text{future-token semantic representation}. } 6. projection back to d the source then applies: x = self.projection(x) the projection is: m_k:\mathbb r^{2d}\rightarrow\mathbb r^d. therefore: \boxed{ [b,l,2d] \rightarrow [b,l,d]. } this is exactly the purpose described in the source's chapter 5 derivation: concatenate the two normalized d -dimensional vectors, then use a linear projection to return to the model's normal dimension. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 7. the mathematical form the source's conceptual equation can be represented as: \boxed{ h_i^{\prime k} = m_k \left[ \operatorname{norm}(h_i^{k-1}); \operatorname{norm}(e(t_{i+k})) \right] } where: [\,;\,] means concatenation, m_k is the projection matrix, h_i^{k-1} is the previous hidden state, e(t_{i+k}) is the future token embedding. the source explicitly gives this as its equation 5.1 description. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) important source distinction chapter 5's conceptual implementation shows separate normalization of the hidden state and future embedding before concatenation using rmsnorm. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the simplified chapter 6 mtpmodule listing directly concatenates h_prev and next_token_embeds and does not show those separate normalization layers. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so for our mini-deepseek implementation, we follow the chapter 6 code rather than silently inserting the chapter 5 normalization. 8. why does the module contain a full transformerblock? this is one of the most important ideas. after projection: h_i^{\prime k} does not immediately go to the output head. it goes through: \boxed{ trm_k } a dedicated transformer block. the source explicitly stresses that this is a full transformer computation , not merely a linear transformation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) in our mini-deepseek code: h_k, _ = self.block( x, attn_mask=... ) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so: \boxed{ h^k=trm_k(h^{\prime k}). } 9. why is that powerful? the projection merely merges: h^{k-1} with: e(t_{i+k}). the transformer block can then perform a much richer transformation over that representation. the source explains this as asking, conceptually: given my current understanding and the future-token information, what is my updated understanding? thus the module doesn't merely generate a token. it generates a new latent state . that new state becomes useful to the next stage. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 10. the causal chain now the entire process for three mtp stages is: h_i^0 ↓ \boxed{ [h_i^0;e(t_{i+1})] } ↓ m_1 ↓ trm_1 ↓ h_i^1 ↓ \boxed{ [h_i^1;e(t_{i+2})] } ↓ m_2 ↓ trm_2 ↓ h_i^2 ↓ \boxed{ [h_i^2;e(t_{i+3})] } ↓ m_3 ↓ trm_3 ↓ h_i^3. the source explicitly says the refined state from head 1 becomes the input hidden state for head 2, then head 2 feeds head 3. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 11. why does h_prev keep changing? look at the full-model logic from the source: h_prev = h_main for depth_k in range(1, self.num_mtp_heads + 1): ... h_curr = self.mtp_modules[ depth_k - 1 ]( h_prev_sliced, future_token_embeds ) ... h_prev = h_curr (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the critical line is: h_prev = h_curr that is what turns multiple modules into a chain . without it: m_2(h^0,\cdot) would be independent of: m_1. with it: \boxed{ m_2(h^1,\cdot) } depends on the refinement performed by mtp 1. 12. now understand the sequence shrinking suppose: s=20. with three mtp stages, the source's conceptual verification example produces: \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \text{main} &: [2,20,1000]\\ \text{mtp 1} &: [2,19,1000]\\ \text{mtp 2} &: [2,18,1000]\\ \text{mtp 3} &: [2,17,1000]. \end{aligned} } the source explicitly reports these shapes and says the shrinking middle dimension confirms the causal chain. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) in the mini-deepseek code, the same: self.lm_head is invoked for the main output and every mtp module. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so conceptually: h_main ────────┐ │ h¹ ────────────┤ ├──→ shared lm head → vocabulary logits h² ────────────┤ │ h³ ────────────┘ this avoids creating a separate huge vocabulary projection for every mtp stage. 17. why not use separate output heads? suppose: d=768 and: v=50,257. one vocabulary projection already contains roughly: 768\times50,257 weights. creating a completely independent one for every mtp stage would multiply that cost. the source instead uses a shared output layer, reducing redundant parameters and maintaining a common vocabulary projection. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) correction: scope correction: chapter5 uses lambda/d times summed stage losses; chapter6 listing shows mtp_weight per stage and abbreviated ce. declare one normalization explicitly; do not claim the displayed chapter6 code already implements the earlier average. complete grounded review 18. now the most important part: the loss the main transformer gives: l_{\text{main}}. each mtp head gives: l_{\text{mtp}}^{(1)}, l_{\text{mtp}}^{(2)}, \ldots, l_{\text{mtp}}^{(d)}. the source combines them as: \boxed{ l = l_{\text{main}} + \frac{\lambda}{d} \sum_{k=1}^{d} l_{\text{mtp}}^{(k)} } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) where: d = number of mtp depths \lambda = mtp loss weight. this is the same formula we derived earlier, now appearing inside the actual model. 19. why divide by d ? suppose: d=3. without normalization, we would add: l_1+l_2+l_3. the contribution from the mtp system grows automatically as we add more heads. the source instead uses: \frac{\lambda}{d} (l_1+l_2+l_3). this gives a weighted average of the mtp losses, multiplied by \lambda . so: \boxed{ \lambda } controls the overall importance of mtp relative to the main objective. 20. why does this create a richer gradient? suppose the total loss is: l= l_{\text{main}} + \frac{\lambda}{d} (l_1+l_2+l_3). then the shared early representations receive gradient contributions from multiple objectives. conceptually: l_main │ ▼ h⁰ / trunk ▲ │ ┌─────────┼──────────┐ │ │ │ l₁ l₂ l₃ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ mtp1 mtp2 mtp3 but because the modules are chained: h^0\rightarrow h^1\rightarrow h^2\rightarrow h^3, the gradients from deeper mtp stages can propagate backward through earlier mtp stages and ultimately into the main trunk. this connects directly to the gradient-flow discussion we completed earlier. the source describes the resulting signal as a rich, multi-faceted gradient signal that improves both immediate prediction and longer-range forecasting. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 21. a concrete chain example let's use a tiny sequence: the cat sat on mat . t0 t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 the main model produces hidden states: h_0^0,h_1^0,h_2^0,\ldots for a particular starting position i=0 : main objective predict the next token: t_1. mtp stage 1 use: h_0^0 together with the appropriate future-token embedding specified by the mtp construction, then create: h_0^1. mtp stage 2 use: h_0^1 and the next future-token embedding to create: h_0^2. mtp stage 3 use: h_0^2 and another future-token embedding to create: h_0^3. each stage produces vocabulary logits and contributes an mtp loss. the source's conceptual description explicitly frames each stage as producing a refined hidden state that is passed onward. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 22. one extremely important point: training vs inference for this source implementation, mtp is primarily a training mechanism . during training: \boxed{ \text{future token embedding = ground truth} } the source explicitly says this. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) therefore the model gets teacher-forced future embeddings while constructing the mtp chain. this is different from ordinary generation, where the next token is not known in advance. 23. so are mtp predictions themselves used to generate the training input? no. during training, the source uses: e(t_{i+k}) from the actual input sequence. so the mtp chain gets the ground-truth future-token embedding , not the model's sampled prediction. this is why the mtp training mechanism can provide a stable training signal. 24. what happens to mtp during normal model inference? the chapter 6 source makes an explicit split in minideepseek.forward() : targets provided ↓ training path ↓ main trunk + mtp versus: targets is none ↓ inference path ↓ kv-cache generation the inference path returns the main logits and updated cache, while the mtp training path is entered when targets are supplied. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1. first see the complete block the source's block is: x │ ▼ layernorm 1 │ ▼ deepseekattention │ ▼ attention h │ ▼ x + h │ ▼ layernorm 2 │ ▼ deepseekmoe │ ▼ moe output │ ▼ (x + h) + moe │ ▼ block output so mathematically: \boxed{ h=x+\operatorname{attention}(\operatorname{ln}_1(x)) } then: \boxed{ y=h+\operatorname{moe}(\operatorname{ln}_2(h)). } that is the complete block. 2. why is it called "pre-norm"? look at the order: x \rightarrow \text{norm} \rightarrow \text{attention} rather than: x \rightarrow \text{attention} \rightarrow \text{norm}. similarly: h \rightarrow \text{norm} \rightarrow \text{moe}. therefore the normalization happens before each major sublayer. hence: \boxed{\text{pre-norm transformer}.} the source explicitly labels its implementation this way. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 3. the source code the source gives: class transformerblock(nn.module): def __init__(self, args: modelargs): super().__init__() # use layernorm for simplicity, # though deepseek uses rmsnorm self.norm1 = nn.layernorm(args.d_model) self.attention = deepseekattention(args) self.norm2 = nn.layernorm(args.d_model) self.feed_forward = deepseekmoe(args) def forward( self, x: torch.tensor, attn_mask: torch.tensor, past_kv: optional[tuple[torch.tensor, torch.tensor]] = none, position_offset: int = 0 ): # attention block with residual connection h, new_cache = self.attention( self.norm1(x), attn_mask, past_kv, position_offset ) x = x + h # feed-forward block with residual connection x = x + self.feed_forward( self.norm2(x) ) return x, new_cache (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) we should understand every line because this is the point where the previous components become one transformer layer. 4. first normalization the source creates: self.norm1 = nn.layernorm(args.d_model) then: self.norm1(x) is fed into attention. at this level, the source is using the standard pre-norm transformer organization. the sequence is: \boxed{ x \rightarrow ln \rightarrow attention \rightarrow residual. } the residual connection means the original representation has a direct path around the attention computation. this gives: x_{\text{new}} = x+ h. 7. attention call the source executes: h, new_cache = self.attention( self.norm1(x), attn_mask, past_kv, position_offset ) (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) notice that four things enter the attention module: 1. normalized hidden state ln_1(x) 2. attention mask attn\_mask 3. previous cache past\_kv 4. position offset position\_offset. this connects the transformer block directly to everything we have already learned about mla, rope, and cached inference. 8. the attention output has two results the function returns: h, new_cache so attention produces: \boxed{h} and: \boxed{new\_cache}. the first is the actual attention output. the second is the updated state needed if the model is doing cached inference. so conceptually: normalized x │ ▼ deepseekattention │ ├────────────→ h │ └────────────→ new_cache 9. first residual connection the source then performs: x = x + h (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this is the first residual connection. so: \boxed{ x_1=x_0+h. } where: h=attention(ln_1(x_0)). therefore: \boxed{ x_1 = x_0+ attention(ln_1(x_0)). } 10. why does the original x remain? claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. r102.0 — reinforcement learning for llms: from next-token prediction to decision-making plan node: b1 · chat order #117 ↩ back to main text: step 5.3 — why grpo instead of ppo? · step 5.7 — the full grpo training algorithm we now begin chapter 7: reinforcement learning — from policy gradients to grpo . this is a major conceptual transition. up to chapter 6, our mini-deepseek was trained with: \boxed{\text{“here is the correct next token. predict it.”}} that is supervised next-token learning. chapter 7 asks a different question: what if we don't specify every correct token, and instead evaluate the completed response and reward the model when it succeeds? that is the basic idea of reinforcement learning for llms. the source explicitly frames chapter 7 as the post-training stage where a pretrained model is pushed toward useful reasoning behavior, eventually connecting rl to grpo and deepseek-r1. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1. why do we need rl after pre-training? our base model already knows how to predict text. but: \boxed{ \text{good next-token prediction} \neq \text{good problem solving} } a model can be excellent at language modeling while still producing poor reasoning solutions. the source therefore distinguishes pre-training from post-training . pre-training learn language patterns: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_t \rightarrow x_{t+1}. reinforcement learning generate a response, evaluate its outcome, and change the policy so successful behavior becomes more likely. the source describes this as moving from simply predicting tokens toward deliberate problem solving. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 2. supervised learning vs reinforcement learning this distinction is foundational. suppose the problem is: roger has 5 tennis balls. he buys 2 cans with 3 balls in each can. how many balls does he have? the answer is: 5+2(3)=11. supervised learning you might provide: prompt: roger has 5 tennis balls... target: 11 or even provide a complete reasoning trace. the model is trained to imitate the supplied target. reinforcement learning you give the model the problem and let it generate a response: prompt ↓ model generates response ↓ verifier checks response ↓ reward you do not necessarily specify the exact sequence of intermediate tokens the model should produce. the source explicitly highlights this distinction: rl does not require the exact correct action at every step; feedback may arrive only after several actions. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 3. first build ordinary rl before translating rl to llms, the source uses a simple agent-environment example: a cleaning robot. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) imagine: robot = agent room = environment at each step: observe state ↓ choose action ↓ environment changes ↓ receive reward ↓ new state ↓ repeat there are four core objects: \boxed{ \text{state} ,\ \text{action} ,\ \text{reward} ,\ \text{policy} } the source deliberately establishes these four before translating them into language generation. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 4. state the state represents the current situation. for the cleaning robot, it might contain: where dust remains, obstacles, battery level, charging-dock location. so: s_t = \text{current situation at time }t. 5. action the robot selects an action: a_t. examples: move forward turn left vacuum return to dock so: \boxed{ a_t=\text{what the agent does next} } 6. reward after taking an action, the environment provides a reward. for example: +1 for cleaning useful dust, and potentially: -1 for wasting battery or colliding with something. the reward tells the agent whether its behavior was beneficial. so: \boxed{ r_t=\text{learning signal about the outcome} } 7. policy the policy is the rule that chooses actions from states. conceptually: \boxed{ \pi(a\mid s) } means: probability of taking action a when in state s . for a neural-network agent, the policy is represented by the model parameters. training changes the parameters so actions associated with higher long-term reward become more likely. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 8. now make the surprising translation to an llm a language model doesn't look like a robot. it does not move around a physical room. but token generation is still a sequential decision process. the source maps the rl components to llm generation as follows. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) rl concept llm equivalent state prompt + tokens generated so far action next sampled token transition append sampled token to context reward score of the completed response policy llm's token probability distribution this table is the conceptual bridge between classical rl and reasoning-model training. 9. let's trace one llm rollout suppose the prompt is: roger has 5 tennis balls... initially: s_0=\text{prompt}. the model samples: a_0=\text{“roger”}. now the state becomes: s_1= \text{prompt}+\text{“roger”}. then the model samples another token. maybe: a_1=\text{“has”}. now: s_2= \text{prompt}+\text{“roger has”}. and so on. therefore: s_0 \xrightarrow{a_0} s_1 \xrightarrow{a_1} s_2 \xrightarrow{a_2} \cdots until the response ends. the source uses essentially this exact progression to explain llm rl. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 10. the action is a token this point is easy to misunderstand. in llm rl, the action is not: “solve the entire math problem.” the action at each generation step is: \boxed{ \text{one sampled next token} } for example: "therefore" is one action. then: " the" is another action. then: " answer" is another. so an entire response is a sequence of actions : a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_t. 11. the policy is the llm itself at every step, the model produces: \pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t). for example, given the current context: "roger has" the model might assign: p(\text{5})=0.10 p(\text{7})=0.03 p(\text{bought})=0.05 and so on. the model samples one of these possible tokens. so the policy is literally the llm's probability distribution over the next token. 12. why sampling matters this is an especially important point in the source. during ordinary inference, you might use: \text{greedy decoding} or low-temperature sampling. but in rl rollouts, sampling is central . why? because rl needs exploration . suppose the model always chooses: \arg\max_a \pi(a\mid s). then it repeatedly follows essentially the same response path. it becomes difficult to discover alternative reasoning paths. instead: \boxed{ \text{sample multiple possible responses} } so the training system can compare them according to their rewards. the source explicitly says this sampling allows exploration of different responses for the same prompt. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 13. one prompt can produce multiple trajectories suppose we give the same problem to the model three times. it might generate: prompt p response a → reward 1 response b → reward 0 response c → reward 1 the responses are different because generation is stochastic. that gives rl useful information: \boxed{ \text{which sampled behaviors tended to succeed?} } this group-based comparison later becomes central to grpo . 14. now the difficult problem: sparse rewards here comes one of the biggest differences between ordinary supervised learning and rl for reasoning. suppose the model generates: token 1 token 2 token 3 ... token 100 and only after the final answer do we know whether it is correct. for the math problem: \text{final answer}=11 might give: r=1. a wrong final answer might give: r=0. the source calls this a sparse reward because the reward arrives only after the sequence of actions is complete. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 15. why sparse reward creates credit assignment suppose the model produced 100 tokens and got: r=0. which token was responsible? maybe: token 14 → misunderstood problem or: token 47 → arithmetic mistake or: token 91 → final answer malformed the final reward alone does not directly identify the cause. that is: \boxed{ \text{credit assignment problem} } the source explicitly raises this issue after introducing sparse rewards. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 16. yet the policy-gradient method has a way to use that reward here is the key idea. suppose the model sampled a response: a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_t and the response receives reward: r. we want: successful response \boxed{ \text{increase probability of the sampled actions} } poor response \boxed{ \text{decrease probability of the sampled actions} } the source introduces policy-gradient methods specifically to make this connection. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 17. policy-gradient intuition the central quantity is the log probability of the sampled actions. a simplified objective can be thought of as: \boxed{ r\sum_t \log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t) } and the corresponding gradient is proportional to: \boxed{ r\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t) } the source explains the intuition: the gradient of the log probability tells us how to change the model so the sampled action becomes more or less likely, while the reward controls the direction and strength. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this is the bridge from: \boxed{\text{reward}} to: \boxed{\text{parameter update}}. 18. successful response suppose: r=1. then, conceptually: +\nabla\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t). we increase the likelihood of the sampled trajectory. so: successful response ↓ positive learning signal ↓ sampled tokens become more likely 19. unsuccessful response now suppose the response receives a lower signal. relative to a baseline, its advantage can be negative. then: a<0. the policy update pushes against the sampled behavior. so: poor response ↓ negative advantage ↓ sampled behavior becomes less likely this is much more informative than simply thinking "reward = number." 20. why raw reward is not enough the source makes an important observation. imagine: prompt a — very easy most responses receive: r=1. prompt b — very difficult most responses receive: r=0. suppose one response from prompt a gets reward 1. that's not necessarily impressive. but a response from difficult prompt b that somehow performs better than most alternatives may still be valuable. so raw reward does not tell us: \boxed{ \text{how good was this response relative to what was expected?} } this motivates the advantage . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 21. advantage the source gives: \boxed{ a_k=r_k-\text{baseline}(s_k) } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) interpret it as: \text{advantage} = \text{actual outcome} - \text{expected outcome}. so: better than expected a>0. worse than expected a<0. about as expected a\approx0. correction: the unbiased baseline identity requires action-independent b(s) under the sampled policy. group-dependent estimates and normalization can introduce finite-sample differences; reduced variance is not an unconditional theorem for every implementation. complete grounded review 22. why the baseline helps without a baseline: r can be noisy. with a baseline: a=r-b. we ask: did this response do unusually well or unusually badly relative to the reference level? the source says the baseline does not change which actions are optimal, but can dramatically reduce variance, producing more stable training. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so: \boxed{ \text{baseline} \rightarrow \text{lower variance} \rightarrow \text{more stable updates} } 23. a concrete example suppose three responses to the same prompt produce rewards: r_1=1 r_2=0 r_3=0.5. suppose the baseline is: b=0.5. then: a_1=1-0.5=+0.5 a_2=0-0.5=-0.5 a_3=0.5-0.5=0. therefore: response 1 → positive signal → reinforce response 2 → negative signal → discourage response 3 → approximately neutral this is the intuition that will eventually lead us to grpo. 24. why this is especially powerful for reasoning suppose we don't know the ideal reasoning chain. maybe there are 20 valid ways to solve the same problem. supervised learning asks: which exact target sequence should i imitate? rl can instead ask: did the response actually solve the problem? that is why reward-based reasoning is interesting. the model can explore different token sequences as long as the resulting behavior receives useful reward. the source connects this idea to deepseek-r1 and objectively verifiable reasoning tasks. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 25. but there is a limitation sparse reward is powerful, but the credit assignment is imperfect. if an entire 100-token answer gets reward: r=1, the simple policy-gradient interpretation can apply that positive signal across the generated response tokens. the source later explicitly explains that the completion-level advantage is applied across generated tokens, which is useful statistically but is not perfect token-level credit assignment. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this is an important limitation to remember. 26. the entire rl rollout we can now draw the complete process: prompt │ ▼ state s₀ │ ▼ llm policy πθ │ ▼ sample token a₀ │ ▼ new state s₁ │ ▼ llm policy πθ │ ▼ sample token a₁ │ ▼ ... │ ▼ complete response │ ▼ verifier / reward │ ▼ r │ ▼ advantage a │ ▼ policy-gradient update │ ▼ updated θ this is the fundamental rl-for-llms pipeline introduced by the source. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 27. now compare this with our chapter 6 training chapter 6 — pre-training x ↓ transformer ↓ logits ↓ cross entropy with known y ↓ backward ↓ adamw the target token is explicitly available. chapter 7 — rl prompt ↓ sample response ↓ verifier / reward ↓ advantage ↓ policy-gradient objective ↓ backward ↓ optimizer the training signal comes from the outcome rather than an explicitly supplied target sequence. that is the fundamental conceptual shift. 28. where ppo enters the source's next step is ppo — proximal policy optimization . why do we need it? because a naive policy-gradient update can change the model's probabilities too aggressively. suppose the old policy produced a rollout. then we update the model. if the new model becomes radically different from the old one in a single update, the rollout data becomes a poor basis for that update. ppo therefore introduces a mechanism to keep the policy update close to the old policy. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) that gives the next progression: \boxed{ \text{policy gradient} \rightarrow \text{advantage} \rightarrow \text{ppo} \rightarrow \text{grpo} } 29. the key knowledge graph so far reinforcement learning │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ ▼ ▼ state action │ │ prompt + generated tokens sampled next token │ │ └──────────┬──────────────┘ ▼ policy πθ(a | s) │ ▼ response │ ▼ reward │ ▼ sparse feedback │ ▼ advantage │ ▼ policy gradient │ ▼ ppo │ ▼ grpo 30. what you should be able to answer now q: what is the state in llm rl? \boxed{\text{prompt + generated tokens so far}} q: what is the action? \boxed{\text{next sampled token}} q: what is the policy? \boxed{\text{llm probability distribution over actions}} q: what is the reward? \boxed{\text{score of the generated response}} q: why is it sparse? \boxed{\text{reward often arrives only after the complete response}} q: what is the credit-assignment problem? \boxed{\text{the final reward doesn't directly identify which token caused success/failure}} q: why use advantage instead of raw reward? \boxed{\text{to measure outcome relative to a baseline and reduce variance}} all of these mappings come directly from the chapter 7 framework. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1. start from what we already have our rl pipeline is currently: prompt ↓ llm policy πθ ↓ sample response ↓ reward ↓ advantage a ↓ update policy suppose the sampled token was: a_k. the policy assigned it probability: \pi_\theta(a_k\mid s_k). the basic policy-gradient idea says: \boxed{ \text{increase probability of actions with positive advantage} } and: \boxed{ \text{decrease probability of actions with negative advantage}. } so why isn't that enough? 2. the problem with a large policy update suppose our current policy assigns: p_{\text{old}}(a)=0.20. the rollout tells us that this action was good. a naive gradient step might push it to: p_{\text{new}}(a)=0.90. that sounds good because we increased the probability of a rewarded action. but notice what happened: 0.20\rightarrow0.90. that's a massive behavioral change from one update. the source's motivation for ppo is exactly this: if the model changes too much after the sampled rollouts, the training signal can become unreliable because the new policy may assign very different probabilities to the actions on which the rollout was based. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 3. think of the rollout as evidence from the old policy this is the key conceptual setup. at time of sampling, we had: \pi_{\text{old}}. it generated: (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_t). then we calculate rewards and use that data to train a new policy: \pi_\theta. but the data was generated by: \pi_{\text{old}} not by the new policy. therefore we need to ask: \boxed{ \text{how different is }\pi_\theta\text{ from }\pi_{\text{old}}\text{ on the sampled actions?} } ppo answers this with a probability ratio . 4. the ppo probability ratio the source defines: \boxed{ r_k(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(a_k\mid s_k) }{ \pi_{\text{old}}(a_k\mid s_k) } } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) read it literally: \boxed{ r = \frac{\text{new probability}} {\text{old probability}} } 5. why the ratio is useful suppose: \pi_{\text{old}}(a\mid s)=0.20 and the new policy gives: \pi_\theta(a\mid s)=0.22. then: r=\frac{0.22}{0.20}=1.10. the new policy made the sampled action: 10\% more likely. that's a relatively small change. 6. example: large increase suppose: p_{\text{old}}=0.20 and: p_{\text{new}}=0.60. then: r=\frac{0.60}{0.20}=3. the new policy is assigning: \boxed{3\times} the old probability. that's a very large policy change. 7. example: probability decreased suppose: p_{\text{old}}=0.20 and: p_{\text{new}}=0.10. then: r=\frac{0.10}{0.20}=0.5. so the new policy assigns only half the old probability. 8. the meaning of the three important values \boxed{r=1} means: \text{new probability = old probability}. so the policy hasn't changed for that sampled action. \boxed{r>1} means the new policy makes that action more likely. \boxed{r<1} means the new policy makes that action less likely. this interpretation is directly given in the source. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 9. now combine ratio with advantage we already have: a_k. suppose: a_k>0. that means: this sampled action was better than expected. we therefore want: r_k>1. we want to increase its probability. conversely, if: a_k<0, we want: r_k<1. so the natural quantity is: \boxed{ r_k a_k } because the advantage tells us direction , while the ratio tells us how much the probability moved relative to the rollout policy . 10. why not just maximize ra ? because then the optimizer could try to make: r\rightarrow\infty for positive-advantage actions. for example: a>0 encourages: r=1.1\rightarrow2\rightarrow5\rightarrow10\rightarrow\cdots there is nothing in the basic ratio term itself preventing a very large policy change. that's why ppo introduces clipping . correction: the clipped term uses a ratio inside[.8,1.2], but the actual new-policy ratio is not constrained to that interval. ppo clipping is an incentive saturation rule, not a hard probability constraint. complete grounded review 11. ppo clipping the source says ppo clips the ratio to prevent overly large updates. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the standard clipped form is: \boxed{ \operatorname{clip}(r,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) } where \epsilon is a small allowed deviation. for example, if: \epsilon=0.2, then: 1-\epsilon=0.8 and: 1+\epsilon=1.2. so the ratio is constrained to: \boxed{[0.8,1.2]} inside the clipped term. 12. what clipping means intuitively think of: r=1 as: “the new policy is identical to the old policy for this action.” ppo says: you can move away from 1, but don't let one update gain unlimited benefit from moving very far away. so: old policy │ │ ▼ r=1 / \ 0.8 1.2 │ │ lower upper boundary this is the "proximal" idea. stay reasonably close to where you started. 13. the full clipped surrogate idea the source later uses the standard structure: \boxed{ \min\left( r_k a_k,\; \operatorname{clip}(r_k,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)a_k \right) } this is the core ppo/grpo surrogate term. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) the reason for the min is crucial. it chooses the more conservative improvement estimate. 14. let's understand this with a positive advantage suppose: a=+2. and: \epsilon=0.2. therefore the upper bound is: 1.2. suppose the new policy produces: r=1.1. then: ra=1.1\times2=2.2. clipped: 1.1\times2=2.2. so: \min(2.2,2.2)=2.2. no problem. 15. positive advantage, large ratio now suppose: r=1.8. then unclipped: 1.8\times2=3.6. but clipping gives: 1.2\times2=2.4. therefore: \min(3.6,2.4)=2.4. the optimizer cannot keep gaining objective value simply by making this rewarded action increasingly probable. that is the central stabilization mechanism. 16. negative advantage now suppose: a=-2. suppose: r=0.5. then: ra=0.5(-2)=-1. the clipped ratio is: 0.8. so: 0.8(-2)=-1.6. the objective takes: \min(-1,-1.6)=-1.6. the negative side is therefore also bounded by the clipping mechanism. the important conceptual point is not memorizing individual arithmetic cases, but understanding that ppo prevents the optimizer from exploiting arbitrarily large policy changes. 17. ppo therefore has two policies this is important. old policy \boxed{\pi_{\text{old}}} this generated the rollout. current/trainable policy \boxed{\pi_\theta} this is being optimized. their probability ratio is: \boxed{ \frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{old}}} } the source explicitly emphasizes this comparison. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 18. now introduce the four ppo components for llm post-training, the source describes four components. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) ppo training ┌─────────────────┐ │ policy model │ │ trainable llm │ └────────┬────────┘ │ generates │ ▼ responses │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ▼ ▼ reward value model signal / critic │ │ └───────┬─────────┘ ▼ advantage │ ▼ ppo update ▲ │ reference model (frozen, kl) let's separate their roles. 19. component 1 — policy model this is the actual llm we are training. \boxed{\pi_\theta} it chooses the next token. its parameters are updated. 20. component 2 — reward the response receives some reward. the source allows for: a learned reward model, or a verifier. so: \boxed{ \text{response} \rightarrow r } the exact reward source depends on the task. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 21. component 3 — value model this is new. the value model estimates: \boxed{ v_\phi(s_k) } which represents expected future reward from the current state. the source describes it as a learned critic that predicts how promising a partial response is. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 22. value model gives us the baseline recall: a_k=r_k-\text{baseline}(s_k). in ppo, the source gives the baseline specifically as: \boxed{ a_k=r_k-v_\phi(s_k) } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so: state ↓ value model ↓ vφ(s) ↓ expected reward and then: r-v_\phi(s) tells us whether the sampled outcome was better or worse than expected. 23. what exactly is the value model learning? suppose the model is halfway through a response. current state: prompt + "let's calculate..." the value model asks: from this point, how much reward do i expect this trajectory to eventually produce? so: v_\phi(s_k) \approx e[\text{future return}\mid s_k]. this is why the value model is sometimes called the critic . the policy says: what action should i take? the value model says: how promising is the current state? 24. why does ppo need a learned value model? because the baseline should depend on the current state. different partial responses can have different expected outcomes. for example: state a → already doing correct algebra expected reward high state b → made a conceptual mistake expected reward low a learned value function can distinguish them. thus: a=r-v_\phi(s) can be much more informative than: a=r-\text{one constant}. 25. the cost of the value model but the source points out an important engineering drawback. the value model adds: memory, forward passes, training losses, optimization complexity. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) for very large llms, this matters enormously. and this sets up the motivation for grpo. 26. component 4 — reference model the fourth component is: \boxed{\pi_{\text{ref}}} a frozen reference model. the source describes it as usually a frozen copy of the model before rl training. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) its purpose is different from the value model. do not confuse: \boxed{\text{value model}} with: \boxed{\text{reference model}}. 27. value model vs reference model value model purpose: \boxed{\text{estimate expected reward}} trainable: \boxed{\text{yes}} used for: \boxed{\text{advantage}} reference model purpose: \boxed{\text{keep policy from drifting too far}} frozen: \boxed{\text{yes}} used for: \boxed{\text{kl control}} this distinction is explicitly emphasized by the source. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 28. why do we need a reference model? suppose our reward only checks: \text{math answer correct?} the model might discover a weird way to maximize that reward while harming general behavior. or a learned reward model might contain exploitable quirks. so we want: \boxed{ \text{improve reward} + \text{stay reasonably close to the original model} } the reference policy supplies the second constraint. the source explains that a kl penalty discourages excessive drift from the pretrained/reference distribution. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 29. kl in this context conceptually we calculate something like: kl(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}). if this becomes large: \boxed{\text{the trained policy has drifted substantially}} and a penalty is applied. so the training pressure becomes: reward pressure ↓ "become better" │ ▼ πθ improves ▲ │ kl pressure │ "don't move too far from reference" the source specifically notes that in ppo-style llm training, kl can be computed token by token for generated tokens. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 30. ppo therefore balances three forces conceptually: \boxed{ \text{reward improvement} } versus: \boxed{ \text{policy-update stability} } versus: \boxed{ \text{reference-policy stability} } more concretely: \boxed{ \text{advantage} + \text{clipping} + \text{reference kl control} } this exact combination becomes important again when we arrive at grpo. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 31. full ppo conceptual pipeline now we can finally draw ppo end-to-end: prompt │ ▼ trainable policy πθ │ sample tokens │ ▼ response │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ▼ ▼ reward r value model vφ │ │ └────────┬──────────┘ ▼ advantage a │ ▼ compare πθ with πold │ ▼ ratio r │ ▼ clip │ + reference kl │ ▼ ppo loss │ ▼ backward() │ ▼ update πθ 32. important: old policy and reference policy are not the same thing this is an extremely common confusion. we have: \boxed{\pi_{\text{old}}} and: \boxed{\pi_{\text{ref}}}. they serve different purposes. old policy used for: \boxed{ r= \frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{old}}} } it tells us how much the current policy changed relative to the policy that generated the rollout. reference policy used for: \boxed{ kl(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) } it acts as the stable anchor. the source's later grpo explanation preserves both of these mechanisms. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 33. why does this lead directly to grpo? now we can see the expensive part of ppo. we need: \boxed{ \text{policy} + \text{reward} + \text{value model} + \text{reference model} } the source's next question is therefore: can we get a useful baseline without training a separate value model? this is exactly what group relative policy optimization (grpo) does. instead of: a_i=r_i-v_\phi(s_i), grpo uses the rewards of multiple completions for the same prompt to construct a group-relative advantage. the source explicitly identifies this as its key simplification. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 34. the big picture we have now reached: \boxed{ \text{policy gradient} \rightarrow \text{advantage} \rightarrow \text{ppo} } and next: \boxed{ \text{ppo} \rightarrow \text{grpo} } the conceptual transformation will be: \boxed{ \text{learned value baseline} \rightarrow \text{group-relative reward baseline} } while keeping important ppo ideas such as: \boxed{ \text{old-policy ratio} + \text{clipping} + \text{reference-policy kl} } the source explicitly states that grpo removes the value model , not the entire ppo stabilization machinery. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) r102.1 checkpoint you should now be able to explain: \boxed{ r_k= \frac{\pi_\theta(a_k|s_k)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(a_k|s_k)} } as: how much more or less likely is the sampled action under the new policy than under the policy that generated the rollout? and: \boxed{ a_k=r_k-v_\phi(s_k) } as: how much better or worse was the observed outcome than the value model expected? and finally: \boxed{ \text{ppo clipping} } as: a mechanism preventing one rl update from gaining unlimited benefit by moving the policy too far from the rollout policy.

\text{group statistics from multiple sampled completions} } grpo was introduced in deepseekmath , and the source describes the same family of ideas as later being used in the deepseek-r1 training recipe. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 1. first remember why ppo was expensive ppo-style llm training had four major pieces: ppo │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ policy reward value model πθ r vφ │ ▼ advantage + reference model πref the expensive part is the value model . it must learn: v_\phi(s) and provide the baseline for: a=r-v_\phi(s). the source explicitly notes that the value model adds memory, forward passes, loss terms, and engineering complexity. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so deepseek asks: can we obtain a useful baseline without training another value model? 2. the grpo idea instead of producing one response and asking a value model: how good was this response compared with expectation? we produce multiple responses to the same prompt . for example: same prompt p ┌─ response 1 → reward 1 prompt ─┼─ response 2 → reward 1 ├─ response 3 → reward 0 └─ response 4 → reward 0 now we can compare these responses against one another . the source's key statement is: a completion is good if it is better than the other completions sampled for the same prompt, and bad if it is worse than the group. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) that is the "group-relative" part of grpo. 3. why must the prompt be the same? this is extremely important. suppose: prompt a = easy problem prompt b = extremely hard problem and: a → reward 1 b → reward 0 comparing those rewards directly can be misleading. maybe the response to b was actually much better than most responses to b. grpo instead creates: \boxed{ \text{local comparison within the same prompt} } so for each prompt: p_i \rightarrow \{c_{i1},c_{i2},...,c_{ig}\}. each completion in the group is judged relative to the others. the source specifically says this makes the baseline prompt-specific and avoids mixing easy and hard prompts together. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 4. what is a grpo group? suppose: g=4. for one prompt: prompt: solve 5 + 2 × 3 completion 1 → 11 → reward 1 completion 2 → 11 → reward 1 completion 3 → 8 → reward 0 completion 4 → 9 → reward 0 so the reward vector is: \boxed{ [1,1,0,0] } 5. compute the group mean the source uses the group mean as part of the group-relative baseline: \mu= \frac1g\sum_{j=1}^{g}r_j. for: [1,1,0,0], we have: \mu= \frac{1+1+0+0}{4} = \boxed{0.5}. therefore: response 1: 1 → above mean response 2: 1 → above mean response 3: 0 → below mean response 4: 0 → below mean 6. compute the group-relative advantage the source gives: \boxed{ a_i= \frac{ r_i-\operatorname{mean}(r_1,\ldots,r_g) }{ \operatorname{std}(r_1,\ldots,r_g)+\epsilon } } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this is the central grpo formula. break it into pieces: r_i-\mu asks: is this completion better or worse than its group's average? then dividing by: \sigma+\epsilon normalizes the scale. 7. numerical example using the rewards: [1,1,0,0], the mean is: 0.5. for illustration, using the population standard deviation: \sigma=0.5. then approximately: completion 1 a_1= \frac{1-0.5}{0.5+\epsilon} \approx+1 completion 2 a_2\approx+1 completion 3 a_3\approx-1 completion 4 a_4\approx-1. so: \boxed{ a\approx[+1,+1,-1,-1] } the source does not specify the exact standard-deviation convention in the displayed formula, so the exact numerical magnitude can depend on implementation; the important source-derived result is that correct-above-group responses get positive advantages and below-group responses get negative ones. 8. now the magic happens we no longer need: v_\phi(s). instead: same prompt ↓ sample g completions ↓ reward each completion ↓ group mean/std ↓ group-relative advantages therefore: \boxed{ \text{no learned value model} } the model can learn which sampled trajectories were relatively better using only the reward distribution within the group. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 9. compare ppo and grpo advantage calculation ppo \boxed{ a_i=r_i-v_\phi(s_i) } where v_\phi is a learned value function. grpo \boxed{ a_i= \frac{r_i-\mu_{\text{group}}} {\sigma_{\text{group}}+\epsilon} } where \mu and \sigma come from the sampled group. that's the fundamental algorithmic change. 10. why is this called "relative"? because grpo does not simply ask: is reward = 1 good? it asks: how good was this response relative to the other responses for the same prompt? suppose: prompt a: [1, 1, 1, 0] the single incorrect answer is clearly worse than the group. now suppose: prompt b: [0, 0, 0, 0] no completion is better than the others. the group contains no obvious preference signal. this is one reason group composition matters. 11. what happens if every completion gets the same reward? this is a subtle implementation issue explicitly noted by the source. suppose: [1,1,1,1]. then: \mu=1 and: \sigma\approx0. without protection, we'd divide by zero. therefore the formula includes: \boxed{\epsilon} for numerical stability. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) more fundamentally, when all completions have essentially identical reward, there is little relative information telling the policy which completion was better. 12. why sample multiple completions? this is not just batching. suppose we sample only: g=1. then there is no meaningful within-prompt comparison. grpo requires: \boxed{ g>1 } in practice so that the reward distribution has some comparative information. the source explicitly emphasizes that grpo requires multiple completions per prompt so the group baseline is meaningful. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 13. bigger group vs smaller group there is a trade-off. larger group more completions: g\uparrow can give a better estimate of the prompt's reward distribution. but it requires more rollout compute. smaller group cheaper: g\downarrow but the group statistics can become noisier. the source explicitly frames group size as a compute-versus-baseline-quality trade-off. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so grpo doesn't eliminate the computational cost of sampling. it changes where the computation is spent . 14. very important correction to a common misconception grpo is not : "ppo, but it samples only one response." it is almost the opposite. grpo explicitly samples: \boxed{ \text{multiple completions per prompt} } the source says grpo is not cheaper because it samples fewer completions. under a fair comparison with the same total sampled completions, it is cheaper because it removes the value-model training path. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 15. what remains from ppo? this is another critical point. grpo removes: \boxed{\text{value model}} but it retains important ppo-style machinery: \boxed{ \text{old-policy probability ratio} } \boxed{ \text{clipping} } and: \boxed{ \text{reference-policy kl control} } the source explicitly says the group-relative advantage replaces the value-model advantage, but does not replace the stabilizers . (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so: ppo │ ┌────────┼──────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ratio clip kl │ │ │ └────────┼──────────┘ │ advantage │ vφ(s) becomes: grpo │ ┌────────┼──────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ratio clip kl │ │ │ └────────┼──────────┘ │ group advantage │ no value model 16. the old policy is still needed we still need: \pi_{\text{old}}. why? because we still calculate: \boxed{ r_i(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(a_i\mid s_i) }{ \pi_{\text{old}}(a_i\mid s_i) } } the rollout was generated by the old policy, and the current policy is being optimized. the source explicitly says the old-policy log probabilities and probability ratio remain when moving from ppo to grpo. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 17. the reference model is also still needed we still have: \pi_{\text{ref}}. it remains frozen. its role is: \boxed{ \text{prevent excessive drift from the reference distribution} } the source explicitly warns: \boxed{ \text{grpo removes the value model, not the reference model}. } the reference-policy kl term remains part of deepseek-style training. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 18. so what does the complete grpo update look like? the source gives the full grpo-style objective: \boxed{ l_{\text{grpo}}(\theta) = \mathbb e \left[ \min \left( r_k(\theta)a_i, \operatorname{clip}(r_k(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)a_i \right) - \beta kl(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) \right] } (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) this equation contains three major mechanisms . 19. part 1 — policy improvement r_ka_i this says: use the advantage to push the current policy toward successful sampled behavior. if: a_i>0, increase the probability of that sampled behavior. if: a_i<0, decrease it. 20. part 2 — clipping \operatorname{clip}(r_k,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) this prevents the update from becoming excessively aggressive. so: \boxed{ \text{advantage says where to move} } while: \boxed{ \text{clipping says don't move too far in one update} } 21. part 3 — reference kl -\beta kl(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) penalizes excessive divergence from the frozen reference policy. so: \boxed{ \text{reward pressure} - \text{drift pressure} } is happening simultaneously. the source describes the kl term as discouraging drift from the frozen reference policy. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 22. one subtle sign issue the equation above is written as an objective to maximize . but pytorch optimizers normally minimize losses. therefore the source notes that implementations generally negate this objective when turning it into a minimization loss. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) so conceptually: \max j(\theta) becomes: \boxed{ \min -j(\theta) } in the training code. 23. the whole grpo pipeline now we can finally see it end-to-end: prompt │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ completion 1 completion 2 ... completion g │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ reward reward reward │ │ │ └─────────────┼─────────────┘ ▼ group mean / std │ ▼ group advantages │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ ▼ ▼ old-policy logprobs reference logprobs │ │ ▼ ▼ probability ratio kl │ │ ▼ │ clipping │ │ │ └──────────┬──────────────┘ ▼ grpo objective │ ▼ backward() │ ▼ update policy πθ the source later summarizes the same conceptual hooks as: verifier → group advantage → grpo loss → training step. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 24. now connect this to deepseek reasoning this is where the deepseek story becomes much clearer. we had: \boxed{\text{pretrained base model}} then we sample multiple candidate reasoning trajectories: \boxed{ \text{same problem} \rightarrow \text{many candidate solutions} } a verifier evaluates them. then: \boxed{ \text{better solutions} \rightarrow \text{positive advantage} } \boxed{ \text{worse solutions} \rightarrow \text{negative advantage} } and grpo updates the model. that creates a feedback loop: \boxed{ \text{generate} \rightarrow \text{score} \rightarrow \text{compare} \rightarrow \text{update} \rightarrow \text{generate better solutions} } this is the central mechanism underlying the source's transition from deepseekmath to reasoning-oriented deepseek models. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 25. why grpo is attractive for huge llms compare the systems: ppo policy model + reward + value model + reference model grpo policy model + reward + reference model + multiple completions so grpo saves the: \boxed{\text{value-model path}} rather than eliminating rollout generation. the source explicitly identifies this as the main cost saving. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 26. but grpo is not “simple rl” this distinction matters. removing the critic does not remove: \text{rollout generation} \text{reward design} \text{log-probability computation} \text{kl control} \text{clipping} \text{masking} \text{optimizer engineering}. the source explicitly says: grpo simplifies the model stack, not the entire training problem. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 27. grpo vs ppo — final mental model ppo grpo policy model ✅ ✅ reward ✅ ✅ old-policy ratio ✅ ✅ clipping ✅ ✅ reference model / kl ✅ ✅ learned value model ✅ ❌ multiple completions per prompt useful, but not defining required for group-relative baseline advantage source value estimate group rewards source basis: (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 28. the critical knowledge graph policy gradient │ ▼ raw reward r │ ▼ noisy │ ▼ advantage │ ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ppo grpo │ │ value model vφ sample group g │ │ a=r−vφ(s) rewards r₁...rg │ │ │ mean / std │ │ │ ▼ │ group advantage │ │ └───────────────┬───────────┘ ▼ ppo-style ratio │ clipping │ reference kl │ ▼ policy update 29. one final numerical intuition imagine the model generates 4 solutions for the same math problem: a → correct → 1 b → correct → 1 c → wrong → 0 d → wrong → 0 grpo effectively tells the policy: \boxed{ a,b:\ \text{“do more of behavior like this”} } \boxed{ c,d:\ \text{“do less of behavior like this”} } while clipping prevents the change from becoming too aggressive and kl discourages the entire policy from drifting too far from the reference. that is the complete intuition behind grpo.

alpha) * temperature**2 * kl_loss ) def train_distill( teacher, student, loader, epochs=10, t=3.0, alpha=0.3, lr=1e-3 ): teacher.eval() optimizer = torch.optim.adam( student.parameters(), lr=lr ) for epoch in range(epochs): total = 0.0 for x, y in loader: optimizer.zero_grad() with torch.no_grad(): teacher_logits = teacher(x) student_logits = student(x) loss = distillation_loss( student_logits, teacher_logits, y, temperature=t, alpha=alpha ) loss.backward() optimizer.step() total += loss.item() print( f"epoch {epoch + 1}: " f"{total / len(loader):.4f}" ) this follows the training-loop structure in the source. blocks} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{next token}. the problem is that scaling a normal transformer creates several different bottlenecks. think of them as four separate engineering problems: \boxed{ \begin{array}{ll} \text{inference:} & \text{kv-cache memory}\\ \text{model scaling:} & \text{parameter/compute cost}\\ \text{training:} & \text{memory + communication + throughput}\\ have generated: the student studied machine learning ... and want the next token. at every step, the query for the new token has to attend to all previous tokens. without caching, we would repeatedly recompute old keys and values. so: \boxed{ \text{kv cache} } stores information from previous positions. instead of: \text{recompute old k,v every step}, we do: \text{compute new k,v once} + \text{reuse cache}. that is the foundation for efficient autoregressive inference. 3. but kv cache creates another scaling problem for conventional multi-head attention, the cache contains: k,v for every layer, every head, every previous token. therefore, for long contexts: \boxed{\text{kv-cache memory grows with sequence length}} this leads directly to the next architectural idea. 4. problem 2 — make the kv cache smaller deepseek introduces: \boxed{\text{mla — multi-head latent attention}} instead of storing full key/value representations for every head, mla compresses the content into a lower-dimensional latent representation. conceptually: x \rightarrow c_{kv} \rightarrow \text{store latent} and during attention the necessary representations are reconstructed. thus the key idea is: \boxed{ \text{store a compact latent representation rather than full k,v} } the source explicitly describes mla as targeting the attention memory/speed bottleneck, especially for long sequences. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 8. but moe creates a new problem now tokens must travel to the gpus containing their selected experts. that creates: \boxed{\text{all-to-all communication}} so we traded one bottleneck for another: \text{dense compute cost} \rightarrow \text{sparse compute + communication}. this becomes extremely important when we reach distributed training. 9. problem 4 — improve learning and inference through future prediction the next deepseek innovation is: \boxed{\text{mtp — multi-token prediction}} instead of training only: t_{i+1} from position i , mtp creates additional prediction objectives for future tokens: t_{i+1},t_{i+2},t_{i+3},\ldots depending on the number of mtp modules. the source describes mtp as improving learning and inference speed by predicting multiple future tokens. the interesting possibility is speculative decoding. the main model predicts the next token, while mtp-trained modules can provide information about several future positions. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{predict farther ahead} \rightarrow \text{propose multiple tokens} \rightarrow \text{verify} } so an objective originally introduced during training can also have an inference-time interpretation. 12. problem 5 — training efficiency now imagine the model is too large for one gpu. we need distributed training. start with: \boxed{\text{data parallelism / ddp}} every gpu holds a copy of the model. different gpus process different data. then gradients are synchronized using all-reduce. so: \boxed{ \text{ddp increases throughput} } but: \boxed{ \text{ddp does not reduce model-replica memory} } because every gpu still holds the full model. 13. model too large?
